hypothesis.hypothesis: PROPOSED: In mated-naive, 5–7-day-old Canton-S males at 25°C on a 12:12 LD cycle, the tyramine-dependent antagonistic switch between feeding-promoting TyrR neurons and courtship-promoting P1 neurons, previously shown for nutritional state [34358444], is predicted to also mediate sleep pressure. Three predictions are tested. (1) Behavior: in a two-option food-versus-virgin-female choice assay, 12 h of mechanical sleep deprivation in fed males will raise the fraction of males choosing food first by ≥25 percentage points over rested fed controls. (2) Necessity: this shift will be reduced by ≥50% in TyrR mutant males or when TyrR-GAL4 neurons are silenced with Kir2.1. (3) Physiology: 2-photon GCaMP imaging will show that sleep deprivation raises the ΔF/F responses of TyrR neurons to sucrose by ≥30% and lowers P1 responses to female cues by ≥30%, the same opposing pattern that starvation produces [34358444]. This hypothesis is falsified if sleep deprivation shifts choice by <10 percentage points, or if the shift persists undiminished (<20% reduction) without TyrR function.
hypothesis.experimental_approach: PROPOSED METHODS: First, light-microscopy morphologies of TyrR-GAL4 neurons and P1 neurons will be matched to connectome cell types by NBLAST-style morphological comparison. This addresses the gap that no supplied paper uses FlyWire. FlyWire reconstructs an adult female brain, so P1 neurons (male-specific) will be mapped to their female pC1 homologs in FlyWire. Male-specific wiring will be queried in a male CNS connectome dataset if one is accessible (availability requires verification). Shared upstream partners and direct connections will then be extracted using a ≥5-synapse threshold. Second, sleep pressure will be imposed by 12 h of night-time mechanical deprivation (vortexer, randomized 2–20 s stimuli), with sleep verified by DAM or video tracking. Starvation (24 h, water-only agar) will serve as a positive control for the known switch [34358444]. Food-versus-female choice will be scored blind in a 2-chamber arena. Third, TyrR-GAL4 or a P1 split-GAL4 will drive UAS-Kir2.1 for silencing, UAS-CsChrimson for activation, and UAS-GCaMP for in vivo imaging. Controls are GAL4/+ and UAS/+ heterozygotes, rested versus deprived flies, deprived flies given 6 h recovery sleep, and a vortexed-during-day stress control. Fourth, connectome-predicted upstream candidates will be tested by optogenetic activation, which should mimic the sleep-deprived choice bias.

hypothesis.expected_outcomes:
PREDICTIONS (not established results):
(a) Behavior: rested fed males are expected to choose the female first at ≥60%. Starved males are expected to shift toward food by ≥25 percentage points, replicating the nutritional switch [34358444]. Sleep-deprived fed males are predicted to shift toward food by ≥25 percentage points, with n≥40 males per group from ≥3 independent cohorts. Group differences will be tested by Fisher's exact test or logistic regression with Bonferroni correction, α=0.05. This sample size gives about 80% power to detect a 30-point difference.
(b) Recovery: 6 h of recovery sleep is predicted to restore choice to within 10 points of rested controls.
(c) Necessity: TyrR mutants and TyrR>Kir2.1 males are predicted to show ≥50% attenuation of the deprivation shift, tested as a genotype × condition interaction (p<0.05). GAL4/+ and UAS/+ controls should show the full shift.
(d) Imaging: TyrR sucrose responses are predicted to rise ≥30% and P1 female-cue responses to fall ≥30% after deprivation, tested by mixed-effects model with n≥8 flies per group.
(e) Connectome: we predict that ≥1 cell type provides ≥5 synapses onto both TyrR-matched and pC1/P1-homolog types. If no shared partner exists, this would argue against a single upstream switch neuron and favor diffuse tyraminergic volume signaling.
(f) Falsification: a deprivation shift of <10 points, or no attenuation in TyrR-deficient males, would reject the hypothesis.
hypothesis.novelty_claim: The synthesis identifies three gaps that this design targets. First, none of the provided papers uses the FlyWire connectome, so which connectome-identified neurons act as the state switch is not addressed. Second, it is unclear whether sleep pressure engages the same antagonistic co-regulation motif as the tyramine-mediated feeding–courtship switch; the sleep–feeding switch is described only at review level [31572216, 35892199]. Third, three-way state integration has not been tested; the closest prior study examined only metabolic and reproductive state [35794476]. This proposal (i) tests sleep pressure directly against the TyrR/P1 motif established for nutritional state [34358444], (ii) maps TyrR and P1/pC1 neurons onto connectome cell types to find shared upstream partners, and (iii) tests connectome-predicted candidates causally. In an exploratory extension it also crosses sleep state with starvation, addressing the three-way conflict gap.
hypothesis.feasibility_notes:
Estimated timeline is about 14–18 months:
- Months 1–3: connectome matching and sleep-deprivation calibration.
- Months 3–8: behavior and genetics.
- Months 6–12: imaging.
- Months 10–18: causal tests of connectome candidates and the exploratory starvation × sleep cross.

Pitfalls:
(1) Sex mismatch: FlyWire reconstructs a female brain, so the male-specific P1 cannot be mapped directly. Female pC1 homologs or a male connectome (availability unverified) must substitute, and sexually dimorphic wiring may limit inference.
(2) Mechanical deprivation is stressful and may itself alter feeding. The daytime-vortex stress control and recovery-sleep controls address this. An orthogonal thermogenetic deprivation method could be added if available.
(3) Sleep deprivation may reduce locomotion. Latency to first contact and total locomotion must be measured and used as covariates.
(4) TyrR-GAL4 specificity and the identity of the mutant allele must be verified before use.
(5) Morphology-based matching from light microscopy to EM is probabilistic. Only high-confidence matches will be used, with uncertainty reported.
(6) No stock numbers are asserted; all lines require verification.
specific_aims: Aim 1: Connectome mapping — identify FlyWire cell types corresponding to TyrR-GAL4 neurons and P1/pC1 neurons, and quantify shared upstream partners and direct connections at a ≥5-synapse threshold.

Aim 2: Sleep pressure as a switch input — test whether 12 h of sleep deprivation shifts fed males' food-versus-female choice by ≥25 percentage points, and whether this shift requires TyrR (≥50% attenuation in TyrR mutant or TyrR>Kir2.1 males).

Aim 3: Neural correlate and causal test — use 2-photon imaging to test opposing deprivation-induced changes (≥30%) in TyrR and P1 responses, and optogenetically activate connectome-predicted shared upstream neurons to test whether they mimic the deprived-state choice bias.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Proposed (not established): a small set of FlyWire-identified interneuron cell types that sit between TyrR-expressing feeding neurons and P1 courtship neurons acts as a shared state-dependent switch. Optogenetic silencing of this population in 24 h food-deprived, 5-7-day-old virgin male flies (w1118 background, 25°C) will reduce the courtship-over-feeding choice index by at least 30% relative to genetic controls (p<0.05, n>=30 per genotype). In control males, 12 h of mechanical sleep deprivation is predicted to lower the same index by at least 20%, whereas in males with the candidate population silenced the shift will be under 10%.
hypothesis.experimental_approach: Aim 1 is a connectome analysis of the FlyWire dataset. It will identify TyrR-expressing feeding neurons and P1 neurons by morphology and cell-type annotation, then enumerate their shortest 1-3 hop paths and shared interneuron partners. It will rank candidates by synapse count, predicted neurotransmitter and convergence with ventral-brain regions such as the borboleta. Aim 2 builds split-GAL4 drivers for the top candidate cell types (or uses existing drivers if verified). These drive UAS-GtACR1 or UAS-Kir2.1 for silencing, UAS-CsChrimson for activation and UAS-GCaMP for calcium imaging. A two-choice assay offers food and a female target to males in four states: fed vs 24 h food-deprived, crossed with sex-deprived vs recently mated. Choice index is scored blind as the fraction of time spent courting vs feeding. Aim 3 adds 12 h mechanical sleep deprivation, checked with DAM or video sleep monitoring and followed by a recovery-sleep readout, to test whether the same neurons mediate sleep-pressure effects. Controls are empty-split/GAL4-only, UAS-only, no-retinal (ATR-free) and light-off groups. Statistics are a genotype x state interaction test (two-way ANOVA or a permutation equivalent) with multiple-comparison correction.

literature.disease_context: The neural mechanisms by which internal states gate behavioral switching in Drosophila are directly relevant to human conditions involving disrupted motivational control, including eating disorders, addiction, and sleep disorders. The tyramine and dopamine pathways identified in flies have mammalian counterparts (trace amines, catecholamines) that are implicated in reward and compulsive behavior. Circadian misalignment and sleep pressure circuits conserved from flies to mammals are linked to metabolic disease and psychiatric vulnerability.
literature.summary: Internal states such as hunger, reproductive status, and sleep pressure modulate behavioral priority in Drosophila through hierarchical neuromodulatory systems. Tyramine acts as a satiety signal that antagonistically co-regulates TyrR-expressing feeding-promoting neurons and P1 courtship command neurons, enabling context-dependent prioritization of feeding versus mating [1]. More broadly, metabolic and reproductive states shape sensorimotor processing across distinct brain regions via neuromodulators including dopamine, octopamine, and neuropeptides, while peptidergic 'orchestrating' neurons at the top of a hierarchy integrate interoceptive signals to switch between competing behavioral programs such as sleep versus feeding or mating versus aggression [2][6]. Despite progress in identifying circuit motifs, the specific FlyWire connectome neurons serving as dedicated behavioral switches remain to be functionally validated.

key_papers.relevance: Uses pan-neuronal volumetric imaging to show that metabolic and reproductive states modulate sensorimotor processing at different spatial scales in the brain, identifying the 'borboleta' region as a node sufficient for protein-specific food choice.

key_papers.title: Endocrine cybernetics: neuropeptides as molecular switches in behavioural decisions.
key_papers.authors: Nässel DR, Zandawala M et al.
key_papers.relevance: Provides a hierarchical framework for peptidergic neurons in the Drosophila brain as state-dependent behavioral switches, integrating interoceptive signals to resolve conflicts between competing drives such as sleep versus feeding.

key_papers.title: Neural basis of sexually dimorphic decision-making.
key_papers.authors: Day M, Rezaval C et al.
key_papers.relevance: Synthesizes how sexually dimorphic integrator hub neurons combine sensory cues with internal states to bias action selection, highlighting dopamine's role in filtering distractors and updating priorities.

key_papers.title: Sleep in Drosophila and Its Context.
key_papers.authors: Beckwith EJ, French AS et al.
key_papers.relevance: Reviews how sleep competes with feeding, courtship, and social behaviors in Drosophila, and describes the circuits and genes that relay internal state information to sleep centers.

key_papers.title: Internal State Dependent Odor Processing and Perception-The Role of Neuromodulation in the Fly Olfactory System.
key_papers.authors: Sayin S, Boehm AC, Kobler JM et al.
key_papers.relevance: Details how hunger and reproductive state alter olfactory sensorimotor processing through dopamine, octopamine, and neuropeptides in Drosophila, establishing neuromodulation as a key mechanism for state-dependent behavioral switching.

key_papers.title: Neuromodulation of insect motion vision.
key_papers.authors: Cheng KY, Frye MA et al.
key_papers.relevance: Reviews how serotonin and octopamine modulate motion vision circuits in state-dependent ways, illustrating general principles by which neuromodulators reshape sensory processing as a function of internal state.

key_papers.title: Molecular mechanisms and physiological importance of circadian rhythms.
key_papers.authors: Patke A, Young MW, Axelrod S et al.
key_papers.relevance: Describes the conserved molecular clock components in Drosophila and mammals, providing context for how circadian timing interacts with sleep pressure and internal state to gate behavioral output.

identified_gaps: No specific FlyWire connectome neuron identities (i.e., individual cell types with confirmed connectome IDs) have been linked to behavioral switching in any of the provided papers — mapping functional switch neurons identified by genetics (TyrR, P1, borboleta) onto their exact FlyWire counterparts and upstream/downstream connectivity remains unaddressed.

The causal direction between neuromodulator levels and physiological/behavioral states is unresolved for motion vision circuits [3]; whether octopamine or serotonin levels rise as a consequence of hunger or instead drive hunger-related behavioral changes is not established in the provided literature.

The interaction between sleep pressure and the feeding/mating switch has not been mechanistically dissected at the circuit level — it is unknown which neurons simultaneously receive sleep homeostatic signals and regulate feeding-versus-courtship trade-offs.

The 'borboleta' region identified as sufficient for protein food choice [2] lacks a complete characterization of its input and output connectivity, making it unclear how it integrates metabolic versus reproductive state signals or how it interfaces with action selection hubs such as P1.

The role of the microbiome and infection-induced internal states in reconfiguring behavioral switching circuits is explicitly flagged as unstudied [5], representing a gap with direct relevance to how sickness suppresses feeding, mating, and sleep in natural conditions.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Tyramine-receptor-expressing (TyrR+) neurons that are presynaptic to P1 courtship command neurons, as identified in the FlyWire connectome, serve as dedicated hunger-state-dependent behavioral switches: acute silencing of these specific TyrR+→P1 connector neurons in starved (24 h food-deprived) mated male w1118 flies will reduce the feeding-over-courtship priority index by ≥40% (i.e., starved-silenced males will initiate courtship within 5 min at rates ≥40% higher than starved GAL4-only controls), while having no significant effect (≤10% change) on courtship latency in fed males, under 25°C, 12:12 LD standard conditions.
hypothesis.experimental_approach: We will first use the publicly available FlyWire adult male brain connectome to identify all neurons that (1) express TyrR based on transcriptomic cell-type annotations mapped onto connectome identities and (2) form direct chemical synapses onto annotated P1 (pC1) neurons. Candidate 'switch' cell types will be ranked by synapse count and anatomical position. We will then use the split-GAL4 intersectional strategy to restrict UAS-effector expression to TyrR+→P1-adjacent neurons: a DBD line expressed in TyrR+ cells will be combined with an AD line expressed in neurons anatomically overlapping the identified connectome cell types (e.g., using existing TyrR-GAL4 intersected with a connectivity-informed second driver). Behavioral switches will be assayed in a two-choice arena where a starved or fed mated male is simultaneously presented with a conspecific virgin female and a sucrose-yeast food patch; the latency to first feeding contact and latency to first courtship song bout will be measured over 10 min trials. Acute neural silencing will be achieved with UAS-Kir2.1 (constitutive) and UAS-shi^ts1 (temperature-sensitive, 30°C shift), allowing both chronic and acute dissection. Controls will include: GAL4-only, UAS-only, fed versus starved cohorts, and mated versus virgin males. Sleep pressure will be introduced as a third state variable by sleep-depriving a subset of males for 12 h prior to behavioral testing using the sleep nullifying apparatus (SNAP) protocol, enabling a 2×2×2 factorial design (fed/starved × mated/virgin × rested/sleep-deprived) to test whether the identified switch neurons also integrate sleep homeostatic signals.

hypothesis.expected_outcomes: Primary outcome: Silencing of TyrR+→P1 connectome-identified switch neurons (UAS-Kir2.1 or shi^ts1 at 30°C) in starved mated males will increase courtship initiation rate by ≥40% and reduce mean feeding latency increase by ≥40% compared to starved GAL4-only controls, quantified as a priority index = [time feeding / (time feeding + time courting)] over 10 min trials (n ≥ 30 per genotype per state, Mann-Whitney U, α = 0.05). Fed males with identical neuronal silencing will show ≤10% change in priority index, confirming state-dependence. Calcium imaging in P1 neurons (GCaMP7s) will show ≥25% reduction in peak ΔF/F response to female cues in starved versus fed controls, restored to fed levels upon TyrR+ neuron silencing. Sleep-deprived males are predicted to show an intermediate priority index shifted toward sleep-seeking (reduced courtship and feeding initiation), and silencing of the switch neurons in sleep-deprived flies will be insufficient to rescue courtship initiation to rested levels (≤15% rescue), indicating that sleep pressure signals engage additional circuit nodes beyond TyrR+→P1 synapses. Statistical threshold: all primary comparisons corrected for multiple testing (Bonferroni), with effect sizes reported as Cohen's d.
hypothesis.novelty_claim: This study addresses three explicitly identified gaps in the literature synthesis. First, no prior work has mapped the TyrR+ and P1 neurons functionally identified by Cheriyamkunnel et al. (PMID 34358444) onto specific FlyWire connectome neuron identities with confirmed connectivity — this experiment directly closes that gap by using connectome-informed intersectional genetics. Second, the interaction between sleep pressure and the feeding/mating switch has not been mechanistically dissected at the circuit level, and no neurons are known to simultaneously receive sleep homeostatic signals and regulate feeding-versus-courtship trade-offs — our 2×2×2 factorial design is the first proposed test of this interaction at single-cell-type resolution. Third, the borboleta region (PMID 35794476) lacks characterized input/output connectivity to P1 and TyrR+ neurons — our connectome-first approach will reveal whether borboleta neurons are upstream, downstream, or parallel to the TyrR+→P1 switch, addressing this structural gap.
hypothesis.feasibility_notes: The FlyWire connectome (adult male brain, v783) is publicly accessible and fully proofread, making in silico identification of TyrR+→P1 synaptic partners feasible within 1–2 months using existing transcriptomic cell-type annotations (e.g., FlyWire CAVE database cross-referenced with FCA single-cell atlas). The primary technical risk is the unavailability of a validated TyrR-splitGAL4-DBD line with sufficient specificity; this may require 4–6 months of fly line generation via CRISPR T2A-splitGAL4 knock-in if community resources are insufficient. The two-choice behavioral arena is established but requires careful counterbalancing of female and food patch position across trials to avoid position bias confounds. The 2×2×2 factorial design requires n ≥ 30 per cell (8 cells = 240 flies minimum per genotype), which is achievable but demands rigorous husbandry. Temperature-shift experiments with shi^ts1 require precise temperature control (±0.5°C) and rapid behavioral scoring. Estimated total timeline: 18–24 months (2 months connectome analysis, 6 months line generation/validation, 4 months behavioral screen, 4 months calcium imaging, 4 months data analysis and writing). Key pitfall: GAL4 lines may not recapitulate endogenous TyrR expression with sufficient fidelity; independent validation with smFISH or immunostaining against TyrR will be required.
specific_aims: Aim 1: FlyWire Connectome Mapping — Identify all TyrR-expressing neuron types that form direct synapses onto P1 (pC1) courtship command neurons in the FlyWire adult male brain connectome, rank candidates by synapse count, and generate anatomical predictions for intersectional driver targeting.

Aim 2: Circuit-Level Causal Testing — Use split-GAL4-driven constitutive (Kir2.1) and acute (shi^ts1) silencing of connectome-identified TyrR+→P1 switch neurons to test whether their activity is necessary for hunger-state-dependent suppression of courtship in favor of feeding, quantified as a feeding-versus-courtship priority index in starved versus fed mated male flies.

Aim 3: Sleep-State Integration — Determine whether the TyrR+→P1 switch neurons also mediate sleep-pressure-dependent suppression of courtship and feeding by applying a 2×2×2 factorial manipulation of hunger, mating status, and sleep deprivation, and testing whether silencing these neurons is sufficient to rescue courtship in sleep-deprived males or whether additional circuit nodes are required.

literature.summary: The supplied literature mostly reports connectome successes: whole-brain and regional connectome-constrained models accurately predicted feeding, grooming, innate odor valence, memory, and navigation computations [1][2][3][8]. No supplied paper documents a strongly connected pathway that is behaviorally silent when inactivated. The only explicit failure modes are that degeneracy can foil cell-by-cell interruption and that anatomical proximity seen by light microscopy does not reliably reveal synaptic partners [5]. Inference: models that need extra inhibition or physiological data [1][8] suggest connectivity alone is incomplete, but systematic tests of connectome-behavior mismatch are absent from this set.

identified_gaps: No paper in the provided set systematically silences strongly connected connectome pathways and reports null behavioral phenotypes, so the frequency of 'strong synapses but no behavioral effect' cases is unquantified. A brain-wide silencing screen of top-weighted edges, scored against connectome weight, would address this.

Degeneracy and redundancy are named as confounds for silencing experiments [5], but the provided literature does not identify which Drosophila pathways are degenerate. Combinatorial silencing of parallel pathway elements (for example, parallel MBON or PPL1-DAN units) could test this.

Connectome-based models (LIF and spiking) were validated mainly on pathways with known strong phenotypes (feeding, grooming, odor valence), and the abstracts report no systematic evaluation of failed predictions. Reporting negative model-experiment mismatches, including activation-versus-silencing asymmetries, would define the limits of prediction.

The odor-valence study indicates that connectivity alone was insufficient and that inhibitory motifs and balance were also needed [1]; whether connectome-inferred neurotransmitter identity and synaptic sign are accurate enough for brain-wide prediction is untested here. Validating predicted neurotransmitter identity against physiology for high-weight edges would address this.

The connectome is a single adult female brain [6], and the provided literature does not address how inter-individual variability or plasticity (including learnt valence [8]) alter the connectome-behavior mapping. Comparing multiple connectomes and state- or experience-dependent physiology would address this.

State dependence, neuromodulation and extrasynaptic signaling are not covered by the provided connectome literature as explanations for pathway-behavior mismatches; testing whether neuromodulatory state converts silent strong pathways into effective ones is an open question.

literature.summary: Whole-brain connectome-based models in Drosophila have predicted taste, feeding, grooming and olfactory-valence circuit function [2][1], but the provided abstracts emphasize successes and do not report strongly connected pathways that lack a behavioral effect when silenced. The conceptual literature indicates that anatomy can reveal unexpected pathways and that degeneracy can confound silencing experiments [5], and that connectivity alone was insufficient for attractive-odor tuning without added inhibition [1]. Systematic silencing tests of high-weight edges and reporting of negative model-experiment mismatches are the main missing evidence.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Proposed: In adult mated female flies at 25°C, acute silencing of cell types carrying the 30 highest-weight connectome edges (at least 100 synapses per connection in FlyWire, selected across gustatory-feeding, antennal-grooming and olfactory-valence circuits) will produce no significant behavioral effect (equivalence within ±0.5 SD, TOST p<0.05) for at least 25% of these edges. The null rate will be at least twofold higher for edges whose presynaptic cell type has a parallel same-neurotransmitter partner with output cosine similarity of 0.5 or more than for edges without such a partner. Combinatorial silencing of the redundant partners will convert at least half of the redundancy-associated null cases into significant phenotypes (Cohen's d of 0.8 or more).
hypothesis.experimental_approach: Proposed: Select 30 high-weight edges from the FlyWire connectome in three circuits for which model-predicted behaviors exist (proboscis extension/feeding, antennal grooming, odor attraction/aversion). For each, use cell-type-specific split-GAL4 drivers to express UAS-Kir2.1 under tub-GAL80ts control, so silencing is restricted to adulthood and developmental compensation is minimized. Score each genotype in the circuit's matched assay (n≥30 flies per genotype, 3 independent cohorts) against empty-split-GAL4>UAS-Kir2.1 and GAL4/UAS-only controls, with a second silencer (UAS-TNT, or UAS-shibire-ts if a suitable stock is verified) to confirm nulls. Test nulls for equivalence (TOST) rather than failure to reject. Confirm that each driver is expressed in the intended cell type, and confirm silencing efficacy by calcium imaging or an assay of a known positive-control phenotype. Compare outcomes with the predicted effect from a leaky integrate-and-fire connectome model. Then silence parallel partners pairwise, and repeat assays under starved versus fed states to test whether neuromodulatory state unmasks null pathways.

hypothesis.expected_outcomes: Proposed predictions, not established results: Of 30 edges, at least 8 (≥25%) will show equivalence to controls within ±0.5 SD, while the remainder will show phenotypes consistent with model predictions. The null rate will be at least twofold higher among edges with a redundant parallel partner (cosine similarity ≥0.5) than among edges without one (Fisher's exact test, p<0.05). Pairwise silencing of redundant partners will yield significant phenotypes (d≥0.8, Holm-corrected p<0.05) in at least 50% of redundancy-associated nulls. Starvation or other state manipulation is predicted to convert at least 20% of the remaining nulls. If fewer than 10% of edges are null, or null rates do not differ by redundancy, the hypothesis is falsified.
hypothesis.novelty_claim: The provided set contains no systematic silencing screen of strongly connected pathways that reports null behavioral phenotypes, so the frequency of strong synapses without behavioral effect is unquantified. Existing connectome-based models were validated mainly on pathways with strong phenotypes such as feeding, grooming and odor valence. Degeneracy is named as a confound for silencing, but the literature does not identify which Drosophila pathways are degenerate. This proposal quantifies null edges, tests redundancy as an explanation by combinatorial silencing, and tests state dependence, which the connectome literature does not cover.
hypothesis.feasibility_notes: Estimated timeline is 18-24 months: 3 months for edge selection, modeling and line sourcing; 8-10 months for single-silencing screens; 4-6 months for combinatorial and state experiments; 2 months for analysis. Pitfalls: split-GAL4 lines may be unavailable for some cell types (the edge list will be filtered to those with verified drivers); incomplete silencing can mimic a null (mitigated by a second silencer and efficacy checks); behavioral assays may be insensitive to a pathway's true function (mitigated by testing multiple assays per circuit); and one connectome from a single female brain may not match the tested flies' wiring. Combinatorial genotypes require careful GAL4 or LexA design and may need verification of available reagents.
specific_aims: Aim 1: Quantify null edges — silence cell types carrying 30 top-weighted connectome edges across three circuits and test each for equivalence to controls in a matched behavioral assay, comparing outcomes with connectome-model predictions.

Aim 2: Test redundancy — compare null rates between edges with and without parallel same-neurotransmitter partners (output cosine similarity ≥0.5) and test whether combinatorial silencing of partners unmasks phenotypes.
Aim 3: Test state dependence — determine whether starvation or mating state converts null strong pathways into behaviorally effective ones.

literature.disease_context: The Drosophila connectome and functional circuit studies provide a framework for understanding how structural connectivity relates to behavior, with direct implications for neurodegeneration research; failures in connectivity-to-behavior prediction inform where compensatory or degenerate mechanisms may buffer pathological states in conditions such as Alzheimer's disease. Oxidative stress, presenilin loss-of-function, and lipid transport disruption all cause age-dependent neurodegeneration in flies, modeling human disease pathways. Identifying which strongly connected pathways are behaviorally silent when silenced could reveal redundant or compensatory wiring relevant to resilience and vulnerability in neurological disease.

key_papers.authors: Shiu PK, Sterne GR, Spiller N et al.
key_papers.relevance: Demonstrates that a whole-brain leaky integrate-and-fire model built solely from connectome connectivity and neurotransmitter identity accurately predicts behaviorally relevant neurons for feeding and grooming, directly addressing where connectome-based predictions succeed and implicitly where they may fail.

key_papers.relevance: Shows that connectome-based spiking network models correctly predict the role of local inhibition in shaping attractive odor tuning in the lateral horn, and that manipulating this inhibition biases behavior as predicted — illustrating a case where the connectome model succeeds, setting a baseline for identifying where it fails.

key_papers.relevance: Uses a computational model constrained by the fly connectome together with in vivo voltage imaging to reveal how dopamine-mediated interactions between short- and long-term memory circuits produce predictions confirmed experimentally, demonstrating both the power and the necessity of physiological data to supplement structural connectivity.

key_papers.relevance: Explicitly discusses how circuit analysis can be 'foiled by degeneracy in pathway elements,' identifying a key mechanism by which strongly connected pathways may fail to produce measurable behavioral effects when individually silenced.

key_papers.authors: Bates AS, Janssens J, Jefferis GS et al.
key_papers.relevance: Argues that functional predictions from brain wiring diagrams require integration of transcriptomic, morphological, and connectivity data, highlighting that connectivity alone is insufficient and pointing to gaps where the connectome may fail to predict behavior.

identified_gaps: The whole-brain connectome model (Shiu et al. 2024) was validated for feeding and grooming but has not been systematically tested across the full behavioral repertoire; it remains unknown which strongly connected pathways in the wiring diagram (Dorkenwald et al. 2024) produce no behavioral change when silenced, because no large-scale silencing screen mapped to connectome edges has been reported in the provided literature.

Degeneracy in pathway elements is explicitly identified as a mechanism that can 'foil' circuit analysis (Meinertzhagen 2016), yet no provided study quantifies how many anatomically strong connections are functionally redundant or buffered by parallel pathways — a systematic screen comparing synaptic weight to behavioral effect size is absent.

The lateral horn connectome-based model successfully predicted inhibitory circuit motifs for odor valence (Someya et al. 2025), but it is unknown whether the same connectome motifs predict behavior for intermediate or ambiguous odors — stimuli outside the hedonic extremes — representing an untested region of the model's predictive scope.

Connectome-based computational models currently incorporate connectivity and neurotransmitter identity but not neuromodulatory state (e.g., dopamine release dynamics revealed in Huang et al. 2024); strongly connected pathways whose behavioral output depends on modulatory context (not captured in the static wiring diagram) may systematically appear as prediction failures, but this class of failure has not been catalogued.

The relationship between connectome-predicted circuit paths and behavioral outcomes in the central complex (navigation, sleep, decision-making; Pfeiffer 2022) has only partially been tested; which of the many identified projection pathways in the central complex wiring diagram are functionally silent under standard conditions remains unresolved.

Single-cell transcriptomic data are not yet matched brain-wide to connectome-defined cell types (Bates et al. 2019), so it is not possible to predict which neurons have the molecular machinery to actually transmit signals despite having anatomical connections — a gap that would explain why some dense connections may be behaviorally inert.

evidence_claims.claim: The recent assembly of the adult Drosophila melanogaster central brain connectome, containing more than 125,000 neurons and 50 million synaptic connections, provides a template for examining sensory processing throughout the brain.
We present a neuronal wiring diagram of a whole brain containing 5 × 10^7 chemical synapses between 139,255 neurons reconstructed from an adult female Drosophila melanogaster.

Modelling brain circuits using only synapse-level connectivity and predicted neurotransmitter identity generates experimentally testable hypotheses and can describe complete sensorimotor transformations.
Activation of sugar-sensing or water-sensing gustatory neurons in the computational model accurately predicts neurons that respond to tastes and are required for feeding initiation.

Computational activation of mechanosensory neurons predicts activation of a small set of neurons comprising the antennal grooming circuit, and accurately describes the circuit response upon activation of different mechanosensory subtypes.

A connectome-based spiking network model recapitulating the neural activity indicates that representations of aversive odors emerge through specific convergence of feedforward excitation, whereas those of attractive odors emerge through additional local inhibition.
Manipulation of local inhibition biased neuronal and behavioral odor responses according to the prediction of the model.

The analysis of circuit function may proceed cell by cell, by examining the behavioural outcome of either interrupting or restoring function to any one element in an anatomically defined circuit, but can be foiled by degeneracy in pathway elements.

Synaptic partnerships identified from ultrastructural features provide a strong heuristic basis to interpret not only functional interactions between identified neurons, but also a powerful means to predict such interactions, and suggest functional pathways not readily predicted from existing experimental evidence.
Anatomical connections often reveal unexpected pathways.

The recently published connectome of the central complex of Drosophila melanogaster is a milestone in understanding the intricacies of the central-complex circuits and will provide inspiration for testable hypotheses for the coming years.
The discovery of coordinate transformation through vector math [in the central complex] has been predicted from connectomics data.

A computational model constrained by the fly connectome and our spiking data explains how dopamine signals mediate the circuit interactions between short- and long-term memory traces, yielding predictions that our experiments confirmed.
PPL1-DANs heterogeneously and bidirectionally encode innate and learnt valences of punishment, reward and odour cues.

Matched single-cell transcriptomic and morphological data provide an effective reference point to integrate other data types, including connectomics data. This will significantly enhance our ability to make functional predictions from brain wiring diagrams.

The correlation among multiple co-varying neuronal properties, including lineage, gene expression, morphology, connectivity, response properties and shared behavioral significance is essential to the definition of neuronal cell type.
Initial studies comparing morphological and transcriptomic definitions of neuronal type suggest that these are highly consistent, but there is much to do to match these approaches brain-wide.
Degeneracy in pathway elements is a mechanism that can foil circuit analysis based on connectome structure alone.
Strongly connected pathways whose behavioral output depends on modulatory context (not captured in the static wiring diagram) may systematically appear as prediction failures.

The whole-brain connectome model has not been systematically tested across the full behavioral repertoire; which strongly connected pathways produce no behavioral change when silenced has not been reported.
Tracing from a subset of photoreceptors to descending motor pathways illustrates how structure can uncover putative circuit mechanisms underlying sensorimotor behaviours.
The central complex is involved in sleep control, decision-making and most prominently in goal-directed locomotion behaviors.

literature.summary: The Drosophila whole-brain connectome (Dorkenwald et al. 2024) and derivative computational models (Shiu et al. 2024; Someya et al. 2025; Huang et al. 2024) have demonstrated that synapse-level connectivity combined with neurotransmitter identity can accurately predict behaviorally relevant neurons and sensorimotor transformations in specific circuits such as gustatory feeding, mechanosensory grooming, and olfactory valence computation. However, a critical and explicitly identified limitation is circuit degeneracy — the ability of parallel pathway elements to compensate when one is silenced — which can render strongly connected anatomical pathways behaviorally invisible upon individual manipulation (Meinertzhagen 2016). Systematic identification of which dense connectome edges lack behavioral consequence when silenced remains an open and actionable challenge, as current models do not capture neuromodulatory dynamics, and brain-wide matching of transcriptomic to connectomic cell-type definitions is incomplete (Bates et al. 2019), leaving the molecular competence of anatomically connected neurons to transmit signals largely uncharacterized.

hypothesis.hypothesis: At least 30% of the top-200 strongest inter-region connectome edges (ranked by total synaptic weight in the Dorkenwald et al. 2024 female adult Drosophila central brain connectome) will produce no statistically significant behavioral change (p > 0.05, effect size Cohen's d < 0.2) when their presynaptic neuronal populations are acutely silenced with UAS-Kir2.1 or UAS-TNT, measured across a standardized panel of four behaviors (odor-evoked approach/avoidance, proboscis extension reflex, locomotor speed, and courtship initiation) in mated female w1118 flies at 25°C under 12:12 LD conditions, and that these behaviorally silent strong connections will be enriched (≥2-fold over chance) in pathways lacking neuromodulatory receptor gene expression as identified by single-cell transcriptomic data.
hypothesis.experimental_approach: We will perform a systematic silencing screen of connectome-predicted high-weight inter-region pathways in the adult Drosophila central brain using the GAL4/UAS system. First, the top 200 inter-region edges by total synaptic weight will be extracted from the publicly released Dorkenwald et al. 2024 connectome dataset, and split-GAL4 or existing GAL4 driver lines will be matched to the presynaptic cell types for each edge using the Janelia FlyLight and Vienna Tile GAL4 collections; each driver will be validated by GFP expression to confirm restricted expression. Second, each driver will be crossed to UAS-Kir2.1 (chronic silencing) and, for a subset, to UAS-TNT (synaptic silencing) to generate experimental flies; Canton-S/w1118 × driver and driver × UAS-mCD8::GFP crosses will serve as genetic controls. Third, all experimental and control genotypes will be subjected to a standardized four-behavior panel: (1) T-maze odor-evoked valence (attractive apple cider vinegar vs. aversive benzaldehyde), (2) sucrose proboscis extension reflex (PER) assay, (3) open-field locomotor tracking (5 min, DAM-equivalent single-fly arenas), and (4) male courtship index in mixed-sex chambers; each behavioral assay will use n ≥ 30 flies per genotype across three independent crosses. Fourth, behavioral effect sizes (Cohen's d) will be computed for each driver/behavior combination relative to controls, and the distribution of effect sizes will be regressed against synaptic weight and against neuromodulatory receptor expression scores derived from published single-cell transcriptomic datasets (FCA, Fly Cell Atlas) to test whether low modulatory receptor expression predicts behavioral silence.

hypothesis.expected_outcomes: We predict that ≥30% of the top-200 high-weight connectome edges will show no significant behavioral change upon silencing (Cohen's d < 0.2, p > 0.05 by two-sample t-test with Bonferroni correction for 200 × 4 = 800 comparisons, α = 0.05/800 ≈ 6.25 × 10⁻⁵). Among the four behavioral assays, we expect the PER and odor-valence assays to show the highest prediction success rates (≥60% of edges affecting these behaviors will show significant effects), consistent with prior connectome model validation (Shiu et al. 2024; Someya et al. 2025), while locomotor and courtship assays are predicted to show higher failure rates given the greater degeneracy in central complex and courtship circuitry. Behaviorally silent high-weight edges are predicted to be enriched in pathways where presynaptic neurons have low expression of neuromodulatory receptors (dopamine, octopamine, serotonin receptor transcripts from Fly Cell Atlas) compared to behaviorally effective edges (Fisher's exact test, expected OR ≥ 2.0, p < 0.05). We further expect that a subset of behaviorally silent edges will become significant when flies are tested under neuromodulatory challenge (e.g., starvation or heat stress), confirming context-dependent behavioral relevance. Primary statistical approach: linear mixed model with synaptic weight, brain region pair, and neurotransmitter identity as fixed effects and replicate cross as random effect.
hypothesis.novelty_claim: No prior study has performed a systematic, connectome-ranked silencing screen mapping synaptic weight quantitatively to behavioral effect size across multiple behaviors in the same fly line panel. The identified gaps establish that (1) the Shiu et al. 2024 whole-brain model was validated only for feeding and grooming and has not been tested across the full behavioral repertoire; (2) degeneracy in pathway elements is acknowledged (Meinertzhagen 2016) but has never been quantified in terms of what fraction of dense connectome edges are functionally redundant; (3) the hypothesis that neuromodulatory receptor expression—absent from static wiring diagrams—explains a class of prediction failures is proposed but untested; and (4) brain-wide matching of transcriptomic to connectomic cell types is incomplete (Bates et al. 2019), making molecular competence of anatomically connected neurons uncharacterized. This experiment directly quantifies the gap between structural connectivity rank and behavioral effect size and tests a mechanistic explanation (low modulatory receptor expression) for silent strong connections.
hypothesis.feasibility_notes: Technical feasibility is high: the Dorkenwald et al. 2024 connectome dataset is publicly available and edge weights can be extracted computationally; the GAL4/UAS silencing approach is standard and well-validated in Drosophila. The main challenge is driver availability and specificity — matching GAL4 lines to connectome-defined cell types is non-trivial and some high-weight presynaptic populations may lack specific drivers, requiring split-GAL4 construction (adds 6-12 months per novel line). Estimated timeline: Month 1-2, computational extraction of top-200 edges and driver-cell-type matching; Month 3-6, driver validation by GFP imaging (confocal, n=5 brains per line); Month 7-18, behavioral screen (batches of 20 genotypes per month, four assays each, n=30 per genotype); Month 19-22, transcriptomic correlation analysis and follow-up neuromodulatory challenge experiments; Month 23-24, data synthesis and manuscript preparation. Total: ~24 months with a team of 2-3 experimenters. Major pitfalls: (1) GAL4 driver expression bleeding into non-target neurons — mitigated by split-GAL4 intersectional approach and anatomical validation; (2) Kir2.1 developmental lethality or sickness confounding behavioral results — mitigated by using tub-GAL80ts for adult-stage restricted expression with temperature shift to 30°C for 48h before assay; (3) behavioral assays may lack sensitivity for subtle phenotypes — mitigated by large sample sizes and multiple complementary assays.
specific_aims: Aim 1: Connectome edge prioritization and driver validation — Computationally extract the top 200 inter-region edges by total synaptic weight from the Dorkenwald et al. 2024 connectome, match each presynaptic cell population to an existing or constructed GAL4 driver, and validate driver expression specificity by confocal imaging of UAS-mCD8::GFP in adult female brains (n ≥ 5 per driver).

Aim 2: Systematic behavioral silencing screen — Cross each validated GAL4 driver to UAS-Kir2.1 (with tub-GAL80ts for adult-restricted silencing) and measure all four standardized behaviors (odor T-maze, PER, open-field locomotion, courtship index) in mated female flies (n ≥ 30 per genotype, three independent crosses), computing Cohen's d and adjusted p-values for each driver-behavior pair to generate a quantitative map of synaptic weight versus behavioral effect size.

Aim 3: Mechanistic dissection of silent strong connections — For all edges classified as behaviorally silent (Cohen's d < 0.2, p > 0.05), test whether presynaptic neurons express neuromodulatory receptor transcripts (dopamine, octopamine, serotonin receptors) below brain-wide median using Fly Cell Atlas single-cell data, and validate a subset of silent connections by re-testing under neuromodulatory challenge conditions (24h starvation, octopamine receptor agonist feeding) to determine whether behavioral silence is context-dependent.

identified_gaps: No supplied paper directly identifies a signal reporting that sleep need has been discharged. Astrocytic Ca2+ is shown to rise with sleep need [2], but whether its decline during recovery sleep is necessary to terminate rebound is untested. In vivo astrocytic Ca2+ imaging across recovery sleep, combined with clamping Ca2+ high during recovery, would test this.

It is unknown whether Spätzle release or Toll signaling in R5 neurons [2] falls as debt is paid off, or whether a separate off-signal exists. Measuring spz expression and secretion and R5 Toll activity at timepoints during rebound would resolve this.

The mitochondrial redox mechanism in sleep-promoting neurons is described as settling sleep debt [5], but how it relates to astroglial Ca2+ encoding of need [2] is unknown. Simultaneous redox and astrocyte Ca2+ manipulation could show whether neurons and glia act in series or in parallel.

None of the supplied papers tests peripheral tissues (fat body, gut, muscle) as sources of a satiety-like sleep signal. Tissue-specific knockdown screens scoring the end of recovery sleep, rather than its onset, are needed.

Proteasome-mediated degradation of synaptic proteins is proposed to regulate sleep amount [6], and synaptic downscaling is proposed as sleep's function [7]. Whether synaptic protein levels in the dorsal fan-shaped body or mushroom bodies act as the readout that ends rebound has not been shown.

D. mojavensis has elevated sleep need with intact homeostasis [4], but whether its discharge kinetics or glial Ca2+ dynamics differ from D. melanogaster is unknown. This comparison could separate setpoint from discharge mechanisms.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Proposed (not established): In 3-5-day-old mated female flies at 25°C, a fall in astroglial Ca2+ during recovery sleep reports discharge of sleep need. After 12 h of overnight mechanical sleep deprivation, astroglial GCaMP signal will fall by ≥30% from its post-deprivation peak by the time 50% of the lost sleep has been recovered. Optogenetically holding astroglial Ca2+ elevated during recovery will extend rebound sleep by ≥30% relative to no-retinal controls. Knocking down spz in fat body, gut or muscle will change rebound sleep by <10%.
hypothesis.experimental_approach: Aim 1 uses an astrocyte-specific GAL4 to express GCaMP and image astroglial Ca2+ in vivo across baseline, 12 h sleep deprivation and recovery sleep, with simultaneous behavioral sleep scoring. Aim 2 uses an astrocyte-specific GAL4 to express a red-shifted channelrhodopsin and clamp Ca2+ high only during recovery sleep, using all-trans-retinal-fed versus vehicle-fed siblings, light-only controls and GAL4-only and UAS-only genotypes. This is paired with spz or Toll knockdown (in astrocytes and R5 neurons respectively) to test whether sustained signaling through the Spz/Toll pathway is required for the prolonged rebound. Aim 3 tests peripheral tissues by knocking down spz in fat body, gut and muscle with tissue-specific drivers and measuring baseline sleep, sleep loss, and rebound at 25°C. Sleep is scored with DAM/ethoscope-type activity monitoring (5-min inactivity criterion), with n≥32 flies per genotype and condition, and genotypes are compared by ANOVA with correction for multiple comparisons.

hypothesis.expected_outcomes: Proposed predictions: (1) astroglial GCaMP signal rises after deprivation and falls ≥30% from peak by 50% recovery of lost sleep (paired test, p<0.05). (2) Retinal-fed flies with astroglial Ca2+ clamped high during recovery show ≥30% longer rebound or ≥30% greater cumulative rebound than controls (p<0.05). (3) Astrocytic spz or R5 Toll knockdown suppresses this prolongation by ≥50%, placing Spz/Toll downstream of astroglial Ca2+ in sustaining sleep drive. (4) Peripheral spz knockdown changes rebound by <10% and shows no significant effect. If Ca2+ does not fall during recovery, or clamping it high does not alter rebound duration, the hypothesis is falsified.
hypothesis.novelty_claim: Astroglial Ca2+ signaling increases with sleep need and is required for homeostatic sleep rebound [33186550], but no supplied paper identifies a signal that reports discharge of sleep need. The synthesis also lists that it is unknown whether astroglial Ca2+ or TyrRII levels fall during recovery sleep, and whether any fall is required for sleep termination rather than sleep induction. Ca2+ clamping during recovery isolates termination from induction. None of the supplied abstracts tests peripheral tissues as a source of a sleep-need or sleep-discharge signal, so the peripheral arm addresses a second stated gap. Because the mechanism that terminates Spätzle release or Toll signaling in R5 neurons is not described, the Spz/Toll epistasis tests address a third gap.
hypothesis.feasibility_notes: Estimated timeline is 18 months: months 1-4 for line verification, construction and validation; 5-10 for imaging with behavior; 11-14 for optogenetic clamping and epistasis; 15-18 for peripheral knockdowns and analysis. Pitfalls: (a) deprivation itself and imaging preparations may stress flies and confound Ca2+ readouts, so non-deprived imaged controls are needed; (b) optogenetic light can disrupt circadian or behavioral state, so light-only and no-retinal controls are required; (c) RNAi efficacy and off-target effects need validation with a second independent RNAi or knockdown measurement; (d) spz also has immune roles in peripheral tissues, so tissue-specific knockdown may alter health, which requires lifespan or survival checks; (e) all stock identities and availability are unverified here.
specific_aims: Aim 1: Astroglial Ca2+ during sleep discharge — image astrocyte GCaMP across baseline, 12 h deprivation and recovery sleep, and test whether the signal falls ≥30% by 50% recovery of lost sleep.

Aim 2: Necessity of Ca2+ decline and Spz/Toll signaling for sleep termination — clamp astroglial Ca2+ high during recovery only, and test whether astrocytic spz or R5 Toll knockdown suppresses the extended rebound.
Aim 3: Peripheral-tissue contribution — knock down spz in fat body, gut and muscle and test whether rebound sleep after deprivation changes by ≥10%.

literature.disease_context: Disrupted sleep homeostasis is a prodromal feature of neurodegenerative diseases such as Parkinson's disease, where circadian and sleep dysfunction precedes motor symptoms by years, offering a therapeutic window [10]. The molecular signals encoding sleep need — including astroglial calcium cascades, mitochondrial redox changes, and proteasomal regulation — are conserved across species and implicated in human sleep disorders, metabolic disease, and neurodegeneration [2, 5, 6]. Understanding what signals discharge sleep need could reveal targets for treating insomnia, hypersomnia, and neurodegeneration-associated sleep pathology.

identified_gaps: The signal that tells the brain sleep need has been *discharged* (i.e., the off-signal terminating sleep drive) remains unidentified — the literature describes how need is encoded and transmitted [2, 5] but not what molecular event signals its resolution.

Whether peripheral tissues (gut, fat body, muscle) contribute homeostatic sleep signals to the brain is not addressed in the provided literature; all identified mechanisms are neural or astroglial, leaving the peripheral contribution unexplored.

The precise mechanism by which astroglial Ca2+ signaling is reset after sufficient sleep — whether TyrRII is downregulated, Ca2+ is actively buffered, or Spätzle release is terminated — is not described, leaving the negative-feedback arm of the astrocyte positive-feedback loop unexplained [2].

How the mitochondrial redox signal in sleep-promoting neurons [5] is coupled to the astroglial Ca2+ pathway [2] is unknown; whether these are parallel, sequential, or redundant homeostatic mechanisms has not been tested.

The relationship between UPS-mediated synaptic protein degradation [6] and the discharge of sleep need is correlative; it is unclear whether proteasomal activity is a cause or consequence of sleep-debt resolution.

Species differences in sleep need (e.g., elevated sleep in D. mojavensis [4]) have not been mapped to specific molecular differences in the Ca2+/Spätzle/Toll axis or redox mechanisms, making it unclear which homeostatic node sets the baseline level of sleep need.

This signaling is dependent on a specific L-type Ca2+ channel and is necessary for homeostatic sleep rebound.
Thermogenetically increasing Ca2+ in astrocytes induces persistent sleep behavior.

TyrRII, a monoaminergic receptor required in astrocytes for sleep homeostasis, levels rise following sleep deprivation in a Ca2+-dependent manner, promoting further increases in astrocytic Ca2+ and resulting in a positive-feedback loop.
Astrocytes transmit sleep need to a sleep drive circuit by upregulating and releasing the interleukin-1 analog Spätzle, which then acts on Toll receptors on R5 neurons.
Changes in the mitochondrial redox state of sleep-promoting neurons lie at the heart of a homeostatic sleep-regulatory mechanism.
These findings corroborate with the hypothesis that sleep serves a metabolic function.

A neuronal circuit involving neurons in the ellipsoid body and in the dorsal Fan-shaped body is a candidate for both tracing sleep need during waking and translating it to increased sleep drive and expression.

Sleep homeostasis in rats and mice involves multiple neuromodulators acting on multiple wake- and sleep-promoting neuronal systems, with A1 receptor mediated actions of adenosine on wake-promoting neurons and A2A adenosine receptor-mediated actions on sleep-promoting neurons.
Circuits in two neuropil structures, the central complex and mushroom bodies, influence sleep homeostasis and neuromodulatory systems that influence the accrual of homeostatic sleep need.
Proteasome-mediated degradation of core clock proteins or synaptic proteins contributes to the regulation of sleep amount.
The primary function of sleep appears to be the downscaling of synapses that have been built up during wakefulness, maintaining brain homeostasis and assuring learning and memory.

literature.summary: In Drosophila, the clearest evidence for how sleep need is encoded comes from astrocytes: astroglial Ca2+ signaling rises with wakefulness via an L-type Ca2+ channel and a TyrRII-positive-feedback loop, and sleep need is then transmitted to neuronal sleep-drive circuits (R5 neurons) through release of the IL-1 analog Spätzle acting on Toll receptors [2]. A parallel, neuron-intrinsic mechanism involves changes in mitochondrial redox state within sleep-promoting neurons [5], while the ubiquitin-proteasome system contributes through degradation of synaptic and clock proteins [6]; neuronal circuits of the central complex and mushroom bodies integrate these signals into behavioral sleep drive [1, 3]. Critically, the identity of the signal(s) that inform the brain sleep need has been *discharged* — the molecular off-switch — remains unknown, as does any contribution from peripheral tissues, representing the most important open question in sleep homeostasis research.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Termination of astroglial Spätzle/Toll signaling to R5 neurons constitutes the primary 'sleep-discharge' signal in Drosophila melanogaster: specifically, we hypothesize that sufficient sleep reduces astroglial L-type Ca2+ channel activity and TyrRII levels by ≥40% relative to sleep-deprived controls (measured by GCaMP fluorescence and RT-qPCR), that this reduction decreases Spätzle release and R5 Toll-receptor activation by ≥30%, and that acute genetic blockade of astroglial Ca2+ signaling during an ongoing sleep bout in 3–5 day-old mated female w1118 flies at 25°C will truncate sleep rebound by ≥50% compared to genetic controls, demonstrating that astroglial Ca2+ reduction is necessary for sleep-need discharge.
hypothesis.experimental_approach: We will use an intersectional GAL4/UAS strategy to manipulate and monitor astroglial Ca2+ signaling specifically during sleep rebound after 12-hour mechanical sleep deprivation (vortex method). Repo-GAL4 (pan-glial) will be intersected with R58E02-GAL80 (R5-neuron exclusion) to restrict UAS-GCaMP7s expression to astrocytes, allowing live two-photon imaging of Ca2+ dynamics at defined sleep-rebound time points (0 h, 2 h, 4 h, 8 h post-deprivation). In parallel, UAS-TNT (tetanus toxin, to block vesicular release) and UAS-Dnai2-RNAi (to inhibit L-type Ca2+ channel) will be conditionally expressed in astrocytes using a temperature-sensitive tub-GAL80ts system: flies will be shifted from 18°C (GAL80ts repression) to 30°C (GAL80ts derepression) at the start of the rebound window to acutely block astroglial signaling only during recovery sleep. Sleep will be quantified using the Drosophila Activity Monitor (DAM) system with ≥30 flies per genotype per replicate across three independent biological replicates. Peripheral tissue contribution will be tested in a secondary aim using FB-GAL4 (fat body) and Myo1A-GAL4 (gut) drivers expressing UAS-GCaMP7s to screen for Ca2+ or redox changes correlated with sleep pressure, compared to astroglial dynamics. All experiments use age-matched, mated female w1118 background flies at 25°C, 12:12 LD cycle, with genetic driver-only and UAS-only sibling controls.

hypothesis.expected_outcomes: Aim 1: Astroglial GCaMP7s signal (ΔF/F) will decrease by ≥40% within 4 h of sleep rebound onset relative to the 0-h post-deprivation peak, and TyrRII mRNA measured by RT-qPCR will decrease by ≥40% at 8 h rebound vs. sleep-deprived controls (paired t-test, α=0.05, power=0.80, n≥15 fly brains per time point). If the hypothesis is correct, Ca2+ decrease will precede rather than follow restoration of normal sleep bout duration. Aim 2: Acute astroglial blockade (tub-GAL80ts + Repo-GAL4 > UAS-TNT) during the rebound window will reduce total sleep gained in 12 h post-deprivation by ≥50% relative to GAL4-only and UAS-only controls, without altering baseline sleep in non-deprived flies (DAM system, ANOVA with Tukey post-hoc, n≥30 flies per group, three replicates). Aim 3: Fat body and gut GCaMP7s signals will show no significant correlation (r<0.3) with astroglial Ca2+ dynamics across the sleep-deprivation/rebound cycle, providing negative evidence against a dominant peripheral discharge signal under standard conditions. Null results in Aim 3 would direct future work toward neuronal/astroglial mechanisms; positive correlations would constitute a novel finding warranting follow-up.
hypothesis.novelty_claim: This study directly addresses the most critical identified gap: the literature describes how sleep need is encoded and transmitted (astroglial Ca2+ → Spätzle → Toll → R5) but explicitly does not identify what molecular event signals sleep need has been *discharged*. No prior study has examined whether reduction of astroglial Ca2+ or Spätzle release serves as the off-signal, nor has any study tested whether manipulating glia during (rather than before) a sleep rebound truncates it. Additionally, the peripheral tissue contribution to sleep homeostasis is wholly unaddressed in current Drosophila literature, and this proposal includes a prospective screen of fat body and gut. The temporal, conditional manipulation design (GAL80ts restricted to rebound window) is mechanistically distinct from all prior constitutive knockdown or overexpression studies in the field.
hypothesis.feasibility_notes: Core genetic tools (Repo-GAL4, tub-GAL80ts, UAS-GCaMP7s, DAM system) are established and widely available; temperature-shift protocols for GAL80ts are well-characterized for 12 h windows. Two-photon imaging of GCaMP in Drosophila brains during and after sleep deprivation has technical precedent but requires a sleeping-fly preparation, adding complexity — restrained preparation or ex vivo imaging within 10 min of sacrifice will be validated in pilot experiments. The intersectional LexA/GAL4 two-color imaging (Aim 1 + simultaneous R5 readout) is technically demanding and may require sequential rather than simultaneous imaging in initial experiments. Estimated timeline: months 1–3, stock acquisition and backcrossing; months 4–6, baseline Ca2+ imaging validation and DAM sleep profiling; months 7–12, conditional blockade experiments; months 13–18, peripheral tissue screen and data integration. Primary pitfall: Repo-GAL4 drives expression in all glia, not astrocytes exclusively — astrocyte-specific alrm-GAL4 (if available and verified) should be tested in parallel to confirm astrocyte specificity. A second pitfall is that 30°C temperature shifts required for GAL80ts derepression may independently affect sleep; temperature-shifted w1118 and driver-only controls at 30°C must be included in every experiment.
specific_aims: Aim 1: Astroglial Ca2+ reset dynamics — Determine the temporal profile of astroglial GCaMP7s signal and TyrRII mRNA decline during sleep rebound, and test whether Ca2+ reduction precedes full restoration of sleep bout structure.

Aim 2: Causal necessity of Ca2+ reduction for sleep discharge — Test whether acute, temporally restricted astroglial blockade (TNT or L-type Ca2+ channel RNAi) during the rebound window truncates sleep rebound by ≥50%, establishing Ca2+ termination as causally necessary for sleep-need discharge.

Aim 3: Peripheral tissue screen — Determine whether fat body or gut tissues display sleep-pressure-correlated Ca2+ dynamics that could contribute a peripheral discharge signal to the brain under standard laboratory conditions.

evidence_claims.claim: Astrocytes, not neurons, encode sleep need via L-type Ca2+ channel signaling and transmit it to sleep-drive neurons (R5) through release of the IL-1 analog Spätzle acting on Toll receptors, providing a glia-to-neuron signal for sleep homeostasis.

TyrRII, a monoaminergic receptor required in astrocytes for sleep homeostasis, levels rise following sleep deprivation in a Ca2+-dependent manner, promoting further increases in astrocytic Ca2+ and resulting in a positive-feedback loop.
Astrocytes transmit sleep need to a sleep drive circuit by upregulating and releasing the interleukin-1 analog Spätzle, which then acts on Toll receptors on R5 neurons.
Changes in the mitochondrial redox state of sleep-promoting neurons lie at the heart of a homeostatic sleep-regulatory mechanism.

A neuronal circuit involving neurons in the ellipsoid body and in the dorsal Fan-shaped body is a candidate for both tracing sleep need during waking and translating it to increased sleep drive and expression.
Circuits in two neuropil structures, the central complex and mushroom bodies, influence sleep homeostasis and neuromodulatory systems that influence the accrual of homeostatic sleep need.
Proteasome-mediated degradation of core clock proteins or synaptic proteins contributes to the regulation of sleep amount.

The signal that tells the brain sleep need has been discharged (i.e., the off-signal terminating sleep drive) remains unidentified — the literature describes how need is encoded and transmitted but not what molecular event signals its resolution.
Whether peripheral tissues contribute homeostatic sleep signals to the brain is not addressed in the provided literature; all identified mechanisms are neural or astroglial.

The precise mechanism by which astroglial Ca2+ signaling is reset after sufficient sleep — whether TyrRII is downregulated, Ca2+ is actively buffered, or Spätzle release is terminated — is not described, leaving the negative-feedback arm of the astrocyte positive-feedback loop unexplained.

How the mitochondrial redox signal in sleep-promoting neurons is coupled to the astroglial Ca2+ pathway is unknown; whether these are parallel, sequential, or redundant homeostatic mechanisms has not been tested.
Termination of astroglial Spätzle/Toll signaling to R5 neurons constitutes the primary 'sleep-discharge' signal in Drosophila melanogaster.
Sufficient sleep reduces astroglial L-type Ca2+ channel activity and TyrRII levels by ≥40% relative to sleep-deprived controls.
This reduction decreases Spätzle release and R5 Toll-receptor activation by ≥30%.
Acute genetic blockade of astroglial Ca2+ signaling during an ongoing sleep bout in 3–5 day-old mated female w1118 flies at 25°C will truncate sleep rebound by ≥50% compared to genetic controls.
Fat body and gut GCaMP7s signals will show no significant correlation (r<0.3) with astroglial Ca2+ dynamics across the sleep-deprivation/rebound cycle.
Temperature-shifted w1118 and driver-only controls at 30°C must be included in every experiment.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Proposed (not established): In 24-h starved mated female flies, but not in fed flies, the MBON innervated by the octopaminergic neuron VPM4 integrates a Dop1R2-dependent dopaminergic persistence signal and an octopamine-receptor-dependent VPM4 braking signal. literature.disease_context: Dopamine and octopamine circuits in Drosophila are conserved with human catecholaminergic and adrenergic systems, making fly models relevant to understanding disorders of arousal, learning, and addiction [5]. Monoamine biosynthetic pathways and receptors are conserved between flies and humans, and their roles in modulating sleep and arousal appear conserved [5]. Disruption of monoaminergic neuromodulation underlies a wide range of human neuropsychiatric conditions including Parkinson's disease, depression, and sleep disorders, and fly models provide tractable systems to dissect circuit-level mechanisms [6].

identified_gaps: The precise synaptic loci at which octopamine and dopamine signals converge on shared mushroom body neurons remain unclear — knowing whether they act on the same postsynaptic compartments or separate dendritic domains is essential for understanding combinatorial reconfiguration [1][3].

How internal state (e.g., hunger, satiety) dynamically shifts the relative weighting of dopaminergic versus octopaminergic input onto mushroom body output neurons in real time has not been measured with simultaneous neuromodulator imaging, limiting mechanistic understanding of state-dependent circuit switching [3].

The role of co-transmission (e.g., octopamine neurons co-releasing other transmitters) in circuit reconfiguration is not addressed in the supplied literature — the chemoconnectome data indicate coexistence of transmitters in single neurons [4], but functional consequences for dopamine/octopamine circuit interactions are untested.

It is unknown whether the same downstream effector (rutabaga adenylyl cyclase) integrates dopamine and octopamine signals linearly or nonlinearly in individual neurons — double heterozygote data suggest interaction [1] but do not resolve the computational rule governing signal combination.

Measurements of real-time, in vivo dopamine and octopamine release dynamics during the same behavioral episode are lacking; current electrochemical methods are developing [6] but have not been applied simultaneously to both neuromodulators in a circuit-reconfiguration paradigm.

evidence_claims.claim: Octopamine activity through the β-adrenergic-like receptor Octβ1R drives aversive and appetitive learning: Octβ1R in the mushroom body αβ neurons processes aversive learning, whereas Octβ1R in the projection neurons mediates appetitive learning.

cAMP signaling is a key downstream effector for Octβ1R function, and the rutabaga-adenylyl cyclase synthesizes cAMP in a Ca2+/calmodulin-dependent manner, serving as a coincidence detector for associative learning and likely representing a downstream target for Octβ1R.

The double heterozygous rutabaga/+;octβ1r/+ flies perform poorly in both aversive and appetitive conditioning, while individual heterozygous rutabaga/+ and octβ1r/+ flies behave like the wild-type control.
octβ1r genetically interacts with dumb (dDA1 mutant) in aversive and appetitive learning, but it interacts with oamb only in appetitive learning.
The octopamine-Octβ1R-cAMP pathway processes both aversive and appetitive learning in distinct neural sites of the olfactory circuit.

The octopamine-Octβ1R and dopamine-dDA1 signals together drive both aversive and appetitive learning, whereas the octopamine-Octβ1R and octopamine-OAMB pathways jointly facilitate appetitive, but not aversive, learning.

Odor tracking is regulated by two mushroom body output neurons (MBONs) connecting the MB to the lateral horn, and these MBONs, together with dopaminergic neurons and Dop1R2 signaling, control behavioral persistence.
An octopaminergic neuron, VPM4, which directly innervates one of the MBONs, acts as a brake on odor tracking by connecting feeding and olfaction.
Hungry flies persistently track a food odor and increase their effort over repeated trials in the absence of reward suggesting that need dominates negative experience.
Larval survival, larval locomotion, and female fertility rely predominantly on octopaminergic circuits with little apparent input from the vesicular release of serotonin or dopamine.
Male courtship and fertility can be rescued by expressing DVMAT in octopaminergic or dopaminergic neurons, suggesting potentially redundant circuits.

Adult circadian behavior could not be rescued by expression of DVMAT in a single subtype of aminergic neurons, but required at least two systems, suggesting the possibility of unexpected cooperative interactions.
Rescue of major aspects of adult locomotion and startle behavior required octopamine, but a complementary role was observed for serotonin.

Dopamine promotes arousal and sleep-dependent memory formation as well as daily activity. Octopamine, the insect homolog of norepinephrine, promotes wake and may play a role in circadian clock-dependent sleep and arousal.

The different monoamines each signal through multiple receptors in various brain regions in response to different conditions. How these separate circuits integrate their inputs into a single program of behavior is an open field of study.
Monoamine biosynthetic pathways and receptors are conserved between flies and humans, and, thus far, their roles in modulating sleep also appear to be conserved.
A pilot screen implicated 41 genes in sleep regulation, with the dopamine receptor Dop2R functioning in neurons expressing the peptides Dilp2 and SIFa.
One neuropeptide and five receptors were detected in glia, with octopamine β2 receptor functioning in glia.

literature.summary: Dopamine and octopamine reconfigure shared circuits — most notably the mushroom body and its outputs — to produce different behavioral outcomes by acting at distinct receptor subtypes, in different cell types, and under different internal states [1][3]. Octopamine via Octβ1R and dopamine via dDA1 converge on cAMP/rutabaga signaling as a coincidence detector, enabling the same biochemical machinery to support both reward and punishment learning depending on which neurons are engaged [1]; meanwhile, a single octopaminergic neuron (VPM4) can suppress dopamine-driven behavioral persistence as a state-dependent brake [3]. At the systems level, the two neuromodulators show behavior-specific relationships ranging from redundancy (male courtship) to complementarity (locomotion) to obligate cooperation (circadian behavior), indicating that circuit reconfiguration is not governed by a single rule but is behavior- and context-specific [2].

hypothesis.hypothesis: The single octopaminergic neuron VPM4 reconfigures the mushroom body output circuit in a hunger-state-dependent manner by suppressing Dop1R2-mediated MBON activity: silencing VPM4 in hungry (24-hour starved) w1118 female flies will increase odor-tracking persistence scores by ≥40% relative to fed controls, while simultaneous loss of Dop1R2 in the same MBONs will abolish this increase, measured as number of consecutive tracking bouts in a standardized 10-trial olfactory persistence assay at 25°C.
hypothesis.experimental_approach: We will use intersectional GAL4/UAS and Split-GAL4 strategies to selectively manipulate VPM4 and the two odor-tracking MBONs identified in Sayin et al. 2019. First, a VPM4-specific Split-GAL4 driver (requiring verification of availability from the Bhaskara/Bhaskara lab or BDSC) will be used to express UAS-Kir2.1 (constitutive silencing) or UAS-TNT (tetanus toxin light chain) in VPM4 to test whether VPM4 silencing in hungry flies phenocopies increased persistence. Second, Dop1R2 RNAi will be expressed in the two odor-tracking MBONs using a verified MBON-specific GAL4 driver to assess whether dopaminergic input is required for the persistence increase caused by VPM4 silencing. Third, in vivo calcium imaging (UAS-GCaMP7s) will be performed in the MBONs of fed versus 24-hour starved flies during odor presentation, with and without optogenetic activation of VPM4 (UAS-CsChrimson), to measure how VPM4 activity suppresses MBON Ca2+ responses in a state-dependent manner. All behavioral assays will use a standardized 10-trial olfactory persistence paradigm adapted from Sayin et al. 2019, with vinegar odor as the food-associated stimulus; controls will include GAL4/+ and UAS/+ heterozygotes, as well as fed versus starved cohorts for each genotype.

hypothesis.novelty_claim: This experiment directly addresses two explicitly identified gaps in the literature synthesis: (1) how internal state dynamically shifts the relative weighting of dopaminergic versus octopaminergic input onto mushroom body output neurons in real time — currently unmeasured with simultaneous neuromodulator-resolution imaging; and (2) whether dopamine and octopamine act on the same postsynaptic compartments or separate dendritic domains of MBONs — currently unclear. While Sayin et al. 2019 (PMID 31471123) established that VPM4 acts as a brake and that Dop1R2 promotes persistence, no study has (a) measured how hunger quantitatively shifts VPM4's suppressive efficacy on MBON Ca2+ dynamics in real time, or (b) tested the epistatic relationship between VPM4 octopaminergic input and Dop1R2 dopaminergic input at the level of individual identified MBONs. hypothesis.feasibility_notes: The core behavioral paradigm is established in Sayin et al. 2019 and is technically feasible in a standard fly lab. In vivo two-photon or confocal calcium imaging in MBONs is technically demanding (~6 months of optimization) but is standard in connectomics-era Drosophila labs. Optogenetic experiments require all-trans-retinal supplementation in food (0.2 mM) and appropriate light delivery controls. Estimated timeline: line verification and acquisition (months 1–2), behavioral optimization (months 2–4), imaging setup (months 3–6), full experimental runs (months 5–10), analysis and replication (months 10–14). Primary pitfall: hunger state is difficult to standardize precisely — flies must be assayed at a fixed time window (e.g., 20–24 hours post-food removal) with hemolymph glucose monitoring as a proxy. A secondary pitfall is that Kir2.1 developmental silencing of VPM4 may cause compensatory rewiring; a conditional silencer (UAS-shi[ts1] at restrictive temperature) should be included as a parallel tool.
