Odor tracking is regulated by two mushroom body output neurons (MBONs) connecting the MB to the lateral horn, and these MBONs, together with dopaminergic neurons and Dop1R2 signaling, control behavioral persistence.
An octopaminergic neuron, VPM4, which directly innervates one of the MBONs, acts as a brake on odor tracking by connecting feeding and olfaction.
Hungry flies persistently track a food odor and increase their effort over repeated trials in the absence of reward suggesting that need dominates negative experience.

cAMP signaling is a key downstream effector for Octβ1R function, and the rutabaga-adenylyl cyclase synthesizes cAMP in a Ca2+/calmodulin-dependent manner, serving as a coincidence detector for associative learning and likely representing a downstream target for Octβ1R.

The double heterozygous rutabaga/+;octβ1r/+ flies perform poorly in both aversive and appetitive conditioning, while individual heterozygous rutabaga/+ and octβ1r/+ flies behave like the wild-type control.
octβ1r genetically interacts with dumb (dDA1 mutant) in aversive and appetitive learning, but it interacts with oamb only in appetitive learning.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Proposed: in singly reared isogenic w1118 flies at 25C, a fly's stable locomotor turn bias (Y-maze handedness index) reflects left-right asymmetry in central complex columnar neuron synaptic output that is set during pupal development. Predictions: (a) day-to-day test-retest Spearman correlation of the handedness index is >=0.4 over 7 days; (b) per-fly handedness index correlates with left-right asymmetry of a presynaptic marker in columnar neuron terminals measured in the same brains (|Spearman rho| >=0.4, FDR <0.05); (c) transient pupal-stage inhibition of these neurons changes between-fly variance of the handedness index by >=30% versus controls, while equivalent adult-only inhibition does not.
hypothesis.experimental_approach: Individual isogenic flies will be tracked longitudinally in Y-mazes (turn bias) and in a sensory reactivity/habituation assay across 7-14 days, to test whether the two behaviors share an individuality axis. Flies are housed singly to remove the group-level effects seen in replicate groups, and a grouped-housing comparison cohort is included. After behavior, the same brains are fixed and imaged with a columnar-neuron split-GAL4 (driver to be identified and verified) driving a membrane marker and a presynaptic marker such as Brp-short, quantifying left-right asymmetry in synapse number and intensity by blinded analysis. For causality, a tub-GAL80ts; columnar-driver combination drives Kir2.1 or a similar silencer in restricted windows (larval, pupal, adult) with temperature-shifted GAL80ts-only and UAS-only controls. Main readouts are the mean and between-individual variance of the handedness index, compared by Levene/Brown-Forsythe tests and bootstrap variance ratios.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Proposed hypothesis: in an isogenic, individually reared wild-type population, each adult's locomotor turn bias is set during pupal development by left–right asymmetry in central complex columnar neuron arborization. We predict three outcomes. (i) A per-fly left–right asymmetry index of columnar neuron arbors in the protocerebral bridge/fan-shaped body will correlate with that fly's adult turn bias with |Spearman r| ≥ 0.40 (n ≥ 150 flies, p < 0.01). (ii) Conditionally silencing columnar neurons only during pupal development (with function restored before testing) will change the population variance of adult turn bias by ≥30% relative to temperature-matched controls. Silencing only in adulthood, followed by recovery, will not produce a persistent change. (iii) Turn bias will be uncorrelated with visual escape habituation parameters measured in the same individuals (|r| < 0.15). This would indicate that these idiosyncrasies have separable developmental origins. The hypothesis is falsified if the asymmetry index explains <5% of turn-bias variance, or if developmental-window and adult-window silencing have indistinguishable effects.
hypothesis.experimental_approach: Turn bias will be scored in Y-maze arrays in isogenic flies, since nonheritable, lifelong handedness in isogenic flies and its regulation by central complex columnar neurons have been reported [25953337]. Each fly will be re-tested 3 times between days 3 and 10 to confirm repeatability. The same flies will then be tested in a looming-stimulus escape/habituation assay modeled on [41894333]. Afterwards, each fly's brain will be dissected and imaged. A columnar-neuron split-GAL4/GAL4 line drives membrane GFP, and sparse stochastic labeling (MCFO) will be used to score individual columns. The asymmetry index is defined as (L−R)/(L+R) arbor volume and column innervation, quantified blind to behavior. For temporal causality, columnar-GAL4 > UAS-Kir2.1 will be combined with tub-GAL80ts and shifted to 30 °C during either a pupal window (0–96 h APF) or an adult window (days 1–4). hypothesis.expected_outcomes: Aim 1: individual turn bias will be repeatable across sessions (intraclass correlation ≥ 0.3), consistent with [25953337]. The arbor asymmetry index will correlate with turn bias (|Spearman r| ≥ 0.40, n ≥ 150, p < 0.01). A power analysis gives roughly 90% power to detect r = 0.30 at α = 0.01 with n = 150. Aim 2: pupal-window silencing will produce a ≥30% change in the variance of turn bias versus all three controls (Levene/Brown–Forsythe test, p < 0.01, n ≥ 120 per genotype). Adult-window silencing followed by recovery will show <10% change. Aim 3: turn bias and habituation rate/reactivity parameters will be uncorrelated (|r| < 0.15). Variance in turn bias will not differ between isolated and group-reared flies (difference <15%, equivalence test). Results outside these thresholds would refute the corresponding component of the hypothesis.
hypothesis.novelty_claim: The synthesis identifies four gaps that this plan addresses. First, it notes that the developmental variation setting an individual's direction of bias is unidentified, and that longitudinal linking of central complex wiring to each adult's measured bias is needed. Aim 1 provides this per-individual link. Second, handedness is uncorrelated with morphological asymmetries [25953337], so a neural, rather than bodily, asymmetry source remains untested. Third, the relationship between handedness and reactivity/habituation [41894333] has never been measured in the same individuals (Aim 3). Fourth, the relative contributions of social context versus intrinsic developmental noise are unresolved [16153038]. Temporally separating developmental from adult circuit function to explain individuality has not been reported in the provided literature.
hypothesis.feasibility_notes: Estimated timeline: 15–18 months. Months 1–3 cover isogenizing and backcrossing lines (≥6 generations) and validating Y-maze and looming rigs. Months 3–9 cover behavior and imaging of ≥150 flies (Aim 1). Months 6–12 cover the GAL80ts experiments (Aim 2), and months 9–15 cover multi-trait and social-context assays (Aim 3). Pitfalls: (1) The identity of the columnar driver used in [25953337] must be verified. Off-target expression could confound results, so a second independent driver should be tested. (2) Kir2.1 during development may alter neuron survival or morphology. Arbor counts will therefore be imaged in silenced flies. (3) Elevated temperature alone affects individuality, so temperature-matched controls are essential. (4) Imaging-based asymmetry indices may be noisy, so scoring should be blinded with inter-rater reliability ≥0.8. (5) A null result in Aim 1 would still constrain candidate sources, leaving stochastic synaptic or epigenetic variation [15273410] as alternatives.

Aim 3: Shared vs separable origins and social context — measure turn bias and visual escape habituation in the same individuals, and compare isolated versus group rearing, to test whether the idiosyncrasies share an origin and whether social experience contributes.

literature.disease_context: Individual variation in sensory reactivity and habituation in isogenic Drosophila provides a quantitative platform for modeling interindividual differences relevant to neurogenetic diseases, where atypical responses are frequently observed [5]. Epigenetic variation in isogenic populations, studied via quantitative epigenetics approaches in Drosophila, may underlie heritable trait variation without DNA sequence differences, with implications for understanding non-genetic inheritance of complex traits in humans [4]. Stable individual behavioral differences in model organisms may inform understanding of neurodevelopmental and psychiatric conditions where behavioral heterogeneity is a hallmark.

identified_gaps: The specific developmental time windows during which stochastic variation in gene expression or neural circuit wiring is established remain uncharacterized — identifying these windows would clarify whether individuality is set early in neurogenesis or continuously throughout development [1][3].

The mechanistic link between epigenetic variation (e.g., epialleles defined by histone modification) and specific adult behavioral phenotypes in isogenic flies has not been directly demonstrated — such a demonstration would establish epigenetics as a causal, rather than merely correlative, source of behavioral individuality [4].

The degree to which social-environment-driven group behavioral differences feed back to alter individual neural states or gene expression is unknown, yet this is necessary to understand how emergent group behavior produces stable individual differences [2].

Whether the central complex neurons controlling locomotor handedness do so by buffering or amplifying developmental stochasticity in circuit formation — versus modulating moment-to-moment variability — is unresolved, limiting mechanistic understanding of how individuality is encoded [3].

It is not known whether individual differences in sensory reactivity and habituation (as quantified by dynamical modeling) share mechanistic origins with locomotor handedness or other individual behavioral traits, or whether each behavioral dimension has independent stochastic sources [3][5].

evidence_claims.claim: Behavioral differences result from the well-known interplay of nature and nurture.
Environmental factors, epigenetic modifications, and gene expression and function are responsible for generating stochastic behaviors.

Genetically identical individuals display variability in their physiology, morphology, and behaviors, even when reared in essentially identical environments, but there is little mechanistic understanding of the basis of such variation.
Individual flies exhibit significant bias in their left vs. right locomotor choices, with some flies being strongly left biased or right biased.
The biases of individual flies persist for their lifetime and are nonheritable: i.e., mating two left-biased individuals does not yield left-biased progeny.
This locomotor handedness is uncorrelated with other asymmetries, such as the handedness of gut twisting, leg-length asymmetry, and wing-folding preference.
The magnitude of locomotor handedness is under the control of columnar neurons within the central complex, a brain region implicated in motor planning and execution.
When these neurons are silenced, exploratory laterality increases, with more extreme leftiness and rightiness.
This observation intriguingly implies that the brain may be able to dynamically regulate behavioral individuality.
Quantitative properties of individual responses vary greatly even in an isogenic population raised under identical environmental conditions.
Individual reactivity and habituation parameters display substantial temporal stability over a two-week interval, indicating that these behaviors are stable, intrinsic properties of an individual.

The presented framework enables robust stratification of individual behavioral phenotypes and provides a quantitative platform for modeling interindividual differences in sensory processing, including frequently observed atypical responses in neurogenetic diseases.
Genotypes differed in activity, explaining 14.41% of the variation in activity; 8.60% of the variation was explained by a significant genotype x sex interaction.
Differences between replicate groups within genotype accounted for 19.47% variation in activity, and activity was significantly repeatable across scans.
Emergent group behavior explained almost as much variation in activity as the combined sources of genetic variation (23.01%).
This emergent group behavior is likely caused by differences between groups of interacting individuals, even though individuals were genetically identical across groups.

QE analyses assume that epigenetic variation in a population is partly responsible for the trait variation, and the aim is to associate inheritance of the trait with segregation of informative epigenetic polymorphisms, or epialleles.

QE analysis can make use of powerful emerging mapping techniques that allow the positioning of epialleles defined by chromatin variation to individual genes or chromosomal regions, even in the absence of DNA sequence variation.

literature.summary: Isogenic Drosophila melanogaster raised in identical conditions nonetheless exhibit stable, reproducible individual differences in diverse behaviors — including locomotor handedness, sensory reactivity, habituation, and activity levels — demonstrating that neither genetic sequence variation nor shared environment fully determines behavioral phenotype [1][3][5]. Multiple non-genetic mechanisms have been implicated, including developmental stochasticity in neural circuit formation (regulated by central complex columnar neurons), epigenetic variation such as differential histone acetylation and methylation, and emergent social-environment effects among co-housed groups of genetically identical individuals [2][3][4]. A key unresolved challenge is pinpointing the precise developmental mechanisms — whether stochastic gene expression, epigenetic patterning, or circuit-level noise — that initiate and stabilize these individual differences across the lifetime of an animal.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Stochastic variation in histone H3K9 acetylation at promoters of central complex development genes during the larval-to-pupal transition (hours 0–24 APF) causally determines stable adult locomotor handedness bias in isogenic w1118 Drosophila melanogaster, such that pharmacological reduction of HDAC activity (via 5 mM sodium butyrate feeding) during this window will reduce the variance in adult handedness scores (measured as |lateralization index|) by ≥30% compared to vehicle controls, while the same treatment applied outside this window (adult stage) will produce no significant change in handedness variance, in a cohort of ≥200 flies per condition at 25°C on standard food.
hypothesis.experimental_approach: We will use a combination of pharmacological HDAC inhibition (sodium butyrate feeding) applied in temporally restricted windows across Drosophila development to identify the critical period during which epigenetic stochasticity is set. Locomotor handedness will be quantified using a Y-maze assay across ≥200 isogenic w1118 flies per treatment group, scoring left/right choice at each branch point over 20 consecutive trials per fly to compute a lateralization index (LI = (R–L)/(R+L)); variance in |LI| will be the primary endpoint. Concurrently, we will use CUT&RUN chromatin profiling on dissected larval/pupal central complexes at 0, 12, and 24 h APF to map H3K9ac levels at candidate central-complex development gene loci (including rx, ey, and toy) in individual-pooled samples, correlating epigenetic variance with downstream behavioral variance. To establish causal neuronal specificity, we will employ a conditional UAS-dHDAC3-RNAi line driven by the central-complex-specific R9D11-GAL4 driver during pupal development (using a temperature-sensitive GAL80ts to restrict knockdown to 0–24 h APF at 29°C) and measure adult handedness variance. Parallel controls will include vehicle-treated w1118, adult-stage sodium butyrate treatment, and R9D11-GAL4/+ and UAS-dHDAC3-RNAi/+ heterozygous controls.

hypothesis.expected_outcomes: Primary outcome: Sodium butyrate (5 mM) feeding restricted to 0–24 h APF will reduce the variance of |LI| in adult w1118 flies by ≥30% relative to vehicle controls (F-test for variance equality, p < 0.05, n ≥ 200 per group), with mean |LI| unchanged (indicating dampened stochasticity, not a directional shift). Adult-stage sodium butyrate treatment will show <10% change in variance (non-significant). CUT&RUN will reveal that H3K9ac variance across central-complex loci is significantly higher at 12 h APF than at 0 h APF (Levene's test, p < 0.05), and that sodium butyrate reduces this epigenetic variance at the same loci. Pupal-restricted R9D11-GAL4–driven Hdac3-RNAi will phenocopy pharmacological HDAC inhibition, reducing adult |LI| variance by ≥25% relative to GAL4/+ and UAS/+ heterozygous controls (n ≥ 150 per genotype, p < 0.05). Conversely, UAS-HDAC3 overexpression during the same window is predicted to increase variance. If sodium butyrate treatment outside the 0–24 h APF window fails to alter behavioral variance while treatment within it succeeds, this will confirm a critical developmental window for epigenetic individuality.
hypothesis.novelty_claim: This experiment directly addresses two major gaps identified in the literature synthesis. First, the specific developmental time windows during which stochastic variation in gene expression or neural circuit wiring is established remain uncharacterized (Gap 1), and this design uses temporally gated pharmacology and GAL80ts to resolve this. Second, the mechanistic link between epigenetic variation (epialleles defined by histone modification) and specific adult behavioral phenotypes in isogenic flies has not been directly demonstrated — such a demonstration would establish epigenetics as a causal, rather than merely correlative, source of behavioral individuality (Gap 2, referencing PMID 15273410). Prior work showed that central complex columnar neurons regulate handedness magnitude (PMID 25953337) and that histone modification variance exists in isogenic flies (PMID 15273410), but no study has connected a specific developmental epigenetic window in central complex neurons to the establishment of stable adult behavioral individuality. Additionally, this design partially addresses Gap 4 by testing whether central complex neurons buffer developmental stochasticity through chromatin-level mechanisms rather than moment-to-moment neural variability.
hypothesis.feasibility_notes: Sodium butyrate feeding is well established in Drosophila and is technically straightforward; the primary challenge is achieving reliable, non-toxic delivery at the larval-to-pupal transition. CUT&RUN on small numbers of dissected pupal central complexes is technically demanding due to tissue availability — approximately 50 dissected central complexes per replicate will be required, necessitating careful staging. GAL80ts-based temporal restriction is a validated approach in Drosophila but requires careful temperature-shift timing and monitoring of developmental staging at 29°C (which accelerates development). The Y-maze handedness assay is established (PMID 25953337) but requires automation for n ≥ 200 flies; a Raspberry Pi-based or commercial Y-maze array is recommended. UAS-HDAC3 overexpression lines may need to be generated if unavailable from stock centers. Estimated timeline: Aim 1 (pharmacological critical window mapping): 4 months; Aim 2 (CUT&RUN epigenetic profiling): 5 months (concurrent with Aim 1); Aim 3 (neuronal genetic validation): 6 months (including line construction). Total: approximately 12–15 months. Key pitfall: sodium butyrate may affect developmental timing or viability at the pupal stage, requiring dose optimization; lethality controls (eclosion rate, pupal size) must be included. A second pitfall is that R9D11-GAL4 may not exclusively target the columnar neurons implicated in PMID 25953337; immunostaining to confirm driver expression pattern is required before behavioral interpretation.
specific_aims: Aim 1: Critical-window mapping — Determine whether sodium butyrate feeding restricted to defined developmental windows (embryonic 0–24 h, larval L1–L3, 0–24 h APF, 24–48 h APF, or adult day 1–5) reduces variance in adult locomotor handedness (|LI|) in isogenic w1118 flies, identifying the window of maximum effect.

Aim 2: Epigenetic profiling — Characterize the temporal dynamics and inter-individual variance of H3K9ac at central complex developmental gene loci (rx, ey, toy) across the larval-to-pupal transition (0, 12, 24 h APF) using CUT&RUN in staged w1118 pupae, and test whether sodium butyrate treatment during the critical window identified in Aim 1 reduces this epigenetic variance.

Aim 3: Neuronal causal validation — Test whether pupal-restricted (0–24 h APF), central-complex-specific (R9D11-GAL4 with GAL80ts) knockdown of Hdac3 recapitulates the reduction in adult locomotor handedness variance seen with systemic pharmacological HDAC inhibition, establishing cell-autonomous epigenetic stochasticity in central complex neurons as a causal source of behavioral individuality.

identified_gaps: No supplied paper directly tests whether glial manipulation (for example astrocyte- or ensheathing-glia-specific knockdown of Nkt) alters mushroom body-dependent long-term memory; Nkt work [1] measured sleep, so whether Nkt affects consolidation is unknown. A test would be cell-type-specific Nkt knockdown followed by spaced-training olfactory LTM assays.

It is unclear whether the sleep deficit from Nkt loss in astrocytes versus α'β' neurons is the cause of any consolidation defect. Sleep-restoration or sleep-deprivation experiments combined with glial-specific manipulation could separate sleep effects from memory effects.

Glial APOE4 expression disrupted memory and lipid metabolism [5], but the abstract does not separate glial metabolic support from a signaling role in consolidation, nor map effects to specific mushroom body lobes or memory phases.

Existing mushroom body consolidation studies [2, 4] address neuronal requirements only; no supplied study uses temporally restricted glial manipulation (such as post-training inhibition) to define a glial consolidation window distinct from neuronal support.

No supplied data identify glial-derived molecules or receptors on Kenyon cells or mushroom body output neurons that carry consolidation signals, so the mechanism that would distinguish signaling from metabolic support remains untested.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Proposed: In adult flies at 25°C (permissive 18°C for development), astrocyte-specific, adult-restricted knockdown of Nkt (alrm-GAL4; tub-GAL80ts > UAS-Nkt-RNAi) will reduce 24-h aversive olfactory long-term memory after spaced training by at least 30% in performance index relative to genetic controls (p<0.05, n≥12 performance indices per genotype). Immediate memory, Kenyon cell nuclei counts and shock/odor acuity will change by less than 10%, and the LTM deficit will persist when night sleep is pharmacologically normalized, which would indicate a consolidation role for glia separate from sleep loss and neuronal support.
hypothesis.experimental_approach: Mushroom bodies are required for consolidation of short- and long-term courtship memory [10624959], so aversive olfactory spaced-training LTM at 24 h will be the primary readout. Nkt will be knocked down with TARGET (tub-GAL80ts) control, shifting to 29°C for 3 days before training in adult flies only, using astrocyte (alrm-GAL4), ensheathing glia and pan-glia (repo-GAL4) drivers, with α'β' neuron knockdown as a neuronal comparison. Controls are GAL4/+, UAS-RNAi/+, a non-targeting RNAi, and a second independent Nkt RNAi or mutant to guard against off-target effects. Specificity tests include immediate memory, shock and odor acuity, Kenyon cell nuclei counts, mushroom body lobe morphology, and Nile red or BODIPY lipid staining to assess metabolic support. hypothesis.expected_outcomes: Proposed predictions: astrocyte-specific adult Nkt knockdown lowers 24-h spaced-training LTM performance index by ≥30% versus all controls (one-way ANOVA with Tukey post hoc, α=0.05), with unchanged immediate memory, sensory acuity, Kenyon cell count and lobe morphology (<10% difference). Night sleep is expected to be reduced, but pharmacological sleep normalization will not restore LTM beyond 50% of the control-to-knockdown gap if the glial role is separable from sleep. If LTM is restored by sleep normalization, the null alternative (the glial effect is mediated by sleep) is supported. Post-training astrocyte silencing is predicted to reduce LTM by ≥25% when applied 0–6 h after training but not when applied 12–18 h after training, which would define a temporal consolidation window. Lipid staining should not differ by >15% between knockdown and control, arguing against a primarily metabolic cause.
hypothesis.novelty_claim: Nkt is required in astrocytes and in mushroom body α'β' neurons for night sleep [31353186], but no supplied paper tests whether glial manipulation alters mushroom body-dependent long-term memory. Glial APOE4 expression impaired memory and altered lipid metabolism [38537387], but the supplied abstract does not separate metabolic support from signaling. Existing mushroom body consolidation studies [10624959, 24183945] address neuronal requirements only, and none uses temporally restricted glial manipulation to define a glial consolidation window distinct from neuronal support.
hypothesis.feasibility_notes: Estimated 12-15 months: 3 months for stock acquisition, verification of RNAi knockdown efficiency (qPCR, antibody if available) and crossing; 5 months for LTM and sleep behavior; 3 months for histology and lipid staining; 2-4 months for the sleep-rescue and post-training silencing experiments. Pitfalls: the Nkt RNAi lines and drivers require verification, and RNAi knockdown kinetics are slow, so the post-training window depends on shi-ts silencing, which may have non-specific effects on glial physiology and temperature-dependent memory effects. Sleep deprivation or drug treatment may itself affect memory, so sham and drug-only controls are required. Spaced-training LTM has high variance, so adequate sample size and blinded scoring are essential. A negative result would not exclude other glial molecules (the supplied literature does not identify the receptors on Kenyon cells or output neurons).
specific_aims: Aim 1: Glial Nkt requirement for LTM — test whether adult-restricted astrocyte, ensheathing-glia, pan-glia or α'β' neuron Nkt knockdown reduces 24-h spaced-training olfactory memory, with immediate memory and sensory acuity as specificity controls.
Aim 2: Separating sleep from consolidation — measure night sleep in each knockdown genotype and test whether post-training sleep normalization or sleep deprivation alters the LTM deficit.

Aim 3: Signaling versus metabolic support and timing — assess Kenyon cell number, lobe morphology and lipid staining, and use post-training thermogenetic astrocyte silencing to define a temporal consolidation window.

literature.summary: The provided literature establishes that the Drosophila mushroom body is a dedicated site for memory consolidation rather than initial learning [2], and that astrocytes contribute non-redundantly to the sleep-dependent consolidation process via the secreted Ig-domain protein NKT, which is required in both MB α'β' neurons and glia [1]. Beyond this direct consolidation-linked glial role, glial-specific metabolic dysfunction—illustrated by APOE4-driven lipid dysregulation and mitochondrial imbalance causing Kenyon cell loss and memory impairment [5]—and oxidative stress-mediated deterioration of MB synaptic architecture [4] reveal that glia influence memory consolidation through metabolic and structural maintenance functions that go beyond passive neuronal support, though the precise molecular mechanisms coupling glial activity to consolidation-specific synaptic plasticity in the MB remain unresolved.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Astrocyte-specific knockdown of Nkt in MB-associated glia (using alrm-GAL4 or repo-GAL4 restricted to the mushroom body neuropil) will impair 24-hour long-term memory consolidation scores by ≥30% relative to controls in the olfactory aversive conditioning paradigm in 3–5-day-old mated female w1118 flies at 25°C, without reducing immediate recall (3-min post-training performance index), demonstrating a consolidation-specific glial role that is separable from general neuronal support functions. Furthermore, simultaneous glial-specific knockdown of cat and sod1 in the same MB-associated glia will compound this deficit (≥45% LTM reduction) only when combined with Nkt knockdown but not alone at early adult timepoints, indicating that NKT-mediated glial signaling and oxidative stress management are partially independent consolidation-relevant pathways converging at MB-associated astrocytes.
hypothesis.experimental_approach: We will use the GAL4/UAS binary system to achieve tissue-restricted knockdown of candidate genes in MB-associated glia. The primary driver will be alrm-GAL4 (astrocyte-specific) crossed to UAS-Nkt-RNAi lines to knock down Nkt selectively in astrocytes; repo-GAL4 (pan-glial) will serve as a broader glial control driver. To isolate MB-associated glial effects from systemic glial effects, we will employ the intersectional Split-GAL4 or GAL80 suppression strategy using 201Y-GAL80 or MB247-GAL80 to confine or exclude MB neuronal expression, ensuring driver activity is enriched at the MB neuropil-associated glia. Memory consolidation will be assessed using the Pavlovian olfactory aversive conditioning assay (electric shock + odor pairing): performance indexes will be measured at 3 min (immediate recall/short-term memory, STM), 1 hr (middle-term memory, MTM), and 24 hr after a single training session or spaced training (long-term memory, LTM). Controls will include: (1) driver-only (alrm-GAL4/+), (2) UAS-RNAi-only (+/UAS-Nkt-RNAi), (3) UAS-mCD8::GFP to confirm driver expression pattern in MB-associated glia by confocal microscopy with nc82 (Bruchpilot) counterstain, and (4) UAS-Dicer2 co-expression to enhance RNAi efficiency. Neuronal support integrity will be assessed by confocal imaging of Kenyon cell morphology (anti-Fasciclin II, anti-Dachshund), synapse density (nc82), and glial coverage (anti-Repo, anti-Alrm) in experimental versus control animals aged 3–5 days (before overt neurodegeneration). A secondary aim will co-express UAS-cat-RNAi and UAS-sod1-RNAi with UAS-Nkt-RNAi under alrm-GAL4 to test for additive or epistatic effects on LTM, with oxidative stress levels quantified by DHE (dihydroethidium) staining and protein carbonylation assays in dissected brains. All experiments will use n ≥ 20 flies per group per trial with ≥5 independent biological replicates; statistical analysis will use one-way ANOVA with Tukey post-hoc correction, significance threshold p < 0.05.

hypothesis.expected_outcomes: Aim 1: alrm-GAL4>UAS-Nkt-RNAi flies will show ≥30% reduction in 24-hr LTM performance index compared to both parental controls (p < 0.05, ANOVA + Tukey), with no significant difference in 3-min STM performance index (p > 0.05), demonstrating consolidation specificity. MB morphology (Fasciclin II staining, Kenyon cell number by anti-Dachshund) and glial coverage will be indistinguishable from controls at 3–5 days of age (p > 0.05), ruling out structural neuronal support failure as the explanation. Aim 2: repo-GAL4>UAS-Nkt-RNAi will show a ≥40% LTM reduction (expected to be larger than astrocyte-specific knockdown due to broader glial coverage), providing a dose-response reference. Aim 3: alrm-GAL4>UAS-cat-RNAi and alrm-GAL4>UAS-sod1-RNAi alone will not significantly impair LTM in 3–5-day-old flies (p > 0.05 vs. controls), but triple knockdown (Nkt-RNAi + cat-RNAi + sod1-RNAi in alrm-GAL4) will produce ≥45% LTM reduction, and DHE staining will show ≥1.5-fold increase in ROS signal in MB neuropil-associated glia (p < 0.05), indicating that oxidative homeostasis and NKT signaling are partially additive consolidation-relevant glial functions. All negative results (STM intact, morphology intact) must reach p > 0.1 in equivalence testing to be interpreted as true null.
hypothesis.novelty_claim: This experiment directly addresses three gaps identified in the literature synthesis: (1) No prior study has manipulated glia specifically within the MB-associated neuropil while leaving neuronal support intact to isolate a purely consolidation-specific glial contribution — our astrocyte-restricted, early-timepoint design fills this gap. (2) The downstream signaling role of secreted NKT from astrocytes in gating MB α'β' neuron-dependent consolidation is unresolved; this experiment isolates the astrocyte arm of NKT requirement from its neuronal arm for the first time. (3) Whether glial metabolic functions (oxidative stress management via cat/sod1) and glial signaling functions (NKT secretion) act as independent or convergent consolidation-relevant pathways at MB-associated glia has not been tested — the triple-knockdown combinatorial aim directly addresses this distinction, moving beyond the whole-CNS APOE4 model that cannot isolate MB-circuit-level effects.
hypothesis.feasibility_notes: The Pavlovian olfactory aversive conditioning assay is well-established in Drosophila and can be performed with standard equipment in most fly neuroscience labs. alrm-GAL4 and repo-GAL4 are widely used and available; however, the extent of MB neuropil astrocyte coverage by alrm-GAL4 must be confirmed empirically by GFP reporter staining before committing to this driver — if coverage is insufficient, substitute with NP3233-GAL4 (reported to label MB-associated cortex glia) or a tethered GAL4 approach. A key pitfall is that pan-glial repo-GAL4 drives expression in neurons under some conditions and may produce off-target effects; this must be monitored by immunostaining. RNAi efficiency for Nkt knockdown must be validated by RT-qPCR on sorted glial cells or by in situ hybridization, as Nkt is expressed at potentially low levels. The triple-knockdown experiment risks developmental lethality or non-specific effects; a conditional temporal control using tub-GAL80ts (shift to 29°C at eclosion) is recommended to restrict knockdown to adult stages. Estimated timeline: 3 months for line establishment and driver characterization, 4 months for behavioral experiments (n ≥ 20 per group × 5 replicates × 6 genotypes × 3 memory timepoints), 2 months for imaging and biochemical assays, 3 months for analysis and replication — total approximately 12 months. Potential pitfall: if alrm-GAL4 expression is too sparse at the MB neuropil, the consolidation phenotype may be below detection threshold; power analysis based on a 30% effect size and σ = 10 PI units indicates n = 22 per group at 80% power (α = 0.05).
specific_aims: Aim 1: Consolidation-specific glial Nkt requirement — Determine whether astrocyte-specific knockdown of Nkt using alrm-GAL4 impairs 24-hr LTM but not 3-min STM in the olfactory aversive conditioning paradigm, without causing detectable Kenyon cell loss or synaptic structural defects at 3–5 days of age

Aim 2: Spatial restriction of glial Nkt requirement to MB-associated astrocytes — Compare LTM deficits produced by alrm-GAL4 (astrocyte-specific), repo-GAL4 (pan-glial), and a GAL80-suppressed intersectional strategy confining expression to MB neuropil-adjacent glia, to determine whether the consolidation-relevant glial Nkt requirement is specifically localized to MB-associated astrocytes rather than distributed across all CNS glia

Aim 3: Epistatic relationship between glial NKT signaling and oxidative stress management in LTM — Test whether combinatorial knockdown of Nkt with cat and sod1 in alrm-GAL4-expressing astrocytes produces additive or synergistic LTM impairment relative to single knockdowns, and quantify ROS levels in MB neuropil glia by DHE staining to determine whether oxidative stress is a convergent downstream effector of NKT pathway disruption

literature.summary: The supplied evidence for a non-supportive glial role in MB memory consolidation is indirect. Nkt is required in both astrocytes and MB α'β' neurons for normal night sleep in adults [1], and MBs are required for consolidation of courtship memory [2], while glial-specific APOE4 expression most strongly elevates CNS lipids alongside memory deficits [5]. As an inference, glia may influence consolidation via sleep regulation or lipid homeostasis, but a direct, sleep-independent role for glia in MB memory consolidation is not demonstrated in these papers and remains an open question.

hypothesis.hypothesis: PROPOSED HYPOTHESIS: Adult-restricted RNAi knockdown of Nkt (CG14141) in astrocytes (alrm-GAL4; tub-GAL80ts, induced at 30°C for 3–5 days post-eclosion) will reduce 24-h courtship-conditioning long-term memory (LTM) in w1118-background males by ≥50% relative to both parental controls, while leaving 1-h short-term memory within 20% of controls. The LTM deficit will persist at ≥50% even when night sleep is pharmacologically restored to within 10% of control levels. Such persistence would indicate that the astrocytic Nkt contribution to mushroom body (MB)-dependent consolidation is separable from its known role in night sleep regulation.
hypothesis.experimental_approach: We propose using the TARGET system (tub-GAL80ts) with the astrocyte driver alrm-GAL4 and, as a comparison, the pan-glial driver repo-GAL4 to knock down Nkt only in adult glia. Adult restriction avoids developmental confounds. Nkt was previously shown to be required in astrocytes and MB α'β' neurons for night sleep [1], and MBs are required for consolidation but not acquisition of courtship memory [2]. Males will receive spaced courtship conditioning with mated females (proposed: 7-h exposure for LTM, 1-h exposure for STM) and will be tested against fresh mated females at 1 h and 24 h. Sleep will be recorded in the same cohorts with DAM monitors for 3 days before training and during the 24-h consolidation window. For Aim 2, a sleep-rescue arm will feed flies the GABA-A agonist gaboxadol (THIP) during the consolidation night, titrated so that knockdown flies match control night sleep. A complementary arm will match sleep loss: control flies will be mechanically deprived to the same amount of sleep loss as knockdown flies. Controls will include GAL4/+ and UAS-RNAi/+ heterozygotes, uninduced 18°C siblings, a second non-overlapping Nkt RNAi line, and qPCR validation of Nkt knockdown in heads. For Aim 3, we will compare knockdown in astrocytes with knockdown in MB α'β' neurons using an α'β'-specific GAL4 to be verified. We will also assess MB integrity by anti-FasII staining, to rule out a degenerative or 'support' explanation.

hypothesis.expected_outcomes:
Predicted results (proposed, not established):
(1) Control genotypes (GAL4/+ and UAS/+, induced) will show significant 24-h LTM, with a learning index (LI) significantly >0 (randomization test, p<0.05; n≥40 males per group). Induced alrm>Nkt-RNAi males will show ≥50% lower LI than both controls (p<0.05 after Bonferroni correction). Uninduced siblings will not differ from controls.
(2) Naive courtship index and 1-h STM in knockdown males will be within 20% of controls. Such a dissociation would be consistent with a consolidation-specific deficit, matching the MB requirement for consolidation but not acquisition [2].
(3) Night sleep in knockdown flies is expected to be reduced, consistent with [1]. THIP will restore night sleep to within 10% of controls (Kruskal-Wallis, Dunn's post hoc), yet LTM will remain ≥50% reduced. Sleep-matched controls under mechanical deprivation will retain ≥70% of normal LTM.
(4) MB lobe morphology and α'β' lobe volume (FasII) will not differ by >10% from controls, arguing against a degenerative or support mechanism.
(5) α'β' neuron knockdown is predicted to produce an LTM deficit of comparable magnitude.
Falsification criteria: The hypothesis is falsified if astrocytic knockdown reduces LTM by <50%. It is also falsified if THIP-mediated sleep restoration rescues LTM to within 20% of controls, which would indicate a sleep-dependent mechanism.
Sample size: Each experiment will be replicated across ≥3 independent cohorts.
hypothesis.novelty_claim: The synthesis notes that no supplied paper directly manipulates glia and measures MB-dependent memory consolidation. It also notes that none addresses whether glial roles in consolidation are separable from the sleep-memory link. This proposal targets both gaps directly. First, it tests astrocytic Nkt [1] in courtship-conditioning LTM [2], as the synthesis recommends. Second, it uncouples glial manipulation from sleep loss through bidirectional sleep controls: pharmacological sleep restoration and matched mechanical deprivation. Third, it addresses the open question of whether astrocytic and α'β' neuronal Nkt contribute to the same consolidation process. It does so by comparing site-specific knockdowns and including MB structural measures, which separate a signaling role from general neuronal support.
hypothesis.feasibility_notes:
Estimated timeline is 18–24 months:
- Months 1–4: Acquire and verify lines, outcross into w1118, and confirm drivers with GFP. Validate knockdown by head qPCR, accepting that glial-restricted knockdown may give modest whole-head reductions.
- Months 4–10: Aim 1 behavior and sleep.
- Months 10–16: Aim 2 sleep-rescue and deprivation arms.
- Months 14–22: Aim 3 site comparison and histology.

Pitfalls:
- Temperature shifts (30°C) alter sleep and courtship. Induced and uninduced controls of every genotype are therefore essential.
- THIP may itself affect memory. A THIP-fed control group is included, and dose titration is needed.
- alrm-GAL4 specificity and the availability of effective Nkt RNAi lines are unverified in the supplied literature and must be confirmed.
- Courtship LTM assays have high variance, so large n (≥40 per group) and blinded scoring are required.
- If Nkt knockdown does not reduce sleep under our conditions, the sleep-rescue arm becomes unnecessary, but the core LTM test remains informative.
specific_aims: Aim 1: Astrocytic Nkt and consolidation — Determine whether adult-restricted astrocytic (alrm) and pan-glial (repo) Nkt knockdown reduces 24-h courtship LTM by ≥50% while sparing 1-h STM and naive courtship.

Aim 2: Dissociating sleep from consolidation — Test whether THIP-mediated restoration of night sleep rescues the LTM deficit in astrocytic Nkt knockdown flies, and whether matched mechanical sleep loss in controls reproduces it.

Aim 3: Glial versus MB neuronal site of action — Compare LTM and MB structure (FasII lobe volume) after adult Nkt knockdown in astrocytes versus α'β' Kenyon cells to distinguish glia-to-MB signaling from structural support.

However, none of the provided papers directly addresses how clock neurons resolve conflicting light and temperature cues, so the central question remains open and the proposed mechanisms are inferential.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Proposed: When a 12h:12h light-dark cycle (LD; 300 lux) is placed in conflict with a 12h:12h 25°C:16°C temperature cycle (TC) that is phase-delayed by 6 h or 12 h, PDF-expressing ventral lateral neurons (LNv) will set the behavioral phase through PDF signaling. In control flies, evening activity peak phase on the first 5 days of free-run (DD, constant 25°C) will lie within ±1.5 h of the light-cycle-predicted phase in ≥70% of individuals, and will otherwise follow the temperature cycle. Proposed prediction: Pdf-GAL4-driven RNAi knockdown of Pdf, or Pdf-GAL4-driven ablation/silencing of PDF neurons, will shift the free-running evening phase by ≥3 h toward the temperature cycle and reduce the proportion of light-aligned flies to ≤35% (Fisher's exact test, p<0.01, n≥48 per genotype). Proposed: this light dominance will be accompanied by a ≥3 h divergence in PER oscillation peak phase between LNv/LNd (light-aligned in controls) and DN1p neurons (temperature-aligned in controls), measured by immunostaining at 4-h intervals on day 3 of DD; PDF loss will collapse this divergence to <1.5 h, with all clusters following temperature.
hypothesis.experimental_approach: Proposed: Use a conflicting-cue entrainment protocol in which flies are entrained for 6 days to LD with a TC offset by 0 h (aligned), 6 h, or 12 h, then released into DD at constant 25°C. Locomotor rhythms are recorded in DAM monitors to quantify evening-peak phase, period, and rhythm strength (FFT/chi-square). Cell-type-specific manipulations use GAL4/UAS and Gal80ts: Pdf-GAL4 for PDF neurons, plus a DN1p-specific driver and a CRY-expressing neuron driver to be verified, driving UAS-Pdf-RNAi, UAS-Kir2.1 (silencing), and UAS-cry-RNAi. Cluster-specific clock phase is read out by anti-PER/anti-PDF immunostaining at ZT/CT 0, 4, 8, 12, 16, 20 in whole-mount brains, with blinded confocal quantification. Controls include GAL4/+ and UAS/+ parents, aligned-cue conditions, LD-only and TC-only entrainments, and temperature-shift controls (Gal80ts permissive vs. restrictive) to avoid confounding developmental effects. Because Gal80ts-based induction itself uses temperature, TARGET experiments will be paired with constitutive-driver experiments as a cross-check.

identified_gaps: None of the provided papers directly address the competition or hierarchy between light and temperature as entraining cues — the specific circuit-level or molecular mechanisms by which clock neurons resolve light-temperature conflicts remain entirely uncharacterized in this literature.

Although the FlyWire connectome identifies novel indirect light input pathways to clock neurons [1], the corresponding temperature input pathways and their synaptic overlap or segregation from light pathways are not described, making it impossible to infer where cue integration occurs anatomically.

The cell-type-specific light-responsive transcripts identified in [2] (analogous to mammalian immediate-early genes) are not linked to temperature-responsive gene expression in the same neuron subtypes, so whether the same or different molecular programs mediate the two entrainment modalities is unknown.

The time-of-day plasticity in E-to-M cell synaptic connectivity shown in [5] is demonstrated only under light-dark conditions; whether this structural remodeling differs under temperature cycles or under conflicting light-temperature schedules has not been tested.

The role of peptidergic signaling — newly implicated in enriching clock network interconnectivity [1] — in weighting competing sensory cues has not been examined; it is unknown whether specific neuropeptides bias the network toward light or temperature entrainment.

literature.summary: The provided literature does not directly address how Drosophila clock neurons arbitrate between conflicting light and temperature zeitgebers. What the literature does establish is that the circadian network comprises ~240 anatomically and transcriptomically distinct neuron subtypes [1][2], that different neuron clusters (sLNvs, LNds, DN1ps) serve distinct entrainment and output roles [3][5], and that synaptic connectivity between these clusters is dynamically remodeled across the day through acetylcholine and glutamate signaling [5]. Light input reaches the clock via both direct (cryptochrome-mediated) and novel indirect synaptic routes [1], and a small set of light-responsive immediate-early-like transcripts are expressed in specific neuron subtypes [2], but temperature input pathways, their anatomical relationship to light pathways, and the mechanisms that weight one cue over the other under conflict conditions are entirely absent from this set of papers.

hypothesis.hypothesis: DN1p clock neurons act as the primary integration site for conflicting light and temperature entrainment cues, and when a 6-hour phase-advanced temperature cycle (20°C:29°C, TC) conflicts with a fixed light-dark cycle (LD 12:12, 25°C mean), silencing DN1p output (via UAS-Kir2.1 driven by Clk856-GAL4) will shift the phase of evening locomotor activity by ≥2 hours toward the LD phase (compared to ≤0.5 hours shift in controls), demonstrating that intact DN1p signaling is required for temperature entrainment to override light entrainment under conflict conditions in mated female w1118-background flies maintained at 25°C.
hypothesis.experimental_approach: Flies will be entrained for 5 days under standard LD 12:12 at 25°C, then transferred to a conflict protocol in which the LD cycle is held fixed while a TC (20°C:29°C, 12:12, warm phase advanced 6 h relative to lights-off) is applied for 7 days; locomotor activity will be recorded continuously by DAM system. Four genotypes will be compared: (1) Clk856-GAL4/UAS-Kir2.1 (DN1p-silenced), (2) Clk856-GAL4/+ (GAL4 control), (3) +/UAS-Kir2.1 (UAS control), and (4) w1118 wild-type. Evening activity peak phase (ZT referenced to LD lights-off) will be extracted for each fly; population-level phase distributions will be compared by Watson-Williams circular statistics (α=0.05). To confirm that DN1ps receive temperature input, we will perform anti-TIM immunostaining of DN1p neurons in LD-only, TC-only, and conflict conditions (n≥10 brains/condition) and quantify TIM cycling phase as a molecular phase readout. As a complementary circuit dissection, we will use CaLexA-based calcium reporter imaging in DN1ps during the first 24 h of conflict exposure to ask whether DN1p activity correlates with temperature or light phase.

DN1p-silenced flies (Clk856-GAL4/UAS-Kir2.1) are predicted to show evening peak phase locked to ZT12 (LD lights-off ± 0.5 h), indicating failure of TC-driven phase advance (mean phase shift ≤0.5 h vs. ≥2 h in controls; Watson-Williams test p<0.05, n≥32 flies/genotype). TIM immunostaining in DN1p neurons is expected to show a phase-advanced TIM peak (~3 h earlier) in TC and conflict conditions compared to LD-only, confirming that DN1ps molecularly track temperature even under conflict. CaLexA signal in DN1ps should be elevated during the warm phase of TC regardless of LD phase, supporting temperature-dominant input to DN1ps. sLNv-silenced flies (pdf-GAL4/UAS-Kir2.1) are predicted to show enhanced phase advance toward TC (evening peak ~ZT9 ± 1 h), suggesting that sLNv PDF signaling normally restrains temperature-driven phase shifts.
hypothesis.novelty_claim: The literature synthesis explicitly identifies that 'the specific circuit-level or molecular mechanisms by which clock neurons resolve light-temperature conflicts remain entirely uncharacterized' and that 'temperature input pathways, their anatomical relationship to light pathways, and the mechanisms that weight one cue over the other under conflict conditions are entirely absent' from available studies. Although [39638801] reveals novel indirect light input pathways and extensive peptidergic connectivity, no study maps corresponding temperature inputs or their overlap with light pathways. Although [28360128] establishes that different clock neuron clusters serve distinct entrainment roles, no study has used targeted silencing to dissect which cluster is causally required for light vs. temperature dominance under explicit conflict. This design directly tests causal circuit hierarchy — not merely correlation — between DN1p activity and cue-conflict resolution, filling a gap unaddressed by any paper in the synthesis.
hypothesis.feasibility_notes: All core transgenic tools (GAL4/UAS, Kir2.1, CaLexA) are established and widely used in circadian biology. The TC conflict paradigm is technically straightforward using Peltier-equipped incubators with programmable ramps; 0.5°C/min ramp rates are standard. The main pitfall is that Clk856-GAL4 drives expression in DN1ps plus a subset of LNds, so observed effects cannot be attributed to DN1ps alone without additional intersectional controls (e.g., split-GAL4 lines specific to DN1ps — these would need to be obtained or generated, adding ~4 months if not available). A second pitfall is lethality or developmental defects with chronic Kir2.1 expression; if observed, temporal control using TARGET (tub-GAL80ts) should be implemented to restrict silencing to adulthood. CaLexA imaging requires ex vivo brain prep and confocal access — standard in most Drosophila neuroscience labs. Estimated timeline: Aim 1 (locomotor behavior) 6 months; Aim 2 (TIM immunostaining + CaLexA) 5 months; Aim 3 (dTRPA1 thermogenetic activation + sLNv controls) 5 months; total ~14–16 months with overlap.
specific_aims: Aim 1: DN1p silencing under conflict — Test whether chronic silencing of DN1p neurons via Clk856-GAL4/UAS-Kir2.1 eliminates temperature-driven phase advance of evening locomotor activity under a 6-h phase-advanced TC conflicting with fixed LD 12:12, quantified as mean evening peak phase shift ≥2 h in controls vs. ≤0.5 h in silenced flies

Aim 2: Molecular phase tracking in DN1ps — Determine whether DN1p neurons molecularly track the TC phase (TIM immunostaining peak advanced ≥2 h in TC and conflict conditions vs. LD-only) and whether DN1p calcium activity (CaLexA) correlates with warm-phase timing rather than lights-off timing under conflict

Aim 3: sLNv vs. DN1p circuit hierarchy — Test whether silencing sLNv PDF neurons (pdf-GAL4/UAS-Kir2.1) produces the opposite behavioral outcome (enhanced TC-driven phase advance, evening peak at ZT9 ± 1 h) compared to DN1p silencing, and whether acute thermogenetic activation of DN1ps (UAS-dTRPA1) during the LD-predicted rest phase is sufficient to phase-advance evening activity by ≥1.5 h

The light-dependent immediate-early-like transcripts [2] were profiled under LD vs DD only. Profiling them under temperature cycles, and under light/temperature cycles set out of phase, would reveal whether temperature suppresses or competes with light-driven gene expression in specific subtypes.

literature.summary: The supplied literature does not directly address how clock neurons resolve conflicting light and temperature cues; it contains no temperature-entrainment data. It does describe candidate integration machinery. The network has ~240 neurons with indirect light inputs and dense contralateral and peptidergic connectivity [1]. M cells set the phase of about half the network via PDF and receive time-of-day-dependent cholinergic feedback from E cells [5]. Within this network, most time-of-day gene regulation in clock neurons is transcriptional and circadian, with only a small number of light-dependent transcripts [2]. Post-transcriptional regulation also contributes: miR-375 acting in l-LNv neurons modulates rhythm and sleep by targeting timeless [6]. By inference only, cue arbitration may depend on which subtypes receive each cue and on the PDF-based hierarchy, but this remains untested here.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Proposed: In male w1118 flies entrained for 6 days to a 12:12 h light-dark (LD) cycle combined with a 12:12 h 25°C:18°C temperature cycle (TC) advanced by 6 h relative to LD, the evening activity peak during the first 2 days of constant darkness at 25°C will lie within 2 h of the light-predicted phase. In flies lacking PDF signaling (Pdf null mutant, or Pdfr RNAi in clock neurons), the evening peak will shift by at least 4 h toward the temperature-predicted phase. The test is a genotype × entrainment-condition interaction in a two-way ANOVA (p<0.05, n≥32 flies per genotype per condition). This outcome would indicate a PDF-dependent hierarchy in which M-cell phase dominates network phase under light/temperature conflict.
hypothesis.experimental_approach: We propose a cue-conflict paradigm using incubators that independently control light and temperature. Four conditions will be compared: LD+TC in phase, LD+TC with TC advanced by 6 h (conflict), LD only at constant 25°C, and TC only in constant darkness. Each condition will be followed by at least 5 days of DD at 25°C. PDF signaling will be removed genetically with a Pdf null allele and by GAL4/UAS-driven Pdfr RNAi in clock neurons. E-cell cholinergic output to M cells will be reduced with UAS-ChAT RNAi under an E-cell-restricted driver. Adult-restricted manipulations will use tub-GAL80ts so that developmental effects are excluded. Behavioral phase will be measured by Drosophila Activity Monitor (DAM) recordings. Molecular phase will be measured by PER and TIM immunostaining at 6 time points in s-LNv, l-LNv, LNd and DN1–3 groups. Light-responsive immediate-early-like transcripts will be profiled in sorted clock-neuron subtypes. Controls are GAL4/+ and UAS/+ heterozygotes in the matched background, plus the in-phase and single-cue conditions.

hypothesis.expected_outcomes: Predicted (not established) outcomes: (1) In w1118 and GAL4/+ and UAS/+ controls under the 6 h conflict, the evening-peak phase in DD days 1–2 will lie within 2 h of the LD-only phase. (2) In Pdf null and Clk856>Pdfr-RNAi flies, the evening peak will shift by at least 4 h toward the TC-only phase. The supporting statistic is a significant genotype × condition interaction (two-way ANOVA p<0.05, Tukey post hoc), and circular statistics (Rayleigh test) will confirm phase clustering. (3) PER nuclear-accumulation peaks in M cells will follow light in all genotypes (within 2 h of the LD-only phase). In PDF-deficient flies, PER peaks in LNd and DN groups will instead decouple from M cells by at least 3 h and move toward the TC phase. (4) E-cell ChAT knockdown will produce an intermediate phase, shifted 1–3 h toward temperature, if E-to-M feedback contributes to arbitration. (5) Light-responsive immediate-early-like transcripts in the responsive subtypes will show at least 30% reduced induction amplitude under conflict compared with in-phase cycles (FDR<0.05) if temperature competes with light-driven gene expression. Null results will also be informative. Equal phases across genotypes would falsify the PDF-hierarchy hypothesis. Wild-type phase following temperature would falsify light dominance under these conditions.
hypothesis.novelty_claim: The literature synthesis states that no supplied paper directly tests light and temperature cues presented in conflict. It also notes as unknown whether the PDF-dependent hierarchy, in which M cells set the phase of about half the network, is maintained when temperature opposes light. This plan addresses that gap directly by combining Pdf/Pdfr manipulation with a cue-conflict paradigm. It further addresses two other identified gaps. First, it asks whether E-to-M cholinergic plasticity shifts the balance of phase control under conflicting cues. Second, it extends immediate-early-like transcript profiling, previously done under LD vs DD only, to temperature and conflict conditions.
hypothesis.feasibility_notes: Estimated timeline is 14–18 months. Stock acquisition, backcrossing and validation will take 3–4 months. Behavioral conflict assays will take 4–5 months. Immunostaining time courses will take 4 months. Transcript profiling will take 4–5 months, overlapping with the immunostaining. Programmable incubators with independent light and temperature control are required. Potential pitfalls: (a) temperature cycles may mask activity directly rather than entrain it, so phase must be read out in DD at constant temperature. (b) Pdf null flies show weakened DD rhythms, so evening-peak phase may be hard to score; anticipatory activity under the cycles and molecular phase will serve as complementary readouts. (c) RNAi efficacy must be verified by immunostaining or qPCR. (d) The thermosensory input routes to clock neurons are not described in the supplied literature, which limits mechanistic interpretation. (e) Genetic background effects will be controlled by backcrossing and matched heterozygote controls. (f) The 6 h offset may be modified (e.g., to 12 h) after pilot experiments.
specific_aims: Aim 1: Behavioral arbitration — Determine whether loss of PDF signaling (Pdf null; Clk856>Pdfr-RNAi) shifts behavioral phase toward the temperature cycle under 6 h light/temperature conflict.

Aim 2: Network molecular phase — Map PER/TIM phase in s-LNv, l-LNv, LNd and DN1–3 under conflict in control, PDF-deficient and E-cell ChAT-knockdown flies to identify which subgroups follow light vs temperature.

Aim 3: Subtype transcriptional competition — Profile light-responsive immediate-early-like transcripts in sorted clock-neuron subtypes under in-phase, conflicting and single-cue cycles to test whether temperature suppresses light-driven induction.

identified_gaps: Shut-off mechanism of the Dilp8 'growth not finished' signal is not directly shown in the supplied papers. It is unknown whether the signal ends through reduced dilp8 transcription in the disc, Dilp8 clearance or degradation, or Lgr3 desensitization or its constitutive activity. Time-resolved Dilp8 protein measurements and Lgr3 activity reporters during catch-up growth would test this.

The ecdysone–epidermal dilp8 feedback loop [3] has not been tested as an 'off' switch for the damage- or Gαq-induced Dilp8 signal from the disc [2][7]. Epidermal versus disc dilp8 sources should be separated by tissue-specific manipulation during regeneration or delay.

How the disc senses 'not yet final size' is unresolved. It is unknown whether mechanical feedback [11], Ca2+/Gαq stress signaling [2][7], or apoptosis-linked injury [12] encodes size deficit or only damage, so these inputs should be compared in the same assay.

The Gαq–Dilp8 link is shown by overexpression and rescue with Dilp8 knockdown [2]. It is unclear whether endogenous Gαq/IP3R activity is required for Dilp8 induction in physiological growth perturbations such as local growth retardation.

Circuits downstream of Lgr3 are only partly mapped. Mip descending neurons act downstream of Dilp8–Lgr3 for pupariation behavior [9], but the pathway from Lgr3 neurons to prothoracic ecdysone suppression in the delay response is not defined in the supplied papers.

Dilp8 and Lgr3 also act in adult ovarian–neural communication [1][6], but it is untested whether the larval size-checkpoint and adult follicle-sensing functions share receptor-level shut-off mechanisms.

literature.summary: Dilp8 is the best-supported inter-organ signal reporting tissue growth status, acting through Lgr3-positive neurons to gate developmental progression [9][10]. Gαq–Ca2+ signaling in the wing disc can raise Dilp8 and delay pupariation, while a later ecdysone-triggered epidermal Dilp8 peak at the end of juvenile growth adjusts wing size [2][3][7]. Mechanisms that switch the signal off are not directly demonstrated in the supplied papers (inference: the ecdysone-Dilp8 feedback in [3] may be part of it).

hypothesis.hypothesis: Proposed: After a transient 24 h pulse of Gαq overexpression in the wing pouch (rn-GAL4 with tub-GAL80ts, shifted to 29°C at ~72 h AEL, then returned to 18°C), the Dilp8-dependent pupariation delay ends because disc dilp8 transcription falls, not because Lgr3 signaling desensitizes or Dilp8 protein is slowly cleared. Specifically, within 12 h of the return to 18°C, wing-disc dilp8 mRNA will fall to ≤1.5-fold of GAL80ts-only controls, and the pupariation delay will be ≥50% shorter than with sustained Gαq expression. If dilp8 is forced to stay on in the pouch after the pulse (UAS-dilp8), the delay will persist at ≥24 h versus controls, showing that Lgr3 signaling is not desensitized.
hypothesis.experimental_approach: A temperature-controlled pulse-chase design uses rn-GAL4 with tub-GAL80ts to drive UAS-Gαq in the wing pouch for a defined 24 h window. Sustained expression, pulse-only, and GAL80ts-only controls are compared. Readouts are pupariation timing (hourly scoring of staged cohorts, n≥100 per genotype, log-rank test), wing-disc dilp8 mRNA (RT-qPCR and HCR/in situ at 0, 6, 12, 24 h after the pulse), Dilp8 protein (tagged or antibody-based reporter, to be verified), and adult wing size. Epistasis tests use the Gαq pulse combined with (a) IP3R RNAi in the pouch, (b) pulsed UAS-dilp8 as a clearance control, (c) Lgr3 knockdown in Lgr3-positive neurons, and (d) epidermal dilp8 knockdown with an epidermal driver, to separate disc and epidermal Dilp8 sources. A separate physiological perturbation, local growth retardation in the pouch, tests whether endogenous Gαq/IP3R is needed for dilp8 induction. Statistical thresholds: Mann-Whitney or log-rank tests with Bonferroni correction, α=0.05.

hypothesis.expected_outcomes: Proposed predictions, not established results. (1) The Gαq pulse induces dilp8 mRNA ≥3-fold and a pupariation delay of ≥12 h. After the pulse ends, dilp8 mRNA returns to ≤1.5-fold of controls within 12 h and the delay is ≥50% shorter than with sustained expression (p<0.01). (2) UAS-dilp8 after the pulse maintains a delay ≥24 h, indicating intact Lgr3 responsiveness and arguing against desensitization. (3) IP3R knockdown reduces pulse-induced dilp8 mRNA by ≥50%. (4) If epidermal dilp8 knockdown prolongs the delay by ≥6 h, this would support a role for the ecdysone-linked epidermal peak in terminating the signal. (5) Lgr3 knockdown abolishes the delay. If dilp8 mRNA remains high while the delay ends, transcriptional shut-off is falsified and receptor desensitization or Dilp8 clearance must be favored.
hypothesis.novelty_claim: The shut-off mechanism of the Dilp8 signal is not directly shown in the supplied literature, and the literature synthesis lists as open whether it ends through reduced disc dilp8 transcription, Dilp8 clearance, or Lgr3 desensitization. Gαq overexpression in wing discs triggers Dilp8 secretion and an IP3R-dependent delay [41131630], but that work used sustained overexpression and did not test reversibility. The ecdysone-triggered epidermal dilp8 peak at the end of juvenile growth [36163439] has not been tested as an off switch for the disc-derived signal. This design adds a reversible pulse, separates disc from epidermal dilp8 sources, and tests the receptor side in one assay.
hypothesis.feasibility_notes: Estimated 12-15 months: 3 months for stock acquisition, verification and recombination; 4 months for Aim 1 kinetics; 3 months for Aim 2; 3 months for Aim 3 and analysis. Pitfalls: GAL80ts leakiness at 18°C could cause background delay, so controls and shift-timing calibration are needed. Temperature shifts themselves alter developmental timing, so all genotypes must be shifted in parallel. Dilp8 protein detection may be limited by the absence of validated reagents. Gαq overexpression may cause apoptosis or tissue damage, so cell death markers should be checked to avoid conflating Gαq signaling with injury. An epidermal driver specific enough to avoid disc expression needs validation. Line identities and availability are unconfirmed.
specific_aims: Aim 1: Kinetics of signal termination — measure dilp8 mRNA, Dilp8 protein and pupariation delay after a 24 h pouch Gαq pulse versus sustained expression to distinguish transcriptional shut-off from clearance

Aim 2: Receptor-side test — use post-pulse forced dilp8 expression and Lgr3 manipulation to test whether Lgr3 signaling desensitizes, and test whether endogenous Gαq/IP3R is required for dilp8 induction in a physiological local growth-retardation model
Aim 3: Source separation — use tissue-specific dilp8 knockdown (disc versus epidermis) to test whether the ecdysone-linked epidermal dilp8 peak contributes to terminating the disc-derived delay

literature.disease_context: The Dilp8/Lgr3 signaling axis—whereby a growing or damaged organ secretes a relaxin-like hormone to delay systemic maturation until growth is complete—has direct parallels to human relaxin receptor (RXFP1/2) biology involved in reproduction and tissue remodeling [6][14]. Gαq, whose hyperactivating mutations underlie Sturge-Weber syndrome and uveal melanoma, controls organ size and developmental timing partly by inducing Dilp8 secretion from wing discs, linking GPCR-driven pathology to systemic growth coordination [2]. Understanding how organs signal incomplete growth to the rest of the body may inform therapeutic strategies for developmental disorders and cancers involving dysregulated organ size checkpoints.

identified_gaps: The molecular mechanism by which Lgr3-positive neurons translate Dilp8 binding into inhibition of ecdysone production in the prothoracic gland remains unknown — identifying the downstream neural circuit and neuropeptidergic relay would close a critical mechanistic gap [9][10].

It is unclear what cell-autonomous signal within a growing organ sets the threshold at which dilp8 expression is turned off — specifically, whether organ-intrinsic size sensors (mechanical, morphogen gradient, or metabolic) directly repress dilp8 transcription or whether this is entirely controlled by rising ecdysone levels [3][10].

The Ca2+-independent mechanism by which Gαq controls wing size (as distinct from the IP3R/Ca2+-dependent pupariation delay) has not been identified, leaving an unexplained arm of GPCR-linked size control [7].
The identity of the Lgr3-downstream signaling cascade within neurons that antagonizes oogenesis progression remains undefined — the paper notes this explicitly as an 'undefined mechanism' [6].

It is unknown whether the epidermis-specific dilp8 peak observed during the size-adjustment time window in larval development [3] uses the same or distinct upstream regulators compared to stress- or damage-induced dilp8 expression in imaginal discs, which could reveal whether there are multiple separable inputs to the same signal.

literature.summary: In Drosophila, the insulin-like relaxin hormone Dilp8 (ILP8) is the central signal by which growing or damaged organs communicate incomplete or perturbed growth status to the rest of the body, delaying ecdysone-driven maturation until organ size and bilateral symmetry are achieved [3][10][33023929]. Dilp8 is expressed in imaginal disc cells under stress, damage, or Gαq/Ca2+ dysregulation, and in the epidermis as a sharp peak at the end of juvenile growth triggered by ecdysone itself, creating a reciprocal feedback loop; it is shut off when ecdysone signaling resolves and appropriate size is reached [3][2][7]. The signal is received by Lgr3-positive neurons in the CNS, which gate progression of the pupariation motor program through downstream Mip command neurons, and the same Dilp8-Lgr3 axis is redeployed in adult reproductive physiology to sense mature follicle accumulation in the ovary and regulate ovulation timing [9][1][6].

hypothesis.hypothesis: The cell-autonomous shutdown of dilp8 expression in the wing imaginal disc at the end of the larval size-adjustment window is controlled by a mechanical/morphogen size-sensing threshold intrinsic to the disc rather than solely by rising systemic ecdysone levels; specifically, loss of disc-intrinsic Hippo pathway activity (as a proxy for reaching final disc size) will maintain dilp8 expression ≥2-fold above wild-type levels at 96 h after egg laying (AEL) in w1118 larvae at 25°C, and will extend the median time to pupariation by ≥8 hours compared to controls, independently of exogenous ecdysone manipulation.
hypothesis.experimental_approach: We will use the GAL4/UAS system to manipulate disc-intrinsic size-sensing pathways (Hippo pathway via UAS-yki overexpression and UAS-wts-RNAi) specifically in wing imaginal discs using nub-GAL4, while simultaneously monitoring dilp8-GFP reporter fluorescence as a real-time readout of dilp8 transcriptional activity. Larvae will be staged precisely by 4-hour egg-collection windows, and disc-specific dilp8-GFP intensity will be quantified by confocal microscopy at 84, 96, 108, and 120 h AEL to capture the normal and perturbed temporal profiles of the dilp8 peak. Pupariation timing will be recorded in cohorts of 30 larvae per vial in triplicate to determine whether disc-autonomous size-sensing manipulation alters developmental timing independently of upstream G alphaQ/IP3R/Ca2+ perturbation. Ecdysone levels will be measured by ELISA from whole-larval homogenates at each time point to distinguish disc-intrinsic repression of dilp8 from ecdysone-driven repression. Controls will include nub-GAL4/+ heterozygotes, UAS-transgene/+ heterozygotes, dilp8-GFP/+ reporters without GAL4, and a positive control using UAS-Galphaq overexpression (known to upregulate dilp8) to validate the assay sensitivity.

hypothesis.expected_outcomes: If the hypothesis is correct: (1) nub-GAL4>UAS-yki larvae will show dilp8-GFP fluorescence intensity ≥2-fold above nub-GAL4/+ controls at 96–108 h AEL as measured by mean integrated fluorescence per disc (n ≥ 15 discs per time point, two-tailed t-test, p < 0.05); (2) median time to pupariation in nub-GAL4>UAS-yki cohorts will be delayed by ≥8 hours relative to both parental controls (log-rank test on pupariation curves, p < 0.01, n = 90 larvae per genotype across 3 replicates); (3) larval ecdysone titers at 96 h AEL will not be significantly reduced in nub-GAL4>UAS-yki versus controls (confirming the dilp8 upregulation is not driven by reduced ecdysone), and the pupariation delay will be at least partially rescued by simultaneous dilp8 knockdown (nub-GAL4>UAS-yki + UAS-dilp8-RNAi), with rescue of ≥50% of the delay. If the hypothesis is incorrect and dilp8 shutdown is entirely ecdysone-controlled, nub-GAL4>UAS-yki will not prolong the dilp8-GFP peak, and ecdysone titers will be suppressed in parallel with any pupariation delay.
hypothesis.novelty_claim: Current literature establishes that the dilp8 peak at the end of juvenile growth is triggered and shut off by ecdysone signaling in the epidermis (PMID 36163439) and that disc perturbations (via Galphaq/IP3R/Ca2+) can upregulate dilp8 (PMID 41131630, 36711848). However, a major identified gap in the literature is that 'it is unclear what cell-autonomous signal within a growing organ sets the threshold at which dilp8 expression is turned off — specifically, whether organ-intrinsic size sensors (mechanical, morphogen gradient, or metabolic) directly repress dilp8 transcription or whether this is entirely controlled by rising ecdysone levels.' No published study has directly tested whether disc-intrinsic Hippo pathway growth arrest contributes to dilp8 shutdown independently of systemic ecdysone, nor whether Hippo pathway status in the disc constitutes the organ-side input that, when satisfied, allows ecdysone to terminate dilp8 expression. This experiment also addresses the gap regarding the Ca2+-independent arm of Galpahq-linked size control by testing whether a non-Ca2+ size-sensing pathway (Hippo/Yorkie) independently feeds into dilp8 regulation.
hypothesis.feasibility_notes: All proposed genetic tools (nub-GAL4, UAS-yki.S168A, UAS-wts-RNAi, dilp8-GFP reporter) are well-established in the Drosophila community; BDSC stock numbers cited require verification before ordering. The dilp8-GFP reporter-based assay for temporal profiling has been validated in prior work (PMID 36163439). Ecdysone ELISA from Drosophila larvae is technically demanding but established, requiring ~50 larvae per sample for reliable signal; this may require optimization. A potential pitfall is that strong Yki overexpression via nub-GAL4 causes disc overgrowth and lethality at later stages, which could complicate pupariation scoring — use of a weaker UAS-yki allele or temperature-sensitive GAL80 (tub-GAL80ts at 18°C→29°C shift) is recommended to titrate expression. Another pitfall is that nub-GAL4 is active in the wing disc but low-level expression in other tissues could confound disc-specific interpretations; disc dissection and cell-type-resolved GFP quantification will mitigate this. hypothesis.hypothesis: Proposed (not established): In wing discs of wandering third-instar w1118 larvae at 25°C, where anteroposterior (A-P) pouch length is varied at least 1.5-fold by larval yeast restriction, the pMad gradient decay length will scale with pouch length with a log-log slope of at least 0.7 up to a critical size L*, and the slope will fall below 0.3 above L*; wing-pouch pent knockdown will reduce the sub-L* slope to 0.3 or less, and wing-pouch Rab11 dominant-negative expression will reduce it by at least 50%, with the Rab11 effect persisting after Pent is restored.
hypothesis.experimental_approach: Larvae will be raised on graded yeast concentrations (and, as a second axis, at different temperatures) to produce small and large wing discs. Discs will be stained for pMad and quantified as A-P profiles normalized to the anterior-posterior boundary, and decay length will be fit as a function of pouch length. Pouch-restricted GAL4 (e.g. nub-GAL4 or rn-GAL4, to be verified) with tub-GAL80ts temporal control will drive UAS-pent-RNAi, a Rab11 dominant-negative, or a Pent-overexpression/restoration transgene. Dpp endocytosis and re-exocytosis will be assessed with a fluorescently tagged Dpp (availability to be verified) using a pulse-chase or recycling assay. Pent range will be tested with clones and in situ staining, and Tkv and Dally levels will be measured in the same discs, so that Pent range, receptor levels and recycling flux are quantified together. Controls are GAL4-only, UAS-only, a non-targeting RNAi, and same-diet siblings imaged in parallel. Statistics will use ANCOVA for slope differences with n ≥ 15 discs per size bin.

hypothesis.novelty_claim: Ben-Zvi et al. reported that scaling is abolished when pent is ubiquitously expressed (PMID 21835621). Zhu et al. reported that Pent acts only within a few cell diameters and proposed a receptor/co-receptor feedback model that predicts a size limit to scaling (PMID 32574592). Romanova-Michaelides et al. reported that scaling depends on recycling of endocytosed Dpp, with Pent-modulating binding rates (PMID 34937053). The literature synthesis identifies two gaps: these models have not been reconciled in the same discs, and the size limit has not been tested against natural size variation between small and large flies. The proposed work addresses both by measuring Pent range, receptor levels and recycling flux together across a size series.

Disease relevance is not established in the supplied literature; any link to BMP2/4 biology is inference.
