identified_gaps: The molecular identity of the niche-derived diffusible signals that directly sense dietary amino acid composition (versus sugar) to regulate ISC proliferation rates remains undefined — clarifying these signals would reveal how the gut encodes qualitative dietary information [2].

It is unknown how olfactory-circuit-derived brain signals are transduced systemically to act on germline cysts to prevent apoptosis — identifying the downstream neuropeptide or hormonal relay would establish the full sensory-to-germline axis [5].

The mechanism by which cap cells are lost and regained during dietary shifts without apoptosis or cell division is unresolved; whether reversible epithelial-to-mesenchymal-like fate transitions between cap cells and escort cells underlie niche plasticity requires direct lineage-tracing evidence [6].

How CkII-dependent phosphorylation of eIF3d1 is itself regulated by niche-derived JAK/STAT signals at a biochemical level is not established — defining this link would complete the niche-to-translational-output circuit in testis stem cells [11].

The relationship between diet-dependent niche size changes in the germline and the parallel diet-dependent uncoupling of ISC proliferation from niche signals in the midgut has not been studied in the same animal or dietary paradigm, so it is unknown whether a shared systemic nutrient-sensing mechanism coordinates both tissues simultaneously [2][6].

Whether lipid-droplet-mediated antioxidant protection of niche glia for neuroblasts during starvation [8] is engaged during dietary restriction in gut or germline niches — and whether this represents a general niche-protective mechanism — has not been tested.

evidence_claims.claim: The gut is the primary interface between an animal and food, but how it adapts to qualitative dietary variation is poorly defined.
A panel of nutrients collectively promote gut growth, which sugar opposes.
Diet influences absolute and relative levels of enterocyte loss and stem cell proliferation, which together determine cell numbers.
A high sugar diet inhibits translation and uncouples intestinal stem cell proliferation from expression of niche-derived signals.
Reducing enterocyte-autonomous TOR signaling was sufficient to attenuate diet-dependent midgut resizing.
When stem cell proliferation was deficient, diet's impact on enterocyte size was enhanced.
The Drosophila ovary germline stem cell (GSC) niche is a well-studied model, which is comprised of cap cells that provide anchorage and maintenance signals for GSCs to maintain oogenesis.
The Drosophila ovary GSC cap cell niche is a dynamic structure, which can contract and expand in fluctuating dietary conditions.
Cap cells are lost when adult flies are shifted to nutrient poor diet and are restored after returning flies to nutrient-rich medium.
Notch signalling in cap and escort cells is similarly reduced and restored by dietary shifts to nutrient poor and rich media.
In old flies decreased Notch signalling is associated with decreased robustness of the niche to dietary changes.
Changes in niche size were not associated with apoptosis or cell division.
Notch can act in cap cells to prevent their loss while activation of Notch in the flanking escort cells results in expansion of the niche.
Dietary changes alone are sufficient to alter Notch signalling and reversibly change niche size in the adult in wild type flies.
Lack of olfactory inputs during development causes a reduction in germline stem cells.
Although germline stem cells proliferate normally, the germline cysts undergo caspase-mediated apoptosis, leading to decreased follicle production and egg-laying in flies with defective olfaction.
Activation of olfactory circuits is sufficient to boost egg production, demonstrating that chemosensory-activated brain-derived inputs promote gamete development.
Olfactory-stimulated systemic regulation evolved tightly with downstream diet-responsive pathways to control germline physiology in response to nutritional status.
Sensory-mediated stem cell maintenance is a generalizable mechanism spanning a myriad of neuronal circuits, systems and species.
Global translation rates are high in CySCs and decrease during differentiation, and that JAK/STAT signaling regulates translation.
The cap binding complex, eIF4F, is dispensable in differentiating cells, but is specifically required in CySCs for self-renewal, acting downstream of JAK/STAT activity.
eIF3d1 is a key regulator of CySC fate, and two eIF3d1 residues subject to regulation by phosphorylation are critical to maintain CySC self-renewal.

Casein Kinase II (CkII) controls eIF3d1 phosphorylation, influences the binding of eIF3d and eIF4F in mammalian cells, and CkII expression is sufficient to restore CySC function in the absence of JAK/STAT.
Niche signals regulate a specific translation programme in which only some mRNAs are translated, allowing stem cells to switch between modes of translation.

The testis niche secretes a ligand to activate the Janus kinase (JAK)/signal transducer and activator of transcription (STAT) pathway in two stem cell populations, germline stem cells (GSCs) and somatic cyst stem cells (CySCs).
Germ-line stem cells physically attach to the niche via localized adherens junctions that provide a polarity cue for orientation of centrosomes in interphase and the spindle in mitosis.
Transit-amplifying cells can revert to the stem cell state if they reoccupy the niche.

Maintenance of stem cell state in the Drosophila male germ line is regulated by cytokine-like signals from hub cells that activate the transcription factor STAT and TGF-beta class signals from surrounding support cells that repress expression of a key differentiation factor.
Cell competition is a conserved, fitness-based process in which 'winner' cells eliminate or displace less-fit 'loser' neighbors, thereby shaping development, tissue homeostasis, and disease.

The adult Drosophila testis provides a genetically tractable model where neutral competition provides a baseline for stem cell turnover, and defined genetic perturbations bias competition to favor specific clones.
Stem cell competition is framed as a driver of aging, clonal evolution, and cancer risk.

Lipid droplets that form in niche glia during oxidative stress limit the levels of reactive oxygen species (ROS) and inhibit the oxidation of polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs), protecting glia and neuroblasts from peroxidation chain reactions.
The antioxidant mechanism involves diverting PUFAs, including diet-derived linoleic acid, away from membranes to the core of lipid droplets, where they are less vulnerable to peroxidation.
Stem-cell-based tumorigenesis occurs through niche appropriation in the posterior midgut and through stem-cell competition for niche occupancy in the testis.

The niche includes all cellular and non-cellular components that interact in order to control the adult stem cell, and these interactions can often be broken down into physical contact and diffusible factors.

It has traditionally been believed that the mesenchymal myofibroblasts play an important role in the crosstalk between ISCs and the niche; however, recent evidence in Drosophila and in vertebrates suggests that epithelial cells also contribute to the niche.

Multiple signalling pathways are utilised to regulate stemness within the intestinal niche, including members of the Wnt, BMP and Hedgehog pathways, and aberrations in these signals lead to disruption of the normal crypt-villus axis.

Studies in Drosophila melanogaster have led our growing understanding of how germline stem cell (GSC) lineages maintain their function and adjust their behavior according to varying environmental and/or physiological conditions.
Diet and diet-dependent factors, mating, and microorganisms modulate GSCs and their developing progeny.
Whether lipid-droplet-mediated antioxidant protection of niche glia for neuroblasts during starvation is engaged during dietary restriction in gut or germline niches has not been tested.

The relationship between diet-dependent niche size changes in the germline and the parallel diet-dependent uncoupling of ISC proliferation from niche signals in the midgut has not been studied in the same animal or dietary paradigm.

literature.summary: In Drosophila, both germline and intestinal stem cell niches are dynamic, diet-responsive structures whose size and signaling output adjust stem cell proliferation and differentiation to match nutritional and physiological status [2][6][31488592]. Diet modulates germline niche size reversibly through Notch signaling in cap and escort cells [6], while in the midgut a high-sugar diet uncouples ISC proliferation from niche signals and enterocyte-autonomous TOR signaling independently controls organ size [2]; additional systemic inputs such as olfactory-circuit-derived brain signals further tune germline output by suppressing cyst apoptosis [5]. At the molecular level, niche-derived JAK/STAT signals in the testis control not only transcription but also specific modes of translation initiation via eIF4F and phospho-eIF3d1/CkII, revealing a post-transcriptional layer by which niches rapidly reprogram stem cell gene expression in response to external stimuli [11].

hypothesis.hypothesis: In adult mated female w1118 Drosophila melanogaster, a shared systemic nutrient-sensing mechanism coordinately regulates both germline stem cell niche size (cap cell number) and intestinal stem cell proliferation uncoupling from niche signals; specifically, we hypothesize that under high-sugar diet (10% sucrose, 0.5% yeast) for 7 days, (1) cap cell number will decrease by ≥30% relative to holidic standard diet controls, (2) ISC mitotic index (phospho-histone H3-positive cells per midgut) will increase by ≥40% relative to controls, (3) both phenotypes will be suppressed (restored to ≤15% deviation from control) by simultaneous gut-specific knockdown of TOR (using Myo1A-GAL4 > UAS-TorRNAi) and ovary-specific Notch activation (using nos-GAL4 > UAS-Notch-ICD), and (4) tissue-specific rescues will fail to fully suppress the contralateral tissue phenotype, demonstrating that at least one systemic intermediary is required for cross-tissue coordination, under 25°C, 12:12 LD cycle conditions.
hypothesis.experimental_approach: Adult mated female flies (day 3 post-eclosion) will be transferred to defined holidic medium or high-sugar medium (10% sucrose, 0.5% yeast) for 0, 3, 7, and 14 days; ovaries will be dissected and stained with anti-Fasciclin III (cap cell marker) and anti-Vasa to quantify cap cell number per germarium by confocal microscopy, while midguts will be stained with anti-phospho-histone H3 (pH3) to quantify ISC mitotic index and with anti-Dl (Delta) to confirm ISC identity. To test tissue-autonomous versus systemic coordination, a 2×2 tissue-specific rescue design will be implemented: (A) gut-specific TOR knockdown (Myo1A-GAL4 > UAS-TorRNAi) to attenuate ISC uncoupling, (B) germline-specific Notch activation (nos-GAL4 > UAS-Notch-ICD) to stabilize cap cell number, (C) both rescues simultaneously, and (D) neither rescue (dietary controls), with all genotypes carrying tub-GAL80ts for temporal control (shift to 29°C at day 0 of dietary treatment). Hemolymph insulin-like peptide (DILP2, DILP5) levels will be measured by ELISA at each time point as a candidate systemic intermediary. For the olfactory axis, orco1 mutants and wild-type controls will be subjected to the same dietary paradigm to determine whether loss of olfactory input exacerbates or decouples the two tissue phenotypes.

hypothesis.expected_outcomes: Under high-sugar diet for 7 days: (1) cap cell number per germarium will decrease by ≥30% (from ~8 to ≤5.6 cap cells per germarium) in w1118 controls, consistent with established niche contraction; (2) midgut pH3+ cell count will increase by ≥40% per midgut (from a baseline of ~5 to ≥7 pH3+ cells per midgut), consistent with ISC proliferative uncoupling from niche signals; (3) gut-only TOR knockdown (arm A) will suppress the ISC mitotic phenotype to ≤15% above standard diet but will leave cap cell number unchanged (>25% reduction persists), demonstrating tissue autonomy of the enterocyte TOR mechanism; (4) germline-only Notch activation (arm B) will maintain cap cell number (≤10% reduction) but will not suppress ISC uncoupling, similarly demonstrating tissue autonomy; (5) the dual-rescue arm (C) will suppress both phenotypes to ≤15% of standard diet levels, but hemolymph DILP levels will remain altered, indicating a systemic signal remains perturbed; (6) orco1 mutants will show exacerbated cap cell loss (≥45% reduction) and may decouple the ISC response, indicating olfactory input contributes to the coordination. Statistical thresholds: all comparisons by one-way ANOVA with Tukey post-hoc, α = 0.05, n ≥ 20 females per genotype per time point, three biological replicates.
hypothesis.novelty_claim: This experiment directly addresses the identified gap that 'the relationship between diet-dependent niche size changes in the germline and the parallel diet-dependent uncoupling of ISC proliferation from niche signals in the midgut has not been studied in the same animal or dietary paradigm, so it is unknown whether a shared systemic nutrient-sensing mechanism coordinates both tissues simultaneously.' No prior study has simultaneously quantified germline niche contraction and ISC proliferative uncoupling in the same individual fly under identical dietary conditions, nor tested whether tissue-autonomous rescues (gut TOR, germline Notch) are sufficient to suppress the contralateral tissue's response — a prediction that would definitively establish or refute systemic coordination. Additionally, the inclusion of orco1 mutants tests the further gap that 'it is unknown how olfactory-circuit-derived brain signals are transduced systemically to act on germline cysts' by asking whether olfactory input is also required for the cross-tissue coordinated dietary response.
hypothesis.feasibility_notes: All core assays (anti-FasIII immunostaining of germaria, pH3 staining of midguts, confocal microscopy) are standard in Drosophila biology labs and can be completed by a single trained researcher. The tub-GAL80ts temperature-shift strategy is well-established and eliminates developmental confounds. Primary concerns: (1) nos-GAL4 may drive expression in early germline cells rather than cap/escort cells — if so, tj-GAL4 (traffic jam) should be substituted as it drives expression in escort and cap cells (BDSC stock 36,480, requires verification); (2) Notch-ICD overexpression in the germline can cause tumorous germaria, so low-temperature titration (25°C induction) and short experimental windows (≤7 days) will be used to avoid this; (3) DILP ELISA requires hemolymph pooling from ~50 flies per condition and the assay requires either commercial kit or antibody availability (anti-DILP2 antibody from Tatar lab or equivalent); (4) simultaneous dissection and staining of ovaries and midguts from the same individual requires careful dissection scheduling. Estimated timeline: 6 months — month 1-2: line establishment and crossing scheme validation; month 3-4: dietary phenotype characterization (w1118 and orco1); month 5-6: rescue experiments and DILP measurements. Potential pitfall: if cap cell loss on high-sugar diet is less penetrant than the 30% threshold, the dietary concentration or duration should be increased to 15% sucrose or 14 days based on Bonfini et al. 2021 and 2015 parameters.
specific_aims: Aim 1: Simultaneous phenotypic mapping — Quantify germline niche cap cell number and midgut ISC mitotic index in the same individual w1118 and orco1 females across a dietary time course (standard vs. 10% sucrose diet, days 0/3/7/14) to establish whether the two tissue responses are temporally correlated within individual flies.

Aim 2: Tissue-autonomous versus systemic rescue — Use a 2×2 tissue-specific GAL4/UAS rescue design (gut TOR knockdown, germline Notch activation, both, neither) with tub-GAL80ts temporal control to determine whether each tissue's diet response can be independently suppressed without affecting the other, thereby testing for a required systemic intermediary.

Aim 3: Systemic signal identification — Measure hemolymph DILP2 and DILP5 levels by ELISA and perform MARCM clonal lineage tracing of cap-cell-to-escort-cell fate transitions in high-sugar-diet flies to identify a candidate systemic hormonal relay and resolve the cellular mechanism of reversible niche contraction.

identified_gaps: No supplied study compares, within one experiment, whole-body versus tissue-specific manipulation of the same gene using matched drivers, so the question of whether tissue-specific interventions match whole-body effect size cannot be answered quantitatively. This matters because the Ucp4a abstract reports mutant and muscle-knockdown extension without a stated head-to-head magnitude comparison [2].

The tissue(s) responsible for Methioninase-mediated lifespan extension are not identified in the supplied abstract, so it is unclear which tissue is rate-limiting for methionine restriction [6]. Testing muscle, fat body, gut and neuron drivers in parallel with a ubiquitous driver would resolve this.

Tissue-specific lifespan effects may be confounded by genetic-background or insertion-site effects. Mocs1 near the TrIP attP integration site may lengthen female lifespan independently of the targeted gene [5]. Published tissue-specific RNAi lifespan results need controls at the same landing site.

Tissue requirements are shown to be partial and context-dependent. Intestinal Tor silencing only partly reduced extension by Salicornia extract [1], and DR required gut and fat body GCN2 [3]. It is unknown whether other tissues (muscle, CNS, oenocytes) account for the remaining Tor- or GCN2-dependent effect.

Sex-specificity is untested across tissue-specific interventions. The Salicornia effect is female-only [1], while Ucp4a, Methioninase and GCN2 tissue effects are not described by sex in the abstracts, so tissue rate-limitation may differ between sexes.

Cell-autonomous versus endocrine mechanisms are unresolved. The nervous system can act through both routes in IIS-mediated lifespan extension [4], and head fat body dFOXO changed ilp2 mRNA only under high yeast [9]. Experiments are needed to determine whether remote tissues mediate the extension, for example by tracking circulating ILP levels or using inter-organ signaling mutants.

literature.summary: In the supplied literature, several single-tissue manipulations extend Drosophila lifespan: muscle Ucp4a knockdown [2], tissue-specific Methioninase expression [6], and head fat body dFOXO overexpression under high yeast [9]. Other interventions need several tissues, such as gut and fat body GCN2 for dietary restriction [3], or are only partly explained by one tissue, such as intestinal Tor for the Salicornia extract [1]. No supplied abstract quantitatively compares matched tissue-specific and whole-body effect sizes, and transgene insertion-site effects [5] are a confound, so the answer to whether tissue-specific interventions can equal whole-body ones remains intervention-dependent and unresolved.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Proposed: In a matched-driver comparison using a single UAS-Methioninase insertion in one isogenic background at 25°C, fat body-driven Methioninase expression will recover at least 70% of the median lifespan extension produced by ubiquitous expression in mated females, whereas muscle-, neuron-, gut- or oenocyte-restricted expression will each recover no more than 40%, and no single tissue will fully equal whole-body extension.
hypothesis.experimental_approach: Express a single UAS-Methioninase insertion with a ubiquitous driver and in parallel with fat body, muscle, neuron, gut and oenocyte drivers, all in the same isogenic background and on the same standard diet. Adult-restricted expression (tub-GAL80ts temperature shift or GeneSwitch with RU486 and vehicle-fed controls) separates adult effects from developmental effects. Each driver-alone and UAS-alone control is run in parallel, plus a landing-site-matched control transgene (for example UAS-neutral reporter at the same attP site), because the transgene insertion site used for tissue-specific RNAi can itself lengthen lifespan. Each genotype is run in both sexes (at least 200 flies per genotype per sex, 10 vials of 20, flies transferred 3 times per week). Median lifespan is analysed by log-rank and Cox models with a driver x sex interaction and Bonferroni correction, and the fraction of whole-body extension recovered is reported with bootstrap 95% CIs. Hemolymph or whole-fly methionine and related metabolites are measured by LC-MS at day 10 and day 30 to test whether the rate-limiting tissue acts through systemic methionine depletion or cell-autonomously.

hypothesis.expected_outcomes: Proposed predictions, not established results: ubiquitous Methioninase will extend median lifespan by at least 20% over the matched controls. Fat body expression is predicted to recover at least 70% of this gain, and muscle, neuron, gut and oenocyte expression each no more than 40% (log-rank p < 0.01 after correction). If any single tissue recovers 80% or more, or if fat body recovers under 50%, the hypothesis is falsified. Hemolymph methionine is expected to fall in proportion to lifespan recovery across drivers (Spearman rho > 0.7), which would support a systemic mechanism over a cell-autonomous one. Landing-site control flies are expected to differ from driver-alone controls by under 5% in median lifespan; a larger difference would indicate an insertion-site artefact. A driver x sex interaction with p < 0.05 would indicate that tissue rate-limitation differs between sexes.
hypothesis.novelty_claim: Parkhitko et al. reported that both whole-body and tissue-specific Methioninase expression can dramatically extend lifespan [34588310], but the literature synthesis found that the tissues responsible for Methioninase-mediated extension are not identified in the supplied abstract. No supplied study compares, within one experiment, whole-body versus tissue-specific manipulation of the same gene using matched drivers. This design fills that gap by testing five tissue drivers and a ubiquitous driver side by side with a landing-site-matched control, and it also addresses the untested sex-specificity of tissue-specific interventions.
hypothesis.feasibility_notes: Estimated timeline is 18-24 months: 3 months for line verification, backcrossing and construction of the control transgene; 8-10 months for lifespan cohorts of both sexes, run in two staggered replicates; 3 months for LC-MS metabolomics; 3 months for analysis. Pitfalls: (1) the Methioninase transgene and some drivers may not be available and may need to be rebuilt; (2) some drivers have leaky or ectopic expression, which should be verified with a reporter; (3) Methioninase is a bacterial enzyme and may affect the microbiome or feeding, so food intake (CAFE or dye assay) should be measured; (4) GeneSwitch RU486 can itself affect lifespan, so vehicle and drug controls are required; (5) background effects require backcrossing for at least 6 generations into a common background; (6) enzyme secretion or leakage could mean that the tissue of expression is not the tissue of action, which the hemolymph measurements are designed to detect.
specific_aims: Aim 1: Matched-driver lifespan comparison — measure median and maximum lifespan of ubiquitous versus fat body, muscle, neuron, gut and oenocyte Methioninase expression in a single isogenic background, and calculate the fraction of whole-body extension recovered by each tissue.

Aim 2: Insertion-site and driver controls — use a landing-site-matched control transgene, driver-alone and UAS-alone lines, and adult-restricted induction (GAL80ts or GeneSwitch) to determine how much of each tissue's apparent effect is due to the insertion site, the driver or developmental expression.

Aim 3: Sex and mechanism — test each tissue driver in males and females for driver x sex interaction, and measure hemolymph methionine and related metabolites to determine whether the rate-limiting tissue acts systemically or cell-autonomously.

literature.disease_context: Identifying rate-limiting tissues for lifespan is directly relevant to human aging and age-related diseases, including neurodegeneration, metabolic syndrome, and cancer, because tissue-specific interventions could offer targeted therapies with fewer systemic side effects than whole-body treatments. Studies in Drosophila have linked gut integrity, muscle proteostasis, neuronal insulin signaling, and fat body nutrient sensing to organismal lifespan, mirroring conserved mechanisms operative in human tissues. Tissue-specific manipulation of pathways such as IIS, TOR, and methionine metabolism in flies demonstrates that interventions confined to a single organ can sometimes recapitulate whole-body lifespan extension, suggesting that analogous targeted strategies could be therapeutically viable in humans.

identified_gaps: No single study has performed a systematic head-to-head comparison of tissue-specific versus whole-body interventions across multiple longevity pathways (IIS, TOR, methionine restriction) in the same genetic background, making it impossible to quantitatively rank tissues by their rate-limiting contribution to lifespan.

The mechanism by which muscle-specific mitochondrial perturbation (Ucp4a loss) communicates with other tissues to extend whole-organism lifespan remains undefined — the identity and targets of the proposed retrograde mitochondrial signal are unknown [2].

For gut-dependent lifespan effects (e.g., SEE/TOR, GCN2 in gut/fat body), it is unclear whether individual intestinal cell types (enterocytes, enteroendocrine cells, intestinal stem cells) are functionally redundant or whether a specific cell type is the dominant driver of the systemic signal [1][3].

Whether tissue-specific methionine restriction via Methioninase expression in a single tissue (e.g., fat body alone vs. gut alone) is sufficient to match whole-body Methioninase expression in lifespan extension has not been tested with equal statistical rigor across all candidate tissues [6].

The interaction between sex-specific lifespan responses (SEE extends only female lifespan; dFOXO effects can be sex-biased) and tissue-specific mechanisms is largely unexplored — it is unknown whether the same tissues are rate-limiting in males and females [1][9].

Studies on neuronal IIS and lifespan extension rely heavily on candidate-driven approaches; unbiased screens for which specific neuronal populations or circuits are rate-limiting for IIS-mediated longevity have not been reported in the provided literature [4].

evidence_claims.claim: Tissue-specific silencing of the Tor signaling pathway in different cellular compartments of the intestine reduced, but did not altogether abolish, the lifespan-prolonging effect in females.

Knockdown of Ucp4a in muscles, but not neurons, fat, or intestine, to extend lifespan and also eliminate polyubiquitinated protein aggregates, which accumulate with aging and are associated with lifespan.
These findings suggest a retrograde mitochondrial signaling process initiated by reduced cytosol aspartate level culminates in muscle protein aggregate removal and lifespan extension.
The knockdown of GCN2 in the gut and fat body, an energy sensing organ in Drosophila, abolished the beneficial effect of GCN2 in lifespan extension upon dietary restriction of amino acids.

One tissue of particular importance for lifespan extension in diverse organisms is the CNS (central nervous system). Although lowered IIS in the CNS can extend lifespan, IIS is also widely recognized as being neuroprotective and important for growth and survival of neurons.
The nervous system can play both endocrine and cell-autonomous roles in extension of lifespan by IIS, and the effects of IIS on lifespan and neuronal function can be uncoupled to some extent.

Identifying rate-limiting tissues for lifespan is directly relevant to human aging and age-related diseases, including neurodegeneration, metabolic syndrome, and cancer, because tissue-specific interventions could offer targeted therapies with fewer systemic side effects than whole-body treatments.

No single study has performed a systematic head-to-head comparison of tissue-specific versus whole-body interventions across multiple longevity pathways (IIS, TOR, methionine restriction) in the same genetic background, making it impossible to quantitatively rank tissues by their rate-limiting contribution to lifespan.

literature.summary: Evidence from multiple Drosophila studies indicates that no single tissue is universally rate-limiting for lifespan; instead, the identity of the critical tissue depends on the intervention: muscle is rate-limiting for Ucp4a-mediated longevity [2], gut and fat body are required for GCN2-dependent dietary restriction benefits [3], and the CNS plays a privileged role in IIS-mediated lifespan extension [4]. Crucially, tissue-specific interventions — including muscle-restricted Ucp4a knockdown [2] and tissue-specific Methioninase expression [6] — can match or substantially recapitulate whole-body longevity benefits, demonstrating that organismal aging can be rate-limited by a single organ for specific pathways. However, when multiple tissues contribute redundantly (as with intestinal TOR silencing [1] or GCN2 in both gut and fat body [3]), partial tissue restriction yields only partial lifespan extension, underscoring that the architecture of tissue control is pathway-specific and that systematic cross-tissue comparisons remain an open and critical research priority.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Fat-body-specific overexpression of dFOXO (using ppl-GAL4 > UAS-dFOXO) will extend median lifespan of mated female w1118 flies by ≥15% relative to whole-body dFOXO overexpression (da-GAL4 > UAS-dFOXO) under standard 25°C, ad libitum SY food conditions, whereas muscle-specific dFOXO overexpression (Mhc-GAL4 > UAS-dFOXO) and gut-specific dFOXO overexpression (NP1-GAL4 > UAS-dFOXO) will each extend median lifespan by <10% relative to w1118 GAL4/+ controls, demonstrating that the fat body is the dominant rate-limiting tissue for IIS/dFOXO-mediated longevity and that its tissue-specific manipulation is sufficient to recapitulate ≥75% of the whole-body intervention effect in the same isogenic background.
hypothesis.experimental_approach: We will use the GAL4/UAS binary expression system to overexpress UAS-dFOXO in a panel of tissues (whole-body via da-GAL4, fat body via ppl-GAL4, muscle via Mhc-GAL4, gut enterocytes via NP1-GAL4, and neurons via elav-GAL4) in age-matched mated female and male w1118 flies in the same isogenic background. Each experimental genotype (GAL4/+; UAS-dFOXO/+) will be compared against two controls per tissue driver: the GAL4/+ driver-only control (to detect GAL4 toxicity) and the UAS-dFOXO/+ transgene-only control (to detect leaky UAS expression), with ≥200 flies per genotype across three independent biological replicates (n ≥ 600 per group total). Primary endpoint is median and maximum (90th percentile) lifespan assessed by daily mortality scoring; secondary endpoints include intestinal barrier integrity (Smurf assay at 30, 45, and 60 days), climbing assay for locomotor healthspan (weekly from day 10), and fat body dFOXO nuclear localization confirmed by anti-dFOXO immunofluorescence. In parallel, fat-body RNA-seq at day 15 and day 40 will compare transcriptional signatures of tissue-specific versus whole-body dFOXO overexpression to identify shared versus unique downstream effectors, with particular attention to ilp2 and ilp5 transcript levels as established dFOXO targets.

hypothesis.expected_outcomes: Based on prior evidence that dFOXO overexpression in the head fat body extends lifespan under high-yeast conditions, we predict: (1) fat-body-specific dFOXO overexpression (ppl-GAL4) will extend female median lifespan by 15–25% over GAL4/+ controls, approximating ≥75% of the whole-body (da-GAL4) effect; (2) whole-body da-GAL4 > UAS-dFOXO will extend female median lifespan by 20–30% consistent with published benchmarks; (3) muscle-specific and gut-specific overexpression will yield <10% median lifespan extension in females, confirming these tissues as non-rate-limiting for dFOXO-mediated longevity; (4) neuronal overexpression will yield an intermediate effect (10–15%) consistent with CNS IIS literature; (5) ilp2 and ilp5 mRNA will be suppressed ≥1.5-fold in fat-body RNA-seq of ppl-GAL4 > UAS-dFOXO flies versus controls; (6) Smurf assay positivity will be delayed by ≥5 days in fat-body and whole-body dFOXO lines relative to controls. Statistical thresholds: log-rank p < 0.01 for lifespan comparisons with Bonferroni correction for multiple tissue comparisons; effect sizes reported as hazard ratios with 95% CIs. Male cohorts are run in parallel; sex-specific effects will be analyzed separately given documented sex bias in dFOXO and TOR interventions.
hypothesis.novelty_claim: No single study has performed a systematic, head-to-head, same-genetic-background comparison of dFOXO overexpression across fat body, muscle, gut, and neurons alongside a whole-body positive control with quantitative ranking of tissue contributions to lifespan — a gap explicitly identified in the literature synthesis. While dFOXO overexpression in the head fat body has been shown to extend lifespan in a diet-dependent manner, its effect has never been directly benchmarked against whole-body dFOXO overexpression in a single unified experiment with matched controls and multiple pathway-relevant secondary endpoints. Furthermore, the literature identifies that muscle is rate-limiting for Ucp4a-mediated longevity and gut/fat body for GCN2-mediated longevity, but the rate-limiting tissue for dFOXO/IIS-specific longevity across multiple tissues simultaneously has not been determined. The inclusion of adult-onset induction via GAL80ts addresses the unresolved confound of developmental dFOXO activity. Finally, the parallel male cohort directly addresses the identified gap that sex-specific tissue rate-limiting effects are largely unexplored.
hypothesis.feasibility_notes: All GAL4 drivers proposed (ppl, da, Mhc, NP1, elav) are widely used in aging studies and are expected to be available from BDSC, though stock numbers require verification before ordering. The UAS-dFOXO line is well-characterized in the literature; if BDSC availability is uncertain, it can be obtained from collaborating labs (e.g., Partridge, Bhatt, or Tatar labs). The experimental design is technically straightforward using established GAL4/UAS methodology. Primary lifespan assays require 90–100 days per cohort; with three biological replicates staggered by 4 weeks, total lifespan data collection spans approximately 8–10 months. RNA-seq adds 2–3 months of analysis. Potential pitfalls include: (1) GAL4 driver leakiness — mitigated by UAS-only and GAL4-only controls; (2) dFOXO overexpression toxicity at high levels (especially da-GAL4) — mitigated by GAL80ts for adult-onset induction in a parallel arm; (3) ppl-GAL4 may have expression in some non-fat-body tissues — expression pattern should be confirmed by crossing to UAS-GFP reporter and imaging; (4) diet-dependence of dFOXO effects requires standardized SY food preparation across all replicates with batch verification. Estimated total timeline: 14–16 months from line acquisition to manuscript submission. Budget considerations: lifespan assays at scale require dedicated incubator space and fly pushing labor; RNA-seq costs approximately $300–500 per sample (20–24 samples total).

literature.summary: The supplied literature indicates that specific nutrients rather than calories drive Drosophila DR longevity [2], and that DR lifespan extension can occur independently of dFOXO and ilp5 [3], with little evidence that any gene is required [2]. Single-amino-acid restriction has distinct effects from total protein restriction on stress resistance [4], and amino-acid-specific signalling such as cystine–TORC1 is described in fasting contexts [1][6]. However, necessity and sufficiency of specific amino acids, total protein, or sugar ratio for lifespan are not directly resolved by these abstracts, and sugar ratio in particular is not addressed.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Proposed: In mated female Drosophila melanogaster (w1118 background, 25°C, 12:12 light:dark, measured food intake), lowering dietary isoleucine and methionine together to 25% of the reference concentration on a chemically defined diet, with all other amino acids, sucrose and total energy held constant, will extend median lifespan by ≥15% over the reference diet (log-rank P<0.01) and will reproduce ≥50% of the extension produced by lowering all essential amino acids to 25%. Restoring isoleucine and methionine to reference levels in the low-essential-amino-acid diet will remove ≥50% of that extension. Varying sucrose alone over a 4-fold range at fixed amino acid concentrations will change median lifespan by <5%.
hypothesis.experimental_approach: Proposed: A geometric-framework design on a chemically defined (holidic-type) diet in mated w1118 females, with 150-200 flies per condition across at least 3 independent cohorts. Diet arms: (i) a grid of total amino acid concentration × sucrose concentration, which separates protein, sugar and protein:carbohydrate ratio effects; (ii) single or paired amino acid reduction (Ile, Met, Ile+Met, and the remaining essential amino acids pooled) with compensation for total nitrogen and energy; (iii) add-back arms for necessity and subtractive arms for sufficiency. Food intake will be measured per diet (e.g., CAFE or dye-based consumption) so that any lifespan effect can be separated from altered feeding, and fecundity will be recorded as a covariate. Lifespan will be analysed by log-rank and Cox models with diet as a covariate, and by fitting nutrient response surfaces. In a follow-up arm, Thor (4E-BP) loss-of-function and adult fat-body Tor knockdown flies will be tested on the informative diets to see whether TORC1 pathway components are required for any amino-acid-driven extension, with genotype-matched controls and adult-restricted induction to avoid developmental confounds.

hypothesis.expected_outcomes: Proposed predictions, not established results: (1) Median lifespan rises monotonically as total amino acids fall, with sucrose varied 4-fold changing median lifespan by <5% at fixed amino acids. (2) Ile+Met reduction alone gives ≥15% median extension, i.e. ≥50% of the effect of total essential amino acid reduction. (3) Add-back of Ile+Met reduces the DR extension by ≥50%. (4) Intake differences between diets will be <15%, so the effects cannot be attributed to altered consumption. (5) If Thor loss or fat-body Tor knockdown abolishes ≥50% of the amino-acid effect (genotype × diet interaction P<0.05), TORC1/4E-BP is implicated. If the extension persists, it is TORC1/4E-BP-independent. Falsification: if Ile+Met reduction gives <5% extension, or sucrose variation shifts median lifespan by ≥10%, the hypothesis is rejected.
hypothesis.novelty_claim: The literature synthesis reports that specific nutrients, not calories, mediate longevity in Drosophila. This finding is from 21187139. Dietary restriction extended lifespan in the presence and absence of dFOXO, as shown in 18221413. Isoleucine deprivation protected against several stressors and was not replicated by protein restriction in females, as shown in 39106944, but that work measured stress resistance, not lifespan. No supplied paper tests lifespan under single-amino-acid restriction versus total protein restriction in a full geometric-framework design with measured intake. The sugar component and protein:carbohydrate ratio are also not tested for lifespan in the supplied abstracts, and the requirement for TORC1 or amino-acid sensing components in DR lifespan extension is untested. This proposal addresses these gaps together by crossing amino acid identity, total protein and sugar in one lifespan design.
hypothesis.feasibility_notes: Proposed timeline of about 14-18 months: 2-3 months for diet formulation and intake validation, 8-10 months for lifespan cohorts (median lifespan on chemically defined diets may be around 60-80 days; cohorts run in parallel), and 3-4 months for the genetic arm and analysis. Pitfalls: chemically defined diets may give shorter baseline lifespan than yeast-based diets; single amino acid reduction may change feeding (compensatory intake), which is addressed by intake measurement; amino acid interactions (e.g., Ile/Leu/Val antagonism) may complicate add-back; and sex and genetic background effects may limit generality (males and a second background are proposed as extensions). Stock numbers and allele identities must be verified before ordering. The numbers of flies are sized for log-rank detection of a ~10-15% median change; power calculations should be finalized with pilot data.
specific_aims: Aim 1: Separate protein, amino acid and sugar axes — map lifespan response surfaces across a total amino acid × sucrose grid on a chemically defined diet with measured intake, and test the prediction that sucrose alone changes median lifespan by <5%.

Aim 2: Necessity and sufficiency of specific amino acids — test whether reducing Ile and Met (alone and together) is sufficient for ≥50% of the extension from total essential amino acid reduction, and whether their add-back is necessary to remove ≥50% of the extension.
Aim 3: Genetic requirement for TORC1/4E-BP — test whether Thor loss-of-function or adult fat-body Tor knockdown blocks the amino-acid-driven lifespan extension (genotype × diet interaction).

literature.disease_context: Understanding which dietary components mediate lifespan extension has direct relevance to age-related diseases including obesity, type 2 diabetes, and non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD), where amino acid availability and signaling intersect with insulin resistance and lipid metabolism [9]. Precision nutrition strategies targeting specific amino acids (e.g., histidine, isoleucine) or protein intake may offer therapeutic avenues for extending healthspan and treating metabolic diseases in humans [5]. The mechanistic pathways identified in Drosophila, including IIS, TORC1, and FOXO signaling, are conserved in mammals and thus findings from fly models have translational potential [3][8].

identified_gaps: The relative contributions of individual essential amino acids versus total protein to lifespan extension remain poorly resolved — the geometric framework shows protein matters more than calories [2], but which specific amino acids are sufficient or necessary for longevity (as opposed to stress resistance) has not been systematically determined across all 20 amino acids in Drosophila.

The sex-specificity of amino acid restriction effects (e.g., isoleucine deprivation protects females but not males from nicotine and other stressors [4]) has not been extended to lifespan endpoints, leaving open whether sex-specific amino acid sensing translates to differential longevity responses.

No single gene has been demonstrated to be strictly required for DR to extend Drosophila lifespan [2][3]; the downstream transcriptional effectors and tissue-specific mediators of amino acid sensing in the context of longevity remain unidentified.

The role of dietary sugar (carbohydrate) ratios relative to protein in lifespan modulation is underexplored in the provided literature — the geometric framework addresses protein-to-calorie ratios but the protein-to-carbohydrate ratio as a specific lifespan determinant independent of total caloric intake is not resolved [2].

The mechanisms by which lysosomal amino acid mobilization (e.g., cystine export and acetyl-CoA production [6]) communicates with TORC1 to regulate autophagy and longevity during dietary restriction have not been causally linked to lifespan extension in intact animals.

literature.summary: Evidence from Drosophila studies using geometric framework nutrition and chemically defined diets demonstrates that specific nutrients — particularly protein/amino acid content rather than total calories — are the primary mediators of dietary restriction-induced lifespan extension [2]. Crucially, restriction of individual amino acids (such as isoleucine) confers benefits that cannot be replicated by bulk protein restriction, and these effects are sex-specific [4], while amino acid sensing via lysosomal cystine export modulates TORC1 and autophagy during fasting [6]. Despite substantial evidence implicating amino acid sensing pathways, no single gene — including those in the insulin/IGF signaling pathway or dFOXO — has been shown to be strictly required for DR to extend lifespan in Drosophila [2][3], leaving the necessary and sufficient molecular mediators of amino acid-driven longevity unresolved.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Dietary restriction of isoleucine alone (to 10% of holidic diet standard concentration, with all other amino acids and sugar held constant) will extend median lifespan by ≥15% in mated female w1118 Drosophila melanogaster at 25°C compared to flies on a complete holidic diet, while equivalent restriction of total protein (all amino acids reduced to 10% of standard) will produce a smaller or equivalent lifespan extension (≥15%), and this isoleucine-specific lifespan extension will be abolished in females with fat-body-specific TOR hyperactivation (r4-GAL4 > UAS-Rheb) but not in dFOXO null mutants, demonstrating that isoleucine sensing acts through TORC1 rather than IIS to extend lifespan in a sex-specific manner.
hypothesis.experimental_approach: Female w1118 flies (mated, 25°C, n≥150 per dietary group) will be maintained on chemically defined holidic diets with systematic single-amino-acid restriction: (1) complete holidic diet control, (2) isoleucine restricted to 10% standard, (3) total protein restricted to 10% standard (all amino acids reduced proportionally), (4) leucine restricted to 10% standard (closely related branched-chain amino acid control), (5) isoleucine-restricted diet with sugar (sucrose) increased 2-fold to control for caloric compensation, and (6) sugar-only restriction (sucrose reduced to 10%) keeping amino acids constant. Lifespan assays will be conducted in triplicate cohorts with weekly food changes and blind scoring. Genetic dissection will use fat-body-specific TOR activation (r4-GAL4 > UAS-Rheb) and dFOXO null mutants on isoleucine-restricted vs. complete holidic diets to test pathway requirements. TORC1 activity will be measured by western blot (phospho-S6K/total S6K ratio) in fat body tissue at days 10, 20, and 30. Fecundity will be scored weekly as an independent fitness endpoint to assess reproduction-lifespan trade-offs. All dietary groups will be compared using log-rank tests with Bonferroni correction (α=0.05), and Cox proportional hazards models will assess genotype-by-diet interactions.

hypothesis.expected_outcomes: Primary endpoint: Isoleucine restriction (10% standard) will extend median female lifespan by ≥15% relative to complete holidic diet control (e.g., from ~60 days to ≥69 days median survival; log-rank p<0.05). Total protein restriction will also extend lifespan by ≥15%, but the magnitude of isoleucine-specific extension will be statistically non-inferior to total protein restriction (overlapping 95% CIs), supporting sufficiency of isoleucine restriction. Leucine restriction will extend lifespan by <10% (or not significantly), establishing amino-acid specificity. Sugar-only restriction will not significantly extend lifespan (p>0.05), confirming that carbohydrate ratio is not the primary driver. Caloric compensation (isoleucine restricted + 2x sucrose) will not diminish the isoleucine-restriction lifespan benefit (<5% difference from isoleucine restriction alone), confirming a calorie-independent mechanism. TORC1 activity (phospho-S6K/S6K ratio) will be reduced ≥30% in fat body of isoleucine-restricted females relative to controls at day 10. Fat-body TOR hyperactivation (r4-GAL4>UAS-Rheb) will abolish the isoleucine-restriction lifespan extension (median lifespan on ILe-restricted diet not significantly different from complete-diet controls; p>0.05), while dFOXO null flies will retain ≥10% median lifespan extension under isoleucine restriction (p<0.05), confirming TORC1-dependence and IIS-independence. Fecundity on isoleucine-restricted diet will be reduced ≥20% relative to complete diet, demonstrating a reproduction-lifespan trade-off.
hypothesis.novelty_claim: This experiment directly addresses two key gaps identified in the literature synthesis: (1) which specific amino acids are necessary and sufficient for lifespan extension (as opposed to stress resistance) has not been systematically tested — prior work showed isoleucine deprivation confers stress resistance but did not measure lifespan endpoints; (2) no causal pathway linking individual amino acid sensing to longevity has been established — the role of TORC1 vs. IIS in mediating isoleucine-specific (rather than bulk protein) lifespan extension is unresolved. Additionally, this design directly tests whether dietary sugar ratio influences lifespan independently of protein content, a question identified as underexplored in the geometric framework literature. The parallel genetic epistasis design (TORC1 hyperactivation vs. dFOXO null) in the context of single-amino-acid restriction is novel and will causally distinguish pathway requirements that prior genetic studies conducted only in the context of bulk yeast-based dietary restriction.
hypothesis.feasibility_notes: Holidic (chemically defined) diets for Drosophila are established and published; the exact isoleucine-restricted holidic diet formulation requires calibration against published holidic diet recipes (e.g., Piper et al. 2014, Nature Protocols) to confirm palatability and consumption rates before lifespan assays begin (estimated 1 month optimization). Lifespan assays require 3–4 months per complete cohort; with three biological replicates run in parallel, total lifespan data collection is estimated at 4–5 months. Western blotting for phospho-S6K in Drosophila fat body is technically established but requires dissection of ≥20 fat bodies per sample for sufficient protein yield — this is technically demanding but routine. Potential pitfall: isoleucine restriction may reduce food intake non-specifically (dietary aversion), confounding calorie-independent interpretations — this will be controlled by measuring food intake via CAFE assay or dye-based consumption assays in a separate cohort. BDSC stock numbers for r4-GAL4 and UAS-Rheb require verification before ordering. Sex-specific analysis requires male cohorts to be run in parallel (adding ~30% additional workload) to assess whether effects are female-specific as predicted. Total estimated timeline: 8–10 months including optimization, lifespan assays, and molecular endpoint collection.
specific_aims: Aim 1: Isoleucine sufficiency for lifespan extension — Determine whether restriction of isoleucine alone (to 10% standard on holidic diet) is sufficient to extend median female lifespan by ≥15%, and compare the magnitude to total protein restriction and leucine restriction, to establish amino-acid specificity of the longevity effect.

Aim 2: Sugar-to-protein ratio independence — Test whether altering dietary sucrose concentration (10% or 200% of standard) while holding all amino acids constant produces significant lifespan changes, and whether caloric compensation via sucrose supplementation during isoleucine restriction negates lifespan extension, to determine whether carbohydrate ratio is an independent or dependent variable in DR-mediated longevity.

Aim 3: TORC1 vs. IIS pathway requirement — Use fat-body-specific TOR hyperactivation (r4-GAL4>UAS-Rheb) and dFOXO null mutants to causally determine whether isoleucine-restriction-induced lifespan extension requires TORC1 suppression in the fat body and is independent of dFOXO/IIS, and validate pathway engagement by measuring phospho-S6K levels in fat body tissue across dietary conditions.

identified_gaps: Apparent conflict on NPF's effect on intake in mated females: [1] reports gut NPF promotes consumption of protein-containing food, whereas [5] reports EEC-derived NPF inhibits feeding; whether this reflects nutrient-specific versus total intake, different EEC subsets, or assay differences should be tested by measuring sugar, yeast and total intake side-by-side under the same EEC-specific NPF manipulations.

The routes of gut NPF to its targets are incompletely resolved: [1] implicates AKH signaling, [4] brain insulin-producing neurons, and [5] two dopaminergic NPFR+ enteric neurons; it is unknown whether these act in parallel or in series, which could be tested with cell-specific NPFR knockdown combined with two-choice food assays.

Only L-glutamate has a defined EEC receptor mechanism (mGluR) [5]; the receptors by which EECs detect dietary sugar and yeast to differentially release NPF [4] are not identified in the supplied abstracts.

The supplied primary studies focus almost exclusively on NPF; whether other enteroendocrine peptides carry distinct nutrient information to the brain is not addressed, and the identity of the enteroendocrine hormones that remodel enteric neurons in [7] is not specified in the abstract.
Male versus female function: gut NPF effects on food choice and lifespan are reported for females [1][4][5]; whether males use the same gut-brain NPF signaling for food choice remains untested.

Inference: NPF appears to be a central enteroendocrine carrier of nutritional status, but its net effect on feeding seems context- and nutrient-dependent.

identified_gaps: Gut NPF is reported to suppress sugar appetite and raise protein intake via AKH [1], and also to inhibit feeding overall via dopaminergic enteric neurons [5]. It is unresolved whether these are the same or parallel pathways, and how an overall anorexigenic signal produces nutrient-specific choice. Testing this requires epistasis between the NPFR-expressing enteric neurons and AKH-producing cells.

Only L-glutamate sensing through mGluR is mechanistically resolved in the provided literature [5]. The receptors and cell types that detect dietary sugar and yeast to drive differential NPF secretion are not identified in the abstracts [4], and this limits understanding of how sugar versus protein status is distinguished.

The provided literature is dominated by NPF. Other enteroendocrine signals that might carry nutritional status to the brain for food choice are not established here; [7] mentions enteroendocrine hormones remodelling enteric neurons without naming them in the abstract. A comparative analysis of EEC subtype-specific peptides under defined nutrient states is needed.

NPF effects on feeding are reported in mated females [1][5], and [1] states a female-specific function in promoting protein consumption. Whether the gut NPF pathway operates in males or virgin females, and how mating state gates it, remains unclear.

It is unknown whether the feeding and food-choice roles of gut NPF [1][5] are mechanistically coupled to the NPF to insulin to juvenile hormone longevity axis [4]. Testing requires measuring feeding phenotypes under the manipulations that alter lifespan.

literature.summary: Enteroendocrine cells of the Drosophila gut sense nutrients and release NPF, the best-supported gut-to-brain signal for feeding in the provided literature [1][5]. Gut NPF acts through AKH signalling to suppress sugar appetite and favour protein intake [1], and via NPFR-expressing dopaminergic enteric neurons to relay an anorexigenic signal to the brain [5]. Gut NPF also modulates insulin signalling and juvenile hormone to influence lifespan [4]. Other enteroendocrine signals, the sugar and protein sensing mechanisms, and the integration of these pathways remain poorly defined.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Proposed: in mated adult female flies on a w1118 background at 25°C, adult-onset, enteroendocrine-cell-specific NPF overexpression acts through two dissociable, parallel arms. (i) NPFR in dopaminergic enteric neurons accounts for at least 50% of the reduction in total food intake but not for the shift in macronutrient choice. (ii) AKH-producing cells account for at least 50% of the shift in sugar:yeast preference (a ≥30% decrease in sugar preference index) but not for the reduction in total intake. Falsification: if NPFR knockdown in dopaminergic enteric neurons blocks the sugar-preference shift by ≥50%, or if Akh knockdown blocks the total-intake reduction by ≥50%, the parallel-arm model is rejected in favour of a serial pathway.
hypothesis.experimental_approach: Use temporally controlled GAL4/UAS (tub-GAL80ts) to overexpress NPF in adult enteroendocrine cells with a gut-restricted driver, and confirm that the driver does not express in the brain. Cross this to cell-type-specific knockdown or manipulation of the candidate downstream arms. For the enteric neuron arm, use NPFR RNAi in dopaminergic neurons with a gut-restricted intersectional strategy (TH-GAL4 combined with a brain-restricting GAL80). For the AKH arm, use Akh-GAL4 or Akh RNAi, with Akh mutants as a secondary test. Feeding is measured in mated females with the FlyPAD or CAFE assay, in two ways: total intake on a single diet, and a two-choice assay (sucrose vs. yeast) that yields a sugar preference index. Controls are UAS-only and GAL4-only genotypes, GAL80ts permissive vs. restrictive temperature, matched age and mating status, and a starvation-state control. Genotype × manipulation interactions are tested by two-way ANOVA, with n ≥ 30 flies per genotype across ≥3 independent replicates.

hypothesis.expected_outcomes: Proposed predictions, not established results: (1) Gut NPF overexpression reduces total intake by ≥30% and sugar preference index by ≥30% vs. controls (p<0.05, Bonferroni-corrected). (2) NPFR knockdown in dopaminergic enteric neurons restores ≥50% of total intake but restores <25% of the sugar preference shift. (3) Akh knockdown restores ≥50% of the sugar preference shift but restores <25% of the total intake reduction. A significant genotype × manipulation interaction in each case would support dissociable parallel arms. Double manipulation is predicted to be additive for the sum of the two phenotypes. If instead both knockdowns block both phenotypes, the pathways are serial or converge.
hypothesis.novelty_claim: Gut NPF has been reported to act through AKH to suppress sugar appetite and raise protein intake in PMID 36344765, and separately to inhibit feeding through NPFR-expressing dopaminergic enteric neurons in PMID 38664401. The literature synthesis identifies as unresolved whether these are the same or parallel pathways and how an overall anorexigenic signal produces nutrient-specific choice. No supplied study tests the two arms by epistasis in a single design with separable readouts for total intake and macronutrient choice. This proposal does so.
hypothesis.feasibility_notes: Estimated timeline is 12-14 months: 3 months for line construction, verification and driver validation (including gut restriction); 6 months for feeding assays; 3 months for epistasis and double manipulations; 2 months for analysis. Pitfalls: (a) the intersectional driver for dopaminergic enteric neurons is unverified and may leak or fail; (b) RNAi efficiency must be checked by qPCR or reporter; (c) feeding readouts differ between FlyPAD and CAFE, so key results should be confirmed with both; (d) mating and diet history strongly modulate feeding, so these must be standardised; (e) developmental effects are avoided by GAL80ts but need temperature controls; (f) AKH also affects metabolism and locomotion, which may confound feeding readouts.
specific_aims: Aim 1: Define the gut NPF behavioural phenotype — quantify total intake and sugar:yeast preference after adult-onset EEC-specific NPF overexpression in mated females, with GAL80ts and brain-restriction controls.
Aim 2: Test the NPFR-enteric-dopaminergic-neuron arm — determine how much of the total-intake and macronutrient-choice phenotypes depends on NPFR in dopaminergic enteric neurons.
Aim 3: Test the AKH arm and epistasis — determine how much of each phenotype depends on AKH-producing cells, and run double manipulations to distinguish parallel from serial pathways.

literature.disease_context: Enteroendocrine signaling pathways identified in Drosophila, particularly the NPF/NPY gut-brain axis and insulin/glucagon-like hormone cascades, are highly conserved in mammals and directly relevant to obesity, diabetes, and metabolic syndrome [1][2][4]. Dysregulation of gut-to-brain nutrient sensing may underlie maladaptive food choices, overeating, and related disorders. The observation that human incretins and their analogs, already used clinically to treat obesity and diabetes, may impact aging through mechanisms paralleling those in Drosophila highlights the translational significance of this model [2][4].

identified_gaps: The precise receptor subtypes and second-messenger cascades on insulin-producing neurons (IPCs) that transduce gut NPF signals into graded insulin secretion remain uncharacterized — clarifying this would define the full molecular logic of the nutrient-to-brain relay [2][4].

How EECs integrate simultaneous signals from multiple macronutrients (sugar, amino acids, fat) to produce a composite hormonal output is unknown; current studies address sugar and L-glutamate largely in isolation [1][5].

The identity and circuitry of the dopaminergic enteric neurons that relay NPF signals toward the brain have only been partially described; their axonal targets in the CNS and the downstream circuits governing macronutrient-specific food choice remain unmapped [5].

The sex- and mating-state specificity of gut NPF signaling in food choice and reproduction has been described phenomenologically, but the molecular mechanisms by which mating-induced steroid hormones reprogram EEC or enteric neuron output are not yet defined [1][7].

Whether the gut microbiota modulates EEC neuropeptide secretion (e.g., NPF) to shape food choice has not been directly tested in Drosophila, despite evidence that microbiota affects gut-brain communication and gut homeostasis [6][9][11].

The temporal dynamics of EEC hormone secretion in freely feeding animals — how rapidly NPF levels rise and fall in response to a meal, and how this kinetics translates into behavioral switching between sugar and protein food sources — have not been measured in real time [1][5].

evidence_claims.claim: Enteroendocrine cells of the adult female Drosophila midgut sense nutrients and in response release neuropeptide F (NPF), which is an ortholog of mammalian neuropeptide Y-family gut-brain hormones.

Gut-derived NPF acts on glucagon-like adipokinetic hormone (AKH) signalling to induce sugar satiety and increase consumption of protein-rich food, and on adipose tissue to promote storage of ingested nutrients.
Suppression of NPF-mediated gut signalling leads to overconsumption of dietary sugar while simultaneously decreasing intake of protein-rich yeast.
Gut-derived NPF has a female-specific function in promoting consumption of protein-containing food in mated females.

Gut NPF-to-AKH signalling modulates specific appetites and regulates food choice to ensure homeostatic consumption of nutrients, providing insight into the hormonal mechanisms that underlie nutrient-specific hungers.
Specific enteroendocrine cells differentially respond to dietary sugar and yeast.
Female lifespan is increased when gut NPF is genetically depleted, and this manipulation is sufficient to blunt the longevity benefit conferred by dietary restriction.
Depletion of NPF receptors at insulin-producing neurons of the brain also increases female lifespan, consistent with observations where loss of gut NPF decreases neuronal insulin secretion.
The longevity conferred by repressing gut NPF and brain NPF receptors is reversed by treating adults with a juvenile hormone (JH) analog.

Inhibition of the insulin receptor at the corpora allata decreases JH titer and extends lifespan in both males and females, while this longevity is restored to wild type by treating adults with a JH analog.

EEC of the gut modulate Drosophila aging through interorgan communication mediated by a gut-brain-corpora allata axis, and insulin produced in the brain impacts lifespan through its control of JH titer.
Human incretins and their analogs, which are used to treat obesity and diabetes, may impact aging.
Drosophila neuropeptide F (NPF) from mated female EECs inhibits feeding, similar to human PYY.
Dietary L-Glutamate acts through the metabotropic glutamate receptor mGluR to decelerate calcium oscillations in EECs, thereby causing reduced NPF secretion via dense-core vesicles.
Two dopaminergic enteric neurons expressing NPFR perceive EEC-derived NPF and relay an anorexigenic signal to the brain.
EECs directly percept dietary amino acids and secrete regulatory peptides, providing mechanistic insights into how EECs assess food quality.
Gut-innervating neurons with sex- and reproductive state-specific activity sustain the increased food intake of mothers during reproduction.

Steroid and enteroendocrine hormones functionally remodel enteric neurons, which leads to the release of their neuropeptide onto the muscles of the crop after mating, changing the dynamics of crop enlargement and resulting in increased food intake.
Preventing the post-mating remodelling of enteric neurons reduces both reproductive hyperphagia and reproductive fitness.

Sensing of nutrients by the gut plays a critical role in transmitting food-related signals to the brain and other tissues informing the composition of ingested food to digestive processes, and these signals modulate feeding behaviors, food intake, metabolism, insulin secretion, and energy balance.
Sleep loss caused by mechanical sleep deprivation and sss mutants disturbs ISC proliferation and intestinal epithelial repair through the brain-gut axis.
Gut microbiota and the GABA signalling pathway both partially played a role in the sss regulation of ISC proliferation and gut function.
Bidirectional communication between the gastrointestinal tract and the central nervous system is emerging as a fundamental regulatory principle across animal phyla.
The microbiota impacts the development of the gut and its communication with the nervous system.
Whether the gut microbiota modulates EEC neuropeptide secretion (e.g., NPF) to shape food choice has not been directly tested in Drosophila.

literature.summary: Drosophila enteroendocrine cells (EECs) act as nutrient sensors that translate dietary composition into hormonal signals shaping food choice and systemic physiology. The gut peptide NPF — ortholog of mammalian NPY/PYY — is secreted by EECs in response to dietary sugar and amino acids: L-glutamate sensed via mGluR dampens calcium oscillations in EECs to reduce NPF release, while elevated circulating NPF suppresses sugar appetite and promotes protein-food intake through AKH signaling and dopaminergic enteric neuron relays to the brain [1][5]. Beyond acute food choice, this gut-brain NPF axis modulates brain insulin-producing neuron activity, juvenile hormone titer from the corpora allata, and ultimately lifespan, establishing a conserved gut-brain-endocrine axis that integrates nutritional status with metabolic aging [2][4].

hypothesis.hypothesis: Gut enteroendocrine cell (EEC)-derived NPF signals to brain insulin-producing neurons (IPCs) via NPFR expressed on the two dopaminergic enteric relay neurons, and this relay is necessary and sufficient for macronutrient-specific food choice: specifically, we hypothesize that selective silencing of NPFR in dopaminergic enteric neurons will phenocopy EEC-specific NPF knockdown (≥30% increase in sucrose intake and ≥25% decrease in yeast intake relative to controls in a two-choice capillary feeding assay in mated female w1118 flies at 25°C, 12:12 LD), and that acute optogenetic activation of NPFR-expressing dopaminergic enteric neurons will suppress sucrose intake by ≥30% within 30 minutes of stimulation under the same conditions.
hypothesis.experimental_approach: We will use the split-GAL4 intersectional strategy to isolate the two NPFR-expressing dopaminergic enteric neurons identified in PMID 38664401, crossing a TH-GAL4 (dopaminergic) driver hemidrive with an NPFR-LexA or NPFR-GAL4 hemidrive to restrict expression to the relevant neurons. Food choice will be quantified using the two-choice capillary feeding assay (CAFE) with 5% sucrose vs. 5% yeast extract solutions over 24-hour intervals in individual vials; total intake, macronutrient preference index (PI = [sucrose consumed − yeast consumed] / [sucrose + yeast consumed]), and meal bout frequency/duration will be recorded. For loss-of-function, UAS-Kir2.1 (electrical silencing) and UAS-npfr-RNAi lines will be expressed in NPFR dopaminergic enteric neurons; for gain-of-function, UAS-CsChrimson will enable red-light (620 nm, 20 µW/mm²) optogenetic activation of these neurons in freely feeding flies on all-trans retinal-supplemented food. Controls will include: (1) driver-only crosses (no UAS effector), (2) UAS-only crosses (no driver), (3) UAS-mCD8-GFP crosses for anatomical confirmation of split-GAL4 specificity, and (4) virgin vs. mated female cohorts to assess reproductive-state dependence. Downstream IPC activity will be assessed by in vivo calcium imaging (UAS-GCaMP7s in dilp2-GAL4 IPCs) combined with ex vivo gut-to-brain preparation during nutrient perfusion experiments to determine whether enteric neuron silencing blunts the IPC calcium response to sucrose stimulation. All experiments will use ≥10 biological replicates per genotype per condition; statistical analysis will use one-way ANOVA with Tukey's post hoc correction, α = 0.05.

hypothesis.expected_outcomes: Aim 1: Silencing NPFR in TH∩NPFR dopaminergic enteric neurons will increase the sucrose preference index by ≥0.30 units (absolute) relative to driver-only and UAS-only controls (expected PI shift from ~0.0 to ≥+0.30) and decrease yeast intake by ≥25%, measured over 24 h in mated female flies. This result would confirm necessity of the dopaminergic relay. Aim 2: CsChrimson-mediated acute activation of the same neurons (30 min red-light pulse) will reduce sucrose intake by ≥30% relative to non-stimulated retinal-fed controls and non-retinal red-light controls, confirming sufficiency. Aim 3: IPC GCaMP7s calcium responses to gut sucrose perfusion will be reduced by ≥40% (ΔF/F peak amplitude) when the dopaminergic enteric neurons are simultaneously silenced with Kir2.1, compared to Kir2.1-absent controls, establishing the mechanistic link between the enteric relay and IPC activity. Virgin females are predicted to show attenuated effects relative to mated females (consistent with PMID 36344765 sex-specificity findings). All comparisons require p < 0.05 after Tukey correction with n ≥ 10 per group.
hypothesis.novelty_claim: Existing work (PMID 38664401) identified two NPFR-expressing dopaminergic enteric neurons as mediators of the gut NPF-to-brain relay but did not (1) functionally establish their necessity and sufficiency for macronutrient-specific food choice using bidirectional manipulations, (2) map their axonal targets in the CNS, or (3) link their activity causally to downstream IPC calcium dynamics. This experiment fills the gap explicitly identified in the literature synthesis: 'The identity and circuitry of the dopaminergic enteric neurons that relay NPF signals toward the brain have only been partially described; their axonal targets in the CNS and the downstream circuits governing macronutrient-specific food choice remain unmapped.' Additionally, no prior study has combined optogenetic gain-of-function with calcium imaging of IPCs in the same experimental framework to close the circuit from gut EEC → enteric dopaminergic relay → brain IPC.
hypothesis.feasibility_notes: The core behavioral assays (CAFE two-choice) and GAL4/UAS manipulations are standard in Drosophila neuroscience and are achievable in a well-equipped fly lab. The primary technical challenge is the split-GAL4 intersection: if existing NPFR-GAL4 or LexA drivers do not recapitulate the precise two-neuron expression pattern described in PMID 38664401, CRISPR-mediated T2A-GAL4 knock-in at the npfr locus may be required (~3–6 additional months). Ex vivo gut-brain calcium imaging requires intact semi-dissected preparations with nutrient perfusion, which demands training but is established in the field. Estimated timeline: Aim 1 behavioral characterization 3–4 months; Aim 2 optogenetics 2–3 months; Aim 3 calcium imaging 4–6 months; total ~12–18 months. identified_gaps: Causality is not resolved by the provided abstracts: [1] shows barrier dysfunction predicts death, whereas [2] only describes an emerging concept that targeting barrier integrity promotes longevity. Fly experiments that restore barrier integrity (e.g., tissue-specific tight/septate junction or enterocyte-protective manipulations) after onset of dysfunction, with lifespan and mortality as readouts, would distinguish cause from marker.

The upstream trigger of spontaneous age-onset barrier failure is unclear. Diet-induced disruption involves enterocyte complex III superoxide and Hif-1α [3], but whether the same mechanism operates in normally aged flies on standard diet is untested in the provided literature.

The relative contributions of microbiota change, immune activation and stem cell dysfunction to barrier failure are not separated; the supplied reviews describe associations [2][4][6]. Germ-free or gnotobiotic flies, with AMP and ISC manipulations and barrier-failure timing measured per individual, would clarify their order.

The relationship between insulin/IGF-FOXO signaling and barrier failure is only correlative: [1] reports reduced Akt activation and dFOXO target upregulation in barrier-compromised flies, but [10] finds dietary restriction extends lifespan without dFOXO. Whether dietary restriction delays barrier failure through an IIS-independent route is untested.

Non-autonomous control of gut barrier by other tissues is only partly characterized: neuronal BNIP3 mitophagy improves intestinal homeostasis [5], but whether it specifically delays barrier failure or the barrier is the mediator of lifespan extension is not established.

literature.summary: In Drosophila, intestinal barrier dysfunction strongly predicts imminent death independent of chronological age and tracks with immune activation and metabolic signaling changes [1]. Evidence that barrier integrity is causal is suggestive, from reviews citing fly and mouse interventions [2], and a diet-induced trigger via enterocyte mitochondrial superoxide is shown [3]. The supplied literature does not resolve the triggers of spontaneous age-onset failure or definitively separate cause from marker.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Proposed (not established): In mated female flies on standard diet at 25°C, adult-onset, enterocyte-specific inhibition of complex III superoxide signaling, by S3QEL feeding or enterocyte Hif-1α knockdown started at day 20, will delay median time to Smurf (barrier-failure) conversion by at least 15% and extend median lifespan by at least 10% versus vehicle or control-RNAi flies (log-rank p<0.01). The same interventions started only after an individual fly converts to Smurf will extend median post-Smurf survival by at least 25%. If Smurf delay occurs without lifespan extension, or post-Smurf intervention has no effect, barrier failure is more likely a marker than a cause.
hypothesis.experimental_approach: Use a longitudinal, individual-fly Smurf assay (blue food dye) in mated females to record the time of barrier failure and the survival that follows it. Drive enterocyte-restricted, adult-inducible manipulations with an enterocyte GeneSwitch or TubGAL80ts-controlled driver to avoid developmental effects. The manipulations are Hif-1α RNAi and a pharmacological S3QEL arm, each with matched controls (control RNAi plus RU486 or temperature shift; vehicle-fed). Intervention timing is a three-way design: from day 20 (pre-failure), from day 40 or at first Smurf conversion (post-onset), and never. Secondary readouts are Dpt and Drs transcript levels by qPCR in dissected guts from pre-Smurf versus Smurf flies, to confirm barrier-linked immune activation. Barrier integrity is confirmed by a second permeability measure, and enterocyte apoptosis is assessed by staining. Axenic versus conventionally reared flies are compared to place microbiota in the sequence of events. Lifespan cohorts of at least 200 flies per arm are used, with Cox regression and a Smurf-state time-varying covariate.
