literature.summary: The supplied literature identifies tau-toxicity modifiers (synapse- and Ca2+ homeostasis-related genes, HNRNPA2B1, MEPCE) [1][6] and reports Hsp70 as a suppressor in polyglutamine and Parkinson's disease fly models [8]. It contains no TDP-43 fly data, so no modifier can be shown to act across tau, α-synuclein and TDP-43 models; this negative conclusion is an inference from the limited set. The cross-model question needs direct parallel testing of candidate modifiers.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Proposed (not established): In a single-driver, single-readout parallel comparison, neuronal overexpression of Hsp70 (e.g., Hsp70Aa/Hsp70Ab) will suppress neurodegeneration in all three models (human tau, human alpha-synuclein, human TDP-43) at 25°C. Specifically, in the GMR-GAL4 eye model, Hsp70 co-expression will reduce the ommatidial degeneration score by ≥30% relative to UAS-LacZ (or UAS-GFP) co-expression controls (n≥15 eyes per genotype, ≥3 independent crosses, Bonferroni-corrected p<0.01), and in the elav-GAL4 adult model it will improve day-30 climbing performance by ≥25%. In contrast, RNAi knockdown of the tau enhancers HNRNPA2B1 and MEPCE orthologs will modify tau toxicity but will change alpha-synuclein and TDP-43 toxicity by <15% (i.e., be tau-selective). This hypothesis will be rejected if Hsp70 suppresses fewer than three models by ≥30% or if the tau-enhancer orthologs shift all three models by ≥15% in the same direction.
hypothesis.experimental_approach: Use the GAL4/UAS system with a matched design: the same driver (GMR-GAL4 for the eye, elav-GAL4 for pan-neuronal adult phenotypes), the same temperature (25°C), the same genetic background, and the same blinded quantitative readouts (external eye degeneration score or eye-area quantification; day-30 negative geotaxis; TUNEL or vacuole counting in brain sections) for UAS-tau, UAS-alpha-synuclein and UAS-TDP-43. Because tau modifier eye-screen protocols are available (Dourlen et al. 2024), they will be adapted as the readout framework. Candidate modifiers are Hsp70 (a suppressor in polyglutamine and Parkinson's disease fly models; Bonini et al. 2002), the fly orthologs of HNRNPA2B1 and MEPCE (tau enhancers; Leventhal et al. 2025) and synaptic/Ca2+ homeostasis genes (tau modifiers; Praschberger et al. 2023). Candidates will be tested by overexpression or RNAi, with UAS-LacZ/GFP and a UAS-RNAi control (e.g., mCherry RNAi or white RNAi) for dosage-matched GAL4 titration. Transgene expression (western blot or qPCR) will be measured to rule out modifier effects on proteinopathy transgene levels, and a modifier will be classed as 'pan-proteinopathy' only if it passes the threshold in all three models with the same sign.

hypothesis.expected_outcomes: Proposed predictions: (1) each proteinopathy transgene will produce a reproducible eye or climbing phenotype in the matched system. (2) Hsp70 co-expression will lower the degeneration score ≥30% in all three eye models and improve day-30 climbing ≥25% (one-way ANOVA with Tukey/Bonferroni, p<0.01) with no reduction in transgene protein level >20%; reduction in transgene level would classify the effect as expression-mediated. (3) HNRNPA2B1- and MEPCE-ortholog knockdown will alter tau toxicity (direction to be determined, because the screen reported them as tau enhancers) but change alpha-synuclein and TDP-43 phenotypes by <15%, indicating tau selectivity. (4) If Hsp70 fails in one model (e.g., TDP-43), that is a meaningful negative result showing partial overlap only. Overall, we expect 0 to 2 modifiers among those tested to meet the all-three criterion.
hypothesis.novelty_claim: The supplied literature contains no TDP-43 fly model or modifier data, and only Praschberger et al. (2023) compares alpha-synuclein and tau in the same system. Hsp70 is reported to suppress polyglutamine and Parkinson's disease phenotypes (Bonini et al. 2002), but its effect on tau, alpha-synuclein-specific or TDP-43 toxicity is not shown in the supplied abstracts, and HNRNPA2B1/MEPCE have not been reported to be tested outside tau (Leventhal et al. 2025). Existing screens use non-comparable readouts (Yang et al. 2023; Dourlen et al. 2024). This design directly fills these gaps with a harmonized three-model, one-driver, one-readout comparison.
hypothesis.feasibility_notes: Estimated 12-15 months: months 1-3 line acquisition, verification and recombination/standardization of transgene strength; months 3-7 eye screen of candidates across the three models; months 7-12 elav-GAL4 climbing and histology of hits, plus expression controls; months 12-15 replication and analysis. Pitfalls: UAS-transgene insertion site and strength differences will confound cross-model comparison (mitigate by using same-landing-site lines or adjusting expression and quantifying protein); GAL4 titration by multiple UAS elements (controlled by dosage-matched UAS controls); eye phenotypes may be too severe or mild for TDP-43 (tune temperature or driver); ortholog assignment for MEPCE and HNRNPA2B1 requires verification; RNAi off-target effects require two independent lines; eye phenotypes may not reflect adult neuronal degeneration (hence the elav validation).
specific_aims: Aim 1: Harmonized models — establish matched GMR-GAL4 and elav-GAL4 tau, alpha-synuclein and TDP-43 fly models with quantified, blinded degeneration readouts and equalized transgene expression.
Aim 2: Hsp70 cross-model test — determine whether Hsp70 overexpression suppresses degeneration by ≥30% in each of the three models independent of changes in transgene protein level.

Aim 3: Tau-enhancer specificity — test whether knockdown of HNRNPA2B1 and MEPCE orthologs and selected synaptic/Ca2+ homeostasis modifiers is tau-selective or also modifies alpha-synuclein and TDP-43 toxicity by ≥15%.

literature.disease_context: Identifying genetic modifiers that suppress neurodegeneration across multiple proteinopathy models — tau, alpha-synuclein, and TDP-43 — is critical for uncovering shared therapeutic targets for Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, and ALS/FTD. Drosophila provides a powerful platform for unbiased genetic screens that can reveal cell-type-intrinsic vulnerability factors and pathway-level suppressors relevant to human disease [1][6][8][13]. Modifiers acting across all three models would represent prime candidates for broadly neuroprotective interventions, though the current literature provides limited direct evidence for genes that simultaneously suppress all three proteinopathies.

identified_gaps: No single gene has been demonstrated in the provided literature to suppress neurodegeneration across all three models (tau, alpha-synuclein, AND TDP-43) simultaneously — this explicit cross-model comparison has not yet been performed in the studies surveyed, and targeted screens designed to test the same modifier panel in all three fly proteinopathy models are needed.

Hsp70 suppresses polyglutamine and Parkinson's disease (alpha-synuclein) phenotypes in Drosophila [8], but its functional effect on tau and TDP-43 toxicity specifically has not been addressed in the provided literature, leaving its candidacy as a universal suppressor unverified.

The synapse- and Ca2+ homeostasis-related genes identified as tau toxicity modifiers [1] have not been tested in alpha-synuclein or TDP-43 fly models in the provided studies, making it unknown whether these modifiers are tau-specific or represent shared vulnerability mechanisms.

TDP-43 proteinopathy models are mentioned in the context of ALS in the review [13] but no specific genetic modifiers of TDP-43 toxicity are identified or tested in the provided literature, representing a critical gap for cross-model comparisons.

The HNRNPA2B1 and MEPCE modifiers of tau toxicity identified by the integrative screen [6] have not been evaluated in alpha-synuclein or TDP-43 fly models, and it is unknown whether their effects are tau-selective or broadly neuroprotective.

All modifier screens identified in the provided literature focus on neuronal survival or morphological readouts (rough eye); functional cross-validation of modifier effects on behavioral phenotypes (locomotion, memory) across tau, alpha-synuclein, and TDP-43 models is lacking.

literature.summary: The provided literature identifies several classes of genetic modifiers that suppress tau toxicity in Drosophila — including synapse- and Ca2+-homeostasis-related genes [1], HNRNPA2B1/MEPCE/CSNK2A1/NOTCH1 [6], lipophorin receptors lpr1/lpr2 [5], and broadly the chaperone Hsp70 which acts across polyglutamine and alpha-synuclein (Parkinson's disease) models [8]. However, no single modifier has been directly demonstrated across tau, alpha-synuclein, AND TDP-43 fly models in the available studies; Hsp70 is the strongest cross-model candidate but its tau and TDP-43 activity has not been confirmed in the provided literature. A critical gap is the absence of any TDP-43-specific modifier data in the surveyed papers, making definitive identification of genes acting in all three proteinopathy models impossible from this literature alone.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Overexpression of Hsp70 (UAS-Hsp70) pan-neuronally (elav-GAL4) will suppress neurodegeneration by ≥30% (measured as ommatidial disorganization score in the eye) and improve climbing speed by ≥25% relative to disease-model controls in all three Drosophila proteinopathy models — human tau (UAS-tauV337M), human alpha-synuclein (UAS-αSyn-A53T), and human TDP-43 (UAS-TDP-43) — tested in a w1118 background at 25°C, thereby identifying Hsp70 as a pan-proteinopathy suppressor; and a secondary panel of five candidate synaptic/Ca2+-homeostasis genes identified from single-cell transcriptomics (including EB1 and dTau) will suppress neurodegeneration in ≥2 of 3 models by ≥20%, establishing partial cross-model suppressor activity.
hypothesis.experimental_approach: Three established Drosophila eye-degeneration and behavioral models will be built using the GAL4/UAS system driven by elav-GAL4 (pan-neuronal) for behavioral assays and GMR-GAL4 (eye-specific) for morphological screens: (1) UAS-tauV337M, (2) UAS-αSyn-A53T, and (3) UAS-TDP-43WT or UAS-TDP-43G298S. Each disease model will be crossed to UAS-Hsp70 (co-expression via UAS-Hsp70; elav-GAL4 or GMR-GAL4) and to UAS-RNAi lines targeting five candidate synaptic/Ca2+-homeostasis genes (EB1, dTau, and three additional top candidates from PMID 36948206 to be selected after full-text review). Primary readouts will be: (a) quantitative scoring of external eye roughness and deep pseudopupil integrity at day 10 post-eclosion (GMR-GAL4 crosses), (b) negative geotaxis climbing assay (RING assay, 10-day and 20-day time points, elav-GAL4 crosses), and (c) lifespan analysis. Controls will include: disease model alone (GAL4 + UAS-disease gene), UAS-Hsp70 or UAS-RNAi alone (no disease transgene), GAL4 alone, and w1118 wild-type. All experiments will use ≥100 flies per genotype per assay replicated across ≥3 independent biological replicates with the experimenter blinded to genotype during scoring.

hypothesis.expected_outcomes: Aim 1: Hsp70 overexpression will reduce ommatidial disorganization (GMR-GAL4 crosses, day 10) by ≥30% vs. disease-model controls in the alpha-synuclein model (consistent with PMID 12149445), and by ≥30% in the tau model and TDP-43 model (proposed, unverified). A ≥25% improvement in 10-day climbing speed (RING assay, elav-GAL4 crosses) is expected in all three models. Failure to reach these thresholds in any model will indicate model-specific limits of Hsp70 suppression. Aim 2: At least 2 of 5 candidate synaptic/Ca2+ homeostasis gene RNAi lines will suppress neurodegeneration by ≥20% in ≥2 of 3 disease models; genes that suppress all three at ≥20% will be designated pan-proteinopathy modifiers. Aim 3: Lifespan extension of ≥10% over disease-model controls is expected for Hsp70 co-expression in elav-GAL4-driven tau and TDP-43 models. Statistical analysis will use one-way ANOVA with Tukey post-hoc correction (p < 0.05) for eye scores and climbing assays, and log-rank test for lifespan (p < 0.05, n ≥ 100 per group). All negative results are interpretable as evidence against Hsp70 universality.
hypothesis.novelty_claim: The literature synthesis explicitly identifies that 'no single gene has been demonstrated in the provided literature to suppress neurodegeneration across all three models (tau, alpha-synuclein, AND TDP-43) simultaneously' and that 'Hsp70 suppresses polyglutamine and Parkinson's disease (alpha-synuclein) phenotypes in Drosophila, but its functional effect on tau and TDP-43 toxicity specifically has not been addressed in the provided literature.' Additionally, 'synapse- and Ca2+ homeostasis-related genes identified as tau toxicity modifiers have not been tested in alpha-synuclein or TDP-43 fly models,' and 'functional cross-validation of modifier effects on behavioral phenotypes across tau, alpha-synuclein, and TDP-43 models is lacking.' This study directly fills these gaps by performing the first systematic, side-by-side cross-model validation of Hsp70 and synaptic/Ca2+-homeostasis modifiers in all three proteinopathy fly models using both morphological and behavioral endpoints.
hypothesis.feasibility_notes: All three disease models (tau, alpha-synuclein, TDP-43) are well-established in Drosophila and have been used in multiple labs; the GAL4/UAS system is routine. The primary technical risk is sourcing the exact UAS-tauV337M, UAS-αSyn-A53T, and UAS-TDP-43 lines with confirmed expression levels — these must be obtained from originating labs or verified BDSC stocks before crosses begin. A key pitfall is variation in transgene insertion site and expression level across lines, which could confound cross-model comparisons; UAS-GFP controls should be included to verify GAL4 driver activity. Temperature sensitivity of GAL4 expression (25°C standard) must be maintained consistently. Blind scoring of eye roughness requires training and inter-rater reliability checks. Estimated timeline: 3 months for line acquisition and verification; 4 months for cross setup and F1 collection; 4 months for behavioral assays and lifespan; 2 months for data analysis and histology — total approximately 13 months. The secondary candidate panel (synaptic/Ca2+ genes) requires full-text review of PMID 36948206 to finalize gene selection, which is a prerequisite before ordering RNAi lines.
specific_aims: Aim 1: Hsp70 as pan-proteinopathy suppressor — Test whether UAS-Hsp70 co-expression with elav-GAL4 and GMR-GAL4 suppresses neurodegeneration (eye disorganization ≥30%, climbing speed improvement ≥25%) in tau-V337M, alpha-synuclein-A53T, and TDP-43 fly models simultaneously

Aim 2: Synaptic/Ca2+ homeostasis modifiers across models — Screen five candidate synaptic and Ca2+-homeostasis gene RNAi lines (including EB1 and dTau, derived from PMID 36948206) for suppression of neurodegeneration in all three proteinopathy models, identifying modifiers active in ≥2 of 3 models

Aim 3: Behavioral and lifespan cross-validation — Validate top cross-model suppressors from Aims 1-2 using longitudinal climbing (RING assay, days 1, 10, 20) and lifespan assays (elav-GAL4 background) to determine whether morphological suppression translates to functional neurological rescue across proteinopathy models

hypothesis.hypothesis: Proposed: In a blinded, pre-specified benchmark of 72 ClinVar-classified missense variants (36 pathogenic/likely pathogenic and 36 benign/likely benign) across 6 genes with fly orthologs, a two-assay humanized Drosophila pipeline will classify variants as functionally abnormal or normal with sensitivity ≥80% and specificity ≥90% against clinical classification (Cohen's kappa ≥0.6). The pipeline combines T2A-GAL4 rescue of ortholog loss with GAL4/UAS overexpression of human cDNA, and each variant is compared with the reference allele at a single attP site. Rescue-only scoring will show ≥25 percentage points lower sensitivity than the combined pipeline for gain-of-function variants (as for MRTFB), which will make the combined readout necessary for scalable VUS classification.
hypothesis.experimental_approach: For each of 6 genes (to be selected for a fly ortholog with a scorable null phenotype, e.g. lethality or a viable morphological defect, and ≥10 ClinVar P/LP plus ≥10 B/LB missense variants; selection requires verification), a T2A-GAL4 gene-replacement or knock-in allele will be generated or sourced, and UAS-human cDNA reference and variant constructs will be integrated at the same attP landing site to equalize expression. Assay 1 is rescue of the T2A-GAL4 loss-of-function phenotype by reference versus variant cDNA, scored as fraction of expected eclosion, lifespan, or climbing as appropriate. Assay 2 is overexpression with a ubiquitous driver and a tissue-restricted driver (e.g. a wing-pouch or neuronal driver), scored for wing or eye morphology, viability, or locomotion, including MRTFB-like gain-of-function readouts. Variants will be coded and scored blind, with transgene expression verified by western blot or qPCR, and with reference cDNA, empty-vector, and known-null variant controls in every batch. Thresholds for 'abnormal' will be fixed before unblinding as >2 SD from the reference-allele distribution with Benjamini-Hochberg-corrected p<0.05. Concordance will be reported as sensitivity, specificity, and kappa with 95% Wilson confidence intervals, stratified by gene, mechanism (LoF vs GoF), and assay.

hypothesis.novelty_claim: The literature synthesis shows that no supplied paper quantifies concordance between fly assay outcomes and clinical variant classification across a variant set. The MRTFB study covers only two variants [37013900], the UDN protocol allows any scorable phenotype without reported false-positive or false-negative rates [31498321], and humanization resources are described without throughput or cost estimates [29951825]. Aim 3: Prospectively classify VUS — test ~30 VUS in the validated genes, issue fly-based calls before clinical review, and compare them with subsequent clinical reclassification or segregation evidence.

literature.disease_context: Humanized Drosophila models provide a scalable in vivo platform for classifying human variants of uncertain significance (VUS), particularly in rare neurodevelopmental and neurodegenerative diseases where clinical data are sparse [1][2]. By replacing the endogenous fly ortholog with a human reference or variant transgene, differences in organismal phenotype can distinguish pathogenic from benign alleles and can reveal gain-of-function versus loss-of-function mechanisms [1][2]. This approach has direct relevance to human conditions ranging from undiagnosed neurodevelopmental syndromes to Alzheimer's disease risk-gene biology [1][4].

literature.summary: Humanized Drosophila models — in which the endogenous fly gene is replaced by a human reference or variant transgene and evaluated through rescue and overexpression assays — represent a scalable, in vivo platform for functional classification of VUS, as demonstrated by the UDN Drosophila Core protocol [2] and applied to de novo MRTFB variants that were classified as gain-of-function through wing morphology and actin-binding readouts [1]. The Drosophila toolkit, including GAL4/UAS-human-ORF lines and MARRVEL-guided variant prioritization, lowers the barrier to rapid cross-species functional studies for both coding and, to a lesser extent, noncoding variants [2][3]. However, the provided literature does not report systematic, quantitative concordance between fly-based VUS classifications and independent clinical or ClinVar adjudications, leaving the actual accuracy and scalability of this approach in need of rigorous benchmarking.

hypothesis.hypothesis: A standardized two-pronged GAL4/UAS humanization pipeline applied to ≥50 human VUS across ≥5 genes (MRTFB, ABCA1, ABCA7, PICALM, and one additional AD-risk gene) with established ClinVar pathogenicity adjudications will achieve ≥80% concordance between fly-based functional classifications (pathogenic vs. benign) and clinical ground-truth labels, as measured by sensitivity and specificity of wing morphology rescue scores, viability indices, and neuronal lipid droplet formation assays under 25°C standard conditions in w1118 background flies.
hypothesis.experimental_approach: We propose a benchmarking study using the two-pronged UAS/GAL4 rescue-plus-overexpression workflow (Harnish et al. 2019, PMID 31498321) applied to a curated panel of ≥50 coding missense VUS drawn from ClinVar with known Pathogenic (P), Likely Pathogenic (LP), Benign (B), or Likely Benign (LB) interpretations, spanning MRTFB, ABCA1, ABCA7, PICALM, and VPS35. For each gene, the endogenous fly ortholog will be replaced via T2A-GAL4 knock-in or MiMIC insertion with a UAS-human-reference or UAS-human-variant cDNA transgene; viability/rescue of lethal or morphological null phenotype (wing, eye, or neuronal) will be the primary readout. As a secondary assay, a ROS-induced neuronal lipid droplet formation assay (adapted from Moulton et al. 2021, PMID 34949639) will be applied to humanized lines for ABCA1, ABCA7, and PICALM to provide a pathway-relevant, quantitative neuronal endpoint. All variant classification calls from flies will be made blinded to ClinVar status by two independent scorers, and concordance (sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value) will be computed against ClinVar P/LP vs. B/LB ground truth using a pre-registered analysis plan. Appropriate controls include wildtype w1118, null-ortholog (rescue-negative), and human-reference-transgene lines for each gene.

hypothesis.expected_outcomes: Primary outcome: ≥80% overall concordance (sensitivity ≥75%, specificity ≥80%) between fly-based classifications and ClinVar P/LP vs. B/LB ground truth across ≥50 VUS. We predict that rescue-positive (viability restored to ≥70% of wildtype) and morphology-normal variants will classify as B/LB, while rescue-negative or morphology-disrupted variants will classify as P/LP. For the lipid droplet assay, we predict that variants in ABCA1, ABCA7, and PICALM classified as P/LP will reduce glial lipid droplet number by ≥30% relative to reference-transgene controls under ROS induction, consistent with the loss-of-function effects documented in PMID 34949639. Inter-rater reliability between blinded scorers should reach κ ≥ 0.75. Discordant cases (fly P/LP but ClinVar B/LB, or vice versa) will be catalogued as a secondary outcome to identify gene-specific or assay-specific failure modes. Statistical thresholds: Fisher's exact test for concordance, p < 0.05; 95% confidence intervals reported for sensitivity and specificity.
hypothesis.novelty_claim: The literature synthesis explicitly identifies the absence of quantitative concordance data between fly VUS classifications and clinical/ClinVar adjudications as the primary unaddressed gap: 'No quantitative concordance data between fly VUS classifications and clinical/ClinVar adjudications are reported in the provided literature — the scale and accuracy of agreement between fly functional results and established clinical classifications remains unmeasured.' No paper in the synthesis reports sensitivity, specificity, or PPV of fly-based calls against a clinical ground truth at scale. Additionally, the synthesis notes that throughput and scalability benchmarks are entirely absent from the provided papers. This study is the first proposed systematic, blinded benchmarking of the two-pronged humanization pipeline across multiple genes and ≥50 variants with pre-registered concordance metrics, directly addressing both gaps. Furthermore, the integration of a pathway-relevant neuronal lipid droplet assay for AD-risk gene VUS (extending PMID 34949639) alongside rescue/morphology endpoints provides a multi-assay classification framework not present in any cited work.
hypothesis.feasibility_notes: The two-pronged GAL4/UAS humanization workflow is technically established (PMID 31498321) and the Drosophila genetic toolkit for gene replacement is mature (PMID 29951825). Key technical challenges include: (1) generating ≥50 site-directed variant transgenes via PhiC31 integration into matched attP sites — estimated 6–8 months for cloning, injection, and line establishment; (2) identifying ≥50 ClinVar-adjudicated P/LP and B/LB coding missense VUS with sufficient balance across the 5 target genes — feasible given ClinVar database scale but requires careful curation to avoid VUS-labeled entries; (3) ensuring sufficient fly-human orthology for humanization to be informative — MRTFB, ABCA1, PICALM, and VPS35 have well-documented fly orthologs, but conservation scores should be confirmed via MARRVEL before committing to a gene. Potential pitfalls: low penetrance of rescue phenotypes for some variants may require scoring ≥100 adult flies per genotype; the lipid droplet assay requires confocal imaging and is lower-throughput than wing scoring. Estimated overall timeline: 18–24 months (6–8 months transgene generation, 6 months phenotypic scoring, 4 months data analysis and concordance calculation). Cost is dominated by injection services (~$300–500 per line) and confocal imaging time.

identified_gaps: The cacophony study used Drosophila primary neuronal cultures and the toxin MPP+ [2]; it is not known whether cac-dependent Ca2+ load differs between the vulnerable parkin-null cluster and non-degenerating dopaminergic clusters in vivo. Cluster-resolved Ca2+ imaging in intact park mutants would test this.

In parkin-null flies, sustained mitochondrial H2O2 elevation marks vulnerable neurons [4], but whether it causes degeneration or is a consequence remains unresolved. Folic acid improved survival and climbing yet did not mitigate whole-brain oxidative stress, and its H2O2 effect was only transient. Cluster-specific manipulation of mitochondrial glutathione or H2O2 scavengers would test causality.

The DGRP screen identified SNP-associated genes for dopaminergic loss [3], but the abstract does not say whether these genes act cell-autonomously in specific dopaminergic subtypes or converge on Ca2+, redox, or ER stress pathways. Subtype-resolved expression and knockdown analysis is needed.

Inference: the DOPAL hypothesis [1] is a review-level proposal and is not tested in the supplied fly papers. Testing whether subtype-specific dopamine synthesis or metabolism (for example DOPAL accumulation) tracks with fly vulnerability would link it to the selective loss.

TMBIM6 is reduced in vulnerable human dopaminergic neurons [5], but the fly experiment used whole-animal TMBIM6 downregulation with rotenone. It is unknown whether UPR/IRE1a signaling differs between vulnerable and resistant fly dopaminergic clusters.

literature.summary: Fly work supports several non-exclusive candidate explanations for selective dopaminergic vulnerability: Ca2+ channel dependence [2], sustained mitochondrial H2O2 and glutathione redox dysregulation in vulnerable parkin-null neurons compared with non-degenerating neighbors [4], and natural genetic variation [3]. These mechanisms have not been integrated, and the dopamine-metabolite hypothesis [1] comes from review rather than fly data. Papers [8]-[12] concern other topics (Alzheimer's models, ethanol and ion channels, aging memory, adipose-brain signaling) and were not used to support the conclusions.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Proposed (not established): in park null (park25/park25) flies at 25°C, the vulnerable dopaminergic cluster has higher cac-dependent cytosolic Ca2+ load than a non-degenerating dopaminergic cluster, and this Ca2+ load acts upstream of sustained mitochondrial H2O2 elevation and neuron loss. Specifically, (a) baseline and depolarization-evoked GCaMP signal will be ≥30% higher in vulnerable than in resistant neurons of park nulls; (b) cac RNAi restricted to dopaminergic neurons will reduce mitochondrial H2O2 (roGFP2-Orp1 oxidation) in the vulnerable cluster by ≥30% and rescue ≥50% of neuron loss at day 30; and (c) mitochondria-targeted H2O2 scavenging will rescue neuron loss without lowering cac-dependent Ca2+ signals.
hypothesis.experimental_approach: Use park25 homozygous and heterozygous control flies (allele identity to be verified) with GAL4/UAS tools. Cluster-resolved drivers (TH-GAL4 as a pan-dopaminergic driver, plus split-GAL4 lines for the vulnerable and resistant clusters, which require verification) will express cytosolic GCaMP, mito-roGFP2-Orp1 or mito-roGFP2-Grx1 sensors, and cac RNAi or a mitochondrial H2O2 scavenger. Ex vivo whole-brain imaging will measure Ca2+ and redox signals separately in the vulnerable and resistant clusters at days 5, 15 and 30. Neuron survival will be scored by anti-TH immunostaining with blinded cluster counts, and climbing (negative geotaxis) will be measured as a behavioral readout. Controls are park/+ siblings, driver-only and UAS-only genotypes, a second non-overlapping cac RNAi, and a non-targeting RNAi. Epistasis will be tested by comparing cac knockdown, mitochondrial scavenger expression, and both together in park nulls, in both sexes, with sex-stratified analysis.

hypothesis.expected_outcomes: Proposed predictions: park nulls will show ≥30% higher Ca2+ signal in the vulnerable cluster than in the resistant cluster (p<0.05, mixed-effects model, n≥10 brains per genotype and age). cac RNAi will reduce vulnerable-cluster mito-roGFP2-Orp1 oxidation by ≥30% and increase surviving neuron counts by ≥50% of the park-null deficit at day 30. The mitochondrial scavenger will improve survival without changing GCaMP signals, which would place H2O2 downstream of Ca2+. If cac knockdown fails to change H2O2, or if the vulnerable cluster does not show higher Ca2+ load, the hypothesis is falsified. A scavenger that rescues survival while cac knockdown does not would indicate a Ca2+-independent source of H2O2.
hypothesis.novelty_claim: Parkin-null flies show sustained mitochondrial H2O2 elevation in vulnerable but not neighboring non-degenerating dopaminergic neurons [36290790], and cacophony-mutant dopaminergic neurons resist MPP+ toxicity in primary cultures [25445363]. The literature synthesis notes that it is not known whether cac-dependent Ca2+ load differs between vulnerable and non-degenerating clusters in vivo, and that causality of H2O2 elevation remains unresolved. This plan tests the two mechanisms together in intact park mutants with cluster-resolved readouts.
hypothesis.feasibility_notes: Estimated 14-18 months: 3 months for line acquisition, verification and cluster driver validation; 5 months for imaging (Aim 1); 6 months for knockdown and rescue with aging to day 30 (Aims 2-3); 2-3 months for analysis. Pitfalls: ex vivo Ca2+ imaging may not reflect in vivo activity; roGFP sensors need calibration with DTT and diamide; RNAi efficiency and off-target effects need two independent lines; cac is essential, so strong knockdown could cause developmental or behavioral confounds (consider temporal control with tub-GAL80ts); park nulls may have modest neuron loss and age-dependent variability, requiring adequate power. Cluster-specific drivers may not exist for every cluster of interest.
specific_aims: Aim 1: Cluster-resolved Ca2+ and redox profiling — measure GCaMP and mito-roGFP2 signals in vulnerable vs resistant dopaminergic clusters of park nulls and controls at days 5, 15 and 30.
Aim 2: Necessity of cac — test whether dopaminergic-neuron-specific cac knockdown lowers mitochondrial H2O2 and rescues neuron loss and climbing in park nulls.
Aim 3: Causal order of Ca2+ and H2O2 — test whether mitochondrial H2O2 scavenging rescues degeneration without altering cac-dependent Ca2+ signals, and whether combined manipulation is additive.

literature.disease_context: Selective vulnerability of specific dopaminergic neuron populations is a defining feature of Parkinson's disease (PD), mirroring the human substantia nigra pars compacta degeneration seen clinically. Drosophila models expressing PD-associated genes (parkin, pink1, SNCA) or exposed to dopaminergic toxins (MPP+, rotenone, 6-OHDA) recapitulate this selective loss, allowing mechanistic dissection of why neighboring neurons survive [4][5][7]. Understanding the cell-intrinsic factors—including calcium dysregulation, mitochondrial oxidative stress, ER stress, and dopamine metabolite toxicity—that render specific neurons vulnerable may reveal therapeutic targets applicable to human PD.

identified_gaps: The parkin-null fly model shows that vulnerable DA neuron clusters have sustained mitochondrial H2O2 elevation while non-degenerating neighboring DA neurons show only transient increases [4], but the molecular basis for this difference in redox buffering capacity between adjacent neuron clusters is unknown — identifying the specific antioxidant or mitochondrial quality-control factors differentially expressed between these populations would be actionable.

Calcium channel (cacophony/Cav2) activity confers vulnerability to MPP+ toxicity in Drosophila DA neurons [2], but it remains unclear whether different DA neuron subtypes in the fly brain express different levels or subtypes of Ca2+ channels, and whether subtype-specific channel expression patterns map onto the known pattern of selective degeneration across DA clusters.

The genome-wide DGRP screen [3] identified SNP-associated genes linked to DA neuron vulnerability, but functional validation was limited; whether the identified genes act cell-autonomously within DA neurons or via non-cell-autonomous mechanisms from glia or neighboring neurons has not been determined.

The TMBIM6/IRE1α ER-stress pathway modulates DA neuron survival in fly rotenone models [5], yet it is unknown whether ER stress is differentially activated between vulnerable and resistant DA neuron subtypes in the same fly brain, and what upstream signals (e.g., alpha-synuclein load, lipid composition) determine subtype-specific ER stress magnitude.

Dopamine metabolites such as DOPAL are proposed to link DA metabolism to alpha-synuclein aggregation and selective vulnerability [1], but direct in vivo Drosophila evidence measuring DOPAL levels or DOPAL-alpha-synuclein interactions specifically within vulnerable versus resistant DA neuron clusters is lacking.

literature.summary: In Drosophila PD models, selective DA neuron vulnerability is driven by a convergence of cell-intrinsic factors rather than a single mechanism: vulnerable neuron clusters exhibit sustained mitochondrial oxidative stress and dysregulated glutathione redox equilibrium in parkin-null flies [4], and calcium channel (cacophony) activity confers susceptibility to MPP+ toxicity [2], while neighboring DA neurons escape degeneration. ER stress via the TMBIM6/IRE1α axis and dopamine metabolite-driven alpha-synuclein aggregation further link the biochemical identity of dopaminergic neurons to their selective demise [1][5]. Genome-wide approaches in Drosophila are beginning to identify additional genetic modifiers of DA neuron resilience [3], but the precise molecular differences between vulnerable and resistant DA neuron subtypes within the same brain—including differential calcium channel expression, antioxidant capacity, and ER stress buffering—remain insufficiently characterized.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Vulnerable dopaminergic neuron clusters (PPL1) in parkin-null Drosophila melanogaster express significantly higher levels of the voltage-gated calcium channel cacophony (cac) and lower levels of the ER-stress regulator TMBIM6 ortholog compared to resistant DA neuron clusters (PPM1/2), and that cluster-specific RNAi knockdown of cac in PPL1 neurons will reduce mitochondrial H2O2 accumulation by ≥40% and rescue ≥30% of PPL1 neuron number in 30-day-old parkin-null flies at 25°C relative to parkin-null controls, while concomitant DA-neuron-specific overexpression of the TMBIM6 ortholog will independently rescue ≥25% of PPL1 neuron number under the same conditions.
hypothesis.experimental_approach: We will use the GAL4/UAS system to achieve cluster-restricted transgene expression in Drosophila DA neurons. First, single-nucleus or single-cell RNA sequencing of dissected adult fly brains from parkin-null (park25/park25) and w1118 control flies at day 10 and day 30 will be performed to quantify differential expression of cac, the TMBIM6 fly ortholog (CG9775, requiring verification), antioxidant genes (sod1, cat), and ER-stress effectors (Ire1, Xbp1) across all annotated DA neuron clusters (PPL1, PPL2, PPM1/2, PPM3, PAL). Second, TH-GAL4-driven RNAi of cac (UAS-cac-RNAi) specifically in DA neurons of parkin-null flies will be combined with the mitochondrial H2O2 sensor UAS-mito-roGFP2-Orp1 to measure real-time redox status in PPL1 versus PPM1/2 clusters by confocal imaging at day 10 and day 30. Third, DA-neuron-specific overexpression of UAS-CG9775 (TMBIM6 ortholog) in parkin-null flies will be assessed for PPL1 neuron survival by TH immunostaining. All experiments include w1118, park25/park25; TH-GAL4/+, and UAS transgene/+ heterozygous controls; locomotor performance (negative geotaxis) will serve as a functional readout alongside neuronal counts.

hypothesis.expected_outcomes: Aim 1 (snRNA-seq): PPL1 DA neurons from parkin-null flies at day 30 are predicted to show ≥2-fold higher cac mRNA and ≤0.5-fold TMBIM6 ortholog mRNA relative to PPM1/2 neurons in the same brain (adjusted p < 0.05, DESeq2). Aim 2 (cac RNAi + redox imaging): TH-GAL4>UAS-cac-RNAi in park25 flies is predicted to reduce mito-roGFP2-Orp1 oxidation ratio in PPL1 neurons by ≥40% and rescue PPL1 neuron count from ~50% loss (expected in parkin-null controls at day 30 based on PMID 36290790) to ≤25% loss (≥30% rescue, n ≥ 20 brains/genotype, ANOVA with Tukey post-hoc, p < 0.05). Aim 3 (TMBIM6 OE): TH-GAL4>UAS-CG9775 in park25 flies is predicted to rescue PPL1 neuron number by ≥25% relative to park25; TH-GAL4/+ controls at day 30 (p < 0.05). Locomotor climbing index is predicted to improve by ≥20% in rescued genotypes relative to parkin-null controls at day 30.
hypothesis.novelty_claim: This experiment directly addresses three unresolved gaps identified in the literature synthesis: (1) The molecular basis for differential redox buffering between adjacent vulnerable (PPL1) and resistant (PPM1/2) DA neuron clusters in parkin-null flies is unknown (Gap 1 from synthesis, PMID 36290790); no study has directly compared cac expression levels across DA neuron subtypes within the same fly brain, nor tested whether cluster-specific cac knockdown is sufficient to rescue PPL1 neurons in a genetic PD model (Gap 2, PMID 25445363). (2) The TMBIM6/IRE1α axis has been implicated in DA neuron survival but it is unknown whether ER stress is differentially activated between vulnerable and resistant DA neuron subtypes in the same fly brain (Gap 4, PMID 41932887). (3) No prior study has combined cluster-resolved transcriptomics (snRNA-seq) with real-time mitochondrial redox imaging and subtype-specific genetic intervention in the same parkin-null model to causally link calcium channel expression levels to cluster-specific oxidative stress and degeneration.
hypothesis.feasibility_notes: TH-GAL4-driven tools for DA-neuron-specific transgene expression in Drosophila are well established; parkin-null flies with documented PPL1-selective loss are available. The mito-roGFP2-Orp1 sensor is validated for in vivo Drosophila redox imaging. Potential pitfalls include: (1) TH-GAL4 may not provide sufficient cluster-specificity to distinguish PPL1 from PPM1/2 — a split-GAL4 or intersectional approach (e.g., PPL1-specific GAL4 driver, availability requiring verification at BDSC) may be needed; (2) CG9775 as TMBIM6 ortholog requires bioinformatic confirmation (BLASTP/OrthoFinder analysis) before UAS line construction; (3) snRNA-seq of Drosophila adult brain requires optimization for cell dissociation and sufficient DA neuron capture given their small number (~120 total per brain); (4) parkin-null flies have reduced viability requiring larger starting populations. Estimated timeline: months 1–4 snRNA-seq profiling and data analysis; months 3–8 cac RNAi redox imaging experiments; months 6–14 TMBIM6 ortholog UAS line validation and overexpression rescue experiments; months 12–18 integration and replication. Total estimated timeline: 18 months.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Proposed (not established): Neuronal activity level sets how strongly dopaminergic (DA) neuron survival depends on PINK1/Parkin. In Pink1B9 null males, chronic thermogenetic activation of TH-GAL4-positive neurons (UAS-TrpA1, 29°C for 12 h/day from day 3) will cause at least 30% greater loss of PPL1-cluster DA neurons at day 25 than in Pink1B9 males with the same genotype kept at 22°C. Chronic Kir2.1 silencing (with tub-GAL80ts restricting expression to adults) will reduce PPL1 neuron loss in Pink1B9 males by at least 30% relative to Pink1B9 controls without Kir2.1. DA-neuron-specific knockdown of Cisd or of the IP3 receptor (Itpr) will suppress the activity-dependent excess loss by at least 50%.
hypothesis.experimental_approach: Use a 2 x 3 design crossing genotype (Pink1B9 vs. Pink1B9/+ heterozygous controls on an isogenic background) with activity state (TrpA1 activation, Kir2.1 silencing, GAL4-only or UAS-only baseline). TH-GAL4 drives expression in DA neurons. Adult-restricted expression uses tub-GAL80ts, with 29°C-matched and 22°C-matched controls for every genotype to separate temperature effects from activation effects. Primary endpoints are the number of TH-immunoreactive PPL1 neurons at days 10, 25 and 40, and climbing performance. Mitophagy is quantified with a mito-QC or mt-Keima reporter in DA neurons, together with phospho-Ub immunostaining. Activity-evoked calcium is measured by GCaMP imaging in dissected brains or explants. Rescue arms add UAS-Cisd RNAi or UAS-Itpr RNAi in the Pink1B9 TrpA1 background. Parkin (park) mutants are used to test whether the findings generalize beyond Pink1. Analysis is blind to genotype, with at least 10 brains per group and 3 independent crosses. Counts are compared by two-way ANOVA with Tukey post-hoc tests, using alpha = 0.05.

hypothesis.expected_outcomes: Proposed predictions: (1) At 22°C, Pink1B9 males lose a baseline fraction of PPL1 neurons. TrpA1 activation at 29°C increases this loss by at least 30% over temperature-matched Pink1B9 controls without activation (p < 0.05, two-way ANOVA genotype x activity interaction). (2) Kir2.1 silencing reduces loss by at least 30%. (3) Mito-QC puncta and phospho-Ub signal are elevated by activation in controls, and the Pink1B9 mutant fails to show this adaptive mitophagy response. (4) Activity-evoked calcium transients are larger in Pink1B9 neurons, and Itpr or Cisd knockdown reduces them and suppresses at least 50% of the activity-dependent excess neuron loss. Falsification: if the genotype x activity interaction is not significant (p ≥ 0.05) or the effect is under 15%, the hypothesis of activity-dependent PINK1/Parkin requirement is rejected for this paradigm.
hypothesis.novelty_claim: Huang et al. (PMID 27054334) showed that PINK1 and Parkin protect against constitutively active TRP channel-induced retinal degeneration, but that model involves constitutive calcium influx rather than graded physiological activity. Ham et al. (PMID 37626046) showed that loss of PINK1/Parkin increases IP3R-mediated ER calcium release through CISD1/Cisd. Martinez et al. (PMID 38273330) reported that Cisd accumulates in Pink1/parkin mutants and blocks mitophagy. No supplied study manipulates neuronal firing or excitability in Pink1/parkin mutant Drosophila neurons and measures mitophagy and survival, so the activity-dependence of the PINK1/parkin requirement is untested. Imai et al. (PMID 32035987) noted stronger phospho-ubiquitin signals in DA neurons than other neurons, and whether this reflects higher intrinsic activity is also untested.
hypothesis.feasibility_notes: Estimated timeline is 12-16 months: 3 months for line construction and validation, 6 months for aging and survival cohorts (to day 40), and 3-4 months for imaging and analysis. Pitfalls: (a) 29°C alone may stress Pink1 mutants, so every genotype needs temperature-matched controls and a TrpA1-independent heat control. (b) Pink1B9 flies have baseline phenotypes (flight muscle defects, reduced viability), so the isogenic background must be controlled. (c) TH-GAL4 also marks some non-DA cells, so confirm with anti-TH counts. (d) Adult DA neuron loss in Pink1 mutants is modest, so a power analysis from pilot data is needed and the effect sizes in the predictions are assumptions to be validated. (e) RNAi efficiency for Cisd and Itpr must be verified, and Itpr knockdown may itself be toxic. (f) TrpA1 raises calcium and firing but is not physiological firing, so the findings should be confirmed with a second manipulation such as optogenetics or sensory-driven activity.
specific_aims: Aim 1: Activity-dependent survival — test whether TrpA1-driven activation increases, and Kir2.1 silencing decreases, PPL1 DA neuron loss and motor decline in Pink1B9 (and park) mutants relative to matched controls.

Aim 2: Mitophagy and phospho-Ub readout — quantify mito-QC/mt-Keima and phospho-Ub signal in DA neurons under activation and silencing, to test whether activity drives a PINK1/Parkin-dependent mitophagy response.

Aim 3: Calcium and Cisd/IP3R mechanism — use GCaMP imaging and DA-specific Cisd or Itpr RNAi to test whether activity-evoked ER calcium release and Cisd accumulation mediate the activity-dependent loss in Pink1B9 neurons.

literature.disease_context: Loss-of-function mutations in PINK1 and Parkin cause familial Parkinson's disease, and Drosophila models have demonstrated that their primary role is maintaining mitochondrial quality control in metabolically active neurons, particularly dopaminergic neurons [4, 6]. Neuronal activity generates calcium transients and reactive oxygen species that stress mitochondria; when PINK1/Parkin-mediated mitophagy is impaired, damaged mitochondria accumulate, leading to bioenergetic failure and neuronal death [9, 3]. These mechanisms are broadly relevant to multiple neurodegenerative conditions beyond PD, including ALS/FTD (FUS proteinopathy) and Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease, underscoring the importance of mitochondrial quality control as a general determinant of neuron survival [2, 7].

identified_gaps: The causal direction between neuronal firing rate and PINK1/Parkin activation remains unestablished — it is unknown whether increased neuronal electrical activity per se (independent of pathological calcium overload) quantitatively upregulates PINK1 kinase activity or mitophagy flux in vivo, which would be testable by combining electrophysiological manipulation with phospho-ubiquitin reporters in identified Drosophila neurons.

Phospho-ubiquitin signals are reportedly stronger in dopaminergic neurons than other neurons [4], but whether this reflects higher baseline mitochondrial damage rates, differential PINK1 expression, or activity-dependent regulation has not been experimentally dissected — distinguishing these mechanisms would clarify why DA neurons are selectively vulnerable.

The interaction between neuronal calcium dynamics (activity-driven ER calcium release via IP3R) and PINK1/Parkin-mediated mitophagy is molecularly established [3], but how physiological calcium oscillations (as opposed to pathological overload) regulate CISD1 degradation by Parkin and thereby tune mitophagy rate remains unknown.

Whether USP30-mediated opposition of parkin mitophagy [8] is regulated by neuronal activity state (e.g., via activity-dependent phosphorylation) is unexplored — if USP30 activity is modulated by firing rate, this would constitute a direct activity-to-mitophagy regulatory axis.

The context-dependence of PINK1/Parkin pathway activity — protective in calcium excitotoxicity [9] but detrimental in FUS proteinopathy [2] — suggests that the pathway's net effect on neuron survival depends on the nature of the upstream stress, but the molecular logic determining when pathway activation is protective versus harmful has not been systematically defined.

evidence_claims.claim: Phospho-ubiquitin signals amplified by PINK1 and Parkin are stronger in DA neurons than other neurons, suggesting that PINK1-Parkin signaling is particularly important for DA neuron activity.

PINK1-Parkin signaling also regulates axonal mitochondrial re-distribution in response to reduced mitochondrial membrane potential, which is impaired in the DA neurons of patients with PINK1 and Parkin mutations.
When activated by PINK1, Parkin suppresses mitochondrial transport by reducing Miro levels in Drosophila DA neurons.
Increasing autophagy flux prevented cell death in Trp(P365) mutant flies, and this depended on the PINK1/Parkin pathway.
The retinal degeneration process was also suppressed by the coexpression of PINK1 and Parkin.
Disruption of mitochondrial function was associated with the degenerative process induced by constitutively active TRP(P365) channels.
Loss of PTEN-induced kinase 1 (PINK1) and Parkin leads to dysregulation of inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate receptor (IP3R) activity, robustly increasing ER calcium release.
Suppression of CISD in PINK1 and Parkin null flies rescues PD-related phenotypes including defective locomotor activity and dopaminergic neuronal degeneration.
CDGSH iron sulfur domain 1 (CISD1, also known as mitoNEET) functions downstream of Parkin to directly control IP3R.
Build-up of Cisd is particularly toxic in neurons, resulting in mitochondrial defects and Ser65-phospho-Ubiquitin accumulation.
Age-related increase of Cisd blocks mitophagy and impairs autophagy flux.
Reduction of Cisd levels upregulates mitophagy in vitro and in vivo, and ameliorates pathological phenotypes in locomotion, lifespan and neurodegeneration in Pink1/parkin mutant flies.

Overexpression of USP30 removes ubiquitin attached by parkin onto damaged mitochondria and blocks parkin's ability to drive mitophagy, whereas reducing USP30 activity enhances mitochondrial degradation in neurons.
Knockdown of USP30 in dopaminergic neurons protects flies against paraquat toxicity in vivo, ameliorating defects in dopamine levels, motor function and organismal survival.
Knockdown of USP30 rescues the defective mitophagy caused by pathogenic mutations in parkin and improves mitochondrial integrity in parkin- or PINK1-deficient flies.
Neuron-specific Pink1 knockdown abolishes spermidine-induced improvement of olfactory associative learning.
In a Drosophila aging model, spermidine boosts mitochondrial respiratory capacity, an effect that requires the autophagy regulator Atg7 and the mitophagy mediators Parkin and Pink1.
Down-regulating expression of either Pink1 or Parkin genes ameliorated FUS-induced neurodegeneration phenotypes.
In fly motor neurons expressing FUS, both motility and processivity of mitochondrial axonal transport were reduced by expression of either Wt- or P525L-mutant FUS.
Down-regulating PINK1 or Parkin partially rescued the locomotive defects and enhanced the survival rate in transgenic flies expressing FUS.

The motor defects and mitochondrial dysfunction were successfully restored by PINK1 and parkin, which are Parkinson's disease-associated genes that have critical roles in maintaining mitochondrial function and integrity.
Kinetin riboside, a small molecule amplifying PINK1 activity, also rescued the loss of motor activity in our HSPB8 mutant model.
A signaling active version of Ret (Ret(MEN₂B)) rescues muscle degeneration, disintegration of mitochondria and ATP content of Pink1 mutants.
Corresponding phenotypes of park mutants were not rescued, suggesting that the phenotypes of Pink1 and park mutants have partially different origins.
Overexpression of Ret(MEN₂B) significantly improves electron transport chain complex I function in Pink1 mutant Drosophila.
Elevated α-synuclein levels potently suppressed mitophagic flux, while non-mitochondrial autophagy was preserved.
In human neurons, a twofold increase in wild-type α-synuclein was already sufficient to induce this effect.
PINK1 and parkin activation and mitochondrial translocation of DJ-1 after mitochondrial depolarization were not affected by α-synuclein upregulation.
Overexpression of the actin-severing protein cofilin or treatment with CK666, an inhibitor of the actin-related protein 2/3 (Arp2/3) complex, rescued mitophagy in neurons with increased α-synuclein.
PINK1 mutations in the kinase domain failed to translocate Parkin to mitochondria and to induce mitochondrial aggregation.
Drosophila PINK1 mutants with mutations in the kinase domain (G426D and L464P) did not genetically interact with Parkin.
Rab11, an endosomal recycling protein, serves as an ATG9A carrier that helps in autophagosome formation and maturation.
Loss of Rab11 prevents the fusion of autophagosomes with the late endosomes hampering the autophagy pathway resulting in apoptosis of cells.
Minocycline increased life span and restored the locomotor activity of knockdown parkin flies.
Minocycline protected DAergic neurons against PQ/iron toxicity and significantly abridged lipid peroxidation in TH>parkin-RNAi/+ flies.
USP14 inhibition enhances mitophagy in a PINK1/Parkin-independent manner, relying on expression of the mitochondrial E3 Ubiquitin Ligase MITOL/MARCH5.
USP14 inhibition normalized the mitochondrial defects of Parkin KO human neurons.

Neuronal activity generates calcium transients and reactive oxygen species that stress mitochondria; when PINK1/Parkin-mediated mitophagy is impaired, damaged mitochondria accumulate, leading to bioenergetic failure and neuronal death.

The interaction between neuronal calcium dynamics and PINK1/Parkin-mediated mitophagy is molecularly established, but how physiological calcium oscillations regulate CISD1 degradation by Parkin and thereby tune mitophagy rate remains unknown.

The context-dependence of PINK1/Parkin pathway activity — protective in calcium excitotoxicity but detrimental in FUS proteinopathy — suggests that the pathway's net effect on neuron survival depends on the nature of the upstream stress.

literature.summary: Drosophila studies have established that the PINK1/Parkin mitochondrial quality control pathway is a critical determinant of neuron survival, particularly in metabolically and electrically active neurons such as dopaminergic neurons, where phospho-ubiquitin signaling is disproportionately high [4]. Neuronal activity level interfaces with this pathway primarily through calcium: constitutively elevated calcium influx (via TRP channels) causes mitochondrial dysfunction that is rescued by PINK1/Parkin-dependent mitophagy [9], while PINK1/Parkin loss itself dysregulates ER calcium release through CISD1/IP3R, creating a vicious cycle of calcium imbalance and mitochondrial damage [3, 5]. However, the relationship between pathway activity and neuron survival is context-dependent — PINK1/Parkin is protective against bioenergetic and calcium stress but can be detrimental in the context of proteostatic stress (FUS proteinopathy) [2], highlighting that the net outcome of mitochondrial quality control activation depends on the nature and severity of the upstream neuronal stress.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Increasing neuronal electrical activity in identified Drosophila dopaminergic (DA) neurons by ≥2-fold above baseline (achieved via dTrpA1 thermogenetic activation at 29°C) will upregulate PINK1/Parkin-dependent mitophagy flux by ≥1.5-fold (measured by a mito-Keima reporter signal ratio) and reduce DA neuron number by ≥25% within 20 days in Pink1 null (Pink1B9) flies, whereas wild-type flies subjected to identical activity elevation will show no significant DA neuron loss (≤5%), demonstrating that physiological increases in neuronal firing rate quantitatively engage PINK1/Parkin-dependent mitophagy and that this pathway is required to buffer activity-driven mitochondrial stress in vivo.
hypothesis.experimental_approach: The experiment uses the GAL4/UAS system to co-express the thermogenetic activator UAS-dTrpA1 (for graded neuronal depolarization at 29°C vs. permissive 22°C control), UAS-mito-Keima (ratiometric mitophagy reporter), and UAS-mCD8::GFP (DA neuron morphology marker) under TH-GAL4 (dopaminergic neuron-specific driver) in Pink1B9 null mutant and isogenic wild-type (w1118) backgrounds. Three activity tiers will be established: baseline (22°C, TH-GAL4 driving reporters only), moderate activity (29°C for 4h/day), and sustained high activity (29°C continuous). Mitophagy flux will be quantified by confocal imaging of mito-Keima 561/440 nm excitation ratios in DA neuron soma and axonal fields of the protocerebral posterior lateral (PPL1) cluster at days 5, 10, and 20 post-eclosion. DA neuron survival will be scored by anti-TH immunohistochemistry and GFP-positive cell counts. Phospho-ubiquitin (Ser65) immunostaining will serve as an orthogonal readout of endogenous PINK1 activity. Genetic epistasis controls include Pink1B9; UAS-dTrpA1/TH-GAL4 (no reporter), UAS-dTrpA1/TH-GAL4 in wild-type, and static temperature controls at 22°C for all genotypes. Locomotor performance (negative geotaxis climbing assay, 10 trials/cohort, n≥50 flies/group) will serve as a functional correlate of DA neuron integrity.

hypothesis.expected_outcomes: In wild-type flies, TH-GAL4>dTrpA1 activation at 29°C will increase mito-Keima 561/440 ratio by ≥1.5-fold relative to 22°C controls at day 10, indicating upregulated mitophagy flux; DA neuron number in PPL1 cluster (expected ~12 neurons/hemisphere at baseline) will decrease by ≤5% (not significant, p>0.05 by one-way ANOVA with Tukey correction). In Pink1B9 mutants under identical thermogenetic activation, mito-Keima ratio will be lower than wild-type activated controls (failed mitophagy flux), phospho-ubiquitin puncta will accumulate (≥2-fold increase over wild-type), and DA neuron loss will reach ≥25% by day 20 (p<0.01). Locomotor performance (climbing index) will decline by ≥30% in activated Pink1B9 flies versus activated wild-type by day 15 (p<0.01). Pink1B9 flies at 22°C (unstimulated) will show intermediate phenotypes consistent with published baseline degeneration. Genetic suppression by co-expression of Cisd-RNAi in TH-GAL4 neurons of activated Pink1B9 flies is predicted to rescue DA neuron loss to ≤10% and restore climbing index by ≥50%, providing mechanistic validation of the CISD-IP3R axis. All group sizes: n≥20 brains/timepoint for histology, n≥50 flies/cohort for climbing assay; statistical threshold α=0.05 with Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons.
hypothesis.novelty_claim: This design directly addresses the primary gap identified in the literature synthesis: the causal direction between neuronal firing rate and PINK1/Parkin mitophagy activation has not been experimentally established. While it is known that pathological calcium overload (constitutively active TRP channels) engages PINK1/Parkin mitophagy, and that phospho-ubiquitin is disproportionately high in DA neurons, whether graded physiological increases in electrical activity per se — independent of pathological calcium overload — quantitatively upregulate mitophagy flux in a PINK1-dependent manner in identified neurons in vivo has not been tested. The experimental design also begins to address the second gap: why DA neurons are selectively vulnerable, by providing a controlled activity-titration paradigm that can dissociate activity-dependent mitophagy demand from constitutive PINK1 expression differences. The use of mito-Keima as a continuous flux reporter in TH-positive neurons in a thermogenetically controlled firing paradigm is a novel methodological combination not present in cited literature.
hypothesis.feasibility_notes: All genetic tools (TH-GAL4, UAS-dTrpA1, Pink1B9, UAS-mCD8::GFP) are established Drosophila reagents; the primary technical challenge is the availability of a TH-GAL4-compatible UAS-mito-Keima line, which may require generation or transfer from a collaborating laboratory (estimated 2–3 months for line establishment and validation). Temperature-shift protocols using dTrpA1 are routine. Key pitfalls: (1) dTrpA1 expression in DA neurons may cause developmental lethality or early adult death at sustained 29°C — a daily 4h activation regimen should mitigate this and will be tested in pilot experiments during months 1–2; (2) mito-Keima imaging requires live tissue or rapid fixation with specific excitation settings — confocal protocols must be optimized and standardized across time points; (3) Pink1B9 flies have reduced viability and fecundity, requiring larger crossing schemes; (4) PPL1 cluster neuron counting requires blinded scoring with anti-TH antibody and confocal z-stacks — inter-rater reliability must be established. Estimated timeline: months 1–3 line construction and validation; months 4–6 pilot dose-response and temperature titration; months 7–14 main experimental cohorts with three activity tiers, three genotypes, three time points; months 15–18 epistasis experiments with Cisd-RNAi and data analysis. Total estimated duration: 18 months.
specific_aims: Aim 1: Quantify mitophagy flux as a function of neuronal activity level — determine whether thermogenetic activation of DA neurons via TH-GAL4>dTrpA1 at 29°C increases mito-Keima reporter ratio by ≥1.5-fold in a dose- and time-dependent manner in wild-type (w1118) flies, establishing a causal link between physiological firing rate elevation and mitophagy induction in identified neurons in vivo.

Aim 2: Test PINK1 requirement for activity-induced mitophagy and neuroprotection — compare DA neuron survival (PPL1 anti-TH counts), phospho-ubiquitin accumulation, and climbing performance between TH-GAL4>dTrpA1 Pink1B9 null and isogenic wild-type flies at days 5, 10, and 20 post-eclosion under matched thermogenetic activation, to determine whether PINK1 is necessary to buffer activity-driven mitochondrial stress and prevent DA neuron loss.

Aim 3: Genetic epistasis through CISD to confirm mechanistic axis — test whether neuron-specific knockdown of Cisd (TH-GAL4>Cisd-RNAi) suppresses activity-induced DA neuron degeneration and restores mitophagy flux in Pink1B9 mutants subjected to dTrpA1 activation, validating the CISD/IP3R/ER-calcium pathway as a downstream mediator connecting elevated neuronal activity to PINK1/Parkin-dependent mitochondrial quality control.

evidence_claims.claim: Phospho-ubiquitin signals amplified by PINK1 and Parkin are stronger in DA neurons than other neurons, suggesting that PINK1-Parkin signaling is particularly important for DA neuron activity.
Increasing autophagy flux prevented cell death in Trp(P365) mutant flies, and this depended on the PINK1/Parkin pathway.
Disruption of mitochondrial function was associated with the degenerative process induced by constitutively active TRP(P365) channels.
Loss of PTEN-induced kinase 1 (PINK1) and Parkin leads to dysregulation of inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate receptor (IP3R) activity, robustly increasing ER calcium release.
Suppression of CISD in PINK1 and Parkin null flies rescues PD-related phenotypes including defective locomotor activity and dopaminergic neuronal degeneration.
CDGSH iron sulfur domain 1 (CISD1, also known as mitoNEET) functions downstream of Parkin to directly control IP3R.
Build-up of Cisd is particularly toxic in neurons, resulting in mitochondrial defects and Ser65-phospho-Ubiquitin accumulation.
Reduction of Cisd levels upregulates mitophagy in vitro and in vivo, and ameliorates pathological phenotypes in locomotion, lifespan and neurodegeneration in Pink1/parkin mutant flies.
Down-regulating expression of either Pink1 or Parkin genes ameliorated FUS-induced neurodegeneration phenotypes.

Neuronal activity generates calcium transients and reactive oxygen species that stress mitochondria; when PINK1/Parkin-mediated mitophagy is impaired, damaged mitochondria accumulate, leading to bioenergetic failure and neuronal death.

The causal direction between neuronal firing rate and PINK1/Parkin activation remains unestablished — it is unknown whether increased neuronal electrical activity per se (independent of pathological calcium overload) quantitatively upregulates PINK1 kinase activity or mitophagy flux in vivo.

Whether this reflects higher baseline mitochondrial damage rates, differential PINK1 expression, or activity-dependent regulation has not been experimentally dissected — distinguishing these mechanisms would clarify why DA neurons are selectively vulnerable.

The interaction between neuronal calcium dynamics and PINK1/Parkin-mediated mitophagy is molecularly established, but how physiological calcium oscillations regulate CISD1 degradation by Parkin and thereby tune mitophagy rate remains unknown.

The context-dependence of PINK1/Parkin pathway activity — protective in calcium excitotoxicity but detrimental in FUS proteinopathy — suggests that the pathway's net effect on neuron survival depends on the nature of the upstream stress.

Increasing neuronal electrical activity in identified Drosophila dopaminergic (DA) neurons by ≥2-fold above baseline (achieved via dTrpA1 thermogenetic activation at 29°C) will upregulate PINK1/Parkin-dependent mitophagy flux by ≥1.5-fold (measured by a mito-Keima reporter signal ratio) and reduce DA neuron number by ≥25% within 20 days in Pink1 null (Pink1B9) flies, whereas wild-type flies subjected to identical activity elevation will show no significant DA neuron loss (≤5%).
Genetic suppression by co-expression of Cisd-RNAi in TH-GAL4 neurons of activated Pink1B9 flies is predicted to rescue DA neuron loss to ≤10% and restore climbing index by ≥50%.
The use of mito-Keima as a continuous flux reporter in TH-positive neurons in a thermogenetically controlled firing paradigm is a novel methodological combination not present in cited literature.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Proposed: In mated female flies at 25°C, tumor-specific knockdown of Mmp1 will restore at least 50% of the tumor-induced loss of fat-body triglyceride and of muscle integrity in an eye-antennal disc RasV12 scrib tumor model but less than 20% in a gut ykiAct tumor model, whereas tumor-specific upd3 knockdown will show the reverse pattern, and combined Mmp1 and upd3 knockdown will restore significantly more (p<0.05) than either single knockdown in each model.
hypothesis.experimental_approach: Two tumor models will be compared side by side: an eye-antennal disc RasV12 scrib tumor model and a gut ykiAct tumor model driven by a temperature-inducible enterocyte or progenitor GAL4 (exact driver and tumor genotypes to be verified). Tumor-specific RNAi against Mmp1 and upd3, singly and combined, is driven by the same tumor driver, with UAS-lacZ or UAS-mCherry RNAi controls to equalize UAS dosage. Distant-tissue wasting is scored at matched tumor burden (GFP-positive tumor volume or area) using fat-body triglyceride normalized to protein, Nile Red or BODIPY staining of fat-body lipid droplets, phalloidin staining of thoracic or abdominal muscle, and climbing assays. Fat-body Pepck1 and Pdk transcripts are measured by qPCR as a readout of the Upd3 axis. Controls include tumor-free flies, tumor flies with control RNAi, and RNAi-only flies, and knockdown efficiency in tumor tissue is confirmed by qPCR.

literature.disease_context: Cancer cachexia is a wasting syndrome responsible for up to one-third of cancer-related deaths, characterized by loss of muscle and adipose tissue driven by tumor-secreted factors that disrupt systemic metabolism [1][3]. Fly models have identified conserved tumor-secreted molecules—including Mmp1 and Upd3—that recapitulate key features of human cachexia, with the Upd3/IL-6 and Pepck1/PDK3 axes validated in both mouse and human cancer datasets [2][5]. These findings open potential therapeutic targets to mitigate metabolic dysregulation in cachexia patients [5].

identified_gaps: Different fly tumor models secrete distinct as well as overlapping cachectic factors [1], but a systematic comparison of which specific secreted molecules are necessary versus sufficient across multiple tumor genotypes (e.g., Ras/scrib versus epithelial overgrowth) has not been completed — this matters because it would clarify whether a single anti-cachexia therapeutic could be broadly effective.

While Mmp1 is required for fat body remodeling and muscle detachment [2], the downstream extracellular matrix substrates cleaved by tumor-derived Mmp1 in distant tissues remain unidentified, leaving the molecular bridge between MMP activity and TGF-β pathway activation in the fat body unresolved.

The mechanism by which tumor-secreted Upd3 reaches and signals in the fat body — including receptor identity, signal transduction duration, and whether it acts directly or via relay tissues — is not established from the supplied literature, limiting understanding of how to intercept this axis therapeutically [5].

The relationship between tumor-derived eiger (TNF-α)-mediated systemic insulin restriction [8] and Upd3-mediated gluconeogenic reprogramming [5] in the same cachexia context is unexplored; it is unknown whether these are parallel, sequential, or redundant mechanisms of systemic wasting.

Early biomarkers of cachexia that precede visible organ wasting have not been identified in fly models [3]; defining such markers would enable earlier intervention studies in both fly and mammalian systems.

literature.summary: In Drosophila cachexia models, two classes of tumor-secreted factors have been identified as necessary for wasting of distant tissues: matrix metalloproteinase Mmp1, which disrupts ECM integrity and activates TGF-β signaling in the fat body and muscle to drive fat-body remodeling and muscle detachment [2], and the interleukin-like cytokine Upd3, which activates JAK/STAT signaling to induce gluconeogenic reprogramming (Pepck1, Pdk) in the fat body and thereby disrupts systemic glucose metabolism [5]. Additionally, tumor expression of eiger (TNF-α homolog) causes systemic insulin restriction that further reduces peripheral tissue growth and protein translation [8]. A key open insight is that different tumor models produce both shared and distinct cachectic factors, suggesting mechanistic heterogeneity in cachexia that Drosophila is well positioned to dissect [1].

hypothesis.hypothesis: In the RasV12/scrib Drosophila tumor cachexia model, simultaneous loss of tumor-secreted Upd3 and eiger will reduce fat body triglyceride loss by ≥50% and muscle detachment frequency by ≥40% compared to tumors retaining both factors, whereas single knockdown of either Upd3 or eiger alone will each rescue these phenotypes by <30%, demonstrating that these two secreted factors act in parallel, non-redundant pathways to drive systemic wasting in mated female w1118 background flies at 25°C.
hypothesis.experimental_approach: Eye-antennal disc tumors will be induced using the GMR-GAL4 driver to express UAS-RasV12 in a scrib RNAi background (GMR>RasV12, scrib-IR), which is an established fly cachexia model. Within this tumor genotype, Upd3 and eiger will be knocked down individually and in combination using UAS-RNAi transgenes co-expressed under GMR-GAL4, allowing tumor-specific depletion of each secreted factor while leaving host tissues intact. Wasting endpoints will be quantified at day 10 post-eclosion: fat body lipid content by Nile Red staining and TAG colorimetric assay, muscle detachment scored by phalloidin staining of indirect flight muscles and thoracic wall muscles, systemic glucose levels by colorimetric assay, and fat body Pepck1/Pdk mRNA levels by RT-qPCR as molecular readouts of the gluconeogenic axis. Survival assays (n ≥ 150 females per genotype, three biological replicates) will assess whether rescue of wasting markers translates to lifespan extension. Controls will include: (1) GMR-GAL4 driver alone (no tumor), (2) GMR>RasV12/scrib-IR with UAS-luciferase RNAi as a specificity control, and (3) fat body-specific (r4-GAL4) rescue of JAK/STAT signaling to confirm tissue-autonomy of Upd3 signaling downstream of the tumor.

hypothesis.expected_outcomes: If the hypothesis is correct: (1) Single Upd3 knockdown in tumors will reduce fat body Pepck1 and Pdk mRNA by ≥60% and restore systemic glucose toward control levels (within 20% of tumor-free flies) but rescue muscle detachment by <30%; (2) Single eiger knockdown will reduce muscle detachment frequency by <30% and partially restore fat body TAG content (<30% rescue) by relieving systemic insulin restriction, with minimal effect on gluconeogenic gene expression; (3) Double Upd3/eiger knockdown will reduce fat body TAG loss by ≥50% and muscle detachment by ≥40% relative to RasV12/scrib tumors expressing control RNAi, demonstrating synergy consistent with parallel pathways; (4) Survival will be extended by ≥15% in double knockdown animals relative to full-tumor controls. Statistical analysis: one-way ANOVA with Tukey post-hoc correction, α = 0.05, n ≥ 30 per genotype per biochemical assay, n ≥ 150 per genotype for survival. If double knockdown does not exceed additive rescue of single knockdowns, this would indicate sequential rather than parallel action.
hypothesis.novelty_claim: The literature synthesis identifies as an explicit gap that 'the relationship between tumor-derived eiger (TNF-α)-mediated systemic insulin restriction and Upd3-mediated gluconeogenic reprogramming in the same cachexia context is unexplored; it is unknown whether these are parallel, sequential, or redundant mechanisms of systemic wasting.' No published study has directly tested whether Upd3 and eiger function in the same tumor model with combinatorial genetic loss-of-function to determine epistasis or pathway independence. Additionally, the synthesis notes that 'a systematic comparison of which specific secreted molecules are necessary versus sufficient across multiple tumor genotypes has not been completed,' and this design directly addresses necessity by genetic ablation of each factor in the RasV12/scrib background. This distinguishes the proposed work from Lodge et al. (2021), which focused on Mmp1 in an epithelial overgrowth model, and from Liu et al. (2025), which focused on Upd3/gluconeogenesis without examining eiger interaction.
hypothesis.feasibility_notes: The GMR>RasV12/scrib cachexia model is well-established and produces robust wasting phenotypes by day 10 post-eclosion, providing a reliable experimental window. The primary technical challenge is generating and validating the double UAS-Upd3-IR; UAS-eiger-IR recombinant chromosome, which requires 3–4 months of stock construction and verification by RT-qPCR of knockdown efficiency in dissected eye discs. A potential pitfall is GAL4 dilution when driving multiple UAS transgenes simultaneously, which will be controlled by including UAS-luciferase-IR as a filler transgene in single-knockdown arms. Fat body dissection quality is variable and requires consistent technique; investigators should be blinded to genotype during dissection and quantification. Mated females must be collected within 24 hours of eclosion and maintained at controlled density (20 per vial). Estimated timeline: months 1–4, stock construction and validation; months 5–8, wasting endpoint assays; months 9–12, survival assays and downstream mechanistic experiments. The project is technically feasible within 12 months with one trained fly researcher.
specific_aims: Aim 1: Necessity mapping — Determine whether tumor-secreted Upd3 and eiger are individually necessary for fat body wasting and muscle detachment in the RasV12/scrib cachexia model by quantifying TAG content, Pepck1/Pdk mRNA, systemic glucose, and muscle detachment frequency in single-knockdown animals versus full-tumor controls.

Aim 2: Combinatorial epistasis — Determine whether simultaneous tumor-specific knockdown of Upd3 and eiger produces additive, synergistic, or sub-additive rescue of wasting phenotypes to establish whether these factors act in parallel, sequential, or redundant pathways driving systemic wasting.

Aim 3: Tissue-autonomy validation — Confirm that fat body JAK/STAT signaling (via Stat92E RNAi under r4-GAL4) is the obligate downstream effector of tumor Upd3 in the gluconeogenic wasting axis, and that this is separable from eiger-mediated systemic insulin restriction as measured by fat body InR target gene expression (4EBP, Thor) and S6K phosphorylation.

identified_gaps: The relative contributions of cell-autonomous (Fos/Ets21c/Ftz-F1, Dorsal/Chinmo) versus non-autonomous (JNK propagation, JAK/STAT cytokines, inflammation) mechanisms to invasion are not quantitatively separated; clone-mosaic versus whole-tissue epistasis tests with cell-type-specific manipulations would resolve this [4][5][6].

Ets21c can substitute for polarity loss with Ras, but how scrib loss mechanistically activates JNK and Ets21c, and whether aPKC mislocalization feeds in, is not resolved; testing Ets21c induction in aPKC-inhibited scrib mutants would address this [3][6].

Whether the Toll/NF-κB (Dorsal/Cactus) and Yki-Cactus-JNK axes are upstream, parallel or downstream of Fos/Ets21c in the invasive program is unclear, as is their hierarchy relative to Ras signaling [5][6][10].

Human validity of the invasion-switch mechanisms beyond Scribble-MAPK (e.g., whether JNK/AP-1/ETS and NF-κB hierarchies operate in human Ras plus polarity-loss models) is not tested in the supplied literature [2][6].
The role of autophagy in context-specific support or suppression of RasV12/scrib- invasion and the underlying downstream mechanisms (metabolism, selective autophagy) remain largely unexplored [14].
