literature.summary: In Drosophila, benign Ras-driven overgrowth becomes invasive when polarity loss (scrib) converts JNK from a pro-apoptotic signal into a driver of overgrowth and invasion, acting through Fos, Ets21c and Ftz-F1 to induce MMP1 and other malignancy programs [3][6]. Non-autonomous JNK/JAK-STAT signaling, Toll/NF-κB (Dorsal/Cactus) and Hippo/Yki inputs further contribute, and the Scribble-Ras cooperation is conserved in human epithelial cells via MAPK deregulation [2][4][5][10]. The hierarchy among these inputs and their human relevance remain incompletely defined.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Proposed: In eye-antennal disc clones, the invasive switch in RasV12 scrib-RNAi tissue requires aPKC activity upstream of JNK-dependent Ets21c induction. Specifically, in RasV12; scrib-RNAi clones at 25°C, (a) co-expression of an aPKC-inhibiting transgene (e.g., aPKC-RNAi, line requiring verification) will reduce Ets21c reporter-positive clone area and Mmp1 immunofluorescence by ≥40% relative to RasV12; scrib-RNAi controls, and (b) will reduce the fraction of wandering third-instar larvae with ventral nerve cord (VNC) invasion/dissemination from ≥50% to ≤20%. (c) Restoring Ets21c (UAS-Ets21c) in the aPKC-inhibited background will rescue invasion to ≥60% of control levels. This is a proposed hypothesis, not an established result; significance threshold p<0.05 (Fisher's exact test for incidence, Mann-Whitney for intensity/area, n≥25 discs/larvae per genotype).
hypothesis.experimental_approach: Use MARCM or flip-out (ey-FLP) clonal systems in the eye-antennal disc to generate GFP-marked clones of RasV12 + scrib-RNAi (scrib loss-of-function), with or without aPKC knockdown or an aPKC-inhibitory construct. Readouts at day 6-7 after egg laying: clone volume, Mmp1 immunostaining, an Ets21c transcriptional reporter or Ets21c antibody/in situ (reagent requiring verification), phospho-JNK/TRE-reporter (JNK activity), and VNC invasion scoring. Epistasis: add UAS-bsk-DN to confirm JNK dependence, and UAS-Ets21c to test whether Ets21c can rescue invasion downstream of aPKC inhibition. Controls: RasV12 alone (benign overgrowth), scrib-RNAi alone, GFP/lacZ or white-RNAi, and UAS-dosage controls (UAS-lacZ) to balance GAL4 titration. Include a mosaic-versus-whole-tissue comparison (clones versus adjacent-clone RasV12 and scrib- populations) in Aim 3 to separate cell-autonomous from non-autonomous contributions, addressing a gap in the synthesis.

literature.disease_context: The cooperative transformation of benign oncogenic overgrowth into malignant, invasive cancer by loss of cell polarity is a widely conserved mechanism directly relevant to human epithelial cancers, where SCRIB expression is decreased in many invasive tumors and RAS pathway mutations occur in approximately 30% of all human cancers [2]. The molecular pathways identified in Drosophila—including JNK, NF-κB, JAK/STAT, and Hippo—are conserved in mammals, suggesting that the principles of oncogenic cooperation discovered in flies have direct translational relevance [7]. Understanding how polarity loss switches JNK from a pro-apoptotic to a pro-invasive signal, and how NF-κB, Hippo, and transcription factor networks are co-opted, may reveal new therapeutic targets for human carcinomas [3, 5, 6].

identified_gaps: It remains unclear precisely how the switch in JNK function from pro-apoptotic (in polarity-deficient cells alone) to pro-invasive/pro-growth (in the context of combined oncogene + polarity loss) is molecularly regulated — identifying the upstream switch mechanism would clarify a central question in cooperative oncogenesis [3, 4].

The relative contributions and epistatic relationships among the multiple cooperating signaling axes (JNK, NF-κB/Toll, Hippo/Yki, JAK/STAT, MAPK) in the same tumor cell have not been fully resolved; it is unknown whether these pathways act in parallel, in series, or in a context-dependent hierarchy [5, 7, 10].

Autophagy's role in the RasV12;scrib-/- model is context-specific and largely unexplored: whether autophagy suppresses or supports invasion in this cooperative model, and through which downstream mechanisms, remains unknown [14].

The non-cell-autonomous mechanisms by which JNK signaling propagates from polarity-deficient cells to adjacent wild-type or RasV12 cells to drive cooperative tumor growth are not fully defined at the molecular level — specifically, which secreted factors beyond JAK/STAT cytokines mediate this crosstalk [4].

The differential roles of distinct NF-κB isoforms (DorsalA vs. DorsalB) and their cell-population-specific distribution in invasive versus non-invasive tumor subpopulations have been identified but their mechanistic contributions to invasion are not yet resolved [5].

evidence_claims.claim: Activating mutations in genes of the Ras-mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) pathway occur in approximately 30% of all human cancers; however, mutation of Ras alone is rarely sufficient to induce tumour development.
Scribble is a polarity regulator recently isolated from a Drosophila screen for events that cooperate with Ras mutation to promote tumour progression and cell invasion.
Loss of Scribble promotes invasion of cells through extracellular matrix in an organotypic culture system in human epithelial cells expressing oncogenic Ras or Raf.
The suppression of MAPK signalling is a highly conserved function of Scribble as it also prevents Raf-mediated defects in Drosophila wing development.
Scribble expression is decreased in many invasive human cancers.
JNK normally promotes apoptosis of scrib mutant cells. However, in cooperation with oncogenic activated Ras or Notch signalling, JNK becomes an essential driver of tumour overgrowth and invasion.
aPKC-dependent signalling in scrib mutants cooperates with JNK to significantly enhance oncogene-mediated tumour overgrowth.
Morphological and proliferative defects in scrib mutants are independent of Crumbs function, and instead can be rescued by a dominant negative (kinase dead) aPKC transgene.
Clones of cells bearing different mutations can cooperate to promote tumour growth and invasion in Drosophila.
The Ras(V12) and scrib(-) mutations can also cause tumours when they affect different adjacent epithelial cells.

Interaction between Ras(V12) and scrib(-) clones involves JNK signalling propagation and JNK-induced upregulation of JAK/STAT-activating cytokines, a compensatory growth mechanism for tissue homeostasis.
The development of Ras(V12) tumours can also be triggered by tissue damage, a stress condition that activates JNK signalling.

Malignant transformation of the ras(V12)scrib(1) tumors requires TFs of distinct families, namely the bZIP protein Fos, the ETS-domain factor Ets21c and the nuclear receptor Ftz-F1, all acting downstream of Jun-N-terminal kinase (JNK).
Both Fos and Ftz-F1 synergistically contribute to ras(V12)scrib(1) tumor invasiveness, only Fos is required for JNK-induced differentiation defects and Matrix metalloprotease (MMP1) upregulation.

Ets21c and Ftz-F1 are transcriptionally induced in these tumors in a JNK- and Fos-dependent manner, thereby demonstrating a hierarchy within the tripartite TF network, with Fos acting as the most upstream JNK effector.

Only Ets21c can efficiently substitute for loss of polarity and cooperate with Ras(V12) in inducing malignant clones that, like ras(V12)scrib(1) tumors, invade other tissues and overexpress MMP1 and the Drosophila insulin-like peptide 8 (Dilp8).
The Toll pathway NFκB protein Dorsal as well as cactus/IκΒ show elevated expression in tumors with highest expression in invasive cell populations.
Oncogenic RasV12, and not loss of scribble, confers increased expression and heterogenous distribution of two Dorsal isoforms, DorsalA and DorsalB, in different tumor cell populations.
Dorsal, in concert with the BTB-transcription factor Chinmo, drives growth and malignancy by suppressing differentiation, counteracting apoptosis, and promoting invasion of RasV12, scrib- tumors.
The extracellular Toll pathway components ModSP and PGRP-SA and intracellular signaling Kinase, Pelle/IRAK, are rate-limiting for tumor growth.
Loss of apico-basal polarity is one of the crucial factors that drives epithelial tumor progression.

The components of the Hippo signaling pathway, which is crucial for organ size control and cancer development, were also identified through Drosophila genetic screens as members of 'hyperplastic' tumor-suppressors.

Accumulating evidence implies that these two tumor-suppressor signaling pathways [Scribble/Dlg/Lgl and Hippo] are not mutually exclusive but rather cooperatively act to give rise to highly malignant tumors.
Cact accumulates in the cytoplasm in Drosophila tumor models, similar to squamous cell carcinoma in mice models and human patients where cytoplasmic IκBα favors oncogenic transformation.
Hippo coactivator Yki transcriptionally regulates cact expression, and downregulation of Yki or Cact is sufficient to cause downregulation of JNK-mediated signaling that promotes tumorigenesis.
Yki3SAscribRNAi form invasive neoplastic lethal tumors that induce a systemic inflammatory response.
Dysfunction of Rab5 leads to cell-autonomous accumulation of Eiger (a TNF homolog) and EGF receptor (EGFR), which causes activation of downstream JNK and Ras signaling, respectively.
JNK signaling and its downstream component Cdc42 cooperate with Ras signaling to induce upregulation of a secreted growth factor Upd (an IL-6 homolog) through inactivation of the Hippo pathway.
Autophagy both serves to suppress or support tumor growth. These effects are context-specific, depending on cell type and oncogenic or tumor suppressive lesion.

When surrounded by normal cells, Ras(V12) cells are either apically extruded from the monolayer, or form dynamic basal protrusions and invade the basal matrix. Neither apical extrusion nor basal protrusion formation is observed when Ras(V12) cells are surrounded by other Ras(V12) cells.
E-cadherin knockdown in normal cells surrounding Ras(V12) cells reduces the frequency of apical extrusion, while promoting basal protrusion formation and invasion.

Cooperativity goes beyond cell intrinsic mechanisms as the tumor interacts with the immediate cells of the microenvironment, the immune system and systemic organs to eventually facilitate malignant progression.

The molecular pathways identified in Drosophila—including JNK, NF-κB, JAK/STAT, and Hippo—are conserved in mammals, suggesting that the principles of oncogenic cooperation discovered in flies have direct translational relevance.

Understanding how polarity loss switches JNK from a pro-apoptotic to a pro-invasive signal, and how NF-κB, Hippo, and transcription factor networks are co-opted, may reveal new therapeutic targets for human carcinomas.

Autophagy's role in the RasV12;scrib-/- model is context-specific and largely unexplored: whether autophagy suppresses or supports invasion in this cooperative model, and through which downstream mechanisms, remains unknown.

literature.summary: The conversion of benign oncogenic overgrowth into invasive malignancy requires cooperation between an activating oncogene (classically RasV12) and loss of apico-basal cell polarity (classically loss of scrib), which together activate a multi-arm signaling network that no single lesion can trigger alone [3, 4, 7]. Central to this conversion is a critical switch in JNK signaling: in polarity-deficient cells alone, JNK promotes apoptosis and cell elimination, but in combination with oncogenic Ras or Notch, JNK is redirected to drive tumor overgrowth, tissue invasion, and MMP1 upregulation through a transcription factor cascade involving Fos, Ets21c, and Ftz-F1 [3, 6]. Additional amplifying mechanisms—including non-cell-autonomous JNK propagation and JAK/STAT cytokine induction, Toll-NF-κB activation by oncogenic Ras driving Dorsal/Chinmo-mediated suppression of differentiation and promotion of invasion, and Hippo-Yki-Cactus-JNK inflammatory crosstalk—collectively explain how the combination of oncogene and polarity loss creates a malignant program far exceeding what either mutation alone can produce [4, 5, 10].

hypothesis.hypothesis: Ets21c overexpression in the posterior compartment of Drosophila larval wing imaginal discs (using hh-GAL4) will be sufficient to substitute for scrib loss and cooperate with UAS-RasV12 to produce invasive tumors (defined by MMP1 upregulation ≥3-fold over RasV12 alone by immunofluorescence intensity, tumor mass escaping the disc basement membrane in ≥40% of larvae, and Dilp8 upregulation ≥2-fold) within 10 days at 25°C in a w1118 background, and that this invasive phenotype will be suppressed ≥60% by simultaneous knockdown of Fos (UAS-Fos-RNAi) or Dorsal (UAS-dl-RNAi), demonstrating that the JNK–Fos–Ets21c transcriptional axis and the NF-κB/Dorsal axis are both required downstream of polarity-independent oncogenic cooperation
hypothesis.experimental_approach: Using the GAL4/UAS system, hh-GAL4 will drive co-expression of UAS-RasV12 with UAS-Ets21c in the posterior compartment of larval wing imaginal discs, using the anterior compartment as an internal wild-type control; GFP (UAS-GFP) will mark clones throughout. Tumor invasiveness will be scored by confocal immunofluorescence for MMP1, Dilp8, E-cadherin (loss of epithelial integrity), and phalloidin (basement membrane breach), alongside Dorsal and Cactus localization in tumor subpopulations. Epistasis experiments will use UAS-Fos-RNAi and UAS-dl-RNAi (targeting Dorsal/NF-κB) to dissect the relative requirement of the JNK–Fos–Ets21c axis versus the Toll–NF-κB–Dorsal–Chinmo axis in driving the invasive phenotype. Controls will include: hh-GAL4/UAS-GFP (wild-type), hh-GAL4/UAS-RasV12 alone (benign overgrowth), hh-GAL4/UAS-Ets21c alone (polarity-independent TF overexpression), and hh-GAL4 driving UAS-scrib-RNAi;UAS-RasV12 (the classical invasive model). A minimum of n=30 discs per genotype will be analyzed; statistical comparison will use one-way ANOVA with Tukey post-hoc test, with p<0.05 as significance threshold.

hypothesis.expected_outcomes: Aim 1: hh-GAL4>UAS-RasV12;UAS-Ets21c discs will show ≥3-fold increase in MMP1 immunofluorescence intensity relative to hh-GAL4>UAS-RasV12 alone, basement membrane breach in ≥40% of larvae (scored by confocal z-stack), and ≥2-fold Dilp8 upregulation by qRT-PCR, recapitulating the invasive phenotype of classical RasV12;scrib-/- tumors. Aim 2: Co-expression of UAS-Fos-RNAi in the RasV12;Ets21c background will suppress MMP1 upregulation and basement membrane breach by ≥60%, confirming Fos as a required downstream effector of the JNK-driven invasive transcriptional cascade. Aim 3: Co-expression of UAS-dl-RNAi will independently suppress the invasive phenotype by ≥50% (basement membrane breach frequency and MMP1 levels), and DorsalA/DorsalB immunofluorescence will show highest intensity in invasive subpopulations of RasV12;Ets21c tumors compared to non-invasive RasV12-alone controls, replicating the heterogeneous Dorsal distribution reported in classical tumors. If Fos-RNAi and dl-RNAi each provide only partial rescue (~50-60%), combined double knockdown is predicted to suppress invasion synergistically to <15% of controls, indicating parallel pathway architecture.
hypothesis.novelty_claim: This experiment directly addresses two identified gaps in the literature: (1) The gap that 'the relative contributions and epistatic relationships among the multiple cooperating signaling axes (JNK, NF-κB/Toll, Hippo/Yki, JAK/STAT, MAPK) in the same tumor cell have not been fully resolved; it is unknown whether these pathways act in parallel, in series, or in a context-dependent hierarchy.' By combining Ets21c overexpression (activating the JNK–Fos–Ets21c axis cell-autonomously without polarity loss) with RasV12 and then performing individual versus combined knockdown of Fos and Dorsal, this design resolves the parallel-versus-serial architecture of the JNK–NF-κB axes in the same genetic background. (2) The gap that 'the differential roles of distinct NF-κB isoforms (DorsalA vs. DorsalB) and their cell-population-specific distribution in invasive versus non-invasive tumor subpopulations have been identified but their mechanistic contributions to invasion are not yet resolved.' Using Ets21c to decouple scrib loss from Ras activation allows attribution of Dorsal isoform induction specifically to the RasV12 input (as established by PMID 40294135), while Ets21c provides a clean oncogenic transcription factor input independent of upstream polarity scaffolding. Additionally, the proposed Ets21c-substitution approach tests the sufficiency of a single transcription factor to bypass the entire polarity-loss requirement, a causal mechanistic question not addressed by prior RNAi screens in the classical scrib-/- model.
hypothesis.feasibility_notes: All GAL4/UAS components are standard and the wing disc system is among the most experimentally tractable Drosophila tissues. The hh-GAL4 driver provides strong, spatially controlled expression with a built-in internal control (anterior compartment). Major potential pitfalls: (1) Lethality — co-overexpression of RasV12 and Ets21c may cause larval lethality before disc analysis; mitigation: use a temperature-sensitive GAL80 (tub-GAL80ts) to restrict expression to late L3 by shifting to 29°C for 48h. (2) UAS-Ets21c line availability: the Külshammer et al. 2015 (PMID 26398940) line must be obtained from the originating lab or re-generated by cloning; this adds 2-3 months if re-cloning is required. (3) Incomplete RNAi knockdown: confirm >80% knockdown by qRT-PCR before interpreting epistasis results; use two independent RNAi lines for each target. (4) MMP1 antibody lot variability: include a positive control (hh-GAL4>scrib-RNAi;RasV12) in every staining batch. Estimated timeline: 6-9 months total (2 months line establishment and crosses, 2 months primary phenotype characterization, 3 months epistasis experiments and quantification, 1 month data analysis and validation). The experiment is technically feasible in a standard Drosophila genetics laboratory with confocal microscopy access.
specific_aims: Aim 1: Ets21c sufficiency — Test whether overexpression of Ets21c in hh-GAL4>UAS-RasV12;UAS-Ets21c wing discs is sufficient to substitute for scrib loss and produce quantifiable invasive tumor phenotypes (MMP1 ≥3-fold, basement membrane breach ≥40%, Dilp8 ≥2-fold) compared to RasV12 alone and the classical RasV12;scrib-RNAi positive control

Aim 2: JNK–Fos axis requirement — Determine whether Fos knockdown (UAS-Fos-RNAi) in the RasV12;Ets21c background suppresses invasion ≥60% (MMP1, basement membrane breach), establishing Fos as a required effector of the Ets21c-driven invasive program and confirming the JNK–Fos–Ets21c transcriptional hierarchy in a polarity-independent context

Aim 3: NF-κB/Dorsal axis requirement and isoform distribution — Determine whether Dorsal knockdown (UAS-dl-RNAi) independently suppresses invasion ≥50% in RasV12;Ets21c tumors, and whether DorsalA and DorsalB show highest immunofluorescence intensity in invasive versus non-invasive tumor subpopulations, resolving the mechanistic contribution of NF-κB isoforms to invasion downstream of RasV12

identified_gaps: No provided study reports a systematic denominator of fly-predicted drug rescues that were then tried in patients, so the concordance rate (how often predictions hold) cannot be estimated; a registry of fly-guided treatments with prospective patient outcomes would address this.

The only patient-level evidence is a single ACC case [2], which has no control arm, so benefit cannot be separated from natural history or from the individual patient's tumor biology; N-of-1 designs with predefined response criteria are needed.

For the TRPP2(D511V) chloroquine rescue [1], it is unknown whether the fly rescue translates to human kidney cyst phenotypes or is safe and effective at clinically achievable doses; this requires testing in mammalian or patient-derived kidney models and then in clinical studies.

The brigatinib study [6] shows consistent inhibition across fly, cell and mouse models, but the abstract reports no clinical outcomes and does not compare fly predictions against negative-control drugs, so the fly model's predictive specificity is unquantified.

Reviews of POLG [4] and KCNT1 [3] note that models are of limited quality or do not fully recapitulate human disease; the abstracts do not show whether fly drug responses for these disorders predict patient responses, so variant-specific benchmarking against known clinical drug responses is needed.
No provided paper assesses false negatives (drugs that fail in flies but help patients) or fly-specific pharmacokinetic confounders such as drug uptake and metabolism.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Proposed (not established): In Drosophila models of patient-derived variants (an Alk gain-of-function variant and a Pkd2/TRPP2 D511V-equivalent variant), a standardized rescue assay applied to a blinded panel of ≥40 approved drugs per model will identify rescuers (≥30% rescue of a quantitative phenotype, Benjamini-Hochberg FDR <0.05, with a monotonic dose-response in ≥3 doses) with ≥70% positive predictive value and ≥70% negative predictive value against a pre-registered reference standard of published mammalian or clinical drug responses for the same variant or pathway. Rescue calls that also pass a measured-drug-exposure check (detectable drug in fly tissue by LC-MS) will have a higher concordance than calls without that check, by ≥15 percentage points. The 70% thresholds and the 15-point difference are arbitrary proposed thresholds. If PPV or NPV falls below 50% (the lower bound of the 95% CI must exclude 70%), the hypothesis is rejected.
hypothesis.experimental_approach: Build or obtain fly lines expressing patient-derived variants. Use UAS-driven human or ortholog variant transgenes with a tissue-specific GAL4 (for example, an eye or renal-tubule-relevant driver) paired with a quantitative, blinded readout. Candidate readouts are eye-size or tumor-like overgrowth for Alk and a TRPP2 protein-level or tubule phenotype for Pkd2; the exact assays require verification. Screen each model against an approved-drug library plus clinically inactive negative-control drugs, using a ≥3-point dose series, randomized vial positions, and experimenters blinded to genotype and drug. Include wild-type-allele and vehicle controls and a positive-control drug for each model (brigatinib for Alk, chloroquine for Pkd2 D511V). Compare fly calls against a reference standard fixed before the screen, then compute PPV, NPV, sensitivity, specificity and exact binomial 95% CIs. Measure drug uptake by LC-MS in a subset to separate pharmacokinetic false negatives from true biological non-rescue. Include a Polg disease-variant model as an exploratory stress test, because POLG models are reported to be of limited quality. Design a prospective registry protocol (N-of-1 with predefined response criteria) for any fly-nominated drug that clinicians elect to use.

hypothesis.expected_outcomes: Proposed predictions: (1) Positive controls (brigatinib for Alk, chloroquine for Pkd2 D511V) will rescue at ≥30% with FDR <0.05; failure to recover them invalidates that assay. (2) The fly hit rate will be roughly 5-15% of the library per model. (3) PPV and NPV against the reference standard will each be ≥70%, with 95% CI lower bounds >50%. (4) At least a third of fly false negatives will be explained by low tissue exposure on LC-MS. (5) The exploratory Polg model will show lower concordance than the Alk and Pkd2 models. All tests will be two-sided with α=0.05 after multiple-testing correction, using ≥3 independent biological replicates of ≥30 flies per dose.
hypothesis.novelty_claim: The literature synthesis shows that chloroquine improved the phenotype of flies expressing a TRPP2(D511V) ortholog without patient data, and that one adenoid cystic carcinoma patient received a fly-predicted cocktail with about 12 months of stabilization. No provided study reports a denominator of fly-predicted rescues, so the concordance rate cannot be estimated. The proposal addresses this gap by pre-registering a reference standard and reporting PPV and NPV, including negative-control drugs and fly false negatives, which no provided paper assesses. It also tests whether measuring drug exposure improves prediction, a pharmacokinetic confounder the synthesis identifies as unaddressed.
hypothesis.feasibility_notes: Estimated timeline is 18-24 months: 3 months for line construction and assay validation, 6-9 months for screening and dose-response, 3 months for LC-MS exposure checks, and 3-6 months for analysis and registry protocol and ethics preparation. The main pitfalls are that the reference standard is limited by sparse published patient data, so many comparisons will use mammalian data instead of clinical outcomes, which the paper must state. Other risks are that variant transgene expression levels may cause artifacts, that drug solubility and feeding variability may produce false negatives, and that the library size limits power. Direct patient concordance cannot be measured within this project; the prospective registry is a proposal and requires clinical partners and ethical approval.
specific_aims: Aim 1: Validate variant models and positive controls — establish blinded quantitative rescue assays for the Alk and Pkd2 D511V-equivalent fly models, confirming that brigatinib and chloroquine, respectively, rescue at ≥30%.

Aim 2: Benchmark fly predictions — screen ≥40 approved drugs plus negative controls per model and compute PPV, NPV, sensitivity and specificity with 95% CIs against a pre-registered reference standard.

Aim 3: Quantify pharmacokinetic confounders — use LC-MS tissue exposure to test whether exposure-verified calls have ≥15 points higher concordance and to classify false negatives; add an exploratory Polg model and a prospective N-of-1 registry protocol.

literature.disease_context: Drosophila models of specific patient variants have been used to screen approved drugs and multi-drug combinations, yielding candidates that have been tested—and in at least one case confirmed—in the corresponding human patient. This approach is particularly valuable for rare diseases and cancers where standard therapeutic options are limited or absent. The translation from fly phenotype rescue to patient benefit has been demonstrated in cancer (adenoid cystic carcinoma) and explored in monogenic diseases (ADPKD, KCNT1-epilepsy, POLG-mitochondrial disease), though the frequency of successful clinical translation remains poorly characterized across the field.

identified_gaps: No published systematic dataset exists reporting the hit rate of fly-predicted drug rescues that subsequently hold in the matched human patient — the adenoid cystic carcinoma case [2] is a single n=1 report, and it is unknown whether the fly platform predicts clinical benefit more often than chance across a patient cohort.

Patient-specific Drosophila models have been built for only a handful of variant types (missense destabilizing variants, oncogenic fusions/amplifications); it is unknown whether the approach generalizes to loss-of-function frameshift, splice-site, or dominant-negative variants that are harder to model with UAS-transgene systems.

For KCNT1-epilepsy and POLG-mitochondrial disease, Drosophila models recapitulate some molecular features but current reviews note they do not fully recapitulate the human condition [3][4], so it is unresolved which phenotypic endpoints in flies are predictive of drug response in patients.

Resistance mechanisms observed in the ACC patient after 12 months (new genomic amplifications and deletions) [2] were not modeled in the fly prior to treatment, revealing a gap: fly models built on baseline tumor genomics cannot prospectively predict acquired resistance variants.

The TRPP2(D511V) chloroquine rescue was validated in Drosophila [1] but never tested in a human PKD2 D511V patient or in a mammalian knock-in model, leaving the clinical translatability of the fly rescue unconfirmed.

literature.summary: Drosophila models expressing specific patient variants have successfully identified approved or approved-class drugs that rescue variant-associated phenotypes in vivo, with the strongest translational evidence coming from a patient-specific adenoid cystic carcinoma line where a fly-predicted three-drug cocktail produced 12 months of clinical benefit in the matched patient [2], and a TRPP2(D511V) ADPKD model where chloroquine rescued fly phenotypes [1]. Multi-system validation using Drosophila alongside cell lines and mouse models has also been demonstrated for ALK inhibitors in neuroblastoma [6], and reviews of KCNT1 and POLG disease models confirm Drosophila's mechanistic utility while flagging incomplete phenotypic recapitulation [3][4]. However, published data on the overall rate at which fly-predicted drug rescues translate to patient benefit remain limited to anecdotal cases, and systematic prospective studies across patient cohorts are lacking, representing the central open question in the field.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Drosophila melanogaster lines expressing ≥2 patient-specific variants from a defined cohort of ≥10 rare-disease or cancer patients will correctly predict clinically beneficial approved-drug responses (defined as ≥stable disease or ≥50% seizure reduction or equivalent primary endpoint) in the matched human patient at a rate significantly greater than chance (>30% positive predictive value, compared to a historical chance baseline of ~10%), as assessed prospectively across patients enrolled at a single center under standardized 25°C screening conditions within a 36-month study window.
hypothesis.experimental_approach: For each of ≥10 enrolled patients harboring a specific characterized variant in one of three index genes (PKD2/amo, KCNT1/kcnt1, or a tumor-specific oncogenic driver analogous to the ACC model), a patient-specific UAS-transgene line will be generated carrying the exact human missense or gain-of-function variant via site-directed mutagenesis of a wild-type UAS-cDNA backbone, followed by PhiC31 integrase-mediated insertion at a defined attP landing site to control for position effects. Transgenic flies will be crossed to a tissue-appropriate GAL4 driver (elav-GAL4 for neuronal KCNT1 models, nanos-GAL4 or nephrocyte-specific Dot-GAL4 for PKD2 models, and en-GAL4/ptc-GAL4 for tumor suppressor contexts) to generate a primary phenotype (locomotor defect, wing vein disruption, or lethality assay) that is quantified in a blinded manner. A curated library of ≥80 FDA-approved drugs (drawn from existing approved-drug repurposing sets such as the NIH Clinical Collection) will be fed at two concentrations (1 µM and 10 µM in 5% sucrose/yeast food) in 96-well-format survival or locomotion assays, with at least three biological replicates per drug per patient line; hits are defined as drugs restoring phenotype to within 20% of the wild-type control mean with p<0.05 (one-way ANOVA with Dunnett correction). All patient lines are screened in parallel with a positive control (a previously validated rescue combination where known, e.g., chloroquine for TRPP2-D511V flies) and a vehicle-only negative control. Top fly-predicted drug candidates (≥2 hits per patient) are reported to the treating physician as candidate repurposing options, and patient clinical outcome at 6 and 12 months is assessed using pre-specified endpoints (RECIST 1.1 for tumors, seizure diary for KCNT1, eGFR/cyst volume for PKD2), with outcome assessors blinded to fly results until the 12-month lock.

hypothesis.expected_outcomes: Primary endpoint: Across ≥10 patient lines, the fly platform will identify at least one phenotype-rescuing approved drug in ≥70% of lines (≥7/10), with a positive predictive value for clinical benefit (stable disease or better at 6 months) of ≥30% (≥3 of the first 10 drug-patient matches tested clinically). Secondary endpoints: (1) Mean phenotypic rescue magnitude in hit compounds will be ≥20% improvement over vehicle control (p<0.05, ANOVA with Dunnett correction); (2) Concordance between fly hits and clinical benefit will be significantly greater than a randomized drug-assignment comparator (chi-square or Fisher's exact, p<0.05 one-tailed); (3) At least one patient in each disease category (renal, epilepsy, cancer) will show measurable clinical benefit attributable to a fly-predicted drug not previously prescribed for that variant. Negative outcome: If <2 patients (out of 10) show clinical benefit from fly-predicted drugs, this would be consistent with the null hypothesis that fly screens do not outperform chance and would prompt reassessment of phenotypic endpoints.
hypothesis.novelty_claim: No published systematic dataset exists reporting the hit rate of fly-predicted drug rescues that subsequently hold in the matched human patient — the adenoid cystic carcinoma case (PMID 33733072) is a single n=1 report, and it is unknown whether the fly platform predicts clinical benefit more often than chance across a patient cohort. This study directly addresses that gap by prospectively testing fly predictions in a multi-disease cohort of ≥10 patients under standardized conditions. Additionally, the TRPP2(D511V) chloroquine rescue was validated in Drosophila (PMID 26924047) but never tested in a human PKD2 D511V patient or mammalian knock-in model; this plan includes PKD2 patients as one of the three index disease arms, providing the first prospective clinical test of that fly-predicted drug. Finally, existing reviews note that KCNT1 and POLG Drosophila models do not fully recapitulate the human condition (PMID 40544226, PMID 41199776), so this study will empirically determine which fly phenotypic endpoints (locomotion, lifespan, electrophysiology) correlate with drug response in patients, filling the gap in validated translational biomarkers.
hypothesis.feasibility_notes: Transgene generation via PhiC31 insertion is routine and takes approximately 3-4 months per patient line including sequence verification and balancer establishment. The 96-well drug feeding format has been validated for survival and locomotion assays in published high-throughput fly studies. The main technical risk is that some patient variants (frameshift, splice-site, or dominant-negative) may not produce a robust, drug-sensitive phenotype using UAS-cDNA overexpression; to mitigate this, only missense gain-of-function or dominant-negative missense variants will be accepted for the initial cohort, consistent with variant types that have been successfully modeled (PMID 33733072, PMID 26924047). Clinical translation requires IRB/ethics approval and willing treating physicians; this is a prerequisite and may limit enrollment rate. Patient recruitment for rare diseases (especially PKD2 D511V specifically) may be slow; a 36-month window with rolling enrollment is planned, targeting 3-4 patients per disease arm. A limitation is that tumor models may require somatic mosaic expression strategies rather than simple UAS overexpression, adding complexity for cancer patients. Estimated timeline: months 1-4 for line generation and validation; months 5-10 for drug screening; months 10-36 for clinical follow-up and outcome assessment. Total cost estimated at $250,000-$400,000 USD depending on patient cohort size and clinical data collection infrastructure.
specific_aims: Aim 1: Variant Modeling and Phenotype Validation — Generate and validate ≥10 patient-specific UAS-transgene fly lines (≥3 per disease arm: PKD2, KCNT1, oncogene) carrying exact patient missense variants, confirm a robust, quantifiable, variant-dependent phenotype in the appropriate tissue-specific GAL4 background, and establish that phenotype is rescued by at least one positive control compound where a literature precedent exists (e.g., chloroquine for TRPP2-D511V lines)

Aim 2: Approved-Drug Screen and Hit Identification — Screen ≥80 FDA-approved compounds at two concentrations in each validated patient fly line using a blinded 96-well survival/locomotion assay format, identify per-patient drug hits defined as ≥20% phenotypic rescue with p<0.05, and rank hits by rescue magnitude and drug safety profile for clinical prioritization

Aim 3: Prospective Clinical Correlation — Report top fly-predicted drug candidates to treating physicians for each enrolled patient, prospectively collect clinical outcome data at 6 and 12 months using pre-specified disease-appropriate endpoints (RECIST 1.1, seizure frequency, eGFR), and calculate positive predictive value, sensitivity, and specificity of fly-screen predictions relative to clinical outcome in a blinded analysis

literature.disease_context: Dysregulation of gut immune discrimination between commensals and pathogens in Drosophila parallels inflammatory bowel disease, colorectal cancer, and metabolic disorders in humans [4][5]. Disruption of the microbial balance (dysbiosis) activates aberrant immune responses and stem cell overactivation that can drive dysplasia and tumorigenesis [5]. Because Drosophila gut signaling pathways are molecularly conserved with those in the mammalian gut, findings in flies directly inform understanding of human gut disease [4][6].

identified_gaps: Uracil has been identified as a pathogen-associated metabolic signal triggering Duox-ROS activation [1], but it is not established from the provided literature which specific molecular receptor or sensor detects uracil in gut epithelial cells, leaving the upstream recognition mechanism unresolved.

AMPs and lysozymes regulate both commensals and pathogens using the same effector molecules [7], yet the provided literature does not explain how quantitative or spatial differences in AMP deployment achieve selective pressure against pathogens without eliminating beneficial commensals — a mechanistic gap with direct relevance to therapeutic microbiome modulation.

Multiple signaling pathways (IMD, Toll, JAK/STAT, Duox-ROS, JNK/FOXO) are activated differentially by pathogen type [2], but the provided literature does not clarify how upstream pattern-recognition events are transduced into pathway-specific activation when commensals and pathogens share similar microbial-associated molecular patterns (MAMPs) such as peptidoglycan.

The role of gut microbiota metabolites beyond uracil in pathogen discrimination is not addressed in the provided literature, representing an unexplored chemical space for commensal-versus-pathogen sensing.

Systemic signals such as sleep deprivation via the brain-gut axis [8] and amino acid availability [9] affect ISC function and gut microbiota composition, but how these organismal states modulate the threshold or specificity of immune discrimination between commensals and pathogens has not been investigated in the provided literature.

evidence_claims.claim: Recognition of the bacterial metabolic status in situ, by a sensing of the gut metabolites as a signature of a specific bacterial metabolic activity, has been suggested to be a highly beneficial means for the host to maintain gut-microbe homeostasis.

Bacterial-derived uracil and uracil-modulated intestinal reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation play a pivotal role in diverse aspects of host-microbe interactions, such as pathogen clearance, commensal protection, intestinal cell regeneration, colitogenesis, and possibly also interorgan immunological communication.

The innate immunity of gut epithelia, such as anti-microbial peptide- and reactive oxygen species-based immune systems, actively participate in gut-microbe homeostasis by shaping the commensal community while efficiently eliminating unwanted bacteria.

Distinct immune signaling pathways are activated within the gut when insects ingest pathogens or hazardous materials. The pathway induced depends on the infection or pathogen type; include immune deficiency (imd), Toll, JAK/STAT, Duox-ROS, and JNK/FOXO regulatory pathways.
The gut microbiota initiates various signaling pathways and produces vitamins and minerals that help maintain gut homeostasis.
AMPs and lysozymes are necessary to regulate the total and relative abundance of bacteria in the gut microbiota.

This work shows that immune effectors, typically associated with resistance to pathogenic infections, also help shape the beneficial gut community, consistent with the idea that host-symbiont interactions use the same 'language' typically associated with pathogenesis.
Consequences of the loss of these antimicrobial peptides and lysozymes are exacerbated during aging, and their loss contributes to increased microbiota abundance and shifted composition in old flies.
Dysbiosis, the imbalance of an organism's commensal microbiota, may drive dysplasia and tumorigenesis via aberrant immune response, increased inflammation, and stem cell overactivation.

Microbiota and pathogenic microbes, such as bacteria and viruses, induce multiple innate immune and stress signaling pathways in enterocytes and other gut cells that, in turn, activate mitogens driving regenerative stem cell proliferation.
Wild-type and genetically predisposed intestinal epithelial cells are more likely to initiate tumorigenesis and tissue invasion upon interaction with intestinal microbes.
Gut microbiota have evolutionarily adapted to the host gut environment, serving as key regulators of intestinal stem cells to promote a healthy gut barrier and modulate epithelial self-renewal.
Disruption of these populations has been associated with inflammatory disorders or cancerous lesions of the intestine.
The molecular mechanisms controlling gut-microbe interactions are only partially understood due to the high diversity and biologically dynamic nature of these microorganisms.

Disruption of SSS causes gut microbiota dysbiosis in Drosophila.
Asparagine inhibits the hyperproliferation of aging ISCs in Drosophila, maintains intestinal homeostasis, and extends the lifespan of aging flies.
The increased microbial load in the gut activates the host immune system, the dysregulated microbiota can have direct implications in gut aging.

literature.summary: The Drosophila gut distinguishes commensals from pathogens not solely through classical pattern recognition of shared microbial structures, but crucially through metabolic cues: pathogens secrete uracil, which activates Duox-generated ROS selectively, while commensals are tolerated partly because they lack this signal [1]. Multiple parallel immune pathways (IMD, Toll, JAK/STAT, Duox-ROS, JNK/FOXO) are deployed in a pathogen-type-specific manner [2], and the same immune effectors — AMPs and lysozymes — that kill pathogens also quantitatively sculpt the commensal community, suggesting that discrimination is more a matter of degree and context than of categorically distinct recognition mechanisms [7]. A key unresolved question is precisely how shared microbial patterns fail to trigger full immune activation against commensals, and whether additional metabolic or spatial signals beyond uracil encode commensal identity in vivo [1][3][4].

hypothesis.hypothesis: Bacterial-derived uracil is both necessary and sufficient to shift gut epithelial immune signaling from commensal-tolerant (low Duox-ROS, low IMD-AMP) to pathogen-discriminating (high Duox-ROS, high IMD-AMP) mode in Drosophila melanogaster adult females: specifically, (1) germ-free w1118 flies orally colonized with uracil-secreting commensal Lactobacillus plantarum engineered to overexcrete uracil will display ≥2-fold elevation in gut ROS levels (measured by luminol assay), ≥1.5-fold increase in Diptericin-GFP reporter fluorescence, and ≥30% reduction in viable commensal CFU relative to wild-type L. plantarum-colonized controls within 5 days at 25°C; and (2) germ-free flies orally challenged with the pathogen Erwinia carunculovora (a standard gut pathogen) in the presence of exogenous uracil-degrading enzyme uricase will show ≥50% reduction in gut ROS and ≥40% reduction in pathogen-driven ISC proliferation (assessed by phospho-H3 staining) compared to vehicle-treated pathogen controls, demonstrating that uracil is the primary discrimination signal upstream of Duox activation.
hypothesis.experimental_approach: We will use a two-arm experimental design in adult mated female w1118 flies reared under germ-free (axenic) conditions on autoclaved holidic medium at 25°C, 12h:12h light:dark cycle. Arm 1 tests uracil sufficiency: germ-free flies will be colonized by feeding with standard wild-type Lactobacillus plantarum (WCFS1) or an isogenic uracil-oversecreting strain (pyrE/pyrF deletion mutant, which accumulates uracil due to impaired pyrimidine salvage, constructed in-house or sourced from collaborators) at 10^8 CFU/mL for 24h; gut ROS will be quantified by luminol chemiluminescence assay and DHE staining, AMP induction by a Diptericin-GFP transcriptional reporter line, commensal load by CFU plating, and ISC proliferation by phospho-histone H3 immunostaining. Arm 2 tests uracil necessity: standard pathogen Erwinia carunculovora (Ecc15) oral infection at 10^9 CFU/mL will be performed with simultaneous administration of recombinant uricase (50 U/mL in food) or vehicle control (PBS) to enzymatically degrade luminal uracil; endpoints are identical to Arm 1 plus survival assay. All genotypes will include UAS-Duox-RNAi × esg-GAL4 and UAS-Duox-RNAi × Myo1A-GAL4 crosses as tissue-specific controls to confirm Duox pathway dependency; a catalase-overexpression line (UAS-Cat × Myo1A-GAL4) will serve as ROS-quench positive control. Sample sizes: ≥100 flies per condition per replicate, ≥3 biological replicates; statistical analysis by ANOVA with Tukey post-hoc and survival analysis by log-rank test, significance threshold p<0.05.

hypothesis.novelty_claim: This experiment directly addresses two gaps explicitly identified in the literature synthesis: (1) while uracil has been shown to trigger Duox-ROS activation, the provided literature does not establish whether uracil is sufficient to convert a commensal into an immune-activating entity in vivo, nor whether uracil removal is sufficient to protect a pathogen from clearance — this causal bidirectional test has not been performed; (2) the provided literature does not clarify how upstream recognition events are transduced into pathway-specific activation when commensals and pathogens share MAMPs such as peptidoglycan — by manipulating a single metabolic variable (uracil) while holding MAMP content constant (same bacterial species backbone or same pathogen strain), we isolate the metabolic discrimination signal from MAMP-based recognition, directly testing the metabolic-cue hypothesis in a controlled genetic system. No paper in the synthesis has used uricase delivery to ablate luminal uracil during pathogen infection or used an isogenic uracil-oversecreting commensal to test sufficiency in germ-free Drosophila.
hypothesis.feasibility_notes: Germ-free fly rearing and oral colonization with defined bacterial strains are well-established protocols in Drosophila gut immunology labs. Luminol and DHE ROS assays, phospho-H3 immunostaining, and CFU plating are standard. The main technical challenge is generating or obtaining the L. plantarum pyrE/pyrF uracil-oversecreting mutant — this requires bacterial genetics expertise or collaboration; alternatively, exogenous uracil supplementation (e.g., 1-10 mM uracil added to food) could serve as a surrogate in a pilot experiment to validate the system before committing to mutant generation. Uricase is commercially available (Sigma-Aldrich) and has been used in Drosophila food supplementation studies, though gut stability and delivery efficiency will need to be empirically validated with a uracil-measurement pilot. Estimated timeline: months 1-3, axenic line establishment and bacterial mutant generation/validation; months 4-6, Arm 1 (sufficiency) experiments; months 7-9, Arm 2 (necessity/uricase) experiments; months 10-12, Duox-RNAi mechanistic controls and data analysis. Potential pitfalls include: uricase instability in gut lumen reducing effective uracil degradation (mitigated by dose-response pilot); uracil-oversecreting bacteria having reduced fitness affecting colonization efficiency (mitigated by CFU normalization at inoculation); non-specific ROS sources confounding luminol assay (mitigated by catalase control arm).

Aim 3: Duox Pathway Dependency — Confirm that the uracil-dependent discrimination phenotypes identified in Aims 1 and 2 are specifically mediated through enterocyte Duox activity using tissue-specific Myo1A-GAL4-driven Duox-RNAi and catalase overexpression controls

Bacterial-derived uracil and uracil-modulated intestinal reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation play a pivotal role in diverse aspects of host-microbe interactions, such as pathogen clearance, commensal protection, intestinal cell regeneration, colitogenesis, and possibly also interorgan immunological communication.

Recognition of the bacterial metabolic status in situ, by a sensing of the gut metabolites as a signature of a specific bacterial metabolic activity, has been suggested to be a highly beneficial means for the host to maintain gut-microbe homeostasis.

Uracil has been identified as a pathogen-associated metabolic signal triggering Duox-ROS activation, but it is not established from the provided literature which specific molecular receptor or sensor detects uracil in gut epithelial cells, leaving the upstream recognition mechanism unresolved.

Distinct immune signaling pathways are activated within the gut when insects ingest pathogens or hazardous materials. The pathway induced depends on the infection or pathogen type; include immune deficiency (imd), Toll, JAK/STAT, Duox-ROS, and JNK/FOXO regulatory pathways.

The provided literature does not clarify how upstream pattern-recognition events are transduced into pathway-specific activation when commensals and pathogens share similar microbial-associated molecular patterns (MAMPs) such as peptidoglycan.

The innate immunity of gut epithelia, such as anti-microbial peptide- and reactive oxygen species-based immune systems, actively participate in gut-microbe homeostasis by shaping the commensal community while efficiently eliminating unwanted bacteria.
AMPs and lysozymes are necessary to regulate the total and relative abundance of bacteria in the gut microbiota.

This work shows that immune effectors, typically associated with resistance to pathogenic infections, also help shape the beneficial gut community, consistent with the idea that host-symbiont interactions use the same 'language' typically associated with pathogenesis.
The provided literature does not explain how quantitative or spatial differences in AMP deployment achieve selective pressure against pathogens without eliminating beneficial commensals.
Dysbiosis, the imbalance of an organism's commensal microbiota, may drive dysplasia and tumorigenesis via aberrant immune response, increased inflammation, and stem cell overactivation.

Microbiota and pathogenic microbes, such as bacteria and viruses, induce multiple innate immune and stress signaling pathways in enterocytes and other gut cells that, in turn, activate mitogens driving regenerative stem cell proliferation.
Gut microbiota have evolutionarily adapted to the host gut environment, serving as key regulators of intestinal stem cells to promote a healthy gut barrier and modulate epithelial self-renewal.
The molecular mechanisms controlling gut-microbe interactions are only partially understood due to the high diversity and biologically dynamic nature of these microorganisms.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Proposed (not established): in germ-free adult mated female flies mono-associated at matched CFU, the pathogen Erwinia carotovora carotovora 15 (Ecc15) will elicit at least 2-fold higher Duox-dependent intestinal ROS than the commensal Lactiplantibacillus plantarum at 24 h, and this difference will track bacterial uracil release rather than receptor-level imd activation. Adding uracil to L. plantarum-colonized flies to match Ecc15 gut uracil levels will raise ROS to at least 70% of the Ecc15 level, and enterocyte-specific Duox RNAi will reduce that uracil-driven ROS increase by at least 50%.
hypothesis.experimental_approach: Germ-free, mated female flies of a single defined background (w1118 or an isogenic control matching the GAL4/UAS lines) are mono-associated at 25°C with L. plantarum or Ecc15 at matched CFU. Ecc15 and L. plantarum are my proposed representatives of a pathogen and a commensal and are not taken from the supplied literature. Readouts at 6, 24 and 48 h are: (a) luminal and culture-supernatant uracil by LC-MS; (b) gut ROS by a ROS-sensitive dye or probe; (c) ISC mitoses by anti-phospho-histone H3 counts; (d) Diptericin and Duox transcripts by qPCR; (e) bacterial load by CFU. Causality is tested with enterocyte-specific Duox RNAi (myo1A-GAL4, tub-GAL80ts), with imd pathway loss of function (e.g., a Relish null or enterocyte RNAi) to separate receptor-level from metabolite-level discrimination, and with uracil supplementation of commensal-colonized flies. Controls are germ-free flies, heat-killed bacteria, GAL4-only and UAS-only genotypes, and a non-targeting RNAi. Tests use at least 3 biological replicates and 15 guts per group per replicate.

This plan directly compares uracil output, Duox-ROS and imd dependence across a commensal and a pathogen at matched dose, which targets those gaps. literature.disease_context: Microbial metabolites such as polyamines and acetic acid that extend fly lifespan and regulate intestinal stem cell homeostasis have direct parallels to human gut microbiome research on aging, metabolic syndrome, and inflammatory bowel disease [1][9][11]. Disruption of microbiota-metabolite axes—for example by dietary oxidized proteins—mirrors inflammation-driven accelerated aging seen in human chronic disease [2]. Understanding causal metabolite-host signaling links identified in Drosophila models may inform therapeutic microbiome interventions for age-related diseases in humans [7][11].

identified_gaps: The specific receptors or transport mechanisms by which fly intestinal epithelium senses and imports bacterially derived polyamines (putrescine, spermidine) remain uncharacterized, making it unclear how the signal is transduced to extend lifespan [1].

While acetic acid activates JAK/STAT signaling to balance ISC homeostasis [9] and insulin/steroid signaling to promote larval development [5], it is unknown whether these two acetic acid-dependent axes are coordinated or independent, and whether the same or different cell populations are targeted.

The identity of the gut microbial terpenoid metabolites (e.g., ergosterol acetate) responsible for lifespan extension by yeast mutants has been reported [7], but their host molecular targets and the signaling pathways they activate have not been defined.

Behavioral effects of microbial metabolites are mentioned in general reviews [11] but no paper in this set provides mechanistic dissection of which specific metabolite mediates which specific behavior in Drosophila, representing a major empirical gap.

The extent to which microbiota-derived metabolites interact with or depend on histone deacetylation (Rpd3/HDAC1) or FOXO-mediated transcription [15] during aging has not been tested; linking epigenetic regulators to metabolite-driven longevity programs is an open question.

Causal directionality between metabolic disorder and microbial dysbiosis in diet-induced aging [2] is inferred from correlative metabolomics and sequencing data rather than gnotobiotic rescue experiments, so which comes first remains unresolved.

literature.summary: A convergent set of Drosophila studies identifies acetic acid and polyamines (putrescine, spermidine) as the best-characterized microbial metabolites mediating effects on fly development rate, lifespan and healthspan: acetic acid from Acetobacter species accelerates larval development on restrictive diets via insulin and steroid hormone signaling [5] and maintains intestinal stem cell homeostasis in aging flies through the JAK/STAT pathway [9], while bacterially derived polyamines extend adult lifespan and suppress stress-response genes TotM and Halo, as demonstrated causally in gnotobiotic flies on polyamine-free diets [1]. Yeast-associated terpenoid metabolites such as ergosterol acetate and mitochondrial energy metabolism represent an emerging additional axis [7], whereas diet-induced dysbiosis shortens lifespan and impairs locomotion through a metabolic disorder–inflammatory amplification cascade [2]. Major open questions include the host receptors and downstream signaling for polyamines, whether distinct acetic acid-dependent pathways for development and ISC homeostasis are coordinated, and which specific microbial metabolites mediate behavioral effects—questions addressable by combining gnotobiotic Drosophila with targeted bacterial biosynthetic mutants and metabolite supplementation.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Bacterially derived acetic acid and polyamines (putrescine + spermidine) act through independent, non-overlapping signaling axes in the adult Drosophila intestine — acetic acid via JAK/STAT in intestinal stem cells and polyamines via suppression of TotM/Halo stress genes — such that gnotobiotic w1118 female flies (25°C, standard diet) mono-colonized with wild-type Acetobacter persici will show ≥15% median lifespan extension and ≥30% reduction in esg+ ISC count relative to germ-free controls, mono-colonization with polyamine-producing Lactobacillus plantarum will show ≥15% median lifespan extension and ≥40% reduction in TotM/Halo mRNA relative to germ-free controls, and simultaneous ablation of JAK/STAT signaling in ISCs (esg-GAL4 > UAS-domN) will abolish the Acetobacter-mediated but not the polyamine-mediated lifespan benefit, while spermidine-pathway genetic blockade (nos-GAL4 > UAS-spdsSp RNAi) will abolish the polyamine-mediated but not the Acetobacter-mediated lifespan benefit, demonstrating pathway independence.
hypothesis.experimental_approach: Gnotobiotic flies will be generated by standard bleach-dechorionation of w1118 embryos and rearing on axenic holidic medium (amino-acid-defined, polyamine-free, acetate-free) in individually vented vials. Four bacterial colonization conditions will be established: germ-free (GF), mono-colonized with wild-type Acetobacter persici (AP-WT), mono-colonized with polyamine-biosynthesis-deficient A. persici (AP-ΔspeB, generated by lambda-Red recombineering to delete the agmatinase gene), and mono-colonized with L. plantarum WCFS1 WT vs. its speB/speE double-deletion mutant (LP-Δpoly) to provide the polyamine-null control. Pathway-specific epistasis will be tested by crossing esg-GAL4 (ISC-specific driver) to UAS-domN (dominant-negative Dome/JAK receptor) to block JAK/STAT in ISCs while maintaining systemic signaling, and by using nos-GAL4 > UAS-Spds-RNAi to knock down spermidine synthase in the gut epithelium; all GAL4/UAS experiments will include UAS-only and GAL4-only sibling controls. Primary endpoints are (1) median and maximum lifespan (Kaplan-Meier, log-rank test, n ≥ 150 females per condition across three independent cohorts), (2) larval development rate (egg-to-adult timing on restrictive 0.25× yeast holidic medium, n ≥ 100 larvae per condition), (3) esg+ ISC cell count by confocal imaging of dissected midguts stained with anti-Esg antibody (n ≥ 20 guts per condition), (4) RT-qPCR of TotM, Halo, STAT92E target genes (Socs36E, upd3), ilp2, ilp5, and dfoxo in whole gut and fat body, and (5) open-field locomotion and geotaxis climbing assays at days 10, 30, and 50 to capture behavioral endpoints. Metabolite supplementation rescue experiments will add 5 mM sodium acetate or 100 µM spermidine to axenic holidic medium of GF flies to confirm metabolite sufficiency independent of bacterial colonization.

hypothesis.expected_outcomes: Aim 1 (metabolite sufficiency): GF flies supplemented with 5 mM sodium acetate will show ≥15% extension of median lifespan and ≥30% reduction in esg+ ISC count vs. unsupplemented GF controls (log-rank p < 0.01); GF flies supplemented with 100 µM spermidine will show ≥15% median lifespan extension and ≥40% reduction in TotM and Halo mRNA (RT-qPCR, fold-change vs. GF, p < 0.01 by one-way ANOVA with Tukey correction); larval development on 0.25× yeast medium will be accelerated by ≥10% (hours to pupation) by acetate but not by spermidine supplementation, consistent with the acetic acid-specific developmental signaling axis. Aim 2 (pathway independence): esg-GAL4 > UAS-domN flies mono-colonized with A. persici WT will lose the lifespan benefit of Acetobacter colonization (median lifespan not significantly different from GF controls, log-rank p > 0.05) but will retain ≥80% of the lifespan benefit conferred by L. plantarum WT colonization; conversely, nos-GAL4 > UAS-Spds-RNAi flies will lose ≥80% of the L. plantarum WT lifespan benefit but retain the A. persici WT lifespan benefit, with corresponding RT-qPCR showing STAT target gene expression rescued in Spds-RNAi flies colonized with A. persici. Aim 3 (behavior): Geotaxis climbing speed at day 30 will be ≥25% higher in spermidine-supplemented or L. plantarum WT-colonized flies vs. GF controls (one-way ANOVA p < 0.05, n ≥ 60 per condition), providing the first metabolite-specific behavioral quantification; acetate supplementation will not significantly improve climbing speed (p > 0.05), dissociating the behavioral from the ISC-homeostasis endpoint.
hypothesis.novelty_claim: This experiment directly addresses three identified gaps in the literature: (1) it tests for the first time whether the acetic acid-JAK/STAT-ISC axis and the polyamine-TotM/Halo axis are independent or coordinated, a question explicitly flagged as unresolved in the synthesis; (2) it provides mechanistic dissection of which specific metabolite mediates which specific behavior in Drosophila, identified as 'a major empirical gap' because no paper in the synthesis links a single metabolite causally to a behavioral endpoint; (3) it uses gnotobiotic rescue and bacterial biosynthetic mutants to establish causal directionality, addressing the critique that the metabolic disorder–dysbiosis cascade in diet-induced aging studies is inferred from correlative data rather than gnotobiotic rescue experiments. Additionally, the epistasis design using dominant-negative JAK/STAT combined with spermidine synthase RNAi has not been reported in the polyamine or acetic acid literature synthesized here.
hypothesis.feasibility_notes: Gnotobiotic Drosophila methodology is well established and the holidic medium formulation is published; polyamine-free holidic medium can be prepared by omitting putrescine from the standard recipe. Generation of A. persici speB deletion mutants by lambda-Red recombineering is feasible within 2–3 months but requires Acetobacter-optimized electroporation protocols that may need troubleshooting — an alternative is to use commercially available polyamine biosynthesis inhibitor DFMO (difluoromethylornithine) supplemented to bacterial cultures as a faster fallback. The esg-GAL4 > UAS-domN combination has precedent for blocking JAK/STAT in ISCs without lethality, but dominant-negative expression level must be titrated to avoid gut barrier failure that would confound lifespan results; single-copy UAS insertions and 18°C rearing during development with shift to 25°C in adults can mitigate over-expression toxicity. Total estimated timeline: bacterial mutant construction and validation (3 months), fly line verification and gnotobiotic setup (2 months), Aim 1 lifespan + developmental assays (4 months), Aim 2 epistasis lifespan assays (4 months, overlapping with Aim 1), Aim 3 behavioral assays embedded within lifespan cohorts (concurrent); total ~12–14 months. Key pitfall: if A. persici colonization efficiency in axenic flies is variable, 16S rRNA qPCR on individual fly guts must be used to confirm colonization at experiment start and end, and non-colonized individuals must be excluded post-hoc with pre-specified criteria.
specific_aims: Aim 1: Metabolite Sufficiency — Determine whether exogenous acetic acid and spermidine are each individually sufficient to recapitulate the full lifespan, ISC homeostasis, developmental rate, and behavioral phenotypes observed with bacterial colonization in germ-free w1118 flies on polyamine-free and acetate-free holidic medium

Aim 2: Pathway Independence Epistasis — Test whether JAK/STAT blockade in ISCs (esg-GAL4 > UAS-domN) selectively abolishes the Acetobacter persici-mediated lifespan benefit while leaving the L. plantarum polyamine-mediated benefit intact, and conversely whether gut-specific spermidine synthase RNAi (nos-GAL4 > UAS-Spds-RNAi) selectively abolishes the polyamine-mediated lifespan benefit while leaving the acetic acid-mediated benefit intact

Aim 3: Behavioral Metabolite Mapping — Quantify geotaxis climbing performance, open-field locomotion, and sleep/activity rhythms at days 10, 30, and 50 in GF flies supplemented with acetic acid, spermidine, both, or neither, to provide the first causal single-metabolite-to-behavior map in Drosophila melanogaster

identified_gaps: Only polyamines [1] and acetic acid [9] have gnotobiotic or treatment evidence for a specific microbial metabolite in the supplied papers, and the polyamine study measured lifespan only. Testing whether polyamines also affect development rate or behavior is needed to see if one metabolite acts across traits.

The polyamine study shows suppressed TotM and Halo in polyamine-producing monocolonized flies [1], but no mechanism is shown. Host polyamine uptake or transport mutants and TotM/Halo manipulation are needed to test whether these genes mediate the lifespan effect.

Acetic acid is named as a microbial metabolite for larval growth [5] and was tested for ISC homeostasis in aging [9]. No supplied study tests whether the same acetic acid/JAK-STAT or insulin/steroid mechanism operates across developmental and aging contexts.

The yeast mutant study implicates ergosterol acetate and mitochondrial metabolism [7], but the abstract does not establish which specific metabolites are necessary and sufficient. Metabolite add-back or depletion experiments with germ-free or gnotobiotic flies are needed.

The supplied literature contains little direct evidence on microbial metabolites affecting fly behavior. The oxidized-protein study reports impaired climbing alongside dysbiosis [2], but this is correlative and cannot be assigned to a specific metabolite. Behavioral assays with defined microbial metabolites in gnotobiotic flies are needed.

Dietary restriction in flies can extend lifespan independently of insulin-like signaling [8], and the supplied abstracts do not link microbial metabolites to this pathway. Testing microbe-by-diet interactions would clarify whether metabolites act through IIS or other routes.

literature.summary: The supplied literature shows the strongest direct evidence for microbial metabolites in fly lifespan: bacterial polyamines extend lifespan in gnotobiotic flies [1], and Acetobacter persici-derived acetic acid is linked to JAK/STAT signaling and ISC homeostasis in aging [9]. Acetic acid is also named in a review as a microbial factor promoting larval growth, with insulin and steroid signaling and intestinal protease activity implicated as host responses [5]. Evidence for yeast terpenoids [7] and for dysbiosis-associated aging and impaired climbing [2] is more limited or correlative, and behavior-specific metabolite mediators remain largely unaddressed.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Proposed: In gnotobiotic w1118 flies reared at 25°C on a holidic or defined diet, monocolonization with an E. coli strain that synthesizes polyamines (e.g., spermidine/putrescine) versus an isogenic polyamine-biosynthesis-deficient mutant will, in a metabolite-specific manner, (a) shorten egg-to-pupariation time by ≥8% (about ≥6 h on a ~5-day baseline), (b) extend median adult lifespan by ≥10%, and (c) increase age-matched (day 30) negative-geotaxis climbing performance by ≥15%. Dietary add-back of physiological-range polyamines to flies carrying the mutant will rescue ≥50% of each effect. Fat-body/gut-restricted knockdown of TotM or Halo is predicted to phenocopy the lifespan and climbing effect of bacterial polyamines (≥50% of the difference) without further extension in polyamine-colonized flies (non-additivity). Acetic acid from Acetobacter persici is predicted to be the dominant driver of the developmental-rate effect but not the lifespan or climbing effect, and polyamines the converse, testing whether one metabolite acts across traits or different metabolites mediate different traits.
hypothesis.experimental_approach: Axenic (bleached-embryo) w1118 flies will be re-associated with defined single-species or paired communities: wild-type E. coli, an isogenic E. coli polyamine-biosynthesis mutant (strains from the Shimokawa et al. study, to be requested/verified), wild-type Acetobacter persici, and an A. persici acetate-production-impaired mutant or acetate-depleted condition (to be constructed or verified). A 2x2 design (polyamine-producing vs. non-producing E. coli x A. persici present vs. absent) plus chemical add-back (spermidine, putrescine, acetic acid at titrated doses) on axenic flies will separate the contribution of each metabolite across three phenotypes: developmental timing (egg-to-pupa and egg-to-adult, scored every 4-6 h, ≥6 vials of 30 embryos per condition), lifespan (≥200 mated females per condition, 25°C, 12:12 LD, tipped every 2-3 days, log-rank and Cox models with vial as random effect), and behavior (RING-assay negative geotaxis at days 10/30/50 and, as an additional exploratory readout, locomotor activity in DAM monitors). Host mechanism will be tested using tissue-specific RNAi (e.g., gut driver and fat-body driver, with drivers and RNAi lines to be verified) against TotM and Halo, alongside ilp2/ilp5, foxo and Stat92E readouts by qPCR and, if justified, reporter lines, with microbial load (CFU) and metabolite levels (LC-MS of polyamines, GC/LC-MS of short-chain fatty acids in fly and diet) measured to exclude colonization differences. Controls include driver-only and UAS-only lines, heat-killed bacteria, and matched CFU across colonization groups.

hypothesis.expected_outcomes: Proposed predictions, not established results: (1) Polyamine-producing E. coli will extend median lifespan ≥10% relative to the mutant (log-rank p<0.01, Bonferroni-adjusted), consistent with prior lifespan data [42720309]; this will be repeated in two independent biological replicates. (2) Polyamine add-back to mutant-colonized flies will recover ≥50% of the lifespan difference. (3) A. persici/acetic acid will accelerate development ≥8% but have a smaller (<5%) lifespan effect than polyamines; if acetic acid also extends lifespan, this will be consistent with prior ISC work [41814352]. (4) Day-30 climbing index will be ≥15% higher with polyamines; if not, the metabolite acts on lifespan without a healthspan benefit. (5) TotM or Halo knockdown in the gut/fat body will reduce the colonization-dependent lifespan gap by ≥50%; no change would falsify the TotM/Halo-mediator model. Metabolite-specific dissociation (polyamines vs. acetate across traits) will be assessed by a genotype/colonization-by-treatment interaction term with p<0.05. A null result for developmental timing with polyamines would falsify a single-metabolite, multi-trait model.
hypothesis.novelty_claim: The supplied literature shows polyamines extend lifespan in gnotobiotic flies but measured lifespan only [42720309], and acetic acid is named as a larval-growth metabolite [26827889] and ISC modulator in aging [41814352] without cross-context testing. Gaps identified: no test of whether polyamines affect development or behavior, no host genetic test of TotM/Halo as mediators, no direct comparison of metabolites across development, lifespan and behavior in one gnotobiotic design, and little direct evidence linking defined microbial metabolites to behavior. hypothesis.feasibility_notes: Estimated 14-18 months: months 1-3 strain acquisition/verification, axenic setup and CFU/metabolite method validation; months 3-7 development and metabolite add-back assays; months 4-14 lifespan cohorts (run in parallel, ~3-4 months each for median, longer for max) and behavior; months 8-16 RNAi and molecular readouts; months 16-18 analysis. literature.summary: Evidence in the supplied literature shows a bidirectional trade-off between immunity and reproduction in Drosophila females: mating (via Sex Peptide) persistently suppresses immune defense, while prior infection reduces offspring survivorship without reducing egg number. Pre-copulatory behaviors are preserved despite metabolic costs, and immune challenge effects on reproduction are dose-dependent. Which tissue pays the cost, and the lifespan consequences of immune activation, remain largely untested in the supplied papers.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Proposed: In mated w1118-background female Drosophila at 25°C, adult-restricted Imd pathway activation (UAS-PGRP-LCa under tub-GAL80ts control) in the fat body will shorten median lifespan by at least 20% and reduce offspring egg-to-adult survivorship by at least 15%, without changing 7-day cumulative egg output by more than 10%. Equivalent activation in the ovary, gut or muscle will each change median lifespan by less than 10%. The fat body is therefore predicted to be the tissue that pays the cost of immune activation.
hypothesis.experimental_approach: Use the TARGET system (tub-GAL80ts; tissue-GAL4 > UAS-PGRP-LCa, with UAS-imd as an independent activator) to switch on Imd signaling only in adults, by shifting from 18°C to 29°C after eclosion and mating. Tissue drivers will target fat body, ovary (somatic follicle/gonad cells and germline in separate crosses), gut enterocytes or progenitors, and muscle, with brain/neurons as an optional extra arm; each driver's specificity must be verified. Controls are GAL4-only and UAS-only genotypes, each with tub-GAL80ts and shifted to 29°C, plus permissive-temperature (18°C) siblings and a sham/heat-killed-bacteria comparison. Readouts are lifespan (at least 150 females per genotype, log-rank test with Bonferroni correction), daily egg counts, egg-to-adult survivorship of offspring, Imd target (Diptericin, Attacin) qPCR to confirm tissue-restricted activation, and tissue-resolved TAG, ovariole and apoptosis readouts. Virgin and mated cohorts will be compared to test whether mating-associated immune suppression interacts with activation cost.

hypothesis.expected_outcomes: Predicted, not established: fat body-restricted Imd activation will reduce median lifespan by 20% or more (log-rank p<0.01 versus both parental controls) and reduce offspring egg-to-adult survivorship by 15% or more, while cumulative 7-day egg number stays within ±10% of controls (equivalence test). Ovary, gut and muscle activation will each shift median lifespan by less than 10%. Ovary-restricted activation may reduce offspring survivorship, which would separate a germline or provisioning cost from a fat body systemic cost. Fat body activation is expected to lower fat body and whole-body TAG by 20% or more and reduce ilp2/ilp5 or foxo-target readouts. foxo knockdown is predicted to rescue at least 50% of the lifespan loss. Virgin females are predicted to show a smaller lifespan cost than mated females. If no tissue shows an effect above these thresholds, or if the effect appears equally in all tissues, the single-tissue-payer hypothesis is rejected.
hypothesis.novelty_claim: Prior infection reduces egg-to-adult survivorship but not egg number in mated females (39965650), and a single mating persistently suppresses immune defense (35728669). However, the supplied papers measure these costs at the whole-organism level and none identifies which tissue pays them. Immune elicitation was dose-dependent for reproductive success but not survival (24731072), and the supplied literature contains no test of tissue-restricted or genetically induced chronic immune activation on lifespan or offspring survivorship. The proposed work fills the tissue-resolution and lifespan gaps by combining adult-restricted, tissue-specific Imd activation with lifespan, fecundity, offspring-survival and metabolic readouts. It also tests whether insulin/FOXO signaling mediates the cost, which the synthesis lists as untested for Sex Peptide-linked immune suppression.
hypothesis.feasibility_notes: Estimated timeline is 12-15 months: 2-3 months for line construction and driver validation, 6-7 months for lifespan cohorts run in parallel (egg and offspring assays in the first 4 weeks), and 3-4 months for qPCR, TAG and ovary analyses. Pitfalls include: leaky GAL4 expression at 18°C; driver expression outside the intended tissue (for example, hemocytes with some fat body drivers, or fat body expression from some gut drivers); heat-shift effects on lifespan, which need matched controls; constitutive PGRP-LCa causing toxicity or gut dysbiosis; and variation in microbiota or Wolbachia status across stocks. Offspring survivorship scoring needs standardized egg density and food. Stock availability and exact driver identities must be verified before starting.
specific_aims: Aim 1: Tissue-resolved lifespan and fecundity cost — compare adult-onset Imd activation in fat body, ovary, gut and muscle for median lifespan and 7-day egg output in mated and virgin females.

Aim 2: Mechanism of reduced offspring survivorship — use ovary versus fat body activation, reciprocal crosses to wild-type males, ovary apoptosis and ovariole assays, and AMP transcript measurement in eggs to separate germline damage from maternal provisioning.
Aim 3: Insulin/FOXO mediation of the fat body cost — measure fat body TAG, ilp2/ilp5 and FOXO-target expression after fat body Imd activation, and test rescue by foxo knockdown.

literature.disease_context: The immune-reproduction-lifespan trade-off studied in Drosophila is directly relevant to human conditions in which chronic immune activation (e.g., infection, autoimmunity) impairs fertility or accelerates aging. Sex Peptide-mediated immune suppression after mating parallels postpartum immune vulnerability in mammals, including increased susceptibility to infection. Understanding which tissues bear the cost of immune activation — particularly the fat body (equivalent to the mammalian liver) — may inform therapeutic strategies for sepsis, reproductive immunology, and age-related immune decline.

key_papers.authors: Adhikari K, Lazzaro BP et al.
key_papers.relevance: Demonstrates that the reproduction-immunity trade-off is bidirectional: prior infection reduces offspring survivorship, and mating destabilizes chronic infections, establishing that neither immunity nor reproduction has unconditional priority.

key_papers.authors: Nystrand M, Dowling DK et al.
