key_papers.authors: Rose S, Beckwith EJ, Burmester C et al.
key_papers.relevance: Surprisingly shows that pre-copulatory mating behaviors are maintained during infection, suggesting that behavioral reproductive investment is prioritized over immune economy at least at the pre-mating stage.

key_papers.title: Drosophila Innate Immunity Involves Multiple Signaling Pathways and Coordinated Communication Between Different Tissues.
key_papers.authors: Yu S, Luo F, Xu Y et al.
key_papers.relevance: Reviews the multi-tissue architecture of Drosophila innate immunity, highlighting the fat body as the primary humoral immune effector organ and identifying tissue-level coordination as central to immune cost allocation.

identified_gaps: The specific tissue(s) responsible for paying the reproductive cost of immune activation remain unresolved — while the fat body is the primary AMP-secreting organ [12], it is unknown whether the reproductive cost is borne locally (e.g., ovarian resource depletion) or systemically via fat body resource diversion from vitellogenesis to immune effector production.

The mechanism by which mating destabilizes chronic bacterial infections [2] is unknown — it is unclear whether this involves Sex Peptide signaling, immune suppression, altered pathogen dynamics, or changes in gut microbiota composition, and identifying the pathway would clarify the proximate basis of this reproductive-immune conflict.

It is unresolved whether the persistent immune suppression induced by a single mating [10] is mediated exclusively through Sex Peptide or involves additional seminal fluid proteins, and whether blocking this suppression can restore immune defense without impairing fertility.

The age-dependent decline in AMP inducibility observed in both mated and unmated females [10] has not been mechanistically linked to the immune-reproduction trade-off — it is unknown whether reproductive investment accelerates this immune aging trajectory.

Pre-copulatory behaviors are preserved during infection [1], but it is unknown whether this reflects active prioritization of reproductive investment (e.g., resource shielding) or simply that these behaviors are metabolically cheap enough to be spared, as the energetic budget of courtship relative to immune activation has not been quantified.

evidence_claims.claim: The activation of the immune system upon infection exerts a huge energetic demand on an individual, likely decreasing available resources for other vital processes, like reproduction.
Pre-copulatory reproductive behaviours are preserved in infected flies, despite the significant metabolic cost of infection.

literature.summary: In Drosophila melanogaster, the costs of immune activation and reproduction are reciprocal and bidirectional: infection prior to mating reduces offspring survivorship without affecting egg number, while mating persistently suppresses female immune defense via Sex Peptide transfer from seminal fluid and destabilizes chronic infections [39965650, 35728669]. Genome-wide transcriptomics and dose-response experiments show that immune gene activation is itself a major mechanistic cost of mating, and that even non-pathogenic immune stimulation impairs reproductive output in a dose-dependent manner [19228270, 24731072]. The fat body is the primary tissue paying the humoral immune cost — secreting AMPs via Toll and IMD pathways — while pre-copulatory behaviors are paradoxically preserved during infection, suggesting that behavioral reproductive investment is shielded from immune-driven resource competition, though the tissue-level accounting of these trade-offs remains incompletely resolved [35538789, 35911716].

hypothesis.hypothesis: Fat body-specific constitutive activation of the IMD pathway (via fat body-targeted overexpression of a dominant-active PGRP-LC transgene using Lsp2-GAL4) will reduce fecundity by ≥30% (eggs laid per female per day) and shorten median lifespan by ≥20% in mated w1118 females at 25°C on standard cornmeal-agar medium, compared to GAL4-only and UAS-only controls, while ovary-specific IMD activation (using nos-GAL4) will produce ≤10% fecundity reduction and ≤5% lifespan reduction under identical conditions — demonstrating that the fat body, not the ovary, is the primary tissue bearing the reproductive and longevity cost of immune activation.
hypothesis.experimental_approach: We will use the GAL4/UAS binary expression system to constitutively activate IMD signaling in a tissue-restricted manner: (1) Fat body-specific activation using Lsp2-GAL4 to drive UAS-PGRP-LC (dominant-active isoform) expression, representing the primary AMP-secreting organ; (2) Ovary/germline-specific activation using nos-GAL4 as a tissue compartment control; (3) Hemocyte-specific activation using Hml-GAL4 as a third tissue comparator. All experimental lines will be crossed to the UAS-PGRP-LC line and compared to parental GAL4-only and UAS-only controls, as well as to a ubiquitous-driver positive control (Act5C-GAL4 × UAS-PGRP-LC). Mated females will be collected within 24 h of eclosion, housed individually with w1118 males (refreshed every 3 days), and assessed for: (a) daily egg-laying rate and egg-to-adult survivorship over 30 days, (b) adult lifespan (n ≥ 120 per genotype, three independent replicates), (c) hemolymph AMP activity by colony-forming unit assay against E. coli K12, (d) fat body triglyceride and glycogen content by colorimetric assay to measure resource diversion from energy stores, and (e) RT-qPCR of Drosomycin, Defensin, and Attacin in dissected fat bodies and ovaries to confirm tissue-restricted transgene effect. To validate that the reproductive cost is resource-mediated rather than inflammation-mediated, a subset of fat body-activated females will receive a high-yeast diet (5% yeast w/v) to test whether caloric supplementation rescues fecundity.

hypothesis.expected_outcomes: Primary outcome: Fat body-specific PGRP-LC overexpression (Lsp2-GAL4 × UAS-PGRP-LC) females will lay ≥30% fewer eggs per day compared to both GAL4-only and UAS-only controls (two-way ANOVA with Tukey post-hoc, p < 0.05, n ≥ 120 per genotype per replicate, 3 replicates), and will show ≥20% reduction in median lifespan (log-rank test, p < 0.05). Ovary-specific activation (nos-GAL4 × UAS-PGRP-LC) will produce ≤10% fecundity reduction and ≤5% lifespan reduction, statistically indistinguishable from controls (p > 0.05). Fat body triglyceride levels in Lsp2-GAL4 × UAS-PGRP-LC females will be reduced by ≥25% relative to controls, indicating resource diversion from vitellogenesis. Hemolymph AMP activity will be elevated ≥2-fold in fat body-activated flies compared to controls (CFU assay). High-yeast diet supplementation will rescue ≥50% of the fecundity deficit in fat body-activated females, confirming a resource-allocation rather than inflammation-toxicity mechanism. RT-qPCR will confirm Drosomycin upregulation ≥5-fold in fat body but not ovary of experimental females.
hypothesis.novelty_claim: This experiment directly addresses the primary gap identified in the literature synthesis: 'the specific tissue(s) responsible for paying the reproductive cost of immune activation remain unresolved — while the fat body is the primary AMP-secreting organ, it is unknown whether the reproductive cost is borne locally (e.g., ovarian resource depletion) or systemically via fat body resource diversion from vitellogenesis to immune effector production.' Prior work established that IMD/Toll activation impairs reproduction and lifespan at the whole-organism level, and that the fat body is the primary humoral immune organ, but no study has used tissue-restricted constitutive IMD activation with parallel tissue compartment controls to causally assign the reproductive cost to a specific organ. The dietary rescue arm additionally tests whether the cost is energetic (resource competition between AMP synthesis and vitellogenesis) or inflammatory (immune effector toxicity to reproductive tissues), a distinction not addressed in prior dose-response or transcriptomic studies.
hypothesis.feasibility_notes: The GAL4/UAS approach is well-established in Drosophila and all components are genetically tractable. Key technical risks: (1) Lsp2-GAL4 drives expression in late larval fat body; adult fat body expression must be verified by GFP reporter — if expression is insufficient in adults, the r4-GAL4 or CG-GAL4 drivers (which are more broadly expressed in adult fat body) should be substituted; (2) UAS-PGRP-LC overexpression may cause lethality if ubiquitous — this is why tissue-restricted drivers are used and why Act5C-GAL4 is included as a positive/lethality control; (3) nos-GAL4 has some expression outside the germline in adults — somatic expression should be verified by GFP reporter; (4) Lifespan assays require strict standardization of mating, density, food, and temperature. Estimated timeline: 3 months for line acquisition and verification (GFP reporter crosses); 2 months for experimental cross setup and genotype confirmation; 3 months for concurrent lifespan and fecundity assays; 2 months for biochemical assays (triglyceride, CFU, RT-qPCR) and data analysis. Total: approximately 10–12 months. The dietary rescue experiment can run concurrently with the main lifespan cohort. Statistical power: based on published lifespan variance in w1118 (σ ≈ 8 days, median ~55 days), n = 120 per group gives 90% power to detect a 20% lifespan reduction at α = 0.05.
specific_aims: Aim 1: Tissue-restricted cost mapping — determine whether constitutive fat body IMD activation (Lsp2-GAL4 × UAS-PGRP-LC) reduces fecundity by ≥30% and median lifespan by ≥20% in mated females compared to ovary-specific (nos-GAL4) and hemocyte-specific (Hml-GAL4) IMD activation and driver/transgene-only controls

Aim 2: Resource diversion quantification — measure fat body triglyceride and glycogen stores, and hemolymph AMP activity, in fat body-activated versus tissue-control females to test whether reproductive cost correlates with measurable diversion of energy reserves from vitellogenesis to immune effector synthesis

Aim 3: Energetic rescue test — determine whether high-yeast dietary supplementation rescues ≥50% of the fecundity deficit in fat body-activated females, distinguishing resource-competition from immune-toxicity as the mechanistic basis of the reproductive cost of fat body immune activation

identified_gaps: The provided literature does not resolve the molecular mechanism; the review [4] names only two candidates (immune activation vs. resource competition). A direct test is needed, e.g. comparing protection in immune-pathway mutant flies and measuring host lipid/cholesterol availability in Wolbachia-infected vs. uninfected flies during DCV infection.

Protection can occur with or without a detectable reduction in virus titer [1], which suggests tolerance-like effects as well as resistance. It is unclear which mechanism underlies each outcome; this could be resolved by measuring tissue-specific viral load and pathology in matched Wolbachia+/- flies.

Developmental temperature at 18°C abolishes protection even though Wolbachia is present [3]. Which Wolbachia or host traits (e.g. tissue density, gene expression) change across developmental temperatures is unknown, and comparing these at 18°C vs. 25°C could identify the mechanistic determinant.

Protection correlates with Wolbachia density in larvae and adults [2], but whether density is causal, or whether localization in specific tissues matters, is untested. Density manipulation or tissue-resolved quantification could address this.

Protection against naturally occurring viruses (LJV, NFV) is associated with reduced titres [5], but the abstract does not say whether the mechanism is shared with DCV. Comparing mechanisms across virus families and Wolbachia strains would test generality.

literature.summary: In Drosophila, Wolbachia robustly protects against RNA viruses such as DCV, and protection depends on Wolbachia density, host life stage, developmental temperature, and Wolbachia/virus genotype [1-5]. The molecular mechanism remains unresolved in the provided literature: the review [4] proposes host immune activation or competition for cellular resources, and none of the supplied primary abstracts test these directly.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Proposed: Wolbachia (wMel) protection of adult w1118 female flies against Drosophila C virus (DCV) at 25°C is independent of Imd, Toll and siRNA signalling and instead depends on competition for host cholesterol; protection will persist in Relish, MyD88 and Dcr-2 mutants (Wolbachia+ vs Wolbachia- hazard ratio for death ≤0.5 in each), and 10-fold dietary cholesterol supplementation will reduce the protective effect (log hazard ratio) by ≥50%.
hypothesis.experimental_approach: Use isogenic Wolbachia-infected (wMel) and tetracycline-cured w1118 lines, with gut microbiota restored in cured lines and cured lines allowed several generations to recover. Cross each background into null or loss-of-function mutants of Relish (Imd), MyD88 (Toll) and Dcr-2 (siRNA), with a wild-type control. Raise flies at 25°C, infect 3–5-day-old mated females by intrathoracic DCV injection (a titration of doses plus a buffer-injected control), and score daily survival, with viral RNA by RT-qPCR at 0, 2 and 4 days post-infection. Next, rear flies on defined diets with standard or 10-fold cholesterol (and a lipid-depleted diet), and measure survival, DCV titre, Wolbachia density (qPCR) and whole-body and tissue cholesterol or lipid content (e.g. mass-spectrometry or filipin staining) in Wolbachia+ vs Wolbachia- flies. Finally, compare 18°C vs 25°C developmental temperature, which affects protection, to test whether loss of protection tracks Wolbachia density, tissue distribution or host lipid state. The Wolbachia density and temperature work follows the reported correlation and temperature dependence. Controls: mock injection, cured and infected genotype-matched siblings, matched Wolbachia density across genotypes, and reporting of survival and viral titre separately because protection can be titre-independent.

hypothesis.expected_outcomes: Proposed predictions, not established results: (1) In wild-type flies, Wolbachia+ flies show significantly longer survival than Wolbachia- flies after DCV injection (log-rank p<0.05, n≥100 flies per group over ≥3 biological replicates). (2) In Relish, MyD88 and Dcr-2 mutants, the Wolbachia+ vs Wolbachia- hazard ratio remains ≤0.5, so that ≥50% of wild-type protection is retained; mutants may be more susceptible overall. (3) On 10-fold cholesterol diets, protection (log hazard ratio) falls by ≥50% relative to standard diet (diet x Wolbachia interaction p<0.05), and Wolbachia+ flies show ≥20% lower cholesterol or lipid availability than Wolbachia- flies. (4) At 18°C, protection is lost, which will be compared with Wolbachia density and lipid measures. Falsification: if protection falls by >50% in any immune mutant, or cholesterol supplementation does not change protection, the resource-competition hypothesis is rejected (or only partly supported).
hypothesis.novelty_claim: The mechanism is unresolved and two candidate mechanisms are named: activation of host immunity or competition with the virus for cellular resources (PMID 33584729). Protection can occur with or without a detectable reduction in virus titer (PMID 38006555). Protection depends on developmental temperature (PMID 34488458). Protection correlates with Wolbachia density in larvae and adults (PMID 26407882). The supplied primary abstracts do not directly test immune-pathway mutants against host lipid availability in the same Wolbachia-DCV system, and this design addresses that gap with a factorial test.
hypothesis.feasibility_notes: Estimated timeline is 12–15 months: 2–3 months for generating and validating the Wolbachia+/- mutant lines (including cure verification and microbiota restoration), 3–4 months for the immune-mutant survival assays, 3–4 months for the diet and lipid assays, and 2–3 months for the temperature comparison and analysis. Pitfalls include differences in Wolbachia density between mutant backgrounds (which must be measured and matched), background effects of mutations and incomplete isogenization, altered feeding or fecundity on modified diets, the difficulty of accurately measuring tissue-level cholesterol, and DCV dose dependence. Cholesterol supplementation may affect fly physiology independently of Wolbachia, and the diet x Wolbachia interaction term addresses this. Stock numbers and the availability of specific mutant alleles must be verified before starting.

literature.disease_context: Wolbachia-conferred antiviral protection in insects has direct relevance to human arboviral diseases such as dengue, Zika, West Nile, and chikungunya. Wolbachia-transinfected Aedes aegypti mosquitoes are already being deployed in field settings to block transmission of dengue and Zika viruses to humans [3][6]. Understanding the molecular mechanism of viral blocking is therefore critical to optimizing and predicting the efficacy of this biocontrol strategy across different climates and mosquito populations [3][6].

key_papers.relevance: Notes that Wolbachia protection can occur with or without detectable reduction in virus titer, suggesting the mechanism may involve host tolerance as well as viral restriction.

identified_gaps: The precise molecular mechanism — whether host immunity activation, cellular resource competition, or another pathway — has not been resolved; the provided literature only identifies these as candidate mechanisms without establishing which is causal or primary [4].

It is unknown which specific host immune genes or pathways (e.g., RNAi, Toll, Imd, JAK-STAT) are required for Wolbachia-conferred antiviral protection; none of the provided abstracts name specific Drosophila immune effectors as mechanistically necessary.

The cellular resource competition hypothesis lacks molecular specificity: it is unclear which resources (e.g., lipids, nucleotides, amino acids, cellular membranes) are competed for and by what molecular means Wolbachia limits their availability to viruses [4].

The observation that protection can occur without a detectable reduction in virus titer [1] is mechanistically unexplained — it suggests a tolerance mechanism distinct from viral restriction, but no molecular basis for this tolerance has been identified in the provided literature.

Why developmental temperature at 18°C abolishes protection while adults still require Wolbachia at the time of infection [3] points to a developmentally programmed component of the mechanism that has not been characterized at the molecular level.

Whether the same molecular mechanism operates in Drosophila and in transinfected Aedes aegypti mosquitoes — which have different endogenous immune landscapes — remains untested in the provided literature [6].

evidence_claims.claim: Wolbachia-infected Drosophila melanogaster survive the pathogenic effects of positive-sense single-stranded RNA virus infections at a higher rate than the flies without Wolbachia.
The protection can occur with or without detectable reduction in virus titer.
Recent studies suggest two possible mechanisms: activation of host immunity or competition with virus for cellular resources.
The antiviral effect works against a broad range of RNA viruses and depends on the Wolbachia lineage.
Temperature after infection directly impacts Drosophila C virus (DCV) replication and modulates Wolbachia protection.
At higher temperatures, viruses proliferate more and are more lethal, while Wolbachia confers lower protection.
Host developmental temperature is a determinant of Wolbachia-conferred antiviral protection.
While there is strong protection when flies develop from egg to adult at 25°C, the protection is highly reduced or abolished when flies develop at 18°C.
Wolbachia is still required to be present in adults at the time of infection.
This developmental effect is general, since it was present in different host genotypes, Wolbachia variants, and upon infection with different viruses.
A high Wolbachia density was congruent with antiviral protection in both adults and larvae.
Wolbachia-mediated protection may vary between larval and adult stages of a given Wolbachia-host combination and that the variations in susceptibility by life stage correspond with Wolbachia density.
Wolbachia protection against the sterilizing effect of NFV leads to a net benefit of Wolbachia infection after exposure to the virus.

Flies infected with these viruses have increased mortality rates, and NFV partially sterilizes females. These effects on fitness were reduced in Wolbachia-infected flies, and this was associated with reduced viral titres.
Wolbachia alone also reduces survival, and under our experimental conditions these costs of the symbiont can outweigh the benefits of antiviral protection.
In Drosophila, Wolbachia mediates antiviral protection against a broad range of RNA viruses.
Wolbachia-transinfected Aedes aegypti mosquitoes are currently being deployed to fight transmission of dengue and Zika viruses.
The mechanism of antiviral protection and the factors influencing are still not fully understood.
Dependence of Wolbachia-mediated pathogen blocking on developmental temperature could be used to dissect the mechanistic bases of protection.
Wolbachia may influence the evolution of virus defense on the insect host genome.

The precise molecular mechanism of Wolbachia-conferred antiviral protection remains unresolved, with host immunity activation and cellular resource competition identified as candidates but neither established as causal.

literature.summary: Wolbachia confers broad antiviral protection against RNA viruses in Drosophila melanogaster and other insects, reducing virus-induced mortality and, in many cases, viral titres [4][5], though protection can also occur without detectable titer reduction [1]. Two mechanistic hypotheses have been proposed — activation of host innate immunity and competition with virus for cellular resources — but neither has been established as the primary or causal mechanism [4]. Key modulatory factors including Wolbachia density [2], host developmental temperature [3], and Wolbachia lineage [4] influence the magnitude of protection, and exploiting these variables may help dissect the underlying molecular mechanism, which remains one of the central unresolved questions in the field [3][4].

hypothesis.hypothesis: The JAK-STAT innate immune pathway is the primary molecular mechanism required for Wolbachia-conferred antiviral protection in Drosophila melanogaster: specifically, flies carrying Wolbachia (wMel strain) and a loss-of-function mutation in hopscotch (hop, the JAK-STAT pathway kinase) will show ≥80% loss of Wolbachia-conferred survival benefit compared to Wolbachia-carrying wild-type controls following systemic injection of Drosophila C virus (DCV) at 25°C developmental temperature, while RNAi knockdown of the competing cellular resource hypothesis effectors (fatty acid synthase, FASN) will produce <30% loss of protection, thereby establishing JAK-STAT activation as necessary and lipid competition as insufficient to explain the protection phenotype.
hypothesis.experimental_approach: We will use a genetic epistasis strategy in w1118 Drosophila melanogaster to test whether specific innate immune pathway components (JAK-STAT via hopscotch, Toll via spätzle, Imd via imd, and RNAi via Dicer-2) are individually necessary for Wolbachia (wMel)-conferred antiviral protection against DCV. Each immune pathway will be disrupted using validated loss-of-function mutants or tissue-specific UAS-RNAi lines driven by ubiquitous da-GAL4 or Act5C-GAL4, crossed into Wolbachia-positive and Wolbachia-negative (tetracycline-cured) isogenic backgrounds. The primary endpoint will be survival following intrathoracic injection of DCV (standardized dose of 10^3 TCID50 per fly) in 3–5 day old mated females reared at 25°C throughout development, with viral titer (RT-qPCR) measured at 2, 4, and 6 days post-infection as a secondary endpoint to distinguish resistance from tolerance mechanisms. To test the cellular resource competition hypothesis in parallel, we will knock down FASN (fatty acid synthase) and DHODH (dihydroorotate dehydrogenase, for nucleotide competition) using UAS-RNAi under Act5C-GAL4 in Wolbachia-positive backgrounds and measure the same survival and titer endpoints. All experiments will include four genotype classes: (1) Wolbachia+/immune pathway intact, (2) Wolbachia+/immune pathway disrupted, (3) Wolbachia−/immune pathway intact, and (4) Wolbachia−/immune pathway disrupted, with ≥150 flies per group across three independent biological replicates.

hypothesis.expected_outcomes: If JAK-STAT is the primary mechanism: (1) Wolbachia-positive hop mutant or hop-RNAi flies will show median survival indistinguishable from Wolbachia-negative controls (≤10% survival difference, versus ≥40% benefit in Wolbachia+/intact-JAK-STAT flies) after DCV injection at 25°C; (2) viral titers in Wolbachia-positive hop-disrupted flies will be ≥5-fold higher than in Wolbachia-positive hop-intact flies by day 4 post-infection (RT-qPCR); (3) FASN-RNAi and DHODH-RNAi knockdown in Wolbachia-positive flies will reduce survival benefit by <30%, suggesting lipid/nucleotide competition is not the primary mechanism. If instead RNAi (Dcr-2) disruption abolishes protection, this implicates small RNA antiviral immunity as the mechanism. If no single pathway disruption eliminates protection, this would support redundancy among mechanisms. Statistical thresholds: log-rank test for survival curves (p < 0.01 after Bonferroni correction for multiple pathway comparisons), one-way ANOVA with Tukey HSD for titer data (p < 0.05), with effect sizes reported as hazard ratios and fold-change in titer.
hypothesis.novelty_claim: The literature synthesis explicitly identifies that 'the precise molecular mechanism — whether host immunity activation, cellular resource competition, or another pathway — has not been resolved' and that 'no specific Drosophila immune effectors have been named as mechanistically necessary' for Wolbachia-conferred antiviral protection. No prior study in the supplied literature has used genetic epistasis in Drosophila to test which specific immune pathway (JAK-STAT, Toll, Imd, or RNAi) is individually necessary for protection, nor has any study directly compared the immune activation and resource competition hypotheses in a single controlled experiment. Additionally, the observation that 'protection can occur with or without detectable reduction in virus titer' remains mechanistically unexplained; our parallel titer and survival measurements across immune-disrupted genotypes will distinguish resistance (reduced titer) from tolerance (normal titer, improved survival) as mechanistic outcomes for each pathway.
hypothesis.feasibility_notes: All genetic tools required (GAL4/UAS system, loss-of-function alleles for hop, spz, imd, Dcr-2, STAT92E, and TRiP RNAi lines) are established in Drosophila and most are available from BDSC, though specific stock numbers must be verified before ordering. The DCV infection protocol via intrathoracic injection is standard and well-described in the literature. The main technical pitfall is that hop null alleles cause lethality; hemizygous males or RNAi-mediated knockdown with Act5C-GAL4 will be used to circumvent this. A second pitfall is incomplete Wolbachia elimination by tetracycline; Wolbachia-negative status must be confirmed by diagnostic PCR before experiments. Wolbachia density may vary with temperature, so all flies must be maintained at 25°C throughout development to match the conditions under which protection is established. A third pitfall is GAL4-driver background effects on immunity; Act5C-GAL4 and da-GAL4 controls without UAS transgene must be included. Estimated timeline: 3 months for line generation and Wolbachia status verification; 4 months for survival and titer experiments across all pathway knockdowns; 2 months for data analysis and validation. Total: approximately 9 months for a complete dataset.
specific_aims: Aim 1: JAK-STAT epistasis — Determine whether disruption of the JAK-STAT pathway (hopscotch, STAT92E) abolishes Wolbachia-conferred survival benefit and viral restriction following DCV infection at 25°C in mated female w1118 flies.

Aim 2: Comparative immune pathway screen — Test whether Toll (spätzle), Imd, or antiviral RNAi (Dicer-2) pathways are individually necessary for Wolbachia antiviral protection using the same DCV survival and RT-qPCR titer assays, to identify the primary or redundant immune effectors.

Aim 3: Resource competition hypothesis test — Determine whether knockdown of fatty acid synthase (FASN) or dihydroorotate dehydrogenase (DHODH) in Wolbachia-positive flies phenocopies loss of protection, thereby testing the cellular resource competition hypothesis in direct comparison with the immune activation results from Aims 1 and 2.

identified_gaps: Unclear whether gut memory is in the enterocytes themselves: [3] identifies the gut as the main site of PGRP-SC downregulation, but not which gut cell type (enterocytes vs. intestinal stem cells) carries the H3K9me3 mark. If the mark sits in stem cells, it could persist through epithelial turnover. Lineage-traced, cell-type-specific ChIP is needed.

Unknown duration of hemocyte training: [6] shows protection after sterile injury but does not report how long it lasts, whether it is stored epigenetically in hemocytes, or whether it is pathogen-specific. Time-course challenges and hemocyte ablation after priming would separate true memory from a sustained activated state.

No test of interaction between the two memory sites: it is unknown whether gut epigenetic memory (Imd/PGRP-SC [3]) and hemocyte ROS/Toll/JAK-STAT priming [6] act independently or communicate. Inter-tissue communication is described in general [4], but not in a memory context.

The fat body, the main AMP-secreting tissue [4], has not been tested as a memory site. [3] reports increased AMP expression after priming without resolving whether the fat body contributes. Fat-body-specific PGRP-SC or chromatin-modifier manipulation would address this.
Dscam-hv's role is hypothetical: [10] proposes it as a hypervariable immune molecule, but none of the supplied papers link it to trained-immunity specificity in Drosophila.

The mechanism of transgenerational transfer is unresolved: [2] notes offspring transmission in some insects, but no supplied Drosophila study identifies a germline carrier, for example inheritance of H3K9me3 at PGRP-SC.

literature.summary: Drosophila shows trained-immunity-like protection, with two supported cellular sites. The first is the gut: priming with heat-killed gram-negative bacteria represses PGRP-SC through H3K9me3, which sensitizes Imd signaling, and PGRP-SC overexpression in the gut abolishes the trained protection [3]. The second is hemocytes, where sterile injury induces intracellular H2O2 (via the channel Prip), upd-3 and Toll activation, conferring protection on later infection [6]. Whether these represent durable, cell-intrinsic memory in hemocytes, or involve the fat body, remains untested in the supplied literature.

identified_gaps: Cell-type resolution of gut memory is unknown. Deng et al. [3] show that the gut is the major tissue lowering PGRP-SC and that H3K9me3 rises at the PGRP-SC locus, but the abstract does not say which gut cell types carry the mark or whether it persists through intestinal epithelial turnover. Cell-type-specific H3K9me3 ChIP or CUT&Tag with lineage-restricted PGRP-SC manipulation in enterocytes, enteroendocrine cells and intestinal stem cells would test this.

Whether hemocytes store the memory is untested. Chakrabarti et al. [6] show hemocyte activation and ROS production at injury sites plus protection on later infection, but the abstract does not show that protection depends on hemocytes, how long it lasts, or whether it is epigenetically encoded. Hemocyte depletion, hemocyte transfer and time-course reinfection experiments would resolve this.

The two proposed mechanisms (gut PGRP-SC/H3K9me3 [3] and hemocyte ROS/JAK-STAT/Toll [6]) have not been compared. They use different priming stimuli (heat-killed Gram-negative bacteria versus sterile injury), and it is unknown whether they are redundant, sequential or independent (inference). Testing both priming regimes in the same assay with tissue-specific perturbations would clarify this.

Pathogen specificity is unresolved. Reviews describe pathogen-specific memory in insects [2], but the PGRP-SC study [3] used Gram-negative training, and the supplied literature does not test whether the effect cross-protects against Gram-positive bacteria, fungi or viruses. Cross-challenge matrices would address this.

Mechanisms of transgenerational transmission and long-term persistence are not defined in Drosophila. Krejčová et al. [2] state that memory can be transmitted to offspring in some insects and that the mechanism is not fully understood. Whether H3K9me3 at PGRP-SC or hemocyte priming is inherited is untested.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Proposed (not established): in adult mated female w1118 flies at 25°C, the survival benefit of heat-killed Gram-negative priming is stored cell-autonomously in enterocytes through H3K9me3-linked repression of PGRP-SC, whereas the benefit of sterile-injury training depends on hemocytes. Specifically, (i) enterocyte-restricted restoration of PGRP-SC during the priming window will reduce the priming-induced survival benefit by at least 50% at 7 days post-priming, (ii) hemocyte ablation will reduce the sterile-injury benefit by at least 50% but the heat-killed priming benefit by less than 20%, giving a double dissociation between the two training routes.
hypothesis.experimental_approach: Prior work reports that heat-killed Gram-negative priming improves survival on reinfection and involves gut H3K9me3-mediated repression of PGRP-SC (PMID 42904035). Prior work also reports that sterile injury activates hemocytes and protects flies on later infection (PMID 33176146). We propose a 2x2 design in which flies receive either heat-killed Gram-negative bacteria, sterile injury (PBS puncture), or a naive/PBS control, and are rested 7 days before challenge with a live Gram-negative pathogen. The priming bacterial species, dose and challenge pathogen will be matched to the published protocol and require verification. Tissue-specific perturbations use temperature-sensitive GAL4/GAL80ts control: an enterocyte driver with UAS-PGRP-SC (or a PGRP-SC-restoring construct) induced only during priming, an enterocyte driver with UAS-Su(var)3-9 RNAi to test H3K9me3 dependence, and a hemocyte driver with a UAS pro-apoptotic transgene (rpr or hid) for ablation. Readouts are survival (log-rank test and Cox hazard ratios, n ≥ 150 flies per group across ≥3 biological replicates), bacterial load (CFU at 24 h after challenge), PGRP-SC transcript (RT-qPCR), and H3K9me3 CUT&Tag or ChIP-qPCR at the PGRP-SC locus in isolated enterocytes. Controls are GAL4/+ and UAS/+ parental genotypes, unprimed flies of every genotype, PBS-injured flies, and non-induced (18°C) flies. The priming effect is computed within each genotype (primed vs. its own unprimed control) so that baseline susceptibility differences, especially in hemocyte-ablated flies, do not confound the result.

hypothesis.expected_outcomes: If the hypothesis is correct: (1) heat-killed priming in control flies increases median survival after live challenge by at least 20% over unprimed flies (log-rank p < 0.05, hazard ratio < 0.7), and the sterile-injury benefit is detectable at a comparable or smaller magnitude; (2) primed control gut shows at least 1.5-fold higher H3K9me3 enrichment at PGRP-SC and at least 30% lower PGRP-SC transcript than unprimed controls; (3) enterocyte-specific PGRP-SC restoration or Su(var)3-9 knockdown reduces the priming benefit by at least 50% (genotype x priming interaction p < 0.05 in Cox model) and increases CFU at 24 h relative to primed controls; (4) hemocyte ablation reduces the sterile-injury benefit by at least 50% with less than 20% change in the heat-killed priming benefit. Falsification: if enterocyte perturbation changes the priming benefit by less than 20%, if hemocyte ablation removes the heat-killed priming benefit, or if the two training routes show equivalent dependence on both tissues, the proposed double dissociation is rejected.
hypothesis.novelty_claim: The synthesis identifies that cell-type resolution of gut memory is unknown, that whether hemocytes store memory is untested, and that the gut PGRP-SC/H3K9me3 mechanism (PMID 42904035) and the hemocyte ROS/JAK-STAT/Toll mechanism (PMID 33176146) have not been compared in the same assay. This proposal tests both priming regimes side by side with tissue-restricted, temporally controlled perturbations, and maps the H3K9me3 mark to specific gut cell types, which to our knowledge has not been done in the supplied literature.
hypothesis.feasibility_notes: Estimated timeline is 12-15 months: 2-3 months for line construction, validation and recombination (including any UAS-PGRP-SC cloning); 4-5 months for survival and CFU experiments; 3-4 months for enterocyte isolation, CUT&Tag/ChIP-qPCR and RT-qPCR; 2 months for analysis. Pitfalls: GAL80ts leakiness at 18°C; hemocyte ablation lowers baseline immune competence, so the primed-versus-unprimed effect should be compared within genotype; PGRP-SC overexpression may alter general IMD tone independent of memory (needs a PBS/unprimed control per genotype); H3K9me3 signal from sorted enterocytes may be low and require pooled guts; gut turnover could dilute the mark in ISC-derived lineages, which is a testable limitation. Exact priming and challenge bacteria and doses should be verified from the original protocol before starting.
specific_aims: Aim 1: Gut cell-type storage — test whether enterocyte-restricted PGRP-SC restoration or Su(var)3-9 knockdown during the priming window abolishes the heat-killed priming survival benefit, and map H3K9me3 at PGRP-SC in enterocytes.
Aim 2: Hemocyte dependence — test whether conditional hemocyte ablation removes the sterile-injury training benefit while sparing the heat-killed priming benefit.

Aim 3: Persistence and specificity — measure the duration of both memory types (days 3, 7, 14 post-priming) and test cross-protection against a Gram-positive bacterium, with PGRP-SC transcript and H3K9me3 tracked over time.

literature.disease_context: Trained immunity in insects provides a model for understanding how innate immune memory is established without adaptive immunity, with implications for human inflammatory and infectious diseases where innate immune priming is relevant [1][2][3]. The epigenetic mechanisms identified in Drosophila, particularly H3K9me3-mediated repression of negative regulators like PGRP-SC, parallel mechanisms proposed in mammalian trained immunity, suggesting conserved principles [3]. Understanding these pathways in flies may inform strategies for innate immune modulation in human disease contexts where adaptive immunity is insufficient or absent [1][2].

identified_gaps: The specific cell populations (hemocytes versus gut epithelium versus fat body) that are individually necessary and sufficient for storing trained immunity memory remain unresolved — both hemocytes [6] and gut cells [3] have been implicated, but no study has directly compared or dissected their relative contributions in the same experimental system.

The duration and stability of trained immunity memory in Drosophila is poorly characterized — it is unknown how long the H3K9me3 mark at PGRP-SC loci or the hemocyte ROS-primed state persists, and whether memory decays with fly age.

The mechanism of pathogen specificity in insect immune memory is unresolved — Dscam hypervariability is proposed as one basis [10], but whether and how Dscam isoform selection is coupled to epigenetic or transcriptional memory in trained immunity is unknown.

Trans-generational immune memory (noted as documented in some insects [2]) has not been mechanistically explained in Drosophila — the germline or somatic carrier of epigenetic information across generations is unidentified.

Whether the H3K9me3-mediated PGRP-SC repression described for gram-negative bacterial training [3] generalizes to other pathogen classes (fungi, viruses, gram-positive bacteria) or involves distinct epigenetic marks is untested.

evidence_claims.claim: A growing body of evidence supports the notion that the innate arm of the immune system could show memory traits.
Insects can develop long-term, pathogen-specific immune memory, which in some cases can be transmitted to offspring.

Flies trained with heat-killed gram-negative bacteria exhibited a higher survival rate upon secondary infection compared to unprimed flies, which was associated with increased expression of antimicrobial peptides.

Priming with G- bacteria increased the sensitivity of the immune deficiency pathway to a second bacterial infection owing to lower levels of peptidoglycan recognition protein SC (PGRP-SC) after the first infection.
The gut was the major tissue involved in the downregulation of PGRP-SC expression.
The histone H3 lysine 9 trimethylation (H3K9me3) levels were higher at the PGRP-SC loci in immune-trained flies compared to untrained flies, contributing to the suppression of PGRP-SC expression.
PGRP-SC overexpression in the fly gut abolished the effect of trained immunity.

Hemocyte activation and production of reactive oxygen species (ROS) at the site of a sterile injury provide protection to flies on subsequent infection, demonstrating training of the innate immune system.
Intracellular accumulation of hydrogen peroxide in hemocytes is essential for upd-3 induction and is facilitated by the diffusion of hydrogen peroxide through a channel protein Prip.
There is a change in the transcriptome of hemocytes at the site of tissue injury, with pronounced activation of the Toll signaling pathway.

Thousands of Down syndrome cell adhesion molecules (Dscam) can be generated by alternative splicing of variable exons from a single-locus gene, Dscam-hv, producing 38,016 protein isoforms in Drosophila.
Dscam-hv was implicated in immunity as a hypervariable immune molecule.
Macrophage-like plasmatocytes eliminate intruders through phagocytosis, and lamellocytes encapsulate large particles.
The fat body, equivalent to the mammalian liver, secretes antimicrobial peptides into hemolymph, killing bacteria and fungi.
Drosophila has seven classical antimicrobial peptide (AMP) gene families primarily regulated by the TOLL and IMD NF-κB pathways in response to infection.
The underlying mechanism of insect immune memory is still not fully understood, and a number of fundamental questions remain unanswered.

Both hemocytes [6] and gut cells [3] have been implicated as sites of trained immunity memory storage, but no study has directly compared or dissected their relative contributions in the same experimental system.
Whether the H3K9me3-mediated PGRP-SC repression described for gram-negative bacterial training generalizes to other pathogen classes is untested.

literature.summary: Drosophila melanogaster exhibits trained-immunity-like memory: prior exposure to heat-killed gram-negative bacteria epigenetically represses the negative immune regulator PGRP-SC in gut cells via H3K9me3, sensitizing the Imd pathway to subsequent infection [3], while sterile injury trains hemocytes through ROS-dependent JAK/STAT and Toll activation, conferring protection against later pathogen challenge [6]. These findings collectively demonstrate that trained immunity memory can be stored in at least two distinct tissue compartments — the gut epithelium and macrophage-like hemocytes — with distinct molecular triggers and epigenetic or signaling mechanisms [1][2]. Key open questions include the relative necessity of each cell type, the duration of immune memory, the mechanism of pathogen specificity (potentially involving hypervariable Dscam isoforms [10]), and whether memory can be transmitted trans-generationally in Drosophila [2].

hypothesis.hypothesis: Trained immunity memory in Drosophila melanogaster is stored independently and additively in gut enterocytes and circulating hemocytes, such that selective ablation of trained immunity in gut cells alone (via gut-specific PGRP-SC overexpression using NP1-GAL4) or in hemocytes alone (via hemocyte-specific ROS quenching using hml-GAL4>UAS-cat) will each reduce secondary-infection survival by ≥30% relative to fully trained wild-type w1118 flies, and simultaneous ablation of both compartments will reduce survival by ≥55% (approximating naïve controls), all measured at 7 days post-secondary oral challenge with live Pseudomonas entomophila (OD600 = 0.1) in mated 10-day-old female flies at 25°C, 12:12 h LD.
hypothesis.experimental_approach: Flies will be trained by feeding heat-killed Escherichia coli (gram-negative, OD600 = 10, 24 h exposure) or sterile sucrose (naïve control), following published priming protocols (PMID 42904035; PMID 33176146). After a 5-day rest period to allow epigenetic consolidation, secondary challenge will be delivered by oral infection with live Pseudomonas entomophila. Tissue-specific blockade of memory storage will be achieved using the binary GAL4/UAS system: NP1-GAL4 drives gut-enterocyte-specific transgene expression, hml-GAL4 drives hemocyte-specific expression, and a combined NP1-GAL4; hml-GAL4 intersectional cross will target both compartments simultaneously. In each compartment, trained immunity will be disrupted by two complementary effectors: (1) UAS-PGRP-SC overexpression to restore the negative Imd regulator suppressed by H3K9me3 in the gut, and (2) UAS-cat (catalase) overexpression to quench hemocyte H2O2 and block ROS-dependent upd-3 induction. Survival (Kaplan–Meier, log-rank test, n ≥ 100 flies per genotype per condition, ≥3 independent biological replicates), antimicrobial peptide transcript levels (RT-qPCR for Diptericin and Drosomycin at 6 h post-secondary challenge), and bacterial load (CFU from homogenized flies at 24 h) will be measured as primary endpoints. Epigenetic memory will be confirmed by ChIP-qPCR for H3K9me3 at the PGRP-SC locus in dissected midguts, and hemocyte ROS status will be quantified by DHE fluorescence flow cytometry. All crosses include UAS-only and GAL4-only sibling controls to account for transgene insertion effects.

hypothesis.expected_outcomes: Aim 1: Fully trained w1118 flies will show ≥50% survival at 7 days post-secondary P. entomophila challenge versus ≤20% in naïve controls (log-rank p < 0.001). ChIP-qPCR will confirm ≥2-fold enrichment of H3K9me3 at PGRP-SC loci in trained midguts versus naïve midguts. DHE flow cytometry will show ≥1.5-fold elevated ROS in trained hemocytes versus naïve. Aim 2: NP1-GAL4 > UAS-PGRP-SC trained flies will survive at ≤35% (≥30% reduction from wild-type trained), with abolished H3K9me3 enrichment at PGRP-SC loci but intact hemocyte ROS elevation, and reduced Diptericin induction (≤50% of wild-type trained levels). hml-GAL4 > UAS-cat trained flies will survive at ≤35%, with intact gut H3K9me3 but suppressed hemocyte ROS (≤naïve levels), and reduced upd-3 transcript. Aim 3: Double-compartment ablation (NP1-GAL4; hml-GAL4 > UAS-PGRP-SC; UAS-cat) will reduce survival to ≤20%, statistically indistinguishable from naïve controls (log-rank p > 0.05 vs. naïve; p < 0.001 vs. fully trained), confirming that the two compartments together account for the majority of trained immunity memory storage. Bacterial load (CFU) will inversely correlate with survival outcomes across all genotypes.
hypothesis.novelty_claim: No published study has directly compared the relative and combined contributions of gut enterocytes and hemocytes to trained immunity memory storage within a single controlled experimental system. The literature synthesis explicitly identifies this as the primary unresolved gap: 'both hemocytes and gut cells have been implicated as sites of trained immunity memory storage, but no study has directly compared or dissected their relative contributions in the same experimental system' (gap 1). Prior studies addressed each compartment in isolation — PMID 42904035 focused exclusively on gut H3K9me3/PGRP-SC mechanisms, and PMID 33176146 focused exclusively on hemocyte ROS/upd-3 mechanisms — using different priming stimuli (bacterial feeding vs. sterile injury) and different challenge protocols, making cross-study comparison impossible. This proposed experiment is the first to use a unified bacterial priming stimulus, a common secondary challenge, and tissue-specific genetic dissection in the same genetic background to quantitatively partition trained immunity memory between compartments.
hypothesis.feasibility_notes: All core GAL4 drivers (NP1-GAL4, hml-GAL4) and UAS-cat are established Drosophila tools with well-documented tissue specificity; however, BDSC stock numbers provided require verification at the time of ordering. The UAS-PGRP-SC line must be requested from the Deng/Luo laboratory (PMID 42904035) or re-generated by cloning PGRP-SC CDS into pUAST-attB and injecting into attP landing sites (e.g., BDSC #24749), adding approximately 3 months if re-generation is necessary. Double-driver and double-effector lines require 3–4 generations of crossing (approximately 2–3 months). ChIP-qPCR from dissected Drosophila midgut is technically demanding given low cell numbers; pooling ≥50 midguts per replicate and using validated anti-H3K9me3 antibodies (e.g., Abcam ab8898) is recommended. DHE-based FACS from hemolymph requires immediate processing after bleeding to avoid ROS quenching; this is established but requires optimization of bleeding technique. Total estimated timeline: 12–15 months (2–3 months line construction/acquisition, 2 months optimization, 6 months primary survival and molecular experiments, 2 months data analysis and replication). Key pitfalls: (1) NP1-GAL4 leaky expression in other tissues must be confirmed by GFP reporter; (2) hml-GAL4 may not capture all hemocyte subpopulations (crystal cells, lamellocytes) — plasmatocyte-dominant results should be interpreted accordingly; (3) UAS-cat overexpression may have non-specific metabolic effects requiring careful UAS-only controls.
specific_aims: Aim 1: Establish a unified bacterial trained immunity protocol — Optimize and validate a single experimental system using heat-killed E. coli priming followed by live P. entomophila secondary challenge in w1118 flies, confirming memory-associated survival benefit (≥30% improved survival) and molecular markers (H3K9me3 at PGRP-SC loci in gut; elevated ROS in hemocytes) in the same cohort of flies.

Aim 2: Dissect the independent contribution of gut versus hemocyte compartments — Use NP1-GAL4>UAS-PGRP-SC (gut ablation) and hml-GAL4>UAS-cat (hemocyte ablation) single-compartment disruptions to quantify the proportional reduction in trained immunity survival benefit, AMP induction, and bacterial clearance attributable to each tissue independently.

Aim 3: Determine whether gut and hemocyte compartments together account for total trained immunity memory — Test the double-compartment ablation genotype (NP1-GAL4; hml-GAL4 > UAS-PGRP-SC; UAS-cat) to determine whether combined disruption recapitulates the naïve phenotype, establishing whether additional unidentified compartments (e.g., fat body) must also contribute to complete immune memory.

identified_gaps: No supplied study directly compares RNAi and inducible pathway (Toll/Imd/JAK-STAT) contributions to viral control in the same infection across tissues such as fat body, gut, hemocytes and brain; tissue-specific conditional loss of Dcr-2/Ago2 versus Toll-9 or other pathway components during DCV infection would test the division of labor.

The origin, sorting and amplification of the systemic RNAi signal remain unresolved; it is unknown whether hemocyte-derived exosomal viral siRNAs or nanotube-transferred RNAi components are required for protection of specific distal tissues in vivo.

Toll-9 effects on Dicer2 induction, AKT dephosphorylation and dsRNA binding were shown with DCV in S2 cells, and fly susceptibility was shown with a transposon insertion allele; tissue-specific Toll-9 requirements and whether Toll-9 acts upstream of Dcr-2 in vivo are untested.

Which Dcr-2 interactors (Me31B, Rump, eIF4E1, eIF4G1, Rin, Syncrip) act in which tissues, and how RNA granule association shapes antiviral RNAi, has not been tested in tissue-resolved infection experiments.

The supplied literature does not establish whether classical AMP-inducing Toll/Imd outputs contribute to antiviral control in a tissue-specific manner; the AMP-focused papers address antibacterial and antifungal defense or S2 cell regulation, not viral infection.

literature.summary: Antiviral siRNA RNAi in Drosophila acts cell-autonomously through Dcr-2 and Ago2 and non-cell-autonomously through spread of RNAi signals via hemocyte exosomes and tunneling nanotubes [2][7]. Inducible pathways coordinate immunity across tissues [8], and Toll-9 links receptor signaling to RNAi by raising Dicer2 expression during DCV infection [11]. A direct tissue-by-tissue division of labor between RNAi and inducible pathways is not resolved by the supplied literature (inference).

hypothesis.hypothesis: Proposed: In adult w1118-background Drosophila melanogaster infected by intrathoracic injection of Drosophila C virus (DCV; 1000 TCID50, 25°C), tissue-specific RNAi knockdown of Dcr-2 in hemocytes (hmlΔ-GAL4 or equivalent) will raise whole-fly DCV titer at 3 days post-infection (dpi) by at least 10-fold relative to controls and reduce survival, whereas fat-body-specific Toll-9 knockdown will raise titer by at least 3-fold and will be accompanied by at least a 30% reduction in infection-induced Dcr-2 transcript in fat body. Fat-body Dcr-2 knockdown is predicted to raise titer by at least 10-fold, and Toll-9 knockdown in hemocytes is predicted to have less than a 2-fold effect. Together these outcomes would indicate that the RNAi effector (Dcr-2) is required in both hemocytes and fat body, while the inducible Toll-9 input is required mainly in fat body (proposed, not established).
hypothesis.experimental_approach: Use the GAL4/UAS system with tissue-restricted drivers (hemocyte, fat body, gut enterocyte, pan-neuronal) to express UAS-RNAi against Dcr-2, AGO2, Toll-9, and, as comparison inducible-pathway nodes, spz/Toll and imd/PGRP-LC, with a temperature-sensitive tub-GAL80ts to restrict knockdown to adulthood and avoid developmental confounds. Infect adult females with DCV by injection (with PBS/mock injection controls) and measure survival, DCV RNA by RT-qPCR in dissected tissues and whole animals at 0, 1, 3 and 5 dpi, and viral siRNA accumulation by small-RNA sequencing in selected genotypes. Controls include driver-only, UAS-only, and non-targeting/mCherry RNAi, with at least two independent RNAi lines per gene where possible and knockdown efficiency confirmed by RT-qPCR. Rescue and epistasis tests (fat-body Dcr-2 overexpression in Toll-9 knockdown flies) will test whether Toll-9 acts upstream of Dcr-2 in vivo. A parallel Imd/Toll antimicrobial peptide readout (e.g., Diptericin, Drosomycin RT-qPCR) will test whether classical AMP outputs change in viral infection.

hypothesis.expected_outcomes: Proposed predictions: (1) Hemocyte and fat-body Dcr-2 or AGO2 knockdown increases DCV RNA at 3 dpi by at least 10-fold versus controls (log2 difference, Welch t-test or ANOVA with Dunnett's correction, p<0.05, n≥5 pools of 5 flies per genotype, 3 biological replicates) and shortens median survival by at least 30% (log-rank p<0.05). (2) Fat-body Toll-9 knockdown increases titer at least 3-fold and reduces infection-induced Dcr-2 mRNA by at least 30%, while hemocyte Toll-9 knockdown has less than a 2-fold effect. (3) Fat-body Dcr-2 overexpression partially restores titer in Toll-9-knockdown flies, reducing it by at least 50% of the excess. (4) Spz/imd/PGRP-LC knockdowns change DCV titer by less than 2-fold, with AMP induction not predicted to correlate with viral load. (5) Hemocyte Dcr-2 knockdown is predicted to alter viral siRNA abundance in distal tissue (reduction of at least 30%), consistent with a systemic signal. Failure of these thresholds would falsify the specific division-of-labor model.
hypothesis.novelty_claim: The literature synthesis notes that no supplied study directly compares RNAi and inducible-pathway (Toll/Imd/JAK-STAT) contributions to viral control in the same infection across fat body, gut, hemocytes and brain. It also notes that tissue-specific Toll-9 requirements and whether Toll-9 acts upstream of Dcr-2 in vivo are untested (Toll-9 effects were shown in S2 cells and with an insertion allele [40366172]), and that the requirement of hemocyte-derived RNAi signals for distal tissue protection is unresolved [39926592][23684730]. This proposal addresses those gaps with a single-virus, multi-tissue, conditional knockdown comparison.
hypothesis.feasibility_notes: Estimated timeline 12-15 months: 2-3 months stock acquisition and verification of RNAi efficiency and driver specificity, 4-5 months for infection/titer/survival screens, 3 months for small-RNA sequencing and tissue dissections, 2-3 months for epistasis/rescue and analysis. Pitfalls: driver leakiness or off-target expression (e.g., fat body drivers in hemocytes), incomplete knockdown of Dcr-2, which is already low-abundance, RNAi line off-target effects, DCV-injection variability (control by titrating inoculum and including 0 dpi titers), and tissue dissection contamination by circulating hemocytes. Gut and brain contributions may be small after injection and may require oral or alternate routes. All specified lines must be verified for availability before work begins.
specific_aims: Aim 1: Tissue-resolved requirement of RNAi — Compare DCV titer and survival after adult-restricted Dcr-2 or AGO2 knockdown in hemocytes, fat body, gut and neurons.

Aim 2: Tissue-specific role of Toll-9 and classical inducible pathways — Test Toll-9, spz/Toll and imd/PGRP-LC knockdown in the same tissues and infection, and measure whether AMP induction tracks viral load.

Aim 3: Toll-9 to Dcr-2 hierarchy and systemic signal — Use Dcr-2 overexpression epistasis and tissue-resolved viral siRNA sequencing to test whether Toll-9 acts upstream of Dcr-2 and whether hemocyte Dcr-2 shapes distal tissue siRNA levels.

literature.disease_context: The division of antiviral labor between RNAi and inducible immune pathways in Drosophila mirrors principles conserved in human innate immunity, including parallels between Dicer-2/RNAi and mammalian RIG-I-like receptor (RLR) sensing, and between Toll/IMD NF-κB signaling and mammalian TLR/NF-κB pathways [6, 8, 12]. Understanding how tissues coordinate these complementary defenses in flies informs our understanding of antiviral immunity in vertebrates, where compartmentalized defenses (e.g., interferon responses in distinct tissues) are similarly critical [8]. Disruption of these pathways in humans underlies susceptibility to viral infections and inflammatory diseases, making the fly a tractable model for dissecting their coordination [8, 11].

identified_gaps: The identity, composition, and sorting mechanism of the systemic RNAi signal (e.g., exosomal siRNAs) remain incompletely characterized — it is unknown which specific signals trigger hemocyte exosome secretion and how recipient non-immune cells take up and utilize viral siRNAs to mount protection [1, 2].

It is unclear how Toll-9 endosomal dsRNA sensing is coordinated across tissues in vivo — whether Toll-9 signaling in specific cell types (e.g., hemocytes vs. fat body) is required for systemic versus local antiviral states, and how its induction of Dicer-2 is spatially regulated, remains unresolved [11].

The in vivo relevance of Dicer-2 interactome partners (Me31B, Rump, eIF4E1, eIF4G1, Rin, Syncrip) to tissue-specific antiviral responses is not yet established — functional characterization has been performed primarily in cells and the in vivo tissue distribution of these complexes during infection is unknown [10].

How inducible immune pathways (Toll, IMD, JAK/STAT) and RNAi cooperate or compete in specific tissues such as the gut epithelium versus fat body versus hemocytes during systemic viral infection has not been systematically mapped — the relative contributions of each pathway per tissue type at defined infection time points are not known [8].

Whether the piRNA pathway provides antiviral functions in Drosophila analogous to its proposed role in mosquitoes remains unresolved — data from Drosophila are limited compared to mosquito studies, and the tissue specificity of any such role (e.g., germline vs. soma) is unclear [3].

evidence_claims.claim: In Drosophila melanogaster, the siRNA-directed RNAi pathway provides crucial antiviral defenses.
Cell-autonomously, Dicer-2 (Dcr-2) recognizes and cleaves viral dsRNA into siRNAs, which are incorporated into the RNA-induced silencing complex (RISC).
Argonaute 2 (Ago2) then targets and cleaves viral RNA, preventing replication.
Non-cell-autonomously, infected hemocytes secrete exosomes containing viral siRNAs, spreading antiviral signals to other cells.
Tunneling nanotubes can transfer RNAi components between neighboring cells, further enhancing systemic immunity.
Cell autonomous RNAi may not be sufficient to reach an efficient antiviral response, and the organism might rely on the spread and uptake of an RNAi signal of unknown origin.
Antiviral RNAi has been well described as a cell autonomous response, which is triggered by double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) molecules.
In plants, systemic antiviral immunity has been demonstrated, however much less is known in animals.
Ago-2-defective flies are hypersensitive to infection with a major fruit fly pathogen, Drosophila C virus (DCV), and with Cricket Paralysis virus (CrPV).

DCV encodes a potent suppressor of RNA interference (RNAi). This suppressor binds long double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) and inhibits Dicer-2-mediated processing of dsRNA into short interfering RNA (siRNA).
Toll-9 is crucial for antiviral immunity against Drosophila C virus (DCV), a natural pathogen of Drosophila.

The stable expression of Toll-9 in Drosophila S2 cells results in increased Dicer2 induction and reduced AKT phosphorylation, collectively establishing an antiviral state that inhibits DCV replication.
Toll-9 localizes to endosomes, where it binds viral double-stranded RNA (dsRNA), highlighting its role in detecting viral replication intermediates.
Toll-9 activation during DCV infection leads to the upregulation of Dicer2 and Argonaute2 and dephosphorylation of AKT.
Drosophila Toll-9 functions as a pattern recognition receptor (PRR) for double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) during Drosophila C virus (DCV) infection, akin to mammalian Toll-like receptors (TLRs).
Epithelial tissues function as physical barriers to prevent pathogen invasion.
Macrophage-like plasmatocytes eliminate intruders through phagocytosis, and lamellocytes encapsulate large particles.
The fat body, equivalent to the mammalian liver, secretes antimicrobial peptides into hemolymph, killing bacteria and fungi.
Drosophila and higher organisms share conserved signaling pathways and factors.
The activation of AMP expression is regulated by both immune deficiency (IMD) and the Toll pathway.
PGRP-LC and Toll genes are targeted by SPS1 for regulating these pathways.
The IMD and Toll pathway regulate AMP expression by cross-talking.
Dicer-2 potently restricts viral infection in insects by generating virus-derived siRNAs from viral RNA.
Each virus was uniquely targeted by the RNAi pathway; dicing substrates included dsRNA replication intermediates and intramolecular RNA stem loops.
The RNA species targeted by Dicer-2 can be modulated by the presence of a viral suppressor of RNAi.
The in vivo Dicer-2 interactome analysis uncovers several previously unknown Dicer-2 interactants associated with RNA granules, i.e., Me31B, Rump, eIF4E1, eIF4G1, Rin and Syncrip.
Functional characterization of the candidates, both in cells and in vivo, reveals pro- and antiviral factors in the context of an infection by the picorna-like DCV virus.

ATP binding to dmDcr-2's helicase domain impacts association and dissociation kinetics of dsRNA in a termini-dependent manner, revealing termini-dependent discrimination of dsRNA on a biologically relevant time scale.
The piRNA pathway is suggested to have antiviral functions in mosquitoes, which is unknown for other insects.
In drosophila antimicrobial responses rely on two signaling pathways: the Toll pathway and the IMD pathway.
Seven classical antimicrobial peptide (AMP) gene families were identified in the 1990s. These genes are primarily regulated by the TOLL and IMD NF-κB pathways in response to infection.

Understanding how tissues coordinate these complementary defenses in flies informs our understanding of antiviral immunity in vertebrates, where compartmentalized defenses (e.g., interferon responses in distinct tissues) are similarly critical.

The identity, composition, and sorting mechanism of the systemic RNAi signal (e.g., exosomal siRNAs) remain incompletely characterized — it is unknown which specific signals trigger hemocyte exosome secretion and how recipient non-immune cells take up and utilize viral siRNAs to mount protection.

It is unclear how Toll-9 endosomal dsRNA sensing is coordinated across tissues in vivo — whether Toll-9 signaling in specific cell types (e.g., hemocytes vs. fat body) is required for systemic versus local antiviral states, and how its induction of Dicer-2 is spatially regulated, remains unresolved.

The in vivo relevance of Dicer-2 interactome partners (Me31B, Rump, eIF4E1, eIF4G1, Rin, Syncrip) to tissue-specific antiviral responses is not yet established — functional characterization has been performed primarily in cells and the in vivo tissue distribution of these complexes during infection is unknown.

literature.summary: Antiviral immunity in Drosophila is divided between a constitutive, sequence-specific RNAi arm — where Dicer-2 processes viral dsRNA into siRNAs and Ago2-RISC cleaves viral RNA both cell-autonomously and systemically via hemocyte-secreted exosomes and tunneling nanotubes [2, 1] — and inducible pattern recognition pathways, including Toll, IMD, and JAK/STAT, that coordinate humoral and cellular responses across tissues such as the fat body, hemocytes, and gut [8]. A key emerging link between these arms is Toll-9, which localizes to endosomes, directly binds viral dsRNA, and upregulates Dicer-2 and Ago2 expression, demonstrating that inducible Toll signaling can actively enhance the RNAi machinery rather than operating in parallel [11]. Despite these advances, the mechanisms by which the systemic RNAi signal is sorted and amplified across tissues, the precise tissue-by-tissue division of labor between RNAi and inducible pathways, and the in vivo functions of Dicer-2's newly identified protein interaction network remain critical open questions [1, 10].

hypothesis.hypothesis: Toll-9-mediated upregulation of Dicer-2 is tissue-autonomous and functionally non-redundant: hemocyte-specific loss of Toll-9 (using Hml-GAL4 > UAS-Toll-9-RNAi) will impair systemic but not local antiviral RNAi, reducing whole-fly viral siRNA levels by ≥40% and increasing DCV titer by ≥10-fold at 5 days post-infection (dpi) compared to controls, whereas fat-body-specific Toll-9 knockdown (r4-GAL4 > UAS-Toll-9-RNAi) will impair local fat-body antiviral responses but leave hemocyte-derived exosomal siRNA output intact, predicting a ≥5-fold but <10-fold increase in DCV titer, in mated female w1118 flies at 25°C under standard conditions.
hypothesis.experimental_approach: We will use the GAL4/UAS system to achieve tissue-specific knockdown of Toll-9 (and, as a comparator, Dcr-2) individually in hemocytes (Hml-GAL4), fat body (r4-GAL4), and gut epithelium (NP1-GAL4 [Myo1A-GAL4]), then orally and systemically challenge adult mated female flies with Drosophila C virus (DCV) at a defined infectious dose, harvesting tissues at 3, 5, and 7 dpi. Antiviral outcomes will be assessed by: (1) tissue-dissected small RNA deep sequencing to quantify virus-derived siRNA (vsiRNA) abundance and 5'-nucleotide bias per tissue; (2) RT-qPCR of viral RNA (positive and negative strand) as a proxy for replication; (3) TCID50 plaque assay on whole-fly and dissected-tissue lysates; (4) survival assays with n ≥ 100 flies per genotype across three independent biological replicates. Key controls include: UAS-Toll-9-RNAi/+ (no GAL4), GAL4/+ (no UAS), UAS-Dcr-2-RNAi positive controls, and a ubiquitous knockdown arm (da-GAL4) to establish maximum phenotype magnitude. Exosome fractions will be isolated from hemolymph at 5 dpi by differential ultracentrifugation, and their small RNA cargo will be profiled to determine whether hemocyte Toll-9 loss reduces exosomal vsiRNA loading specifically.

Fat-body-specific Toll-9 knockdown (r4-GAL4 > UAS-Toll-9-RNAi) is predicted to increase DCV titer by ≥5-fold but <10-fold, with exosomal vsiRNA content reduced by <20%, indicating fat body Toll-9 contributes locally but not to the systemic signal. Gut-specific knockdown (NP1-GAL4 > UAS-Toll-9-RNAi) following oral DCV challenge is predicted to show earliest viral titer increases (3 dpi) with a ≥5-fold increase in gut-dissected viral RNA, but a smaller whole-fly survival phenotype (≤2 day median reduction). All tissue knockdowns combined should phenocopy da-GAL4 > UAS-Toll-9-RNAi. Statistical thresholds: ANOVA with Tukey post-hoc for titer/siRNA data; log-rank for survival; p < 0.05 with Bonferroni correction across tissue comparisons.
hypothesis.novelty_claim: This experiment directly addresses two gaps explicitly identified in the literature synthesis: (1) 'It is unclear how Toll-9 endosomal dsRNA sensing is coordinated across tissues in vivo — whether Toll-9 signaling in specific cell types (e.g., hemocytes vs. fat body) is required for systemic versus local antiviral states, and how its induction of Dicer-2 is spatially regulated, remains unresolved' (PMID 40366172); and (2) 'The identity, composition, and sorting mechanism of the systemic RNAi signal (e.g., exosomal siRNAs) remain incompletely characterized — it is unknown which specific signals trigger hemocyte exosome secretion and how recipient non-immune cells take up and utilize viral siRNAs to mount protection' (PMIDs 23684730, 39926592). Prior work established Toll-9 function in S2 cells and whole flies (PMID 40366172) and hemocyte exosome secretion at the organismal level (PMID 39926592), but no study has systematically dissected per-tissue Toll-9 requirements for systemic versus local RNAi deployment. The proposed mechanistic link — that hemocyte Toll-9 is specifically required to license exosomal vsiRNA loading — is a novel proposed causal connection not previously tested.
hypothesis.feasibility_notes: All core genetic tools (GAL4 drivers, TRiP RNAi lines) are standard in the field; DCV is a well-characterized natural pathogen with established infection protocols. Key technical risks: (1) Hml-GAL4 expression may not cover all hemocyte subtypes uniformly — this should be validated with UAS-mCD8::GFP imaging before infection experiments; (2) exosome isolation from Drosophila hemolymph yields small volumes requiring pooling of ≥50 flies per prep, increasing biological replication effort; (3) TRiP line stock numbers for Toll-9-RNAi require verification against current BDSC holdings, as Toll-9 is a recently characterized gene (PMID 40366172, 2025) and a validated TRiP line may not yet be deposited — alternative: generate UAS-Toll-9-RNAi by microinjection using published Toll-9 sequence or obtain from authors of PMID 40366172. Estimated timeline: 6 months total — Month 1–2: stock verification, driver pattern confirmation, DCV stock titration; Month 3–4: survival assays and viral titer measurements; Month 5–6: small RNA deep sequencing, exosome isolation, and data analysis. Potential confound: GAL4 leakiness in non-target tissues; use of tissue-specific GAL4 lines with documented specificity and inclusion of GAL4/+ controls at every step is essential.
specific_aims: Aim 1: Tissue-specific Toll-9 requirement for systemic antiviral RNAi — Determine whether hemocyte-specific Toll-9 knockdown selectively impairs systemic vsiRNA dissemination and whole-fly DCV control compared to fat-body- or gut-specific knockdown, using vsiRNA deep sequencing and TCID50 assays at 5 dpi.

Aim 2: Toll-9-dependent exosomal vsiRNA loading in hemocytes — Quantify and compare exosomal small RNA cargo from hemolymph of hemocyte-specific Toll-9 knockdown versus control flies at 5 dpi to test whether Toll-9 is required for vsiRNA packaging into hemocyte-secreted exosomes.

Aim 3: Tissue-by-tissue additive contribution mapping — Combine pairwise tissue-specific Toll-9 knockdowns (hemocyte + fat body, hemocyte + gut) and compare survival and viral titer outcomes to single-tissue knockdowns, to determine whether tissue contributions are additive or synergistic and to establish a quantitative tissue-resolution map of Toll-9-dependent antiviral defense.

It is unclear how Toll-9 endosomal dsRNA sensing is coordinated across tissues in vivo — whether Toll-9 signaling in specific cell types (e.g., hemocytes vs. fat body) is required for systemic versus local antiviral states, and how its induction of Dicer-2 is spatially regulated, remains unresolved.

The identity, composition, and sorting mechanism of the systemic RNAi signal (e.g., exosomal siRNAs) remain incompletely characterized — it is unknown which specific signals trigger hemocyte exosome secretion and how recipient non-immune cells take up and utilize viral siRNAs to mount protection.
Ago-2-defective flies are hypersensitive to infection with a major fruit fly pathogen, Drosophila C virus (DCV), and with Cricket Paralysis virus (CrPV).

DCV encodes a potent suppressor of RNA interference (RNAi). This suppressor binds long double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) and inhibits Dicer-2-mediated processing of dsRNA into short interfering RNA (siRNA).
The fat body, equivalent to the mammalian liver, secretes antimicrobial peptides into hemolymph, killing bacteria and fungi.
Macrophage-like plasmatocytes eliminate intruders through phagocytosis, and lamellocytes encapsulate large particles.
The in vivo Dicer-2 interactome analysis uncovers several previously unknown Dicer-2 interactants associated with RNA granules, i.e., Me31B, Rump, eIF4E1, eIF4G1, Rin and Syncrip.
Prior work established Toll-9 function in S2 cells and whole flies but no study has systematically dissected per-tissue Toll-9 requirements for systemic versus local RNAi deployment.
The proposed mechanistic link — that hemocyte Toll-9 is specifically required to license exosomal vsiRNA loading — is a novel proposed causal connection not previously tested.

literature.summary: Both papers indicate that enhancer grammar, meaning the combination and arrangement of transcription factor sites, shapes Drosophila embryonic expression: [2] finds pervasive, conserved linked-site patterns across ~100 enhancers, while [1] shows in the t48 enhancer that site affinity and arrangement tune timing, bursting and amplitude to set expression boundaries, with synergy rather than a dominant site. hypothesis.hypothesis: Proposed: In the early Drosophila embryo at 25°C, Dorsal (Dl) binding-site affinity changes in a synthetic minimal enhancer will shift the dorsoventral expression boundary and activation timing (mainly through burst frequency) more than a comparable change in Zelda (Zld) site affinity. Zld site changes will alter amplitude more than Dl changes do. Specifically, a 2-fold-or-greater reduction in Dl site affinity will delay median activation time by ≥2 min and narrow the boundary by ≥10% embryo width. Equivalent Zld site weakening will reduce mean MS2 burst amplitude by ≥25% with a smaller shift in burst frequency. By contrast, changing Dl-Dl spacing by a half helical turn (~5 bp) at constant affinity will change boundary position or burst frequency by <half the effect of the affinity change. Together, affinity and site identity/arrangement are proposed to explain >60% of variance in timing, frequency and amplitude across 4 enhancer backbones in a cross-validated model.
hypothesis.experimental_approach: Use MS2/MCP-GFP live imaging in embryos carrying enhancer-MS2 reporters integrated at one common landing site. Test the t48 enhancer (the system studied in [32541043]) plus 3 additional early enhancers chosen to contain Dl, Zld, Bicoid, Hunchback, Caudal or Twist sites (the linked-site combinations described in [19651877]). For each enhancer, build a matrix of variants: (i) point-mutation series of Dl and Zld sites giving graded affinity; (ii) spacing variants of Bicoid-Dorsal or Dl-Zld pairs, shifted by 5 and 10 bp with affinity held constant; (iii) site-order or orientation swaps. Quantify per-nucleus activation time, burst frequency, burst duration, amplitude and boundary position (≥8 embryos per construct), and fit a regularized regression or kinetic model to compare the predictive power of affinity, spacing and grammar features. Test the proposed Zld potentiation of Dl recruitment with Dl-GFP imaging or ChIP-qPCR on sorted-stage embryos for wild-type versus Zld-site-mutant reporters. Controls: wild-type enhancer-MS2, a no-enhancer MS2 reporter, an a-priori scrambled-site control, and a landing-site-matched reporter in each experiment.

identified_gaps: It remains unclear how the spatial arrangement (spacing and orientation) of binding sites within an enhancer quantitatively controls transcriptional output beyond pairwise linkages — specifically, whether there are general rules governing multi-site grammar that extend beyond the enhancers studied in [1] and [2].

The mechanism by which pioneer factor Zld potentiates Dorsal recruitment to target DNA is proposed but not mechanistically resolved in [1]; determining whether this involves nucleosome remodeling, cooperative binding, or direct protein-protein interaction is an open question.

The functional significance of the observed under-representation of nucleosome positioning sequences in enhancers [2] is raised as a possibility but not experimentally tested; whether this higher-order chromatin structure is causally required for correct enhancer activity is unknown.

The studies focus on early embryonic patterning enhancers; whether the same grammar rules (motif linkage, affinity tuning, pioneer factor roles) generalize to later developmental stages or tissue-specific enhancers in Drosophila is not addressed by the provided literature.
