literature.summary: Together, these two studies establish that enhancer sequence grammar — including the specific identity, affinity, spatial linkage, and arrangement of transcription factor binding sites — is a primary determinant of where and when developmental genes are expressed in the Drosophila embryo [1][2]. At the single-enhancer level, tuning binding affinity at individual Dorsal or Zelda sites within the t48 enhancer shifts expression boundaries primarily through changes in transcriptional timing and bursting frequency, with multiple sites acting synergistically rather than any single dominant site [1]. At the genome scale, conserved pairwise linkages between motifs (e.g., Bicoid-Dorsal, Hunchback-Hunchback) are pervasively found across ~100 developmental enhancers and are functionally important for integrating orthogonal patterning axes, suggesting that non-random motif grammar is a general feature of developmental gene regulation [2].

hypothesis.hypothesis: Systematic alteration of inter-site spacing between Dorsal (Dl) and Zelda (Zld) binding sites within the t48 enhancer by ±5 bp, ±10 bp, and ±20 bp increments will shift the ventral expression boundary of t48 by ≥10% of embryo circumference and alter the timing of transcriptional activation by ≥5 minutes (measured by MS2-MCP live imaging at 25°C in w1118 background mated female embryos), demonstrating that inter-site spacing is an independent, quantitatively predictive parameter of enhancer output separable from binding site affinity, and that spacing rules identified at t48 will generalize to at least one tissue-specific enhancer (eve stripe 2) active at a later developmental stage (stage 5–7).
hypothesis.experimental_approach: We will use site-directed mutagenesis to generate a series of t48 enhancer variants in which the spacing between the two strongest Dl sites, between Dl and Zld sites, and between paired Zld sites is systematically varied (insertions/deletions of 5, 10, 20 bp neutral sequence) while holding binding site sequence and affinity constant, cloned upstream of an MS2-tagged lacZ reporter in the pBDP vector for PhiC31-mediated integration at the attP40 landing site to ensure positional equivalence across constructs. All reporter lines will be crossed into the MCP-GFP; His2Av-RFP stock for live single-molecule fluorescence imaging of nascent transcription in nc13–14 embryos, enabling measurement of transcriptional onset time, bursting frequency, burst duration, and amplitude as a function of dorsoventral position. As a second aim, analogous spacing variants will be introduced into a minimal eve stripe 2 enhancer to test whether spacing rules generalize beyond early DV patterning. Controls include the wild-type t48 enhancer reporter, affinity-null Dl-site mutants (established in PMID 32541043), and an unrelated spacing-scrambled enhancer that preserves dinucleotide composition. Statistical comparisons will use mixed-effects models with embryo as a random factor, with significance threshold p < 0.05 and effect size (Cohen's d) ≥ 0.5 considered biologically meaningful.

hypothesis.expected_outcomes: Aim 1: We expect a monotonic relationship between Dl–Zld inter-site spacing deviation from wild-type and the timing of transcriptional onset (measured in minutes post-nc14 initiation), with ±20 bp variants showing ≥5-minute delays or advances in onset and ≥15% shift in the ventral expression boundary relative to wild-type (assessed as fraction of DV axis circumference expressing MS2 signal above threshold). We expect bursting frequency to be the primary parameter altered (as established for affinity changes in PMID 32541043), while burst amplitude and duration remain within 20% of wild-type values. Aim 2: We expect that eve stripe 2 spacing variants (Bcd–Dl ±10 bp) will similarly shift stripe position by ≥1 cell diameter (≥5 μm) and alter onset timing by ≥3 minutes, demonstrating generalization of spacing grammar to AP patterning and later stages. Aim 3: Computational modeling of spacing–output relationships across all variants will produce a quantitative predictive function; if spacing effects are helical-repeat-dependent, we predict a ~10 bp periodicity in boundary shifts corresponding to one B-DNA helical turn.
hypothesis.novelty_claim: The literature synthesis identifies as an explicit gap that 'it remains unclear how the spatial arrangement (spacing and orientation) of binding sites within an enhancer quantitatively controls transcriptional output beyond pairwise linkages — specifically, whether there are general rules governing multi-site grammar that extend beyond the enhancers studied.' PMID 32541043 established affinity as a quantitative control parameter but did not independently vary spacing while holding affinity constant. PMID 19651877 identified conserved pairwise linkages at genome scale but did not test whether the spacing distance per se (rather than mere co-occurrence) is causally required. No study in the provided literature has used MS2 live imaging to quantitatively disentangle spacing from affinity as independent enhancer grammar parameters, nor has any study tested whether grammar rules from early DV patterning enhancers generalize to later-stage or AP-axis enhancers — another identified gap.
hypothesis.feasibility_notes: All proposed mutagenesis is standard (QuikChange or Gibson assembly); attP40 PhiC31 injection is routine at most fly facilities. MS2-MCP live imaging is an established technique in the field (Garcia lab protocols available). The main technical risk is that small spacing changes (±5 bp) may have effects below the detection threshold of live imaging (~1–2 min temporal resolution, ~2–3 cell spatial resolution); larger spacing changes (±20 bp) may disrupt local DNA structure beyond spacing per se, potentially confounding results — this is addressed by including dinucleotide-composition-matched neutral spacer sequences. The generalization test (eve stripe 2) assumes the minimal stripe 2 enhancer is well-characterized, which is supported by published literature though not directly cited in the synthesis. Estimated timeline: mutagenesis and cloning (2 months), injection and line establishment (3 months), live imaging and data analysis (4 months), computational modeling (2 months), totaling approximately 11–12 months. A potential pitfall is lethality or sterility of dl or zld hypomorph crosses, which can be mitigated by using maternal-zygotic heterozygotes or inducible knockdown.
specific_aims: Aim 1: Spacing-boundary mapping — Determine quantitatively how systematic ±5, ±10, and ±20 bp alterations in Dl–Zld and Dl–Dl inter-site spacing within the t48 enhancer shift the ventral expression boundary and transcriptional kinetic parameters (onset time, burst frequency, amplitude) measured by MS2-MCP live imaging in nc14 embryos.

Aim 2: Generalization testing — Test whether spacing grammar rules identified at t48 apply to the eve stripe 2 enhancer (Bcd–Dl and Hb–Hb motif pairs) by introducing equivalent spacing variants and measuring stripe position, onset timing, and bursting parameters at developmental stages 5–7.

Aim 3: Quantitative modeling — Use the spacing–output data from Aims 1 and 2 to build and validate a quantitative predictive model of enhancer output as a function of inter-site spacing, testing whether a helical-periodicity (~10 bp) signature is detectable and whether the model predicts outputs of held-out variant constructs with ≤15% error.

literature.summary: Drosophila sequence-to-expression models, including thermodynamic and CNN approaches, have been systematically compared on enhancer data [1], and in vivo eQTL maps resolve causal noncoding variants in embryonic enhancers [5]. However, the supplied literature does not link the two by testing model predictions against measured variant effects, so the question of correct in vivo prediction remains open. Most other supplied papers are tangential background.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Proposed: Sequence-to-expression models (the thermodynamics-based model and the CoNSEPT CNN from PMID 34508359) trained only on Drosophila neuroectodermal enhancer data will predict the direction of effect of natural noncoding variants in embryonic enhancers (benchmark from PMID 28024300) with ≥70% accuracy (binomial test vs 50% chance, p<0.05), but will predict effect magnitude only weakly (Spearman rho ≤0.4 between predicted and measured allelic expression ratio). Accuracy for compensatory opposite-effect variant pairs within the same enhancer will be at least 20 percentage points lower than for single variants, and the CNN will outperform the thermodynamic model on held-out variants by ≥0.1 in Spearman rho. Predictions for a prospective set of ≥20 CRISPR-introduced or reporter-based variants, tested in stage 5 embryos at 25°C, will match the retrospective benchmark within 15 percentage points of directional accuracy.
hypothesis.experimental_approach: Proposed: Aim 1 is a retrospective benchmark. Both model classes are trained on the neuroectodermal enhancer set used in PMID 34508359, and variants from the embryonic eQTL maps in PMID 28024300 that fall in enhancers with matching TF inputs are scored in silico. Direction and magnitude are compared with the measured allelic effects, with permutation-based null models and enhancer-level cross-validation. Aim 2 is a prospective in vivo test. Reference and variant alleles of selected enhancers, including single variants and compensatory pairs, are cloned into a lacZ or MS2/fluorescent reporter integrated at a single attP landing site (phiC31) to control position effects. Expression is quantified in stage 5 embryos by in situ hybridization or live imaging, with reference-allele reporters as controls and a scrambled-enhancer reporter as a negative control. Aim 3 tests the models' limits by stratifying errors for compensatory pairs and for variants outside the training tissue. Fly Cell Atlas data (PMID 35239393) could be used to assess generalization, though this is a proposal and not an established use.

hypothesis.expected_outcomes: Proposed: (1) Directional accuracy of ≥70% on the retrospective benchmark for both models, with magnitude correlation of rho ≤0.4. (2) Accuracy on compensatory opposite-effect pairs ≥20 percentage points lower than on single variants, indicating poor capture of epistasis. (3) CNN rho exceeding thermodynamic model rho by ≥0.1 on held-out enhancers, assessed by bootstrap 95% CI excluding zero. (4) Prospective reporter results with directional accuracy within 15 percentage points of the retrospective result, with ≥8 embryos per genotype and Benjamini-Hochberg FDR <0.05. Falsification: directional accuracy ≤55%, or no model difference, would reject the hypothesis.
hypothesis.novelty_claim: The supplied literature indicates that no study tests whether the thermodynamic or CNN models of PMID 34508359 predict the in vivo effect of natural or engineered noncoding variants. It also indicates that the embryonic eQTL variants of PMID 28024300 have not been used as a benchmark for sequence-to-expression models, and that it is unknown which model class best predicts held-out variant effects as opposed to fitting data. This proposal addresses these gaps and explicitly tests compensatory allelic pairs as a probe of epistasis.
hypothesis.feasibility_notes: Estimated 18 months: months 1-4 model training and retrospective benchmarking; 5-14 cloning, transgenesis and embryo imaging; 15-18 analysis. Pitfalls: the eQTL variants may lie in enhancers outside the neuroectodermal training domain, limiting the usable variant number; allele-specific effects in reporters may differ from endogenous context; effect sizes may be small and require quantitative imaging; the models may need retraining to include the relevant TF inputs. Variants affecting post-transcriptional regulation (e.g., ARE-mediated decay) are out of scope for enhancer models and must be excluded or analyzed separately. Stock numbers need verification.

Aim 3: Failure-mode analysis — compare model classes on epistatic pairs and out-of-domain (non-neuroectodermal) enhancers to identify where predictions break down

literature.disease_context: Understanding whether sequence-to-expression models can predict the in vivo effect of noncoding variants is directly relevant to interpreting human disease-causing regulatory mutations. Studies of eQTLs in Drosophila embryos have resolved causal noncoding mutations at near base-pair resolution, revealing allelic interactions within enhancers that buffer expression variation [5]. Drosophila also serves as a platform for testing functional impact of human noncoding elements, including ultra-conserved elements shown to drive reporter expression in fly tissues [2], and knockdown models have been used to characterize variants in genes such as ZMYND8 linked to syndromic intellectual disability [3].

identified_gaps: No provided study directly benchmarks sequence-to-expression model predictions against in vivo allelic expression measurements for specific noncoding variants — the CoNSEPT model [1] predicts enhancer function but is not shown to quantitatively predict the effect of individual natural variants identified in eQTL studies [5].

The buffering effects of allelic interactions within enhancers uncovered by Cannavò et al. [5] — where variants with opposing effects cancel each other out — are not modeled by current CNN or thermodynamic approaches, representing a mechanistic gap for predicting net variant effects.

While Drosophila ultra-conserved elements drive reporter expression in flies [2], it is unknown whether fly-trained sequence models accurately predict the quantitative or tissue-specific expression differences caused by variants within these elements in a native genomic context rather than a reporter assay.

The CoNSEPT model [1] is evaluated on neuroectodermal enhancers but has not been tested across the >250 cell types now catalogued in the Fly Cell Atlas [10], leaving open whether models trained on one developmental context generalize to all tissues and stages.

No provided literature tests whether thermodynamic or CNN models trained on Drosophila can correctly rank the direction and magnitude of expression change for loss-of-function noncoding variants identified in human disease cohorts, even when using humanized fly reporter assays [2].

literature.summary: Current sequence-to-expression models for Drosophila, including thermodynamic frameworks and CNN approaches such as CoNSEPT, can learn enhancer grammar and recover known regulatory mechanisms from sequence alone [1], but systematic benchmarking against in vivo noncoding variant effects remains incomplete. High-resolution Drosophila eQTL studies have demonstrated that natural noncoding variants — including those within enhancer binding sites — quantitatively alter expression in a stage-specific manner, with extensive allelic buffering complicating prediction [5]. Rich resources including the Fly Cell Atlas [10] and humanized fly reporter systems [2] provide the ground-truth expression data and experimental frameworks needed to rigorously evaluate whether sequence models trained on fly data can correctly predict the in vivo consequence of specific noncoding variants, but this direct validation has not yet been demonstrated in the provided literature.

hypothesis.hypothesis: A CoNSEPT-class sequence-to-expression model retrained on Drosophila melanogaster embryonic enhancers genome-wide will correctly predict the direction of allelic expression change for ≥70% of individually validated causal eQTL variants from Cannavò et al. (PMID 28024300), while prediction accuracy will drop to ≤50% (near chance) for variants residing within enhancers harboring opposing-effect allelic interactions (buffered enhancers), quantified as area under the ROC curve (AUC) across ≥200 tested variants at 25°C in stage 5–10 embryos.
hypothesis.experimental_approach: We will use a two-arm benchmarking and reporter-validation strategy. Arm 1 (computational): We will retrain a CoNSEPT-style CNN and thermodynamic model on a genome-wide set of Drosophila developmental enhancers using STARR-seq and ChIP-nexus datasets as training signal, then score each causal eQTL variant from Cannavò et al. 2017 (PMID 28024300) by computing the predicted expression delta between reference and alternative allele sequences in a ±500 bp window. Model predictions will be benchmarked against the measured allelic expression ratios from the published eQTL dataset. Variants will be stratified into 'buffered' (enhancers with ≥2 variants with opposing effect directions) and 'unbuffered' groups, and AUC for direction prediction computed independently for each group. Arm 2 (in vivo reporter validation): For a selected subset of 20–30 eQTL variants spanning both buffered and unbuffered enhancers, we will construct attB-site-integrated reporter transgenes (pBPGUw backbone) carrying reference vs. alternative allele sequences upstream of a minimal hsp70 promoter driving GFP, inserted at the same genomic landing site (e.g., VK37 or 86Fb) to control for position effects. Quantitative GFP fluorescence and smFISH will be measured in stage 5–10 embryos. Controls will include empty vector reporters, reporters with scrambled enhancer sequence, and reporters carrying known-functional Dorsal and Twist binding site mutations. All experiments use w1118 as the host genetic background. A chi-square test and logistic regression will assess whether buffering status is a significant predictor of model failure.

hypothesis.expected_outcomes: We expect the retrained sequence model to achieve AUC ≥0.70 for direction-of-effect prediction on unbuffered eQTL variants (single causal SNP per enhancer), consistent with the CoNSEPT model's demonstrated capacity to learn enhancer grammar (PMID 34508359). For buffered enhancers (those with ≥2 opposing-effect variants per Cannavò et al. PMID 28024300), we predict AUC will fall to 0.45–0.55, indistinguishable from random. Reporter assays are expected to validate at least 80% of computationally predicted direction calls for unbuffered variants (GFP signal ratio reference/alternative allele differing by ≥1.5-fold, p<0.05 by t-test after Bonferroni correction). Buffered-enhancer reporters are expected to show <1.3-fold difference per individual variant, confirming that opposing variants cancel in vivo. A statistically significant interaction between buffering status and model accuracy (logistic regression, p<0.01) would confirm the central hypothesis.
hypothesis.novelty_claim: This experiment directly addresses the primary gap identified in the literature synthesis: no published study has benchmarked sequence-to-expression model predictions against in vivo allelic expression measurements for specific causal noncoding variants (gap 1). Critically, it introduces the first systematic test of whether allelic buffering — extensive opposing-effect interactions within enhancers uncovered by Cannavò et al. (PMID 28024300, gap 2) — is a predictable failure mode for CNN and thermodynamic models. The CoNSEPT model (PMID 34508359) was evaluated only on neuroectodermal enhancers and was not tested on natural eQTL variants; our design extends it to genome-wide developmental enhancers and natural variant alleles, addressing gap 4. The use of phiC31-integrated reporters at fixed landing sites to validate model predictions in native embryonic context rather than in silico is novel relative to the reporter-only approach in Takano-Shimizu-Kouno et al. (PMID 29951825).
hypothesis.feasibility_notes: The computational retraining component requires existing STARR-seq and ChIP-nexus Drosophila embryo datasets (publicly available from modENCODE/ENCODE), GPUs, and approximately 2–3 months. The eQTL variant list and allelic effect measurements are published (PMID 28024300), making benchmarking straightforward. Reporter construction via Gibson assembly and phiC31 integration is routine; 20–30 constructs per arm at ~6–8 weeks per injection-selection cycle gives a 4–5 month wet-lab timeline. Potential pitfalls include: (1) the published eQTL dataset may not contain sufficient per-variant effect size information to separate buffered from unbuffered classes cleanly — mitigation is to contact the originating lab for raw allelic counts; (2) CoNSEPT's original architecture may require substantial modification to accept variable-length input — mitigation is to use a sliding-window or dilated CNN; (3) GFP reporters may not recapitulate endogenous chromatin context — mitigation is to include smFISH as an orthogonal readout. Estimated total timeline: 10–12 months. Primary statistical risk: insufficient power if fewer than 200 variants pass quality filters; power calculation suggests 200 variants gives 85% power to detect AUC difference of 0.20 at α=0.05.
specific_aims: Aim 1: Model retraining and in silico benchmarking — Retrain a CoNSEPT-class model on genome-wide Drosophila embryonic STARR-seq data and compute predicted allelic expression deltas for all causal eQTL variants from Cannavò et al. (PMID 28024300), computing AUC for direction-of-effect prediction separately for buffered vs. unbuffered enhancer variants.

Aim 2: In vivo reporter validation of model predictions — Generate phiC31-integrated GFP reporter lines carrying reference and alternative allele sequences for 20–30 selected eQTL variants spanning buffered and unbuffered enhancers, and quantify allele-specific GFP expression by imaging and smFISH in stage 5–10 w1118 embryos to establish in vivo ground truth.

Aim 3: Mechanistic dissection of buffering as a model failure mode — Computationally and experimentally test whether introducing both opposing variants simultaneously into the same reporter construct recapitulates the buffered (near-neutral) expression phenotype, and whether the thermodynamic model component of CoNSEPT can be extended with a pairwise interaction term to partially recover predictive accuracy for buffered enhancers.

literature.summary: Testis-specific RNAi screens identified 2 of 11 putative de novo genes (goddard, saturn) [1] and 1 of over 40 (atlas) [3] as required for male fertility, so the fraction of de novo genes that is essential appears small but non-zero. Young genes appear to become essential through integration into spermatogenesis, chromatin packaging and regulatory networks [1][2][3], and de novo drivers can create new dependencies on suppressors [5]. However, no supplied study quantifies viability-essential de novo genes, and several retrieved papers are off-topic.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Proposed: In a non-redundant panel of ≥50 putative de novo D. melanogaster genes that includes goddard, saturn and atlas, CRISPR null mutants will show that ≤5% of the genes are required for viability at 25°C, while ≥10% are required for fertility in at least one sex. This fertility fraction would exceed the roughly 6% (3 of ~51) male-fertility hit rate seen in testis-specific RNAi screens. Proposed secondary prediction: knockdown of the transcription factors achintya or vismay in the testis will reduce transcript levels of at least one of goddard, saturn or atlas by ≥50%.
hypothesis.experimental_approach: Merge the candidate sets from the goddard/saturn screen and the atlas screen into one non-redundant list, and apply uniform de novo criteria (no annotated protein similarity, restricted phylogenetic distribution, noncoding syntenic sequence where traceable). For each gene, generate a CRISPR/Cas9 null (deletion or frameshift, with the marker verified by sequencing) in an isogenic w1118 background. Score egg-to-adult viability (≥100 embryos per genotype, expected Mendelian ratio from heterozygous crosses), male fertility and female fertility (single-pair matings, ≥15 pairs per sex per genotype, progeny counts over 7 days), with sterile mutants examined by testis or ovary and sperm cytology. Use ubiquitous (tub-GAL4>UAS-RNAi) and testis-specific (e.g. bam-GAL4>UAS-RNAi) knockdown as an orthogonal check, with GAL4-only and UAS-only controls. Genetic rescue with a genomic transgene is required for each hit. Separately, knock down achintya and vismay in the testis and measure goddard, saturn and atlas expression by RT-qPCR, with the GAL4-only genotype as control.

hypothesis.expected_outcomes: Proposed predictions, not established results: (1) At most 3 of ≥50 genes (≤5%) will show reduced viability, defined as <50% of the expected Mendelian class with p<0.05 by chi-square. (2) At least 5 of ≥50 genes (≥10%) will show fertility defects, defined as ≥80% reduction in progeny per pair versus w1118 (Mann-Whitney, FDR<0.05) in males or females. (3) goddard, saturn and atlas nulls will reproduce male sterility. (4) At least one additional gene will show a female-specific or non-testis phenotype missed by testis-specific RNAi. (5) Knockdown of achintya or vismay will reduce transcript levels of at least one of the three known fertility genes by ≥50% (n≥3 biological replicates, p<0.05). Falsification: if >5% of the genes are viability-essential, or if the fertility fraction is ≤6%, the hypothesis is rejected.

Only about 3 hits (goddard, saturn, atlas) came from roughly 51 screened candidates, and it is unclear whether the two candidate sets overlap. This study would combine the candidate sets under uniform criteria, use null alleles instead of testis-specific RNAi, and score viability and both sexes. The regulatory work on achintya and vismay does not show whether these transcription factors are required for the fertility function of specific de novo genes, which Aim 3 would address. Goddard and saturn could not be traced to a specific noncoding ancestral sequence, so the ancestral-locus question remains open and is outside the scope of this plan.
hypothesis.feasibility_notes: Estimated timeline is 14 months: months 1-2 for candidate curation and gRNA design; months 3-8 for CRISPR mutant generation and validation; months 6-11 for viability and fertility assays; months 9-12 for the RNAi and transcription-factor experiments; months 12-14 for rescue of hits and analysis. Pitfalls: some candidates overlap or are nested in other genes or enhancers, so deletions may disrupt neighboring loci, which makes rescue and sequence-verified alleles essential. Small ORFs are hard to target, and RNAi off-target effects can produce false viability hits. Maternal contribution can mask zygotic lethality. Sterility may be a secondary effect of poor health. A panel of ~50 genes requires substantial crossing effort. Definitions of de novo origin vary, so the ≥50 gene panel must be verified for provenance and overlap, and no line should be assumed available until verified.

literature.disease_context: De novo gene essentiality in Drosophila provides a model for understanding how newly emergent genetic elements contribute to reproductive fitness and, by analogy, how de novo mutations in conserved regulatory complexes (such as CCR4-NOT via CNOT1, or APC/C via FZR1) underlie human neurodevelopmental disorders [6][8]. The discovery that de novo genes in flies are frequently required for spermatogenesis parallels the role of DAZ-family genes in human male infertility, where de novo Y-chromosome deletions cause azoospermia [7]. Understanding regulatory networks controlling de novo gene expression may illuminate why de novo variants in transcriptional regulators so often produce developmental disease phenotypes in humans [2][6][8].

key_papers.relevance: Shows that de novo protamine-derived selfish genes (Dox family) on the X chromosome drive meiotic conflict, and that newly emerged hairpin RNA loci (nmy, tmy) are essential suppressors, demonstrating that de novo genes can become essential components of genome conflict and suppression systems.

identified_gaps: Screens of putative de novo genes for fertility or viability phenotypes have covered only small fractions of candidates (11 in [1], >40 in [3]), leaving the majority of de novo genes uncharacterized; a comprehensive genome-wide RNAi or CRISPR screen is needed to quantify what proportion of all de novo genes are essential.

The regulatory architecture governing de novo gene expression has only begun to be explored through two transcription factors (achintya and vismay) [2]; it remains unknown how many distinct transcription factors are required, whether their regulatory roles are ancestral or co-evolved with the new genes, and how transcription factor duplications mechanistically expand de novo gene regulatory networks.

The evolutionary trajectory from non-essential to essential is poorly resolved: for atlas, chromosomal relocation and gene fusion are implicated [3], but the molecular events that confer essentiality in other de novo genes (goddard, saturn) are uncharacterized, and no systematic framework explains why some de novo genes become essential while most do not.

De novo genes that are essential for viability (rather than fertility) have not been identified in the provided literature; all screens have focused on male reproductive tissues, leaving open whether de novo genes contribute to somatic essential functions in Drosophila.

The mechanistic basis by which de novo Dox-family selfish genes cause male sterility or sex-ratio distortion when derepressed [5] remains incompletely understood; it is unclear whether their protamine-derived protein products directly disrupt chromatin packaging or act through other mechanisms.

evidence_claims.claim: New genes arise through a variety of mechanisms, including the duplication of existing genes and the de novo birth of genes from noncoding DNA sequences.
Many newly evolved genes are expressed in the male reproductive tract, suggesting that these evolutionary innovations may provide advantages to males experiencing sexual selection.

Using testis-specific RNA interference, we screened 11 putative de novo genes in Drosophila melanogaster for effects on male fertility and identified two, goddard and saturn, that are essential for spermatogenesis and sperm function.
Goddard knockdown (KD) males fail to produce mature sperm, while saturn KD males produce few sperm, and these function inefficiently once transferred to females.
Both genes are identifiable only in Drosophila and are predicted to encode proteins with no sequence similarity to any annotated protein.
Goddard is consistently found in single-copy and evolves under purifying selection. In contrast, saturn has diversified through gene duplication and positive selection.
We conducted a functional genetic screen of over 40 putative de novo genes with testis-enriched expression in Drosophila melanogaster and identified one gene, atlas, required for male fertility.

Atlas is required for proper chromatin condensation during the final stages of spermatogenesis. Atlas protein is expressed in spermatid nuclei and facilitates the transition from histone- to protamine-based chromatin packaging.

The protein-coding portion of the gene likely arose at the base of the Drosophila genus on the X chromosome but was unlikely to be essential, as it was then lost in several independent lineages. Within the last ~15 million years, however, the gene moved to an autosome, where it fused with a conserved non-coding RNA and evolved a non-redundant role in male fertility.
Transcription factors do not have the same propensity for regulating de novo genes; some transcription factors regulate more de novo genes than others.

Two key transcription factors, achintya and vismay, and the regulatory architecture of new genes were examined, identifying key transcription factors associated with the expression of de novo genes and highlighting how transcription factors, and possibly their duplications, are linked to the expressional regulation of de novo genes.
A family of de novo, protamine-derived X-linked selfish genes (the Dox gene family) is silenced by a pair of newly emerged hairpin RNA (hpRNA) small interfering RNA (siRNA)-class loci, Nmy and Tmy.
In the w[XD1] genetic background, knockout of nmy derepresses Dox and MDox in testes and depletes male progeny, whereas knockout of tmy causes misexpression of PDox genes and renders males sterile.

These studies support a model in which protamine-derived drivers and hpRNA suppressors drive repeated cycles of sex chromosome conflict and resolution that shape genome evolution and the genetic control of male gametogenesis.
Loss of boule function results in azoospermia; meiotic divisions are blocked, although limited spermatid differentiation occurs.
The primary defect is at the meiotic G2/M transition.
These results support the hypothesis that DAZ is the human AZF, and indicate that Boule and DAZ have an essential meiotic function in fly and human spermatogenesis.
De novo genes can acquire essential roles in male reproduction.
The regulatory programmes governing the expression of de novo genes remain unknown.
All screens have focused on male reproductive tissues, leaving open whether de novo genes contribute to somatic essential functions in Drosophila.

Dox loci are functionally polymorphic within D. simulans, such that both nmy-associated sex ratio bias and tmy-associated sterility can be rescued by wild-type X chromosomes bearing natural deletions in different Dox family genes.

literature.summary: Functional screens in Drosophila have demonstrated that a subset of de novo genes — those arising from non-coding sequences with no detectable homology outside the genus — become essential for male fertility, with identified examples including goddard and saturn (required for spermatogenesis and sperm function [1]), atlas (required for spermatid chromatin condensation [3]), and the hpRNA suppressors nmy and tmy (required to silence selfish Dox-family meiotic drivers [5]). The proportion of de novo genes that become essential remains unclear, as the largest published screens covered only 11–40+ candidates focused on testis-expressed genes, and viability roles in somatic tissues have not been systematically examined. Recent work has begun to reveal the regulatory logic enabling de novo gene integration, identifying specific transcription factors (achintya, vismay) that preferentially regulate de novo genes [2], while evolutionary analyses of atlas show that chromosomal relocation and gene fusion can transform a dispensable ancestral locus into an essential one [3].

hypothesis.hypothesis: A comprehensive, tissue-stratified CRISPR-based loss-of-function screen of all annotated Drosophila melanogaster de novo genes (estimated ≥200 candidates) will reveal that ≥15% are essential for male fertility, ≥5% are essential for female fertility, and ≥2% are essential for viability in somatic tissues, under standard 25°C conditions in a w1118 background; furthermore, de novo genes regulated by achintya and/or vismay will be disproportionately enriched (≥2-fold over chance) among the fertility-essential subset relative to de novo genes lacking these transcription factor binding sites in their promoters.
hypothesis.experimental_approach: We will compile a genome-wide list of Drosophila melanogaster de novo genes (defined as genes with no detectable homolog outside Drosophila by reciprocal BLAST and synteny analysis) from published catalogs and FlyBase annotation, targeting ≥200 candidates. For each candidate, we will generate a CRISPR/Cas9 frameshift or deletion allele using two independent sgRNAs injected into w1118 embryos (or using available TRiP CRISPR lines from BDSC), confirm loss-of-function by Sanger sequencing, and balance over CyO or TM3,Sb to maintain homozygous-lethal alleles. Fertility assays will be conducted by crossing homozygous or transheterozygous knockout males (or females) to w1118 partners and counting progeny over 10 days (n≥30 crosses per genotype); male fertility will be supplemented by phase-contrast microscopy of seminal vesicle contents for sperm motility and morphology. hypothesis.expected_outcomes: Primary screen (CRISPR knockouts, n≥200 de novo genes): We predict ≥30 genes (≥15%) will cause complete or severe male sterility (≤10% progeny relative to w1118 controls, p<0.01 by two-tailed t-test with Bonferroni correction), ≥10 genes (≥5%) will cause female sterility, and ≥4 genes (≥2%) will show homozygous lethality (Mendelian ratio <0.33 of expected homozygotes, p<0.01). Microscopy of sterile males will classify phenotypes into: (a) failed spermatogenesis (no sperm in seminal vesicles), (b) motility defects (immotile sperm), (c) meiotic arrest, or (d) chromatin condensation failure (analogous to atlas). For the transcription factor hypothesis: Fisher's exact test will show ≥2-fold enrichment of fertility-essential genes among achintya/vismay ChIP-seq targets (p<0.05), supporting co-regulation as a mechanism of de novo gene network integration. If the null hypothesis holds (de novo genes are rarely essential somatically and TF targeting is random), we expect <2% somatic lethality and no significant enrichment among TF targets.
hypothesis.novelty_claim: This experiment directly addresses three major gaps identified in the literature synthesis: (1) Prior screens covered only 11 (PMID 28104747) and >40 (PMID 34478447) candidates, leaving the majority of de novo genes uncharacterized — this proposal is the first to attempt genome-wide coverage of all annotated de novo genes; (2) No prior screen has systematically tested de novo genes for somatic viability requirements — all published screens focused exclusively on male reproductive tissues; (3) While achintya and vismay were identified as preferential regulators of de novo genes (PMID 40659874), no study has directly tested whether their transcriptional targets are disproportionately essential, linking regulatory architecture to phenotypic essentiality for the first time.
hypothesis.feasibility_notes: The primary technical challenge is generating and validating ≥200 independent CRISPR knockout alleles, which at a rate of 10–15 lines per month requires approximately 15–20 months for line generation alone; a phased approach prioritizing testis-expressed candidates (using FlyAtlas2 or modENCODE expression data) in the first phase (~80 genes, 6 months) is recommended. Many de novo genes may lack existing RNAi or CRISPR reagents at BDSC/VDRC, necessitating de novo sgRNA design and injection for the majority of candidates — this is feasible but labor-intensive. Off-target CRISPR effects must be controlled by (a) two independent alleles per gene, (b) rescue with a genomic transgene for any essential gene, and (c) whole-genome sequencing of 10% of lines. The achintya/vismay ChIP-seq requires GFP knock-ins that are not currently available and will add 3–4 months. Estimated total timeline: 24–30 months. Potential pitfall: many true de novo genes may have redundant paralogs or may be expressed at levels too low for effective RNAi; CRISPR null alleles are preferred over RNAi for this reason. Genetic background effects (e.g., the w[XD1] background required for Dox/nmy phenotypes per PMID 37289846) must be considered when interpreting sex-ratio or meiotic drive phenotypes.
specific_aims: Aim 1: Genome-wide CRISPR fertility screen — Generate and phenotype CRISPR loss-of-function alleles for ≥200 annotated D. melanogaster de novo genes to quantify the proportion essential for male fertility, female fertility, and somatic viability under standard 25°C w1118 conditions.

Aim 2: Cellular and developmental phenotype classification — For all genes causing fertility or viability defects in Aim 1, use stage-specific GAL4 drivers, phase-contrast and confocal microscopy, and DAPI/protamine staining to classify the developmental stage and cellular mechanism of failure (meiotic arrest, spermatid chromatin defects, motility failure, or somatic lethality).

Aim 3: Transcription factor regulatory enrichment analysis — Generate endogenous GFP-tagged achintya and vismay knock-in lines, perform ChIP-seq in testes, and test whether de novo genes bearing achintya/vismay binding sites in their promoters are disproportionately enriched among the fertility-essential genes identified in Aim 1, using Fisher's exact test with a significance threshold of p<0.05.

All screens have focused on male reproductive tissues, leaving open whether de novo genes contribute to somatic essential functions in Drosophila.

Two key transcription factors, achintya and vismay, and the regulatory architecture of new genes were examined, identifying key transcription factors associated with the expression of de novo genes and highlighting how transcription factors, and possibly their duplications, are linked to the expressional regulation of de novo genes.

The protein-coding portion of the gene likely arose at the base of the Drosophila genus on the X chromosome but was unlikely to be essential, as it was then lost in several independent lineages. Within the last ~15 million years, however, the gene moved to an autosome, where it fused with a conserved non-coding RNA and evolved a non-redundant role in male fertility.

Both genes are identifiable only in Drosophila and are predicted to encode proteins with no sequence similarity to any annotated protein.

identified_gaps: Whether TE expression increases causally drive lifespan limitation in a tissue-specific way is unresolved: Schneider et al. [7] used knockdown of only two TEs (412, Roo) and did not test other families or tissue-restricted manipulation.

The mechanism by which TE expression without increased insertion shortens lifespan is unknown; candidates from transcriptomics (proteolysis and immune genes) [7] need testing, e.g. by determining whether reverse transcription, RNA/DNA intermediates or inflammatory signaling mediate effects.

The reasons for the middle-age TE reduction followed by late-life reactivation [1] are not defined; it is unclear how flamenco/piRNA output relates mechanistically to this pattern across tissues and genotypes.

The contribution of genetic background and TE family specificity to age-related TE changes [4] has not been systematically resolved, nor has the soma versus germline difference been directly compared in the same strains.
Whether Hinfp/Histone1-dependent repression [3] declines naturally with age, and whether restoring it extends lifespan in wild-type flies, was not shown in the supplied abstracts.

literature.summary: Evidence in Drosophila indicates that somatic TE control is dynamic with age, with variable expression changes and reactivation in older flies, and that TE expression (rather than clearly increased insertion) can contribute to lifespan limitation [1][7]. Somatic repressors such as Hinfp/Histone1 and piRNA sources such as flamenco support TE control, and loss of control is associated with DNA damage and aging phenotypes [1][3]. The ovary appears to differ from soma, and effects are strain- and TE-family-specific, so causality and generality remain unresolved [4].

hypothesis.hypothesis: Proposed: adult-onset RNAi knockdown of the retrotransposon 412 restricted to the fat body will extend median lifespan by at least 10% (log-rank p<0.05, n≥200 flies per genotype) in mated female flies at 25°C on standard medium relative to genotype-matched vehicle controls, whereas the same knockdown restricted to neurons will extend median lifespan by less than 5%, and the fat-body extension will occur without a change in 412 genomic copy number in aged fat body DNA.
hypothesis.experimental_approach: Use the GeneSwitch (RU486-inducible) system so knockdown is induced only in adulthood: a fat body GS driver versus a pan-neuronal GS driver, each crossed to UAS-412 RNAi, with a UAS-Roo RNAi arm, a non-targeting RNAi control, and vehicle-fed (no RU486) siblings of every genotype. Prior work showed that knockdown of 412 and Roo extends lifespan, but it did not test tissue-restricted manipulation (PMID 37084379). Lifespan will be scored in mated females at 25°C in the same genetic background, with a minimum of 200 flies per genotype and treatment, and compared by log-rank test with Bonferroni correction. In a second cohort, collected at days 10, 30 and 50, we will measure 412 and Roo transcripts by RT-qPCR, genomic copy number by qPCR/ddPCR on dissected fat body or head DNA, γH2Av foci as a DNA-damage readout, and antimicrobial peptide transcripts as an inflammation readout. To separate expression from insertion, a subset will be fed a reverse-transcriptase inhibitor (proposed; dose and fly-compatibility require verification). A third arm will test whether Hinfp or His1 transcript or protein declines with age in fat body, and whether adult-onset Hinfp overexpression lowers 412 transcript and extends lifespan.

hypothesis.expected_outcomes: Proposed predictions, not established results: (1) Fat body 412 knockdown will increase median lifespan by 10-20% over vehicle-fed controls (log-rank p<0.05), while neuronal knockdown will give less than 5% extension. (2) Aged (day 50) fat body will show at least a 2-fold increase in 412 transcript relative to day 10 in controls, and RNAi will reduce 412 transcript by at least 60%. (3) 412 genomic copy number will not differ by more than 10% between knockdown and control or between young and old flies. (4) Knockdown will reduce γH2Av foci and antimicrobial peptide transcripts by at least 30% at day 50. (5) Hinfp or His1 levels will decline with age in fat body, and adult Hinfp overexpression will reduce 412 transcripts and extend median lifespan by at least 8%. A lifespan extension below 5% in the fat body arm, or one equally strong in the neuronal arm, would falsify the tissue-restricted hypothesis.
hypothesis.novelty_claim: The literature synthesis identified that Schneider et al. used knockdown of only two TEs (412, Roo) and did not test other families or tissue-restricted manipulation (PMID 37084379). This plan fills that gap by comparing tissue-restricted, adult-onset knockdown in fat body and neurons. It also addresses the unresolved question of how TE expression without increased insertion shortens lifespan, by pairing lifespan with copy-number, DNA-damage and inflammation readouts. Finally, it tests whether Hinfp/Histone1-dependent repression declines with age and whether restoring it extends lifespan in wild-type flies, which the supplied abstracts did not show (PMID 34620709).
hypothesis.feasibility_notes: Estimated timeline is 12-15 months: 2 months for line acquisition, RNAi validation and RU486 dose titration; 4-5 months for lifespan cohorts; 3 months for molecular time courses; 3 months for the Hinfp arm and analysis. Main pitfalls: (a) RNAi knockdown of high-copy TEs may be incomplete or may have off-target effects, so at least two independent RNAi constructs should be used if available; (b) RU486 itself can affect lifespan and feeding, hence vehicle controls of every genotype; (c) GeneSwitch drivers can be leaky and tissue specificity must be verified; (d) results are strain- and TE-family-dependent (PMID 31014230), so the effect may not generalize beyond the chosen background; (e) the reverse-transcriptase inhibitor arm requires dose and toxicity validation; (f) in-house construction of a UAS-Hinfp line may be needed.

identified_gaps: Mechanism linking TE expression to lifespan without new insertions is unresolved. Schneider et al. found no age-related insertion increase but lifespan extension upon 412/Roo knockdown [7]. Whether the effect works through TE RNA, reverse-transcribed cDNA, encoded proteins, or immune activation needs testing, for example by combining TE knockdown with immune-pathway mutants or reverse-transcriptase inhibitors.

Causes of the biphasic TE expression trajectory (down in middle age, up in old age) [1] are unknown. Longitudinal, tissue-resolved profiling of flamenco piRNAs, Piwi-pathway components and H3K9me3 at TE loci would show whether the late reactivation reflects failing small-RNA silencing or chromatin silencing.

Insertion detection was limited to thorax and indirect flight muscle nuclei [7]. Whether mitotically active or other tissues (gut stem cells, fat body, brain) accumulate insertions with age remains untested, which matters because the insertion-based model may apply only to specific cell types.

It is unclear whether Hinfp or Histone1 levels decline during normal aging. Hinfp loss enhances aging-related phenotypes [3], but whether Hinfp or Histone1 overexpression in aged somatic tissue suppresses TE reactivation and extends lifespan is untested.

Genetic background and TE family strongly modulate age effects on TEs [4], yet the somatic aging studies examined few strains and families [1,7]. Multi-strain somatic studies are needed to tell general effects from strain-specific ones.

The link between environmental or dietary aging accelerators and TE activity is understudied. A high-fat diet increased somatic P-element activity [2], but whether interventions such as dietary restriction or Rpd3 reduction act partly through TE silencing has not been tested in the supplied literature [11,12].

Review of how TEs and satellites may drive aging and neurodegeneration through DNA damage, insertional mutagenesis and inflammation, with Drosophila as the main model.
Review establishing H3K9me heterochromatin as a conserved TE-silencing mechanism whose disruption correlates with premature aging.
Schneider et al. found no age-related insertion increase but lifespan extension upon 412/Roo knockdown [7].

Whether the effect works through TE RNA, reverse-transcribed cDNA, encoded proteins, or immune activation needs testing, for example by combining TE knockdown with immune-pathway mutants or reverse-transcriptase inhibitors.
Causes of the biphasic TE expression trajectory (down in middle age, up in old age) [1] are unknown.

Longitudinal, tissue-resolved profiling of flamenco piRNAs, Piwi-pathway components and H3K9me3 at TE loci would show whether the late reactivation reflects failing small-RNA silencing or chromatin silencing.
Insertion detection was limited to thorax and indirect flight muscle nuclei [7].

Whether mitotically active or other tissues (gut stem cells, fat body, brain) accumulate insertions with age remains untested, which matters because the insertion-based model may apply only to specific cell types.
Hinfp loss enhances aging-related phenotypes [3], but whether Hinfp or Histone1 overexpression in aged somatic tissue suppresses TE reactivation and extends lifespan is untested.
It is unclear whether Hinfp or Histone1 levels decline during normal aging.
Genetic background and TE family strongly modulate age effects on TEs [4], yet the somatic aging studies examined few strains and families [1,7].
Multi-strain somatic studies are needed to tell general effects from strain-specific ones.

A high-fat diet increased somatic P-element activity [2], but whether interventions such as dietary restriction or Rpd3 reduction act partly through TE silencing has not been tested in the supplied literature [11,12].

Somatic TE control in aging Drosophila is dynamic rather than simply declining: TE expression falls in middle age and rebounds in old flies [1], while new somatic insertions do not measurably increase with age in thoracic and flight muscle nuclei [7].

Causal evidence nonetheless links TEs to lifespan: forced somatic P-element transposition shortens lifespan [2], knockdown of 412 or Roo expression extends it [7], and loss of the Hinfp–Histone1 silencing axis derepresses most TEs, causing DNA damage and aging-related phenotypes [3].

By contrast, aged ovarian tissue shows no global TE derepression and upregulates piRNA machinery [4], suggesting (inference) that loss of TE control is a soma-specific, background- and family-dependent feature of aging.

literature.disease_context: Derepression of transposable elements (TEs) in somatic tissues during aging has been linked to DNA double-strand breaks, genome instability, and inflammatory responses, all of which are implicated in human age-related diseases including neurodegeneration and cancer [1][3][5][6]. TE families such as gypsy, HERV-K, and HERV-W, as well as TDP-43 interactions with TE-derived RNA, have been specifically implicated in neurodegenerative disorders including ALS [5]. Loss of chromatin regulators such as H3K9 methyltransferases (orthologous to Drosophila Su(var)3-9 and setdb1) correlates with impaired tissue identity, premature aging, and malignancy in mammals [8].

identified_gaps: The relative contributions of TE expression versus new somatic insertions to aging remain poorly resolved — single-nucleus sequencing in thorax/muscle found no increase in insertions with age [7], but it is unknown whether other somatic tissues (e.g., brain, gut) accumulate insertions, and whether ultra-rare insertions detectable only at single-cell resolution drive focal pathology.

The flamenco piRNA cluster regulates specific retrotransposons in somatic tissues [1], but the full repertoire of somatic small RNA pathways (piRNA vs. siRNA) that counteract TE reactivation during aging, and how their capacity changes across the lifespan, has not been systematically mapped.

TE derepression during aging appears tissue-specific — somatic tissues show reactivation while reproductive tissues do not show global TE release [4] — but the molecular mechanisms that make reproductive tissues more resistant to age-related TE derepression remain unknown.

The causal chain between TE expression, immune/inflammatory activation, and longevity is unresolved: knockdown of 412 and Roo extended lifespan and altered proteolysis and immune gene expression [7], but it is not known which downstream effectors (e.g., innate immune signaling, cGAS-STING ortholog) are the proximate drivers of lifespan shortening.

The Hinfp-Histone1 pathway suppresses most TEs in Drosophila soma [3], but whether the activity or expression of Hinfp or linker histones declines with normal aging (thereby explaining age-related TE reactivation) has not been tested directly.

evidence_claims.claim: The transposon theory of aging hypothesizes the activation of transposable elements (TEs) in somatic tissues with age, leading to a shortening of the lifespan.
TE activation in aging produces an increase in DNA double-strand breaks, contributing to genome instability and promoting the activation of inflammatory responses.

We found significant variations in the expression levels of all the analyzed TEs during aging, with a trend toward reduction in middle-aged adults and reactivation in older individuals that suggests dynamic regulation during the lifespan.
At least two elements, Copia and 412, are capable of somatic activity in adult Drosophila tissue.
A high-fat diet, known to accelerate aging, increased the frequency of eye color mosaicism and red eyes.
We induced life span shortening by artificially activating somatic transposition of P elements, and the extent of reduction in life span was similar in both sexes.
Loss of function of the conserved zinc-finger transcription factor Hinfp causes dysregulation of many host genes and derepression of most transposable elements.
There is also substantial DNA damage in somatic tissues of Drosophila after loss of Hinfp.
Interference of transposable element mobilization by reverse-transcriptase inhibitors can suppress some of the DNA damage phenotypes.
The key cell-autonomous target of Hinfp in this process is Histone1, which encodes linker histones essential for higher-order chromatin assembly.
Transgenic expression of Hinfp or Histone1, but not Histone4 of core nucleosome, is sufficient to rescue the defects in repressing transposable elements and host genes.
Loss of Hinfp enhances Ras-induced tissue growth and aging-related phenotypes.
Age-related expression changes in late-stage egg chambers tend to occur in genes residing in heterochromatin, particularly on the largely heterochromatic 4th chromosome.
We find no evidence for global TE derepression in reproductive tissues. Rather, the observed effects of aging on TEs are primarily strain and family specific.
An increase in expression of the piRNA machinery [was identified], suggesting an age-related increased investment in the maintenance of genome stability.
Global loss of TE control observed in other studies may be unique to the soma and sensitive to genetic background and TE family.
Analyses of nuclei from thoraces and indirect flight muscles using a newly developed pipeline, Retrofind, revealed no significant increase in the number of transposon insertions with age.
Reducing the expression of two different retrotransposons, 412 and Roo, extended lifespan, but did not alter indicators of health such as stress resistance.
This suggests a key role for transposon expression and not insertion in regulating longevity.

Transcriptomic analyses revealed similar changes to gene expression in 412 and Roo knockdown flies and highlighted changes to genes involved in proteolysis and immune function as potential contributors to the observed changes in longevity.

An association between heterochromatic silencing and longevity has long been recognized in yeast, and in more recent years evidence has accumulated of age-related chromatin changes in Caenorhabditis elegans, Drosophila, and mouse model systems.
A number of studies have linked expression of transposable elements (TEs), as well as changes in the RNAi pathways that cells use to combat TEs, to the aging process.
Alterations in RE expression, retrotransposition, and chromatin microenvironment may shorten lifespan, elicit neurodegeneration, and impair memory and movement.
REs may cause these phenotypes via DNA damage, protein sequestration, insertional mutagenesis, and inflammation.
Studies of TEs in neurodegeneration have focused on Drosophila and, thus, further examination in mammals is needed.

Heterochromatin is characterized by dimethylated or trimethylated histone H3 Lys9 (H3K9me2 or H3K9me3, respectively) and is found at transposable elements, satellite repeats and genes, where it ensures their transcriptional silencing.
Genetic ablation or mistargeting of an individual H3K9 methyltransferase can correlate with impaired cell differentiation, loss of tissue identity, premature aging and/or cancer.
TE derepression in somatic tissues during aging appears tissue-specific — reproductive tissues do not show global TE release with age whereas somatic tissues do.

literature.summary: Multiple lines of evidence from Drosophila melanogaster support the transposon theory of aging: retrotransposon expression increases in aging somatic tissues (though with dynamic mid-life fluctuation) [1], artificial somatic transposition shortens lifespan [2], and RNAi-mediated knockdown of retrotransposons 412 and Roo extends lifespan [7], indicating that TE expression — rather than new insertions — is a key driver of longevity. Mechanistically, somatic TE silencing depends on H3K9 methylation-dependent heterochromatin [6][8] and on the Hinfp-Histone1 pathway, whose disruption causes TE derepression, DNA damage, and enhanced aging phenotypes [3]; the piRNA-generating flamenco cluster also contributes to somatic TE regulation [1]. Strikingly, global TE derepression is soma-specific — reproductive tissues of aged flies show no global TE release and even upregulate piRNA machinery [4] — and the downstream consequences of somatic TE expression, including immune/proteolytic gene dysregulation and potential inflammatory signaling, remain active areas of investigation [5][7].

hypothesis.hypothesis: Age-dependent decline in Hinfp protein expression in the Drosophila somatic fat body (beginning at day 30 post-eclosion at 25°C) causes ≥2-fold upregulation of retrotransposons 412 and Roo by day 45, and fat-body-specific transgenic restoration of Hinfp in aged w1118 mated female flies will suppress this TE reactivation by ≥50%, reduce γH2Av DNA-damage foci by ≥40%, suppress age-related upregulation of immune/antimicrobial peptide genes (e.g., Diptericin, Attacin) by ≥30%, and extend median lifespan by ≥15% relative to age-matched UAS-Hinfp/+ and r4-GAL4/+ controls under standard 25°C, 12:12 LD conditions.
hypothesis.experimental_approach: We will use the GAL4/UAS system to drive fat-body-specific (r4-GAL4) overexpression of Hinfp throughout adulthood in mated female w1118 flies, and separately use RNAi to knock down Hinfp in the fat body to phenocopy natural age-related decline. First, we will establish the age trajectory of endogenous Hinfp protein (western blot, immunofluorescence) and mRNA (RT-qPCR) in dissected fat bodies at days 10, 20, 30, 45, and 60 post-eclosion. Second, we will measure TE expression (RT-qPCR and small RNA-seq targeting 412, Roo, Copia, gypsy, and mdg1) and DNA damage (γH2Av immunostaining, neutral comet assay) in the same age series. Third, lifespan assays (n ≥ 200 flies per genotype, three independent cohorts) will be performed for r4-GAL4 > UAS-Hinfp versus both heterozygous parental controls and a UAS-lacZ transgenic control to confirm GAL4 dosage effects. Fourth, transcriptomic profiling (bulk RNA-seq, ≥3 biological replicates) of fat bodies from day-45 r4-GAL4 > UAS-Hinfp and control flies will identify downstream immune, proteolytic, and DNA-damage-response gene changes. All crosses and assays will include w1118 isogenic background controls, temperature-controlled incubators, and mated females maintained at standard density (20 flies per vial).

hypothesis.expected_outcomes: Primary outcome: Hinfp mRNA and protein in fat body will decline ≥1.5-fold between day 10 and day 45 (RT-qPCR, western blot; significance threshold p < 0.05, Student's t-test with Bonferroni correction across timepoints). TE expression (412, Roo) will increase ≥2-fold in wild-type fat body by day 45 relative to day 10. Fat-body-specific Hinfp overexpression (r4-GAL4 > UAS-Hinfp) will suppress day-45 TE upregulation by ≥50% relative to both parental controls (p < 0.05). γH2Av foci per fat-body nucleus will be reduced ≥40% in r4-GAL4 > UAS-Hinfp flies at day 45 (confocal immunofluorescence, ≥50 nuclei per genotype per replicate, n = 3 biological replicates). Antimicrobial peptide gene expression (Diptericin, Attacin) will be reduced ≥30% in Hinfp-overexpressing fat bodies (RNA-seq, DESeq2 analysis, FDR < 0.05). Median lifespan will extend ≥15% in r4-GAL4 > UAS-Hinfp females relative to both parental controls (log-rank test, p < 0.05, n ≥ 200 per genotype). Conversely, r4-GAL4 > UAS-Hinfp-RNAi flies will show premature TE upregulation by day 20 and lifespan reduction ≥15% relative to controls, confirming the sufficiency of fat-body Hinfp loss.
hypothesis.novelty_claim: This experiment directly tests the untested causal hypothesis that Hinfp expression declines with age in somatic tissues and that this decline is a proximate upstream driver of age-related TE reactivation. The literature synthesis explicitly flags that 'whether the activity or expression of Hinfp or linker histones declines with normal aging (thereby explaining age-related TE derepression) has not been tested directly' (identified gap #5). Additionally, while TE knockdown extends lifespan (PMID 37084379) and Hinfp loss causes TE derepression and aging phenotypes (PMID 34620709), the causal chain linking Hinfp decline → TE reactivation → immune signaling → lifespan shortening has not been assembled in a single tissue-specific in vivo experiment. The experiment also addresses gap #4 — the unresolved identity of downstream effectors (innate immune signaling) connecting TE expression to lifespan shortening — through transcriptome profiling of immune gene expression in fat bodies with manipulated Hinfp levels.
hypothesis.feasibility_notes: GAL4/UAS technology in adult fat body is well-established and r4-GAL4 provides robust adult fat-body expression with minimal developmental confounds. The primary technical risk is the UAS-Hinfp line, which must be generated or obtained from the authors of PMID 34620709; generating it via attP40 injection is standard and takes approximately 3–4 months. A TRiP RNAi line for Hinfp may exist but requires verification against the current BDSC database before ordering. Western blot quantification of endogenous Hinfp across age requires a validated anti-Drosophila-Hinfp antibody, which may need to be commissioned or validated — this is a potential 2–3 month bottleneck. The lifespan assay requires strict standardization of mating, density, food, and temperature; at least three independent biological replicates are needed for statistical power (estimated 6–8 months). RNA-seq on dissected fat bodies from aged flies is technically demanding due to tissue fragility and RNA quality; TRIzol extraction with immediate snap-freezing is recommended. Total estimated timeline: 18–24 months from line acquisition/generation through data analysis. Potential pitfall: if Hinfp overexpression in the fat body causes developmental or metabolic defects, a temporal induction system (e.g., tubGAL80ts; r4-GAL4) should be substituted to restrict overexpression to post-eclosion adulthood.
specific_aims: Aim 1: Age trajectory of Hinfp — Quantify Hinfp mRNA and protein levels in dissected fat bodies of mated female w1118 flies at days 10, 20, 30, 45, and 60 post-eclosion, and correlate with RT-qPCR measurements of 412, Roo, Copia, and gypsy TE expression at the same timepoints to establish whether Hinfp decline precedes or coincides with TE reactivation

literature.disease_context: The supplied abstracts do not directly link Drosophila 3D genome perturbations to specific human diseases or name human orthologs, so no disease relevance is asserted here. One review notes that perturbing enhancer-promoter interactions can affect transcription and physiological outcomes [3]. By inference (unverified by the provided literature), mis-wiring of chromatin contacts could contribute to developmental disorders, but this should be tested directly.

key_papers.authors: Pollex T et al.
key_papers.relevance: Separates loop formation from gene expression by mutating loop anchors versus genes in embryos, showing that loop disruption fine-tunes expression and cross-regulation rather than switching genes on or off.

key_papers.title: Unveiling dynamic enhancer-promoter interactions in Drosophila melanogaster.
key_papers.authors: Deng H et al.
key_papers.relevance: Reviews how multiple competing or cooperating enhancer-enhancer, enhancer-promoter and promoter-promoter interactions, plus insulators and tethering elements, shape transcription. This suggests mechanisms for buffering and for cases where topology is required.

key_papers.title: Chromatin Organization and Function in Drosophila.
key_papers.authors: Llorens-Giralt P et al.
key_papers.relevance: Provides background on Drosophila genome organization across scales, from histone-DNA interactions to chromosome territories and lamina interactions, and its relation to gene expression.

identified_gaps: Which loops are functional: Pollex et al. dissected only three gene-gene loops [2]. Genome-scale anchor-mutation screens are needed to determine what fraction of constitutive loops affect expression and in which tissues.

Context dependence is unexplained: loops can be constitutive yet change function across developmental contexts [2]. The trans-acting factors that convert a scaffold into an activating versus attenuating contact remain unidentified.

The buffering hypothesis is untested in the supplied literature: whether redundant enhancer-promoter and promoter-promoter contacts [3] explain modest perturbation effects requires combinatorial deletion of redundant contacts with quantitative live-imaging of transcriptional bursting.

Phenotypic consequences: the provided abstracts do not show whether the expression changes caused by breaking loops alter organismal fitness or developmental robustness. Assays under stress or sensitized genetic backgrounds are needed.

Which long-range interactions depend on insulators or tethering elements [3] is not systematically defined. A predictive classification by enhancer-promoter distance and element type would clarify when topology matters.

identified_gaps: Only three loops between functionally related genes were dissected in embryos [2]; it is unknown whether the attenuate-or-enhance pattern holds for loops genome-wide or in other tissues and stages, which limits any general account of why architectural disruption is usually modest.

Loop function can change between developmental contexts [2], but the factors that switch a loop between roles (for example, a cooperative versus a competitive enhancer arrangement) are not identified. Testing the same loop deletion across several cell types with single-cell or live transcription readouts would address this.

The supplied literature does not quantify how redundancy among multiple enhancer-promoter interactions [3] buffers expression when one contact is lost. Combinatorial deletion of redundant enhancers or anchors, combined with a 3D perturbation, would test whether buffering explains the modest bulk effects.

The supplied abstracts do not test whether modest average changes in expression hide larger effects on transcriptional bursting or cell-to-cell variability. Live imaging of burst frequency and amplitude after loop or insulator disruption [3] is needed to find out.
The supplied literature does not connect Drosophila 3D genome disruption to a specific human disease phenotype, so when architecture matters for disease cannot be assessed from these sources.

evidence_claims.claim: Breaking a chromatin gene-gene loop in Drosophila embryos led to either attenuation or enhancement of expression of related genes, and altered their relative expression levels and cross-regulation.
The function of a gene-gene loop can differ between developmental contexts even when the loop appears constitutive.
Multiple simultaneous enhancer-enhancer, enhancer-promoter and promoter-promoter interactions can work competitively or cooperatively to maintain appropriate mRNA levels.
For some long-range enhancer-promoter interactions, insulators and tethering elements are required to promote proper interactions and block aberrant ones.
Enhancer and promoter sequence composition affects transcriptional bursting dynamics, including duration, amplitude and frequency.
Modest expression effects of 3D disruption are plausibly explained by redundancy among multiple regulatory interactions and by loops acting as fine-tuning scaffolds rather than on/off switches.

Architecture is most likely to matter when a contact is non-redundant, when insulators or tethering elements are needed to prevent ectopic regulation, or when relative expression of co-regulated genes must be precisely balanced.

Drosophila chromatin is organized from histone-DNA interactions up to chromosome and lamina interactions in the nuclear space, which provides the background for how topology relates to gene regulation.
Human disease relevance of Drosophila 3D genome disruption is unverified in the supplied literature.

literature.summary: In the supplied literature, disrupting a Drosophila gene-gene loop attenuates or enhances expression and shifts relative levels, rather than abolishing expression, and loop function varies with developmental context [2]. Reviews describe multiple simultaneous regulatory interactions and insulator/tethering elements that cooperate or compete to maintain mRNA levels [3]. Redundancy and fine-tuning are therefore a plausible explanation for modest effects, but that is an inference from these sources and not a directly tested conclusion. The fourth supplied paper [4], a computational neuroscience meeting abstract, is irrelevant to this topic and was excluded.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Proposed: in Drosophila melanogaster embryos at 25°C, deleting one anchor of a gene-gene chromatin loop will change bulk mRNA of the looped genes by less than 1.5-fold, yet will raise cell-to-cell variability of nascent transcription (coefficient of variation) by at least 25% through altered burst frequency. Removing a redundant enhancer in the same background will reduce expression at least 2-fold more than expected from the product of the two single perturbations (synergy, p<0.05).
hypothesis.experimental_approach: Proposed: pick 2-3 gene-gene loops from the embryo loop set characterized in the Pollex et al. study (38157845), preferring loops where one anchor can be deleted without removing a coding or promoter sequence. Use CRISPR/Cas9 to make precise anchor deletions (ΔA) and, in a second step, deletions of a candidate redundant enhancer or shadow enhancer (ΔE) of one looped gene, giving WT, ΔA, ΔE and ΔAΔE homozygous lines. Measure bulk expression by RNA-seq and RT-qPCR in staged embryos, and nascent transcription by endogenous MS2 knock-in with MCP-GFP live imaging, quantifying burst frequency, amplitude, duration and cell-to-cell CV. Run the same ΔA comparison in at least two later tissues or stages, using smFISH or MS2, to test whether loop function is context-dependent. Controls: isogenic parental line, a size-matched deletion of non-anchor sequence next to the anchor, and Hi-C or Micro-C or 4C-seq on ΔA embryos to confirm that the loop is actually lost. Synergy is tested with a multiplicative model on log-scale expression across at least 3 biological replicates and at least 20 embryos per genotype for imaging.

hypothesis.expected_outcomes: Proposed predictions, not established results: (1) ΔA gives bulk log2 fold-change within ±0.58 (under 1.5-fold) for looped genes, with at least 80% of tested loops in that range. (2) Despite the modest mean effect, ΔA raises CV of nascent transcription by at least 25% or changes burst frequency by at least 20% relative to WT (Benjamini-Hochberg q<0.05). (3) ΔAΔE reduces expression at least 2-fold below the multiplicative expectation from ΔA and ΔE. (4) At least one loop shows a different sign or magnitude of ΔA effect between stages or tissues. Falsification: if ΔA has no significant effect on variability or burst parameters and ΔAΔE is not synergistic, the redundancy and noise-buffering account is rejected for the tested loops.
hypothesis.novelty_claim: Pollex et al. showed that breaking a gene-gene loop attenuates or enhances expression of related genes in embryos, but only three loops were dissected, so it is unknown whether the pattern generalizes. The Deng et al. review indicates that multiple simultaneous enhancer-promoter interactions can act cooperatively or competitively to maintain mRNA levels, but the supplied literature does not quantify redundancy buffering. This plan combines anchor deletion with removal of a redundant enhancer, and adds live burst-level readouts, to test whether modest bulk effects mask changes in variability.
hypothesis.feasibility_notes: Proposed timeline of about 12-15 months. Months 1-4: select loops, design guides and generate ΔA, ΔE and MS2 knock-ins. Months 5-8: build the double mutants and verify loop loss by Micro-C or 4C. Months 9-13: live imaging, RNA-seq and statistical modeling. Pitfalls: anchor deletions may remove cryptic regulatory sequence, which the adjacent-deletion control addresses. MS2 knock-ins may perturb expression, so tagged WT should be compared with untagged WT. Embryo-to-embryo variability requires adequate replication. Redundant enhancers may be hard to identify without prior mapping. Human disease relevance is not addressed by this design.
specific_aims: Aim 1: Quantify bulk effects of loop anchor loss. Delete one anchor at 2-3 embryonic gene-gene loops, confirm loop loss by Micro-C or 4C, and measure bulk mRNA changes in the looped genes (prediction: under 1.5-fold).

Aim 2: Test whether modest mean changes hide altered transcriptional dynamics. Use endogenous MS2 live imaging to compare burst frequency, amplitude, duration and cell-to-cell CV between WT and ΔA embryos.
Aim 3: Test redundancy buffering and context dependence. Combine ΔA with deletion of a redundant enhancer to test for synergy, and compare ΔA effects across at least two stages or tissues.

literature.disease_context: Disruptions to 3D genome architecture underlie a range of human developmental disorders and cancers, often by rewiring enhancer-promoter contacts or TAD boundaries. Understanding when such disruptions are consequential versus buffered is essential for interpreting non-coding mutations found in patient genomes. Drosophila offers a tractable system to dissect these mechanisms due to its well-characterized regulatory landscape.

key_papers.authors: Llorens-Giralt P, Camilleri-Robles C, Corominas M et al.
key_papers.relevance: Provides a comprehensive review of multi-scale chromatin organization in Drosophila, from histone-DNA interactions to chromosome-lamina contacts, establishing the structural framework within which gene expression regulation operates.
