key_papers.authors: Pollex T, Marco-Ferreres R, Ciglar L et al.
key_papers.relevance: Demonstrates experimentally that chromatin loops between paralogous gene pairs fine-tune co-regulation and that loop disruption produces context-dependent, sometimes subtle, changes in expression—directly addressing why 3D structure perturbations often have modest effects.

key_papers.title: Unveiling dynamic enhancer-promoter interactions in Drosophila melanogaster.
key_papers.authors: Deng H, Jin G, Lim B et al.
key_papers.relevance: Reviews how multiple simultaneous enhancer-enhancer, enhancer-promoter, and promoter-promoter interactions work cooperatively or competitively, explaining how redundancy in the regulatory architecture can buffer single perturbations of 3D contacts.

identified_gaps: The provided literature does not resolve which molecular features (e.g., specific insulator proteins, tethering element sequences, or promoter identity) determine whether a loop disruption is buffered vs. consequential — this distinction is critical for predicting the phenotypic impact of non-coding variants.

Although [2] shows that loops can be 'constitutive' yet functionally context-dependent, the molecular logic governing how the same architectural scaffold is repurposed in different developmental contexts remains undefined.

The role of nuclear lamina interactions in buffering or amplifying effects of chromatin topology perturbations on gene expression is mentioned in [1] but not experimentally dissected in the provided literature.

How transcriptional bursting dynamics (duration, amplitude, frequency) are specifically altered when 3D contacts are disrupted — as opposed to average steady-state mRNA levels — is reviewed in [3] but not experimentally resolved for loop perturbation experiments.

evidence_claims.claim: Eukaryotic genomes are packaged into high-order chromatin structures organized in discrete territories inside the cell nucleus, which is surrounded by the nuclear envelope acting as a barrier.

Chromatin organization is complex and dynamic and, thus, determining the spatial and temporal distribution and folding of chromosomes within the nucleus is critical for understanding the role of chromatin topology in genome function.
Breaking the loop leads to either an attenuation or enhancement of expression and perturbs their relative levels of expression and cross-regulation.
Although many loops appear constitutive across embryogenesis, their function can change in different developmental contexts.

Chromatin gene-gene loops act as architectural scaffolds that can be used in different ways in different contexts to fine-tune the coordinated expression of genes with related functions and sustain their cross-regulation.

By mutating the loop anchor (but not the gene) or the gene (but not loop anchor), [the authors] disentangle loop formation and gene expression and show that the 3D proximity of paralogous gene loci supports their co-regulation.
Proper enhancer-promoter interactions are essential to maintaining specific transcriptional patterns and preventing ectopic gene expression.
3D chromatin topology is also important for proper enhancer-promoter contacts.

By working competitively or cooperatively with one another, multiple, simultaneous enhancer-enhancer, enhancer-promoter, and promoter-promoter interactions often occur to maintain appropriate levels of mRNAs.
For some long-range enhancer-promoter interactions, extra regulatory elements like insulators and tethering elements are required to promote proper interactions while blocking aberrant ones.
At a DNA level, compositions of both enhancer and promoter sequences affect transcriptional dynamics, including duration, amplitude, and frequency of transcriptional bursting.

The redundancy of multiple simultaneous regulatory contacts (enhancer-enhancer, enhancer-promoter, promoter-promoter) can buffer single perturbations of 3D genome structure, explaining why disruptions often have modest effects on gene expression.

Loops become functionally consequential when they mediate fine-tuning of co-regulated paralogous genes, particularly in specific developmental contexts where alternative regulatory redundancy is unavailable.

literature.summary: In Drosophila, 3D genome organization operates across multiple scales — from local enhancer-promoter loops to chromosome-wide lamina interactions [1] — and disrupting individual structural elements often produces modest transcriptional effects because multiple simultaneous enhancer-enhancer, enhancer-promoter, and promoter-promoter contacts act cooperatively or redundantly to buffer single perturbations [3]. However, 3D structure becomes functionally consequential when it mediates fine-tuned co-regulation, as demonstrated by gene-gene chromatin loops between paralogues whose disruption quantitatively alters expression levels and cross-regulation in a context-dependent manner [2]. The emerging picture is that architectural features of chromatin act as scaffolds that matter most when developmental precision in relative gene dosage is required, and when the redundant regulatory network cannot compensate.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Disrupting the CTCF/cohesin-anchored chromatin loop between the paralogous Abd-B and Ubx Hox gene loci in Drosophila melanogaster will produce gene expression changes (≥1.5-fold in at least one paralog) only in developmental contexts (stage 10–14 embryo abdominal segments) where a single non-redundant loop mediates cross-regulation, whereas in larval wing disc tissue where redundant enhancer contacts exist, disruption will produce <20% change in steady-state mRNA levels; furthermore, transcriptional bursting frequency (not amplitude) will be the primary parameter altered upon loop disruption, detectable by single-molecule fluorescence in situ hybridization (smFISH) as a ≥25% reduction in the fraction of actively transcribing nuclei in affected segments at 25°C.
hypothesis.experimental_approach: We will use CRISPR-Cas9 to delete or invert the loop anchor sequences (tethering element/insulator sequences) between Abd-B and Ubx without altering coding or known enhancer sequences, generating anchor-mutant fly lines verified by 4C-seq or Hi-C to confirm loop disruption. GAL4/UAS-based tissue-specific expression of a dCas9-KRAB transcriptional repressor fused to guide RNAs targeting loop anchor sequences will provide an orthogonal, reversible approach to test loop disruption in specific tissues (abdominal neuroblasts via elav-GAL4, wing disc cells via nub-GAL4, and fat body via Lsp2-GAL4 as a non-expressing control). Quantitative RT-qPCR and smFISH with intronic probes will measure both steady-state mRNA levels and transcriptional bursting parameters (burst frequency, amplitude, and duration) in dissected tissues from stage 10–14 embryos and third-instar larval wing discs. Controls will include isogenic w1118 flies, loop-anchor-intact CRISPR lines with synonymous edits, and GAL4 lines without UAS-dCas9-KRAB to account for GAL4 toxicity. 4C-seq from Abd-B and Ubx viewpoints will confirm loop loss in each tissue context.

hypothesis.expected_outcomes: In stage 10–14 embryonic abdominal segments (A5–A8), loop-anchor deletion will reduce Abd-B mRNA levels by ≥1.5-fold and alter Ubx expression by ≥1.5-fold relative to w1118 controls (p<0.05, Mann-Whitney U, n≥20 embryos per genotype), with smFISH revealing ≥25% reduction in burst frequency (fraction of nuclei with nascent transcript foci) but <25% change in burst amplitude (foci intensity per transcribing nucleus). In third-instar larval wing discs (nub-GAL4 territory), the same loop disruption will produce <20% change in Abd-B or Ubx mRNA levels by RT-qPCR (not significant at p>0.05), consistent with regulatory redundancy buffering the perturbation. 4C-seq will confirm ≥50% reduction in inter-locus contact frequency at the anchor in mutant versus control lines. The synonymous-edit control lines and Lsp2-GAL4-driven dCas9-KRAB lines will show no significant expression changes in any tissue (p>0.05), validating specificity.
hypothesis.novelty_claim: This experiment directly addresses three unresolved gaps identified in the literature synthesis: (1) it tests which molecular features — specifically insulator/tethering element sequences at loop anchors — determine whether loop disruption is buffered versus consequential, a distinction explicitly flagged as unresolved; (2) it dissects the developmental-context dependence of a constitutive loop's function by comparing embryonic versus larval disc tissues using the same genetic perturbation, addressing the gap that 'the molecular logic governing how the same architectural scaffold is repurposed in different developmental contexts remains undefined'; and (3) it resolves how transcriptional bursting dynamics (frequency, amplitude, duration) are specifically altered by loop disruption rather than measuring only steady-state mRNA, addressing the gap that bursting parameters 'are reviewed but not experimentally resolved for loop perturbation experiments.' No prior study has simultaneously measured bursting parameters and steady-state expression across multiple developmental tissue contexts for the same loop disruption in Drosophila.
hypothesis.feasibility_notes: CRISPR-Cas9 deletions in Drosophila are routine and achievable within 4–6 months including line establishment and 4C-seq validation. smFISH on Drosophila embryos and larval discs is technically established and compatible with intronic nascent-transcript probes for bursting analysis; the primary challenge is designing probes that distinguish Abd-B and Ubx transcripts given paralogy — this requires careful probe design and validation (~2 months). The dCas9-KRAB approach depends on achieving sufficient repression of the anchor without off-target effects, which may require optimization of sgRNA design and validation by ChIP-seq for KRAB occupancy (~3 months). A potential pitfall is that the loop anchor may overlap with cryptic enhancer sequences not annotated in current databases, making it difficult to separate loop disruption from enhancer disruption — this is mitigated by the synonymous-edit control and by restricting deletions to CTCF motif cores identified by existing ChIP-seq data. Total estimated timeline: 18–24 months from line generation to final analysis. Budget consideration: 4C-seq from multiple viewpoints and tissues represents the largest cost (~$2,000–4,000 per sample). Statistical power analysis: n=20 embryos per genotype provides >80% power to detect a 1.5-fold mRNA difference assuming CV=30% based on published Drosophila smFISH datasets.
specific_aims: Aim 1: Loop anchor deletion — Generate and validate CRISPR-Cas9 lines carrying precise deletion of the Abd-B/Ubx inter-locus tethering element and confirm loop disruption by 4C-seq in embryonic and larval tissues without altering flanking gene or enhancer sequences

Aim 2: Context-dependent expression consequences — Quantify steady-state Abd-B and Ubx mRNA levels by RT-qPCR in stage 10–14 embryonic abdominal segments versus third-instar larval wing discs in loop-anchor deletion versus control lines to test whether expression effects are tissue-context-dependent (≥1.5-fold in embryo, <20% in disc)

Aim 3: Transcriptional bursting dynamics — Use smFISH with intronic probes in stage 12 embryonic abdominal segments to decompose any expression change into burst frequency, amplitude, and duration components, testing the prediction that burst frequency is preferentially reduced (≥25%) while amplitude is preserved (<25% change) upon loop disruption

The relative contributions of MSL-dependent and derepression-based non-canonical compensation [10] on the same X genes, and whether these mechanisms are redundant or additive when MSL targeting fails.

Why ectopic MSL complex on female X chromosomes reduces viability [4]: whether through over-hyperactivation of a two-X dose or off-target binding. Quantitative expression profiling in msl-2-expressing females would resolve this.

literature.summary: X targeting appears to involve MRE recognition by the MSL2 CXC domain for nucleation [12], followed by roX RNA- and acetylation-influenced spreading to active genes [1][6]. Partial or ectopic targeting has consequences: inappropriate MSL assembly on female X reduces viability [4], MSL abundance may tune compensation across tissues [5], and repressive-domain genes can be compensated without MSL occupancy [10]. Quantitative consequences of intermediate targeting remain largely untested.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Proposed: Reducing MSL2 to about 50% of wild-type level in male third-instar larvae will cause non-uniform loss of MSL3 occupancy on the X. Occupancy at high-affinity MRE-rich entry sites will fall by ≤15%, and occupancy at weakly bound, MRE-poor active genes will fall by ≥40%. The X-to-autosome expression ratio of active genes that lose occupancy will fall by ≥10%. X-linked genes in repressive chromatin domains will stay within 5% of control expression.
hypothesis.experimental_approach: Graded msl-2 knockdown will be produced in males with a ubiquitous GAL4 driving a UAS-msl-2 RNAi construct, titrated by rearing temperature (18, 25 and 29°C). Knockdown will be calibrated by qPCR and western blot to about 75%, 50% and 25% of control MSL2 (proposed, requires verification). MSL3 (or MSL1) and H4K16ac occupancy will be profiled by ChIP-seq or CUT&Tag with an exogenous spike-in for absolute normalization. Occupancy changes will be compared between entry sites (MRE-rich), weak/spreading-dependent active genes, and genes in repressive domains defined from published Hi-C/TAD annotations. Expression will be measured by RNA-seq with ERCC spike-ins in 3 biological replicates per condition. Controls are an RNAi against an unrelated gene (e.g., mCherry) and a driver-only line, plus females as a negative control for MSL binding. As a complementary test of the rheostat model, graded UAS-msl-2 expression lacking its 3' UTR will be driven in females (proposed) to define the dose-response of X occupancy, roX dependence and viability.

identified_gaps: The precise biochemical mechanism by which the MSL complex spreads from high-affinity MRE nucleation sites to active genes sequence-independently remains incompletely defined — knowing whether spreading is driven by transcription-coupled chromatin states, RNA Pol II pausing, or roX RNA bridging would clarify how targeting fidelity is maintained across the entire X.

The extent and molecular basis of tissue-specific variation in MSL complex activity (the 'rheostat' model) is supported only by correlational expression data [5]; direct functional manipulation of MSL-2 levels in specific tissues to test whether compensation scales proportionally is lacking.

How non-canonical dosage compensation (derepression of X-linked genes in repressive chromatin domains without MSL occupancy) is mechanistically achieved at the molecular level is unknown [10] — identifying the trans-acting factors responsible would clarify whether this represents a passive or actively regulated process.

Why CRISPR knockout of Anopheles msl-2 causes lethality in both sexes without X chromosome dosage compensation effects [11] raises the question of what the ancestral MSL pathway function was before it was co-opted for dosage compensation in Drosophila — addressing this could reveal constraints on the evolutionary origin of chromosome-wide targeting.

The interplay between MSL-3 acetylation status (controlled by MOF and RPD3) and roX RNA binding [1] as a dynamic regulatory mechanism for spreading has been proposed but not tested in vivo with temporal resolution — determining whether acetylation cycles drive stepwise spreading or merely modulate complex stability remains an open question.

literature.summary: The Drosophila dosage compensation complex (MSL complex) achieves X chromosome specificity through a two-step mechanism: the CXC domain of MSL2 first recognizes high-affinity MSL recognition elements (MREs) on the X via sequence-specific minor groove contacts [25452275], followed by sequence-independent spreading to active genes facilitated by roX noncoding RNAs and regulated by MOF-mediated acetylation of MSL-3 [12769850, 25934013]. Sex-specificity is enforced at the translational level through SXL-mediated repression of msl-2 mRNA in females, involving co-factors Hrp48 and eIF3d [29635389, 7781064]. When MSL targeting is partial — as seen in repressive chromatin domains with low MSL occupancy — dosage compensation can still occur through a non-canonical derepression mechanism analogous to autosomal hemizygous gene derepression, and MSL complex abundance appears to act as a quantitative rheostat tuning compensation levels across tissues [30355339, 25737812].

hypothesis.hypothesis: The MOF-mediated acetylation cycle of MSL-3 (acetylation by MOF, deacetylation by RPD3) drives stepwise spreading of the MSL complex from MRE nucleation sites to active X-linked genes in a temporally ordered manner; specifically, expression of an acetylation-mimetic MSL-3 (K→Q substitution at the MOF target lysine) will increase MSL complex spreading to ectopic autosomal loci by ≥2-fold relative to wild-type MSL-3, while an acetylation-dead MSL-3 (K→R substitution) will reduce spreading to distal X-linked genes (>50 kb from the nearest MRE) by ≥50% compared to wild-type controls, as measured by ChIP-seq occupancy of MSL-2 and H4K16ac in adult male w1118 flies at 25°C under standard conditions.
hypothesis.experimental_approach: We will use the GAL4/UAS system to express UAS-msl-3[WT], UAS-msl-3[K→Q] (acetylation-mimetic), and UAS-msl-3[K→R] (acetylation-dead) transgenes in an msl-3 null background using the ubiquitous da-GAL4 driver, allowing controlled replacement of endogenous MSL-3 with defined acetylation-state variants. ChIP-seq with anti-MSL-2, anti-MSL-3, and anti-H4K16ac antibodies will map complex occupancy genome-wide in adult males of each genotype, comparing binding at MRE-proximal (<10 kb), intermediate (10–50 kb), and distal (>50 kb) X-linked loci, and on autosomes. roX RNA co-immunoprecipitation (RIP) assays will quantify the MSL-3 variant interaction with roX1 and roX2, directly testing whether acetylation status controls roX RNA binding as proposed. RNA-seq on the same genotypes will assess X-linked gene expression levels and dosage compensation ratios (X:autosome expression) to link spreading defects to functional compensation outcomes. Controls include w1118 males (wild-type), msl-3 null males rescued with UAS-msl-3[WT] (positive), and unrescued msl-3 null males (negative lethality control confirming null phenotype).

ChIP-seq: In UAS-msl-3[K→Q] males, MSL-2 and H4K16ac occupancy at autosomal loci will increase ≥2-fold over wild-type, and X-linked loci >50 kb from MREs will show ≥1.5-fold increased occupancy; in UAS-msl-3[K→R] males, MSL-2 occupancy at MRE-distal X loci will decrease ≥50% relative to UAS-msl-3[WT] rescue while MRE-proximal occupancy is maintained (≤20% reduction), demonstrating that acetylation is specifically required for spreading rather than nucleation. 2. RIP assay: MSL-3[K→Q] will co-immunoprecipitate ≥2-fold more roX1/roX2 RNA than MSL-3[K→R], confirming that acetylation status controls roX RNA binding in vivo. 3. RNA-seq: UAS-msl-3[K→R] males will show a reduced X:autosome expression ratio (falling from the expected ~1.0 in males toward ~0.5) specifically for genes >50 kb from MREs (predicted ≥30% reduction in compensation index at distal loci), with statistical significance at FDR < 0.05. 4. rpd3 RNAi males will phenocopy UAS-msl-3[K→Q] spreading patterns, providing independent validation. 5. Viability assays: UAS-msl-3[K→R] males in an msl-3 null background will show reduced eclosion rates relative to UAS-msl-3[WT] rescue (predicted ≥50% reduction), reflecting incomplete dosage compensation.
hypothesis.novelty_claim: This experiment directly addresses the identified gap that 'the interplay between MSL-3 acetylation status (controlled by MOF and RPD3) and roX RNA binding as a dynamic regulatory mechanism for spreading has been proposed but not tested in vivo with temporal resolution' and that 'whether acetylation cycles drive stepwise spreading or merely modulate complex stability remains an open question.' Prior work established that MOF acetylates MSL-3, that RPD3 can deacetylate it, and that acetylation status correlates with roX2 binding in vitro, but no study has used separation-of-function acetylation-mimetic and acetylation-dead MSL-3 transgenes to dissect the spatial consequence of acetylation state on genome-wide MSL spreading versus MRE nucleation in vivo. hypothesis.feasibility_notes: All molecular biology tools (site-directed mutagenesis, pUAST-attB injection, ChIP-seq, RIP, RNA-seq) are standard in Drosophila chromatin biology labs. identified_gaps: Whether reduced protein synthesis via Xrp1–eIF2α phosphorylation is the measured fitness parameter itself or a downstream consequence of loser status is unresolved. The supplied abstracts report it as a common loser feature [2] but do not show that equalizing translation rates abolishes competition across all loser types.

The relationship between the Toll/Rel loser-elimination program in the testis [1] and the Xrp1/eIF2α translation-reduction program [2] is untested in these papers. Epistasis between Rel and Xrp1 in cyst stem cell competition and in imaginal discs would show whether they form one sensing axis or parallel ones.
The ligand or cue that activates Toll in testis loser cells is not identified [1]. Without it, it remains unclear whether losers sense neighbors directly or sense reduced niche signal transduction.

How cell identity and cell affinity differences gate the winner/loser interaction is undefined. In ph mutant tissue, competition operates in both directions and is incomplete [4]; defining which surface or affinity molecules are required for neighbors to compare fitness would distinguish relative-fitness sensing from identity mismatch.

How loser cells are sensed in non-epithelial stem cell niches, where loss means displacement and differentiation rather than apoptosis [1][3], compared with epithelial polarity-defective losers [6] has not been mechanistically compared in the supplied literature.

identified_gaps: No supplied paper defines a single measurable 'fitness' variable. Candidates are protein synthesis rate, polarity integrity, niche signal transduction, adhesion and cell identity. Whether these are distinct readouts or converge on one (e.g. eIF2α phosphorylation) is untested, and quantitative cross-context comparison of clones would be needed to resolve it.

How a loser cell senses the relative difference, rather than its own defect, is unresolved in the supplied literature. Cell-autonomous stress responses (Xrp1/eIF2α) are described [2], but how a comparison with neighbours is encoded and transmitted is not shown. Testing whether Xrp1 activation depends on the presence of wild-type neighbours would address this.

literature.summary: The supplied literature defines cell fitness operationally and relatively: cells that are less fit than their neighbours are eliminated, and no single molecular measure is established [6]. Candidate readouts include reduced protein synthesis through Xrp1-driven eIF2α phosphorylation [2], Toll/Rel signaling in testis stem cell competition [1], polarity module integrity [6], and cell identity/affinity with apoptotic competence [4]. How losers sense a relative disadvantage, and whether these mechanisms are unified, remains unresolved.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Proposed: In the adult Drosophila testis, clonal activation of Rel in germline stem cells (GSCs) lowers the clone's relative protein synthesis (OPP incorporation) by at least 25% compared with neighbouring wild-type GSCs at 7 days after clone induction. This reduction depends on Xrp1 and on the presence of wild-type neighbours. Xrp1 knockdown in Rel-activated clones is predicted to at least double their GSC clone retention at 14 days after clone induction relative to Rel-activated clones with control RNAi. Activating Rel in all germline cells at the same level is predicted to reduce OPP signal by less than 10% relative to controls (p<0.05 thresholds, 25°C).
hypothesis.experimental_approach: Use FLP-out (hs-flp) clonal induction in adult males to create marked GSC clones that express a constitutively active Rel, with or without Xrp1 RNAi, and compare them with neutral marked clones. Measure relative translation by ex vivo OPP incorporation and anti-phospho-eIF2α staining, and measure Xrp1 induction with an Xrp1 reporter, comparing clone to adjacent GSCs within the same niche. Measure clone retention at the niche (hub-contacting GSC clones per testis) at 2, 7 and 14 days after clone induction. To test neighbour dependence, use a temporally controlled germline-wide driver (nos-GAL4 with tub-GAL80ts) to activate Rel in all germline cells and quantify OPP, p-eIF2α and Xrp1 reporter, then compare with the mosaic condition. Controls are neutral FLP-out clones, a non-targeting or mCherry RNAi, a Toll/Rel loss-of-function rescue check, and a GADD34-type eIF2α-phosphatase epistasis arm if a suitable line is verified.

hypothesis.expected_outcomes: Proposed predictions: (1) Rel-activated GSC clones show at least 25% lower OPP signal than neighbouring GSCs, higher p-eIF2α and higher Xrp1 reporter signal, with n of at least 60 niches per genotype and p<0.05 by Mann-Whitney test. (2) Xrp1 RNAi restores OPP to within 10% of neighbours and at least doubles clone retention at 14 days after clone induction, compared with control RNAi. (3) Germline-wide Rel activation causes a smaller (<10%) OPP reduction than the mosaic condition, which would support relative sensing. Falsification: if OPP is unchanged in Rel clones, or Xrp1 knockdown does not alter retention, Rel and Xrp1 act in parallel rather than convergently. If germline-wide Rel activation reduces OPP as strongly as mosaic activation, the effect is cell-autonomous stress rather than relative sensing.
hypothesis.novelty_claim: No supplied paper defines a single measurable fitness variable, and the relationship between Rel/Toll-driven loser elimination in the testis and Xrp1/eIF2α-driven protein synthesis reduction is unknown. This plan tests directly whether Rel activation reduces translation through Xrp1, and whether this depends on wild-type neighbours, which addresses two gaps in the synthesis: convergence of loser pathways and how relative difference is sensed. It also asks whether Rel displaces neutral cells by lowering a fitness-like state (translation) rather than by altering niche adhesion directly.
hypothesis.feasibility_notes: Estimated timeline is 10-14 months: 2-3 months for line verification, construction and validation of Xrp1 RNAi and reporters; 4-5 months for mosaic OPP, p-eIF2α and retention time courses; 3-4 months for germline-wide and epistasis experiments and for analysis. Pitfalls: OPP incorporation in small GSCs gives noisy signal, so normalising each clone to adjacent GSCs in the same niche is needed. Xrp1 RNAi may have off-target effects, so a second independent RNAi or mutant allele should be used. Rel activation may also change niche adhesion independently of translation, so a retention effect alone cannot distinguish the two. Heat-shock clone induction may affect germline health, so no-heat-shock controls are included. The testis-specific role of Xrp1 is not established in the supplied literature and may be absent, which would itself be informative.

literature.disease_context: Cell competition is increasingly recognized as a tumor-suppressive mechanism that eliminates oncogenic or otherwise aberrant cells; however, certain mutations (e.g., in polyhomeotic) can render cells refractory to elimination, allowing tumorous overgrowths to persist [4]. Conversely, competitive dynamics can be co-opted by cancer cells to promote clonal expansion, as seen in clonal hematopoiesis and intestinal 'supercompetitors' [3,5]. Understanding the molecular sensors that distinguish winners from losers—particularly the roles of eIF2α-mediated translational suppression and NF-κB signaling—may reveal therapeutic targets for cancers driven by aberrant clonal selection [2,5].

identified_gaps: The precise molecular sensor that detects relative fitness differences between neighboring cells remains unresolved — it is unclear whether cells measure absolute levels of signaling/protein synthesis or directly compare rates with neighbors through juxtacrine communication, and which upstream inputs trigger eIF2α phosphorylation in each competition context [2].

How loser-fate signals are transmitted non-cell-autonomously to induce elimination is unclear: in the ph mutant model, wild-type cells are also eliminated when surrounded by ph-deficient cells [4], but the identity of the signal(s) from ph mutant cells that redefines neighbor fitness is unknown.

The relationship between the NF-κB/Toll pathway (identified in testis stem cell competition [1]) and the eIF2α/Xrp1 translational stress pathway (identified in epithelial competition [2]) has not been established — it is unknown whether these are parallel, convergent, or context-specific mechanisms for loser sensing.

The threshold at which reduced protein synthesis transitions a cell from 'stressed-but-viable' to committed loser has not been quantitatively defined, making it unclear what magnitude of fitness difference is required to trigger competitive elimination [2].

Whether the partial refractoriness to apoptosis seen in ph mutant losers reflects a general escape mechanism available to oncogenic clones, and which anti-apoptotic factors are responsible, has not been fully characterized [4].

literature.summary: Cell competition measures relative fitness primarily through two identified molecular axes: translational output (with loser cells across multiple contexts showing reduced protein synthesis via eIF2α phosphorylation downstream of the bZIP factor Xrp1 [2]) and niche-signal transduction capacity (with stem cells unable to transduce niche signals being eliminated via differentiation [1,3]). Loser cells sense their status and are eliminated through NF-κB/Toll-Relish signaling in the testis niche [1] and through polarity-complex integrity in epithelial tissues [6], though how these pathways converge or interact remains unresolved. Escape from competitive elimination—as seen in ph-mutant cells that are partially refractory to apoptosis and can paradoxically drive neighbors to become losers [4]—highlights how disruption of normal fitness-sensing machinery underlies oncogenic progression [5].

hypothesis.hypothesis: In Drosophila melanogaster wing imaginal disc epithelial cell competition, Xrp1-mediated eIF2α phosphorylation and NF-κB/Relish activation represent two parallel, non-redundant loser-sensing axes that converge to trigger apoptotic elimination: knocking out both Xrp1 and Rel simultaneously in Minute heterozygous (M/+) loser clones will rescue loser-cell survival by ≥60% compared to single knockouts (each of which rescues ≤35%), as measured by clone area ratio (loser/winner) in third-instar wing discs at 25°C, with statistical significance at p < 0.01 (ANOVA with post-hoc Tukey correction, n ≥ 15 discs per genotype).
hypothesis.experimental_approach: We will use the MARCM (Mosaic Analysis with a Repressible Cell Marker) system combined with the GAL4/UAS system to generate GFP-marked clones homozygous for a Minute mutation (RpS17, a ribosomal protein gene haploinsufficiency that generates canonical losers) in the wing imaginal disc, while simultaneously depleting Xrp1, Rel, or both via UAS-RNAi transgenes driven by act-GAL4 within the clone. Clone induction will be performed by heat-shock FLP recombinase at 48–72 h AEL, and discs will be dissected from wandering third-instar larvae (~120 h AEL). Primary readouts will be: (1) clone area ratio (GFP+ loser clone area / GFP− winner area) by confocal microscopy and ImageJ quantification; (2) apoptotic index within loser clones by anti-cleaved Dcp-1 immunostaining; (3) phospho-eIF2α (Ser51) levels by immunofluorescence; and (4) Rel nuclear translocation as a proxy for NF-κB activation. Controls will include: wild-type clones (no Minute), single-knockdown clones (Xrp1-RNAi only; Rel-RNAi only), and RNAi-only clones without the Minute background. Epistasis will be assessed by comparing the double-knockdown rescue magnitude to expected additive rescue under independence.

hypothesis.expected_outcomes: If the hypothesis is correct: (1) Single Xrp1-RNAi in Minute clones will rescue clone area ratio by 20–35% relative to Minute alone (p < 0.05), and reduce phospho-eIF2α immunostaining intensity by ≥50% within clones; (2) Single Rel-RNAi in Minute clones will rescue clone area ratio by 20–35% (p < 0.05) and reduce Dcp-1+ apoptotic cells by ≥40%; (3) Double Xrp1-RNAi + Rel-RNAi in Minute clones will rescue clone area ratio by ≥60% (p < 0.01) and reduce Dcp-1+ apoptotic index by ≥70%, exceeding the additive expectation of two independent partial rescues, indicating convergence on the same elimination program. If the two pathways are fully redundant (alternative outcome), double knockdown rescue will equal the sum of single rescues (~60–70%), with no synergistic effect. If they are fully independent of apoptosis, neither rescue will affect Dcp-1 staining. Statistical analysis: one-way ANOVA with Tukey post-hoc correction; minimum n = 15 wing discs per genotype; experiments repeated ≥3 independent biological replicates.
hypothesis.novelty_claim: The identified gap states that 'the relationship between the NF-κB/Toll pathway (identified in testis stem cell competition) and the eIF2α/Xrp1 translational stress pathway (identified in epithelial competition) has not been established — it is unknown whether these are parallel, convergent, or context-specific mechanisms for loser sensing.' This experiment directly addresses that gap by: (1) testing both pathways simultaneously in the same tissue (wing imaginal disc epithelium) using the same canonical loser model (Minute), which has not previously been done; (2) providing the first quantitative epistasis analysis between these two molecular axes; and (3) defining whether convergence or independence determines the apoptotic threshold for loser elimination, addressing the further gap that 'the threshold at which reduced protein synthesis transitions a cell from stressed-but-viable to committed loser has not been quantitatively defined.'
hypothesis.feasibility_notes: MARCM-based epithelial competition experiments are well-established in the Drosophila field, and the Minute/+ loser system is a gold-standard model. RNAi knockdown efficiency in imaginal disc clones using act-GAL4 within MARCM is routinely achievable. Key potential pitfalls include: (1) incomplete knockdown by single RNAi lines, which will be mitigated by validating knockdown efficiency via immunostaining and/or RT-qPCR on sorted GFP+ cells; (2) the Rel-RNAi phenotype may be subtle in epithelial (non-stem-cell) tissue if Rel plays a minor role outside the testis niche, which would itself be an informative result; (3) generating the double-UAS recombinant may require 2–3 months of fly genetics. Antibodies for phospho-eIF2α (Ser51; Cell Signaling Technology) and cleaved Dcp-1 (Cell Signaling Technology) are commercially available and validated in Drosophila. Estimated timeline: 3 months for line generation and validation, 4 months for main experiments, 2 months for analysis and repetition — total approximately 9 months. No specialized equipment beyond standard confocal microscopy is required.
specific_aims: Aim 1: Pathway Independence Assessment — Determine whether Xrp1-RNAi and Rel-RNAi each independently and partially rescue Minute loser-clone survival in wing imaginal discs, establishing individual contributions of each axis to loser elimination

Aim 2: Convergence Epistasis Test — Quantify whether simultaneous double knockdown of Xrp1 and Rel in Minute loser clones produces rescue of clone survival greater than additive single-knockdown effects, distinguishing parallel-convergent from fully redundant pathway architectures

Aim 3: Apoptotic Commitment Threshold — Define the relationship between phospho-eIF2α levels, Rel nuclear localization, and Dcp-1-marked apoptotic commitment within individual loser clones across genotypes, to determine whether the two axes must both be active to cross the apoptotic elimination threshold

literature.summary: Drosophila epithelial polarity is maintained by mutual antagonism between apical (Crb, aPKC, Par-6) and basolateral (Scrib, Dlg, Lgl) modules, and Scrib/Dlg also contribute to polarity initiation through adherens junction positioning [3][9]. Polarity regulators are tightly linked to growth control and cell competition, but polarity mechanisms differ between epithelia, as in the midgut [6][10]. The supplied literature gives little direct evidence on how polarity is maintained through rapid successive divisions, which remains an open question (inference).

hypothesis.hypothesis: Proposed (not established): In the larval wing disc pouch, acute (24 h) tub-GAL80ts-controlled scrib knockdown will raise the fraction of cytokinesis events with delayed apical E-cadherin junction re-establishment (>20 min after completion of furrow ingression) from an assumed control level of ≤10% to ≥30%, and this defect will precede detectable basolateral aPKC mislocalization in non-dividing cells; CycE overexpression will increase the frequency of delayed junction re-establishment by ≥1.5-fold relative to scrib knockdown alone (25-29°C, mixed-sex wandering third-instar larvae, n≥150 divisions from ≥8 discs per genotype).
hypothesis.experimental_approach: Background premise: Scrib and Dlg direct initial assembly and positioning of adherens junctions during polarity establishment, which suggests that they may also be needed to re-assemble junctions after each division. Proposed approach: use nub-GAL4 with tub-GAL80ts to drive scrib RNAi in the wing pouch in a temporally restricted way (shift to the restrictive temperature for 24 h before imaging). Live ex vivo disc imaging with endogenously tagged E-cadherin and Crb reporters will score the timing of junction re-establishment, apical Crb restoration and aPKC localization for each cytokinesis event. Division rate will be raised by co-expressing UAS-CycE. Controls are a non-targeting RNAi (e.g., UAS-mCherry RNAi or UAS-lacZ), a second independent scrib RNAi or a scrib allele to exclude off-target effects, GAL80ts-permissive (18°C) discs, and fixed-tissue staining for Dlg, aPKC and cleaved Dcp-1 to separate polarity defects from apoptosis and cell competition. Both the scrib RNAi/CycE and non-dividing-cell comparisons will be analyzed with blinded scoring and mixed-effects statistics (disc as random factor, p<0.05).

hypothesis.expected_outcomes: Predicted (proposed): control discs restore E-cadherin junctions within ~20 min in ≥90% of divisions. Acute scrib knockdown is predicted to increase delayed re-establishment to ≥30% of divisions, with transient mislocalization of Crb or aPKC in daughter cells, while neighboring non-dividing cells keep normal apical-basal polarity at 24 h. Adding CycE overexpression is predicted to raise the frequency of delayed re-establishment ≥1.5-fold above scrib RNAi alone and to increase the fraction of discs showing basolateral aPKC at 48 h. If delayed re-establishment stays ≤15% in scrib knockdown and CycE has no effect (two-sided p>0.05, power 0.8 for the stated effect), the hypothesis is rejected. Integrin knockdown in the scrib background is predicted to increase delays further if integrin-based adhesion compensates.
hypothesis.novelty_claim: The synthesis identifies this gap: No supplied paper directly measures polarity protein turnover, trafficking or localization dynamics across successive rapid cell divisions in growing imaginal discs. It also notes that coupling of Scrib-dependent spindle orientation and tricellular junction formation to junction remodeling after division is undefined. The proposal tests this at single-division resolution with acute, stage-restricted loss of function, which also helps separate polarity initiation from maintenance (the dlg-1 discs of Abbott et al. initially retained polarity yet overgrew, while later work places Scrib/Dlg in polarity initiation).

specific_aims: Aim 1: Junction re-assembly kinetics — quantify timing of E-cadherin and Crb restoration after cytokinesis in control versus acute scrib-depleted wing pouch cells using live imaging.

Aim 2: Proliferative load dependence — test whether CycE-driven increase in division rate enhances junction re-assembly delays and basolateral aPKC mislocalization in scrib-depleted tissue, with apoptosis and JNK activity monitored.

Aim 3: Compensation by integrin adhesion — test whether knockdown of an integrin subunit in scrib-depleted pouch cells worsens re-assembly delays, probing a secondary polarity pathway in proliferating epithelia.

literature.disease_context: Loss of apical-basal polarity is a hallmark of epithelial cancers, and the Scrib/Dlg/Lgl module was originally identified as neoplastic tumor suppressors in Drosophila whose disruption leads to tumorigenesis in mammalian epithelia and is associated with human cancers [1][3][12]. The Dlg protein is homologous to vertebrate ZO-1 and ZO-2, suggesting that tight junction-associated proteins may act as tumor suppressors in humans [13], while fat mutations demonstrate that cadherin-related molecules also couple cell-cell adhesion to growth control [13]. Understanding the molecular mechanisms that maintain polarity during rapid epithelial proliferation therefore directly informs how polarity factor dysfunction drives malignant transformation and may reveal therapeutic targets for epithelial cancers [12][15].
identified_gaps: It remains unknown how apical-basal polarity complexes are dynamically re-established on daughter cells immediately after cytokinesis during rapid epithelial proliferation — the molecular sequence linking mitotic exit to polarity complex reassembly is not defined in the provided literature.

The alternative polarity mechanism identified in the Drosophila midgut (integrin-dependent, canonical-factor-independent) has not been characterized in the context of rapid stem-cell-driven proliferation, leaving open how intestinal progenitors polarize de novo after each division [6].

While Scrib/Dlg are shown to direct adherens junction positioning during polarity initiation [9], it is unclear how planar spindle orientation is coordinated with junction reassembly during successive rapid divisions to prevent polarity errors from accumulating across the tissue.

The role of tissue-scale mechanical coupling (as demonstrated for Dlg1 in mesoderm invagination [4]) in maintaining polarity during proliferation-driven tissue expansion has not been addressed — whether mechanical stress from neighboring cells disrupts or reinforces polarity complexes in dividing cells is unknown.

Cell competition eliminates polarity-deficient clones via Ptp10D/Hippo/JNK [10], but whether this surveillance mechanism is sufficient to correct transient, division-associated polarity asymmetries in wild-type proliferating epithelia (rather than only clonal mutant cells) remains unresolved.

evidence_claims.claim: The Scrib module proteins, Scrib, Dlg, and Lgl, are conserved regulators of cell polarity in diverse biological contexts.

Originally discovered as neoplastic tumor suppressors in the fruit fly Drosophila melanogaster, disruption of Scrib module components leads to tumorigenesis in mammalian epithelia and is associated with human cancers.
Scrib module proteins function as determinants of basolateral identity in epithelial cells with apical-basal polarity while acting as signaling platform scaffold proteins.

Recent studies have further revealed novel roles of the Scrib module in the control of epithelial architecture, ranging from polarity establishment and tricellular junction formation to planar spindle orientation during cell division.

Three tumor suppressors, Discs large (Dlg), Scribble (Scrib) and Lethal giant larvae (Lgl), which localize to the basolateral region of epithelial cells, cooperatively regulate cell polarity, junction formation and cell growth in epithelial cells.

Antagonistic interactions between these tumor suppressors and apical polarity regulators such as Crumbs and aPKC are important for the establishment of apical-basal polarity with organized cell-cell junctions and regulation of cell growth in epithelial cells.
Depletion of the basolateral determinant Dlg1 disrupts the transition between apical constriction and invagination without affecting the rate of apical constriction.
The observed delay in invagination is associated with ineffective apical myosin contractions in the flanking cells that lead to overstretching of their apical domain.
Scribble was originally identified because of its role in apical-basal polarity and epithelial integrity in Drosophila melanogaster.
Scribble acts to assemble and position diverse multiprotein complexes in processes ranging from planar polarity to adhesion to oriented cell division to synaptogenesis.
None of the canonical polarity factors (Crumbs, Stardust, Par-6, aPKC, Bazooka, Scrib, Dlg, Lgl) are required for the polarisation of the endodermal epithelium of the Drosophila adult midgut.
The midgut epithelium forms occluding junctions above adherens junctions and requires the integrin adhesion complex for polarity.
Drosophila contains two types of epithelia that polarise by fundamentally different mechanisms.

In the neoplastic l(1)dlg-1 mutant, wing discs develop convoluted monolayers of epithelial cells characterized by well-defined apical-basal polarity, but late in development clusters or 'rosettes' of separated cells lacking cell-cell junctions and apical-basal polarity form.
Cell-cell interaction and communication is required for termination of disc cell proliferation, which must occur prior to a cellular response to ecdysone.
The tumour suppressor gene scribble (scrib) is required for epithelial polarity and growth control in Drosophila.

Two Scrib protein isoforms result from alternative splicing during scrib transcription, and during morphogenesis each displays a specific pattern of expression in the central and peripheral nervous systems.
Scribble and Dlg are enriched in nascent adherens junctions, are essential for adherens junction positioning and supermolecular assembly, and also play a role in basal junction assembly.
The Scribble/Dlg module plays multiple roles in polarity initiation and different domains of Scribble contribute to these distinct roles.
In Drosophila melanogaster larval epithelial tissues, cells containing mutations in the apico-basal polarity protein, Scrib, are eliminated by cell competition when surrounded by wild-type cells.
RhoGEF2OE cells are eliminated when surrounded by wild-type cells and Ptp10D knockdown increases RhoGEF2OE clone growth.
Mutations in crb partially rescued the elimination of RhoGEF2OE clones, and in this setting JNK and Hippo signaling were elevated whereas EGFR-Ras signaling was reduced.

The proteins localized at septate junctions include the product of the tumor suppressor gene dlg, which is required for septate junction formation, apical basal cell polarity, and the cell interactions that control proliferation.
The migration of the nucleus to the apical surface of the epithelium for mitosis may enable it to interact directly with the junction-associated signalling mechanisms.
Mutations in the fat locus cause hyperplastic imaginal disc overgrowth, in which the imaginal disc cells retain their epithelial structure, junctional complexes, and ability to differentiate.
Loss of the discs large (dlg) gene product results in neoplastic overgrowth of imaginal discs, causes the epithelial cells to lose apical/basal polarity, and prevents them from differentiating.

The Dlg protein is restricted to a specific apical junctional complex in Drosophila epithelial cells, the septate junction, and is the first identified member of a new family of junction-associated proteins that includes ZO-1 and ZO-2.

These results suggest that junctional contacts could play previously unrecognized roles in regulating the growth of epithelial tissues and that ZO-1 and/or ZO-2 may act as tumor suppressor proteins in humans.
The PAR3/PAR6/aPKC complex and the CRUMBS/PALS1/PATJ complex are conserved between species and, along with the SCRIBBLE/DLG/LGL complex, are crucial to the formation of apical junctions.
The exact mechanisms underlying their tight junction construction and maintenance activities are poorly understood.

Work in Drosophila has identified several important components of the polarity machinery and has also established the surprising existence of a secondary cell polarity pathway required only under conditions of energetic stress.
Most cancers are epithelial in origin, and the loss of cell polarity is a critical step towards malignancy.
Apical-basal polarity in most epithelia is established by conserved polarity factors, but recent evidence suggests that the gut epithelium in at least some organisms polarises by novel mechanisms.
SY showed early pupal rescue, preservation of actin filaments, downregulation of MMP1 and cyclin-E in comparison to the untreated in the scrib loss Drosophila model.

literature.summary: Apical-basal polarity in growing Drosophila epithelia is maintained through mutually antagonistic interactions between the apical Crumbs/Par-6/aPKC complex and the basolateral Scrib/Dlg/Lgl module, which together define domain boundaries and couple polarity to junction assembly and growth control [1][3][14]. During cell division, the Scrib module additionally orients the mitotic spindle and positions adherens junctions on daughter cells, placing it at the intersection of polarity maintenance and proliferation [1][9]; cells that lose polarity are eliminated by a Ptp10D/Hippo/JNK-dependent cell competition mechanism, providing a tissue-level surveillance system [10]. Importantly, not all proliferating epithelia rely on canonical polarity factors — the Drosophila midgut uses an integrin-dependent, alternative polarity pathway that more closely resembles vertebrate intestinal epithelium, highlighting that multiple mechanistically distinct strategies for maintaining polarity during rapid proliferation exist within a single organism [6].

hypothesis.hypothesis: During rapid proliferation in the Drosophila larval wing disc epithelium, the Scrib/Dlg basolateral module is re-recruited to daughter cell membranes within ≤15 minutes of cytokinesis completion, and acute, division-synchronized loss of Dlg function (via auxin-inducible degron) will cause ≥30% of post-mitotic cell pairs to display mislocalized Bazooka (apical marker) or fragmented adherens junctions within 20 minutes of mitotic exit, measurable by live imaging in w1118 background under 25°C standard conditions, without triggering Hippo/JNK-dependent cell competition elimination within the 60-minute observation window.
hypothesis.experimental_approach: We will use a dual-strategy approach combining live confocal imaging of endogenously tagged polarity proteins with acute, temporally controlled protein degradation. First, CRISPR-knock-in lines will be used to tag endogenous Dlg with AID (auxin-inducible degron) and mNeonGreen, and endogenous Baz with mCherry, in the same fly line, allowing simultaneous visualization of basolateral and apical markers in real time. Larval wing disc explants will be imaged by spinning-disc confocal microscopy; divisions will be identified by chromatin morphology (using H2B-iRFP), and the temporal sequence of Dlg re-recruitment and Baz re-establishment on daughter cell membranes will be quantified per division event. Acute Dlg degradation will be induced by adding auxin (500 µM indole-3-acetic acid) to the culture medium at defined times relative to cytokinesis (identified from live imaging), and polarity reassembly failures will be scored as mislocalization of Baz beyond a 2-µm apical zone or discontinuous E-cadherin (Arm) signal at daughter-cell junctions. Controls will include: (1) no-auxin vehicle controls, (2) UAS-GFP::dlg rescue in the AID background driven by nub-GAL4 to confirm specificity, and (3) fixed endpoint immunostaining for activated JNK (anti-pJNK) and Hippo pathway output (anti-pYki/Yorkie) to confirm absence of competition signaling during the acute window. A secondary aim will use UAS-RhoGEF2 (overexpression to perturb Rho-actin signaling) driven by act-GAL4 with a temperature-sensitive GAL80 (tub-GAL80ts) to transiently elevate RhoGEF2 during proliferative phases and score polarity error accumulation across 3-5 successive divisions by tracking clonal descendants.

hypothesis.expected_outcomes: Aim 1: Live imaging will reveal that endogenous Dlg::AID-mNeonGreen is re-recruited to nascent daughter cell lateral membranes within 10–20 minutes of cytokinesis (anaphase onset to membrane abscission), and Baz::mCherry apical re-restriction will lag by 5–10 minutes, establishing the sequential order of polarity re-establishment. N ≥ 50 division events from ≥10 discs. Aim 2: Auxin-induced Dlg degradation within a 20-minute window around cytokinesis will result in ≥30% of daughter cell pairs displaying Baz mislocalization (lateral or unpolarized signal) and/or discontinuous Arm::GFP at nascent junctions, compared to <5% in vehicle-only controls (chi-square test, p < 0.01). No significant increase in pJNK or pYki signal in affected cells within 60 minutes post-cytokinesis (two-sample t-test, p > 0.05), indicating that cell competition surveillance is not rapidly activated by transient division-associated polarity errors. Aim 3: Three to five successive divisions under RhoGEF2 overexpression will cause progressive accumulation of polarity errors (>50% of 4th-generation daughter cells with detectable Baz mislocalization vs. <10% in controls), and this will correlate with delayed but eventually activated JNK signaling (elevated pJNK by 120 minutes), suggesting that polarity error accumulation — rather than single-division errors — triggers competition surveillance.
hypothesis.novelty_claim: This experimental plan directly addresses the primary gap identified in the literature synthesis: 'the molecular sequence linking mitotic exit to polarity complex reassembly is not defined.' No published study has used temporally controlled, division-synchronized acute degradation of an endogenous polarity component to dissect the kinetics and sequence of polarity re-establishment on daughter cells in real time in the wing disc. Additionally, the plan tests the unresolved question of whether the Ptp10D/Hippo/JNK cell competition surveillance mechanism — shown to eliminate clonal polarity-deficient cells — is activated by transient, single-division polarity asymmetries in otherwise wild-type proliferating epithelium, a gap explicitly identified in the synthesis. Finally, the successive-division RhoGEF2 experiment addresses the gap regarding whether polarity errors accumulate across rapid successive divisions before triggering tissue-scale surveillance.
hypothesis.feasibility_notes: The major technical challenge is generating the AID-tagged endogenous dlg CRISPR knock-in line; this is feasible with established Drosophila CRISPR protocols (6–9 months including validation). The AID system has been demonstrated in Drosophila and the degron approach is technically established, though OsTIR1 expression levels and degradation efficiency in wing disc tissue require empirical optimization. Wing disc live imaging is technically demanding but routinely performed in multiple labs with established ex vivo culture protocols. The spinning-disc confocal acquisition rate (1 frame per 2 minutes) may miss very rapid polarity events; higher-frequency imaging (30-second intervals) should be tested. Total estimated timeline: 24–30 months. Potential pitfalls: (1) AID degron may be leaky or incomplete, requiring titration of auxin concentration; (2) CRISPR knock-in may affect Dlg function — homozygous viability of the tagged line must be confirmed before experiments; (3) wing disc explant culture conditions (duration, temperature) must be standardized to prevent culture-induced artifacts in polarity; (4) if degradation is too slow, division events may complete before sufficient Dlg depletion — inducible temperature-shift or optogenetic degradation systems may be needed as alternatives.
specific_aims: Aim 1: Temporal mapping — Determine the kinetics and sequential order of Dlg (basolateral) and Baz (apical) re-establishment on daughter cell membranes following cytokinesis in wing disc live imaging using endogenously tagged alleles

Aim 2: Acute perturbation — Test whether auxin-induced Dlg degradation specifically during the cytokinesis window causes quantifiable apical polarity errors in daughter cells, and whether these errors are sufficient to activate Hippo/JNK cell competition signaling within 60 minutes

Aim 3: Error accumulation — Determine whether repeated, successive cell divisions under sustained Rho-actin perturbation (RhoGEF2 overexpression) cause progressive, cumulative polarity errors that eventually cross a threshold for JNK-dependent cell competition elimination

literature.summary: In Drosophila, the death-versus-proliferation decision depends on tissue developmental state, which caspases are active, and the level of caspase activity. Dronc-dependent JNK, ROS/DUOX, Ca2+ and p38 signaling drive proliferation, while factors such as Myo1D restrain lethal effector caspase activity so that cells survive and proliferate [2][4][7]. The upstream switches setting these thresholds, and the links to Hippo/Yki growth control, remain open.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Proposed: In wandering third-instar wing imaginal discs at 25°C, undead-cell apoptosis-induced proliferation (AiP; en-GAL4-driven UAS-hid + UAS-p35 in the posterior compartment) will raise Yki activity, read out by the ex-lacZ reporter, by at least 1.5-fold in neighboring anterior cells within ~10 cell diameters of the A/P boundary, relative to p35-only controls. This increase will depend on Dronc and DUOX, because it will be reduced by at least 50% by posterior Dronc RNAi or Duox RNAi. Knockdown of yki in the anterior compartment will reduce AiP-associated anterior compartment overgrowth (anterior/total area ratio) by at least 30% without reducing Dcp-1 staining in the posterior compartment (p<0.05, n≥15 discs per genotype).
hypothesis.experimental_approach: Undead-cell AiP will be induced in the posterior compartment with en-GAL4 driving UAS-hid and UAS-p35, with tub-GAL80ts for temporal control. Controls are UAS-p35 alone, UAS-hid alone and UAS-GFP. Yki activity in anterior neighbors will be read out with ex-lacZ and a diap1 reporter, alongside anti-Dcp-1, anti-phospho-histone H3, and Wg and Dpp reporters. Epistasis will use UAS-RNAi against Dronc and Duox, UAS-Catalase and UAS-bsk-DN expressed in the posterior (sender) cells to test whether the Dronc-ROS/Ca2+-DUOX-JNK axis is required for the Yki response. Necessity of Yki in responding cells will be tested with a separate binary system, in which a LexA driver in the posterior compartment drives hid/p35 and ci-GAL4 drives yki RNAi in the anterior compartment. Readouts are compartment area ratios, pH3 counts and reporter intensity, with blinded scoring.

literature.disease_context: Misregulation of the balance between apoptosis and apoptosis-induced compensatory proliferation (AiP) is implicated in cancer: apoptotic caspases such as Dronc can paradoxically promote tumor growth when cells fail to die but continue to emit mitogenic signals [1, 2, 5, 6]. The Hippo/YAP pathway, which restrains compensatory proliferation by enforcing contact inhibition, is frequently disrupted in human liver and prostate cancers [8]. Additionally, microbiome-derived metabolites can hijack ROS and JNK signaling to drive intestinal stem cell division and tumor growth in both Drosophila and human colorectal cancer [11].

identified_gaps: The precise molecular switch that determines whether Dronc activity in a stressed cell tips toward committed apoptosis versus AiP signaling without cell death remains unknown — identifying this switch would clarify why some cells die while neighbors proliferate.

The mechanism by which DARE cells maintain Dronc activity below a lethal threshold (with Myo1D preventing effector caspase activation) is only partially understood; how Myo1D senses or limits caspase activity at the mechanistic level is unresolved [7].

It is unclear how tissue developmental state (proliferating vs. differentiating) selects between distinct AiP pathway arms (Dronc/JNK vs. DrICE/Hedgehog) [2]; identifying the upstream context-sensing machinery would explain tissue-specific regenerative capacity.

The role of Ca2+ signaling in AiP has been established in Drosophila [4], but whether the same TRP channel–CICR–DUOX axis operates during vertebrate wound healing or cancer is unverified in the provided literature.

DARE and NARE cells transmit apoptosis resistance to progeny [7], but the epigenetic or transcriptional mechanisms encoding this heritable resistance are unknown, which is directly relevant to radiation-resistant cancer cell populations.
Whether the microbiome-derived Nα-acetyl-L-lysine/Loxl2/H2O2 axis can also activate AiP-like programs in normal intestinal regeneration (as opposed to tumor contexts) has not been tested [11].

evidence_claims.claim: Apoptosis-induced compensatory proliferation (AiP) is a form of compensatory proliferation that is triggered by apoptotic cell death to maintain tissue homeostasis.
Apoptotic caspases can mediate the generation of ROS for promoting AiP.
In proliferating eye and wing tissues, the initiator caspase Dronc coordinates cell death and compensatory proliferation through the Jun N-terminal kinase and p53.
The mitogens Decapentaplegic and Wingless are induced in this process.
In differentiating eye tissues, the effector caspases DrICE and Dcp-1 activate the Hedgehog signaling pathway to induce compensatory proliferation.

Loss of function of Zip leads to compromised epithelial integrity in Drosophila wing imaginal discs as evident from the perturbed expression pattern of cell-cell junction proteins Cadherin, Actin, and Armadillo.
Dronc is responsible for the apoptosis-induced compensatory proliferation due to the loss of Zip function and not the effector caspase Drice/Dcp-1.
Dronc leads to the subsequent activation of Jun N-terminal kinase pathway (JNK) pathway and Wingless (Wg) mitogen that diffuse to the neighboring cells and prompt them to undergo cell division.
Dronc activates the NADPH oxidase DUOX at the plasma membrane, resulting in the production of extracellular reactive oxygen species (ROS) which are required for AiP.
Dronc-dependent Ca2+ entry into the cytosol is a significant factor for DUOX activation and AiP.
Three cell surface Ca2+ channels of the TRP family mediate Ca2+ influx in a non-redundant fashion.
Calcium-induced calcium release (CICR) from the ER was identified as another source of cytosolic Ca2+ during AiP.
DUOX itself acts as a Ca2+ effector in AiP, requiring Ca2+ binding for its activation.
Two apoptosis-resistant epithelial cell populations mediate regeneration after ionizing radiation: Dronc-activating (DARE) and non-activating (NARE) cells.
Dronc activity in DARE cells, independent of Dark and effector caspases, drives regeneration both cell-autonomously and non-cell-autonomously.
The TNFR in DARE cells, Wengen, likely activated by ROS, strongly promotes DARE proliferation, while TNF/Eiger and TNFR Grindelwald moderately suppress it.
p38 MAPK is the main signaling essential for DARE and NARE cell proliferation.
Myo1D ensures DARE survival by preventing lethal effector caspase activation, whereas Myo7A/Crinkled supports moderate caspase activity.
Dying cells trigger DARE induction, and both DARE and NARE transmit apoptosis resistance to progeny, with DARE progeny showing enhanced resistance.
YAP (Yes-associated protein) is inhibited by cell density via the Hippo pathway.
Phosphorylation by the Lats tumor suppressor kinase leads to cytoplasmic translocation and inactivation of the YAP oncoprotein.
YAP protein is elevated and nuclear localized in some human liver and prostate cancers.
Staphylococcus sciuri promotes Drosophila intestinal tumor growth by inducing intestinal stem cell (ISC) division.
Nα-acetyl-L-lysine derived from S. sciuri activates ATR-Chk1 and JNK and subsequently triggers the JAK/STAT pathway required for ISC division and tumor growth.
The Nα-acetyl-L-lysine/Loxl2/H2O2 axis also regulates human colorectal cancer cell division.
Caspases, traditionally viewed as mediators of apoptosis and tumor suppressors, have also been shown to promote cell proliferation and to contribute to tumor growth.
Cell competition is a quality-control mechanism that removes less fit loser cells in favor of healthier winner neighbors.
Misregulation of these processes can contribute to pathological conditions, including cancer.
Whether the same TRP channel–CICR–DUOX axis operates during vertebrate wound healing or cancer is unverified in the provided literature.
The precise molecular switch that determines whether Dronc activity in a stressed cell tips toward committed apoptosis versus AiP signaling without cell death remains unknown.

literature.summary: Current evidence from Drosophila indicates that the fate decision between cell death and compensatory proliferation hinges on the level and context of initiator caspase (Dronc) activity: sub-lethal or apoptosis-uncoupled Dronc activity activates a Ca2+→DUOX→ROS→JNK cascade that emits Wingless and Dpp mitogens to neighboring cells, while the developmental state of the tissue determines which downstream pathway (JNK/p53 in proliferating tissues; Hedgehog via effector caspases in differentiating tissues) is engaged [1, 2, 4, 6]. A recently identified cellular layer of control involves distinct apoptosis-resistant populations (DARE/NARE) that are induced by dying cells and use Dronc, p38 MAPK, and myosin-dependent caspase buffering to orchestrate tissue regeneration without themselves dying [7]. Misregulation of these death–proliferation circuits — including through loss of Hippo/YAP contact inhibition or exploitation by microbiome-derived oxidative metabolites — drives pathological compensatory proliferation relevant to cancer [8, 11].

hypothesis.hypothesis: Myo1D acts as a molecular rheostat that maintains Dronc activity in DARE cells below the effector caspase activation threshold by physically limiting Dark-independent apoptosome assembly; genetic reduction of Myo1D by 50% (one copy removed in a Myo1D heterozygous null background) in irradiated w1118 third-instar wing imaginal discs will convert ≥30% of DARE cells (identified by sub-lethal Dronc reporter activity) into committed apoptotic cells (TUNEL-positive, effector caspase reporter-positive) within 24 hours post-irradiation (40 Gy), and will simultaneously reduce compensatory BrdU incorporation in neighboring cells by ≥40% compared to irradiated wild-type controls, under 25°C standard laboratory conditions.
hypothesis.experimental_approach: We will use the GAL4/UAS system to manipulate Myo1D levels with tissue-specific precision in wing imaginal discs, combining apoptosis reporters (UAS-Apoliner or SCAT3 FRET-based effector caspase sensor), a Dronc activity reporter (UAS-GFP-Dronc cleavage sensor), and proliferation markers (anti-BrdU, anti-pH3). Wing discs from wandering third-instar larvae will be irradiated at 40 Gy using an X-ray source, then cultured ex vivo for 6, 12, and 24 hours before fixation and confocal imaging. Controls will include unirradiated discs, irradiated GAL4-only and UAS-only sibling controls, and a positive control in which full Myo1D knockdown via RNAi is expected to abolish DARE survival entirely. To distinguish DARE from NARE cells, we will co-stain for active Dronc (using antibody to cleaved Dronc or the GFP reporter) alongside effector caspase activity (SCAT3 or anti-cleaved DrICE); DARE cells are defined as Dronc-active/effector-caspase-low and NARE as both-negative. Quantitative confocal image analysis will score the fraction of Dronc-reporter-positive cells that cross into effector caspase positivity and the BrdU incorporation index in immediately adjacent (non-reporter-positive) cells across ≥20 discs per genotype per timepoint.

hypothesis.expected_outcomes: Primary outcome: In irradiated wing discs with 50% Myo1D dosage reduction (Myo1D[1]/+ or ap-GAL4>UAS-Myo1D-RNAi at 25°C), ≥30% of Dronc-reporter-positive (DARE) cells will become doubly positive for effector caspase reporter (SCAT3 FRET ratio shift) and TUNEL at 24 hours post-40 Gy irradiation, compared to <5% conversion in irradiated wild-type controls (Fisher's exact test, p<0.01, n≥20 discs/genotype). Secondary outcome: BrdU incorporation index in cells immediately adjacent to former DARE positions will decrease by ≥40% in Myo1D-reduced discs versus wild-type irradiated controls (Student's t-test, p<0.05). Epistasis prediction: Co-expression of p35 (UAS-p35) in the Myo1D-reduced background should block DARE-to-apoptosis conversion and partially rescue neighboring-cell BrdU incorporation, confirming that effector caspase activation is the downstream mediator. Rescue prediction: Reintroduction of UAS-Myo1D in the heterozygous null background should restore DARE survival (effector caspase conversion rate returning to <10%) and restore BrdU index to within 20% of wild-type irradiated levels. Negative control: Unirradiated discs of all genotypes should show <2% Dronc-reporter-positive cells and no increase in TUNEL, confirming irradiation-dependence of DARE induction.
hypothesis.novelty_claim: The literature identifies Myo1D as necessary for DARE survival by preventing effector caspase activation but explicitly states that 'how Myo1D senses or limits caspase activity at the mechanistic level is unresolved' (identified gap 2, PMID 41345088). No prior study has experimentally titrated Myo1D levels to define a quantitative threshold below which DARE cells convert to committed apoptosis, nor has any study measured the direct consequence of this conversion on neighboring-cell compensatory proliferation in the same disc. Furthermore, while the DARE/NARE distinction is established, the molecular logic by which a single gene (Myo1D) gates the binary death-vs-AiP decision in a dose-dependent manner has not been tested. This directly addresses the overarching gap: 'the precise molecular switch that determines whether Dronc activity in a stressed cell tips toward committed apoptosis versus AiP signaling without cell death remains unknown' (identified gap 1, PMIDs 41345088, 28688927, 18774295).
hypothesis.feasibility_notes: All core genetic tools (irradiation, wing disc culture, BrdU labeling, TUNEL, confocal imaging) are standard in Drosophila developmental biology laboratories. The main technical risk is the availability of validated Dronc activity reporters and SCAT3 lines; if not available from stock centers, SCAT3 has been published and can be requested from originating labs (~2-month delay). The Myo1D null allele is referenced in PMID 41345088 but its BDSC stock number is not confirmed in the literature provided and must be verified or requested from the Braun/Bergmann labs. Ex vivo disc culture after 40 Gy irradiation is established but requires optimization of culture media and timing (potential 1-month optimization phase). Estimated total timeline: 14-18 months (2 months line acquisition/verification, 2 months optimization of irradiation and reporter conditions, 6 months primary experimental replication across three independent biological replicates per aim, 2 months epistasis and rescue experiments, 2 months data analysis and preparation). Key pitfalls: (1) Incomplete penetrance of Myo1D heterozygosity may require use of stronger RNAi, which could introduce off-target effects — addressed by using both approaches and requiring concordant results; (2) DARE cells are rare and may require automated image analysis pipelines for unbiased quantification; (3) ex vivo culture conditions may not fully recapitulate in vivo regeneration — larval recovery experiments at 72 hours post-irradiation will be run in parallel as an in vivo validation.
specific_aims: Aim 1: Quantify Myo1D dosage threshold — determine the minimum reduction in Myo1D levels (heterozygous null, 25% RNAi knockdown, 50% RNAi knockdown, full knockdown) that converts DARE cells from effector-caspase-low to effector-caspase-high in irradiated wing discs, establishing a dose-response curve for the Myo1D caspase-buffering rheostat.

Aim 2: Measure AiP output — quantify BrdU and pH3-positive neighboring-cell proliferation at each Myo1D dosage level from Aim 1 to determine whether DARE-to-apoptosis conversion directly and proportionally reduces compensatory proliferation in adjacent cells, establishing a causal link between Myo1D-gated DARE survival and AiP.

Aim 3: Epistasis and rescue — test whether co-expression of p35 (effector caspase block) rescues AiP in Myo1D-reduced discs and whether re-expression of UAS-Myo1D in the null heterozygous background fully restores both DARE survival and neighboring BrdU incorporation, confirming that Myo1D acts upstream of effector caspase activation to gate the death-vs-proliferation decision.

identified_gaps: How much determinant segregation depends on spindle orientation versus polarity-based cortical localization is not quantified in the supplied papers; mud mutants show polarity is normal [3] while Baz-aPKC-Par6-Insc dominates determinant localization [9]. Testing graded Mud/Pins weakening with live imaging of Mira/Brat/Pros segregation would resolve this.

The mechanism of ordered assembly of competing Pins/Mud and Pins/Insc complexes in vivo is unresolved; phase separation is shown in vitro [1] and Insc:LGN tetramers are not dissociated by NuMA [7]. In vivo tests of whether phase separation-defective Hts or Mud variants weaken spindle orientation are needed.

The abstracts do not quantify the penetrance of tumor-like overproliferation after weakened coupling [4], or whether symmetric division arises solely from orthogonal spindles [3]. Lineage-tracing of mis-oriented neuroblast divisions would address this.

Human relevance of Drosophila Insc/Mud/Hts findings in neural stem cells and disease is largely untested; the human INSC study is in silico only [5]. Functional tests in mammalian neural progenitors are needed.

evidence_claims.claim: In mud mutants, cortical polarity is normal, but the metaphase spindle frequently fails to align with the cortical polarity axis.
When spindle orientation is orthogonal to cell polarity, symmetric division occurs.
In the absence of Mud, spindle misalignment can lead to symmetric segregation of Brat and Prospero, mis-specification of daughter cell fates and tumor-like overproliferation.
Pins binds directly to Mud, and Pins recruits Mud to the neuroblast apical cortex.

Hts is a direct Mud-binding protein, apically polarizes in mitotic neuroblasts, is required for Mud-dependent spindle orientation, and reduces the concentration threshold for Pins/Mud phase separation.
Baz-aPKC-Par6-Insc remain polarized in G protein mutants and are responsible for asymmetric Miranda localization, whereas Pins-Galphai plays a predominant role in spindle orientation.
abs mutants show loss of Insc protein, loss of apical Insc crescents, failure of basal protein targeting and defects in spindle orientation.
Cno functionally interacts with Insc, Galphai and Mud and is required for determinant localization, spindle orientation and unequal-sized daughter cells.
The Insc:LGN complex forms stable tetrameric cores that cannot be dissociated by NuMA.
Loss of Mud randomizes spindle orientation in the wing but does not alter wing shape.
Downregulation of mammalian Insc inhibits vertical divisions and enhances proliferation in rat retinal explants.

Weakening the Pins–Mud link likely produces a context-dependent loss of asymmetry, because spindle misorientation relative to the polarity axis, rather than loss of polarity itself, drives symmetric determinant segregation.
Human INSC protein might be implicated in asymmetrical cell division of human neural stem cells and other stem cells.

literature.summary: In Drosophila neuroblasts, spindle orientation is coupled to apical polarity through a Pins/Galphai–Mud link, with Insc, Cno and Hts acting as additional apical components. Weakening this coupling, as in mud mutants, leaves cortical polarity intact but misaligns spindles, which can cause symmetric Brat/Prospero segregation, fate mis-specification and tumor-like overproliferation. Open questions include how the competing apical complexes assemble in vivo and how far these mechanisms extend to mammalian systems.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Proposed: In third-instar larval central-brain type I neuroblasts at 25°C, graded Mud depletion by worniu-GAL4-driven RNAi will increase the fraction of metaphase spindles misaligned by more than 30 degrees from the apical Pins crescent axis in a dose-dependent manner. Symmetric Miranda partitioning at telophase will track spindle angle rather than genotype: at least 50% of neuroblasts with spindle angles above 60 degrees will partition Miranda symmetrically, versus fewer than 10% of neuroblasts with angles of 30 degrees or less. Apical Pins/aPKC crescents will remain intact in at least 90% of metaphase neuroblasts in every genotype. Hts knockdown is predicted to phenocopy a partial Mud reduction on the same angle-to-segregation curve.
hypothesis.experimental_approach: Use worniu-GAL4 with tub-GAL80ts for neuroblast-specific, temporally controlled knockdown. A series of Mud RNAi lines or temperature and induction regimes will give graded depletion, and Hts RNAi will be tested in parallel. Live imaging of intact larval brain explants will use a Miranda reporter plus a spindle/centrosome marker (e.g., a tubulin or Jupiter reporter) and an apical polarity marker (Pins or aPKC). From these movies, per-cell metaphase spindle angle relative to the apical crescent axis, apical crescent integrity, telophase Miranda partition ratio, and daughter-cell size ratio will be measured. Controls are driver-only and non-targeting RNAi (e.g., mCherry or white RNAi) flies, plus a polarity-perturbation comparison (e.g., insc or baz knockdown) to distinguish orientation-dependent from polarity-dependent segregation failures. The per-cell relationship between spindle angle and segregation outcome will then be compared across genotypes by logistic regression with genotype as a covariate. Fixed-sample analysis of Mira, Pros and Brat will confirm the live-imaging results, and neuroblast counts will be used to assess overproliferation.
