hypothesis.expected_outcomes: Proposed predictions, not established results. (1) Mud knockdown will produce a dose-dependent rise in the fraction of neuroblasts with spindle misalignment above 30 degrees, from under 15% in controls to 40-70% in strong knockdown. (2) Apical crescent integrity will stay at or above 90% in all genotypes. (3) Symmetric Miranda partitioning will be tightly coupled to spindle angle: at least 50% symmetric partitioning above 60 degrees versus under 10% at or below 30 degrees, with no significant genotype effect after controlling for angle (likelihood-ratio test, p > 0.05). (4) Hts knockdown will give a milder shift in the angle distribution that falls on the same curve. (5) Insc or Baz perturbation will break this relationship, giving symmetric partitioning even at well-aligned angles. (6) Strong Mud depletion will increase neuroblast numbers per central-brain lobe by at least 20% over controls. Sample sizes of at least 40 neuroblasts per genotype from at least 8 brains will be used. Falsification: if partition outcome depends significantly on genotype at matched angles, or if angle-misaligned neuroblasts still segregate Miranda asymmetrically at more than 30% frequency, the spindle-orientation-dependent model is rejected.
hypothesis.novelty_claim: The supplied literature shows that in mud mutants cortical polarity is normal but spindles misalign, and that loss of Mud can cause symmetric Brat/Prospero segregation and tumor-like overproliferation. However, it does not quantify how much determinant segregation depends on spindle orientation versus polarity-based cortical localization. The penetrance of overproliferation after weakened coupling is also not quantified. This design tests graded weakening with per-cell live imaging, which converts a qualitative mutant phenotype into a quantitative angle-to-segregation relationship. It also includes a direct comparison with Hts, whose role in Pins/Mud phase separation has only been shown biochemically and in spindle orientation assays.
hypothesis.feasibility_notes: Proposed timeline of about 12-14 months. Months 1-3 cover line construction, verification of RNAi lines and knockdown validation by immunostaining. Months 4-8 cover live imaging and angle/segregation quantification. Months 9-11 cover Hts and Insc/Baz comparisons and fixed Mira/Pros/Brat analysis. Months 12-14 cover neuroblast-number analysis and statistics. Pitfalls include RNAi off-target effects (use at least two independent lines), incomplete knockdown that is difficult to grade (validate by Mud immunostaining intensity per cell), phototoxicity in long live-imaging sessions, neuroblast drift or rotation during imaging, and the difficulty of measuring 3D spindle angle. Stock numbers and the availability of reporters have not been verified and must be checked before starting.
specific_aims: Aim 1: Graded coupling versus spindle angle — quantify how graded Mud knockdown shifts metaphase spindle angle relative to the apical crescent while apical polarity stays intact.

Aim 2: Angle-dependence of determinant segregation — test by live imaging and logistic regression whether telophase Miranda, Pros and Brat partitioning depends on spindle angle rather than genotype, and compare with polarity perturbations (insc or baz).

Aim 3: Hts contribution and tissue consequences — determine whether Hts knockdown phenocopies partial Mud loss on the same angle-to-segregation curve, and measure resulting neuroblast overproliferation.

literature.summary: In neuroblasts, apical Pins-Galphai couples cortical polarity to the spindle by directly binding and recruiting Mud/NuMA [3][4][8]. Hts/Adducin [1] and Canoe [6] support this coupling, while Insc, whose levels Abs controls [2], links Pins to the Baz-aPKC polarity arm [9]. The Baz-aPKC-Insc arm largely drives determinant localization independently of Pins-Galphai [9]. Inference: the coupling is therefore partly modular, and in mud mutants polarity is preserved but determinants segregate symmetrically mainly when the spindle lies orthogonal to the polarity axis [3]. When this happens, Brat/Prospero missegregation leads to fate mis-specification and tumor-like overgrowth [4]. Loss of Mud outside neuroblasts randomizes wing disc spindle orientation without altering wing shape [13].

literature.disease_context: Failure to couple spindle orientation with fate determinant segregation in Drosophila neuroblasts leads to symmetric division, misspecification of daughter cell fates, and tumor-like overproliferation in the nervous system [4]. The core machinery—Pins/LGN, Mud/NuMA, and Insc/mInsc—is conserved in mammals, where loss of correct spindle orientation in neural and mammary progenitors leads to enhanced symmetric proliferative divisions, with implications for cancer and developmental disorders [7, 14]. Understanding the molecular mechanics of apical complex assembly, including phase separation and auxiliary factors like Hts/Adducin, may reveal new therapeutic targets for stem cell-driven cancers.

identified_gaps: The molecular mechanics distinguishing the mutually exclusive Pins/Mud and Pins/Insc apical complexes remain incompletely understood — specifically, how phase separation of Pins/Mud is prevented or outcompeted when Insc is present, and what triggers the switch between these two assemblies during the cell cycle [1].

It is unknown whether the Hts/Adducin-mediated phase separation of the Pins/Mud complex is regulated temporally during mitosis and how the liquid-like properties of these condensates are converted into stable cortical asymmetry for robust spindle capture [1].

The precise mechanism by which spindle misorientation in mud mutants leads to symmetric fate determinant segregation — i.e., whether symmetric division is a direct consequence of spindle misalignment or whether Mud has additional roles in actively tethering fate determinants — is not resolved from the provided literature [3, 4].

The Mud-Ncd (kinesin-14) interaction at spindle poles has been characterized biochemically, but its functional contribution to spindle orientation in neuroblasts versus its role in generic spindle bipolarity has not been dissected in vivo [11].

It remains unclear how the two apical signaling pathways — Pins-Galphai (spindle orientation dominant) and Baz-aPKC-Insc (fate determinant localization dominant) — are quantitatively integrated so that partial loss of coupling does not immediately collapse asymmetry; the identity of buffering or redundancy mechanisms is not established [9].

The contribution of oriented cell divisions versus cell rearrangements differs between tissues (e.g., wing morphogenesis does not require spindle orientation [13] whereas neuroblast asymmetry does [3, 4]), but the tissue-specific factors that determine whether spindle orientation is obligatory for asymmetric outcomes are not identified.

evidence_claims.claim: ACD involves coupling mitotic spindle orientation with cortical polarity cues to direct unequal segregation of cell fate determinants.

In Drosophila neural stem cells (neuroblasts; NBs), spindles orient along an apical-basal polarity axis through a conserved complex of Partner of Inscuteable (Pins; human LGN) and Mushroom body defect (Mud; human NuMA).
Hts is expressed throughout the larval central brain and apically polarizes in mitotic NBs where it is required for Mud-dependent spindle orientation.

Pins undergoes liquid-liquid phase separation with Mud, but not with Insc, suggesting a potential molecular basis for differential assembly mechanics between these two competing apical protein complexes.
Hts binds an intact Pins/Mud complex, reduces the concentration threshold for its phase separation, and alters the liquid-like property of the resulting phase separated droplets.
Pins directly binds, and coimmunoprecipitates with, the NuMA-related Mushroom body defect (Mud) protein; Pins recruits Mud to the neuroblast apical cortex.

In mud mutants, cortical polarity is normal, but the metaphase spindle frequently fails to align with the cortical polarity axis; when spindle orientation is orthogonal to cell polarity, symmetric division occurs.

In the absence of Mud, mitotic spindles in Drosophila neuroblasts fail to align with the polarity axis, leading to symmetric segregation of the cell fate determinants Brat and Prospero, resulting in the mis-specification of daughter cell fates and tumor-like over proliferation in the Drosophila nervous system.

Mud directly associates and colocalizes with Pins at the cell cortex overlying the spindle pole(s) in both neuroblasts and epithelial cells; Mud localizes to centrosomes during mitosis independently of Pins to regulate centrosomal organization.
The Pins-Galphai pathway has a predominant role in spindle orientation, while the Baz-aPKC-Insc pathway retains a dominant but partially independent role in asymmetric Miranda localization.

In Ggamma1 and Gbeta13F mutant NBs, Pins-Galphai no longer distribute asymmetrically; however, Bazooka-atypical PKC-Par6-Inscuteable still remain polarized and responsible for asymmetric Miranda localization.
Cno localizes apically in metaphase NBs and coimmunoprecipitates with Pins in vivo; Cno functionally interacts with Insc, Galphai, and Mud to generate correct neuronal lineages.
Canoe (Cno) regulates the localization of cell-fate determinants, the orientation of the mitotic spindle, and the generation of unequal-sized daughter cells in neuroblasts.

In abs mutants, there is loss of apical Insc crescents, failure in basal protein targeting, and defects in spindle orientation; abs mutants show a striking loss of Insc protein levels but no change of insc RNA levels.

Abstrakt physically interacts with insc RNA, demonstrating a novel role in post-transcriptional regulation of insc expression essential for proper cell polarity, spindle orientation, and distinct sibling cell fates.
Insc:LGN tetramers constitute stable cores of Par3-Insc-LGN-GαiGDP complexes, which cannot be dissociated by NuMA.
In mammary stem cells, the asymmetric domain of Insc bound to LGN:GαiGDP suffices to drive asymmetric fate, and reverts aberrant symmetric divisions induced by p53 loss.

Mud binds directly to the kinesin-14 motor Ncd via a short coiled-coil domain (MudCC) and the N-terminal non-motor microtubule-binding domain of Ncd; Mud binding competes against Ncd self-association and increases NcdnMBD microtubule binding in vitro.

Loss of Mud randomizes spindle orientation but does not alter wing shape, and the absence of oriented cell divisions is compensated by increased contribution of cell rearrangements to wing morphogenesis.

Downregulation of mammalian Inscuteable (mInsc) inhibits vertical divisions in the rat retina, resulting in enhanced proliferation consistent with a higher frequency of symmetric divisions generating two proliferating cells.

Asymmetric centrosome behavior plays a key role in developmentally programmed asymmetric division in both Drosophila male germline stem cells and neuroblasts, coordinating spindle orientation with cell fate decisions.
Human INSC mRNA was expressed in eye, kidney, fetal cochlea, parathyroid tumor, chondrosarcoma, epidermoid carcinoma, and skin tumor.

The molecular mechanics that drive assembly of the cortical Pins/Mud complex remain unclear, particularly with respect to the mutually exclusive Pins complex formed with the apical scaffold protein Inscuteable (Insc).
Mud is a functional orthologue of mammalian NuMA and C. elegans Lin-5, coordinating spindle orientation with cortical polarity to promote asymmetric cell division.
Phase separation of specific protein complexes might regulate ordered assembly within the apical domain to ensure proper signaling output.

literature.summary: In Drosophila neuroblasts, spindle orientation is coupled to fate determinant segregation through a conserved apical complex in which cortically localized Pins recruits Mud (NuMA homolog) via a direct interaction, and Mud in turn links the cortical polarity axis to the mitotic spindle [3, 4, 8]. Two partially distinct apical signaling arms—Pins-Galphai (dominant for spindle orientation) and Baz-aPKC-Insc (dominant for fate determinant asymmetry)—cooperate to ensure that spindle alignment and basal determinant localization are coordinated, with additional regulators including Canoe, Abstrakt, and the newly identified Hts/Adducin modulating complex assembly, potentially through liquid-liquid phase separation [1, 6, 9, 14738736]. When this coupling is weakened—as in mud, pins, or insc mutants—spindles misalign relative to the polarity axis, fate determinants such as Brat and Prospero segregate symmetrically, daughter cell fates are equalized, and the result is tumor-like overproliferation in the nervous system, highlighting the direct mechanistic link between spindle orientation fidelity and stem cell homeostasis [3, 4].

hypothesis.hypothesis: Hts/Adducin-mediated liquid-liquid phase separation of the Pins/Mud complex is required for robust coupling of spindle orientation to fate determinant segregation in Drosophila larval neuroblasts; specifically, neuroblasts expressing a phase-separation-deficient Hts variant (hts-ΔLLPS) will show ≥40% spindle misorientation (>30° deviation from apical-basal axis) compared with ≤15% in controls, ≥35% symmetric co-segregation of Miranda and Prospero between daughter cells, and a ≥2-fold increase in type-II neuroblast clone size within 7 days of clone induction at 25°C in mated female larvae, while cortical Baz/aPKC polarity remains intact in ≥80% of mitotic neuroblasts.
hypothesis.experimental_approach: We will generate a UAS-hts-ΔLLPS transgene encoding Hts with mutations in the predicted phase-separation-driving domain (informed by the Pins/Mud condensate data from PMID 37655159), alongside a UAS-hts-WT rescue control, and express each using the neuroblast-specific worniu-GAL4 driver (wor-GAL4) in an hts-null or strong hypomorphic background to test whether Hts phase-separation activity is required for spindle orientation coupling. Spindle orientation will be quantified by measuring the angle between the metaphase spindle axis (anti-α-tubulin) and the apical Pins/Baz crescent in fixed third-instar larval brain wholemounts using confocal microscopy and automated angle measurement (≥50 mitotic neuroblasts per genotype, ≥3 biological replicates). Fate determinant segregation will be assessed by imaging Miranda-GFP and Pros-RFP co-segregation at anaphase/telophase, scoring symmetric vs. asymmetric segregation; cortical polarity integrity will be confirmed by Baz and aPKC immunostaining. MARCM clone analysis using FLP/FRT-based clonal induction in wor-GAL4 larvae will quantify neuroblast overproliferation as clone cell number and Deadpan-positive neuroblast number per clone at 7 days after clone induction (ACI). Liquid-droplet properties of endogenous Hts/Pins/Mud complexes will be assessed in S2 cells by fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP) of GFP-Mud puncta in the presence and absence of co-expressed Hts-ΔLLPS to confirm dominant-negative or loss-of-function condensate effects before in vivo deployment.

hypothesis.expected_outcomes: Aim 1: hts-null neuroblasts or neuroblasts expressing UAS-hts-ΔLLPS via wor-GAL4 will show ≥40% of mitotic neuroblasts with spindle angles >30° from the apical-basal axis (vs. ≤15% in wor-GAL4/+; hts/+ controls and ≤15% in UAS-hts-WT rescue), with Pins and Baz apical crescents remaining intact in ≥80% of cells, confirming spindle-polarity decoupling without cortical polarity loss. Aim 2: Miranda-GFP and Pros-RFP will co-segregate symmetrically (both markers in equal or near-equal proportions to both daughter cells, defined as <1.5-fold ratio) in ≥35% of anaphase neuroblasts in the hts-ΔLLPS condition vs. ≤10% in controls; this frequency should be significantly lower than in mud[4] mutants (expected ≥60%), indicating partial rather than complete decoupling. Aim 3: MARCM clones in hts-null or hts-ΔLLPS backgrounds will contain ≥2-fold more Deadpan-positive neuroblasts and ≥2-fold more total cells per clone at 7 days ACI compared with wild-type clones (p<0.05, Mann-Whitney U test, n≥20 clones per genotype, ≥3 animals). FRAP of GFP-Mud puncta in S2 cells will show ≥2-fold higher mobile fraction in hts-ΔLLPS co-expression compared with hts-WT co-expression (t½ <30 s vs. >60 s), confirming loss of condensate stability.
hypothesis.novelty_claim: This experimental plan directly addresses two identified gaps in the literature synthesis: (1) It is unknown whether Hts/Adducin-mediated phase separation of the Pins/Mud complex is regulated functionally during mitosis and how liquid-like condensate properties are converted into stable cortical asymmetry sufficient for robust spindle capture [gap 2 from synthesis; PMID 37655159]. (2) The precise mechanism by which spindle misorientation leads to symmetric fate determinant segregation — specifically whether this is a passive geometric consequence of spindle misalignment or whether condensate integrity at the cortex actively tethers fate determinants — has not been resolved [gap 3 from synthesis; PMID 16740476, 16648843]. By genetically separating Hts LLPS activity from total Hts protein levels using a structure-informed ΔLLPS allele expressed in an otherwise normal polarity context, this design provides the first in vivo test of whether condensate assembly per se (rather than Hts protein presence) is the instructive molecular step coupling spindle orientation to fate determinant segregation and tumor suppression in neuroblasts.
hypothesis.feasibility_notes: The core genetic tools (wor-GAL4, mud and pins loss-of-function alleles, MARCM components) are established and widely available, reducing technical risk. The primary novel requirement is generation of UAS-hts-ΔLLPS transgenic flies, which requires prior biochemical domain mapping to identify the minimal LLPS-driving region of Hts in the Pins/Mud context (data partially provided by PMID 37655159 but specific residues must be confirmed); this mapping phase adds approximately 3-4 months. Overall timeline estimate: domain mapping and transgene design (months 1-4), transgenesis and validation in S2 cells (months 4-8), in vivo neuroblast characterization and fixed imaging (months 8-16), MARCM clonal analysis (months 12-18), data analysis and validation (months 18-20). Potential pitfalls include: (a) Hts-ΔLLPS mutations may affect Mud binding independently of phase separation, necessitating binding assays to decouple these activities; (b) partial redundancy with other condensate-promoting factors may buffer the in vivo phenotype, requiring double mutant or dominant-negative strategies; (c) maternal Hts deposition may complicate null analysis, favoring the conditional UAS-hts-ΔLLPS approach; (d) FRAP measurements in vivo in neuroblasts are technically challenging and may require S2 cell validation as a surrogate. The experimental design is feasible within a 20-month window for a team of 2-3 researchers.

literature.disease_context: Understanding how epithelia sense crowding and select cells for extrusion is directly relevant to cancer biology, where dysregulation of cell number control can drive tumor initiation or suppress it via oncogenic cell extrusion. The Hippo/YAP pathway, identified as a key mediator of geometry-dependent apoptosis commitment in Drosophila [2], is frequently dysregulated in human cancers. Notch signaling, also implicated in this process [2], plays broad roles in developmental disorders and malignancies.

key_papers.title: Epithelial apoptotic pattern emerges from global and local regulation by cell apical area
key_papers.authors: Cachoux et al.
key_papers.relevance: Directly demonstrates that apoptosis commitment and extrusion selection in Drosophila epithelium are governed by two geometric features — small global apical area and small relative apical area compared to immediate neighbors — mediated by Hippo/YAP and Notch pathways.

key_papers.title: Assembly, dynamics and remodeling of epithelial cell junctions throughout development
key_papers.authors: Mira-Osuna, Borgne RL et al.
key_papers.relevance: Provides comprehensive mechanistic context for junctional remodeling during extrusion and other morphogenetic events, framing how molecular changes at cell interfaces maintain tissue homeostasis.

identified_gaps: It remains unknown precisely how apical area differences are transduced into Hippo/YAP and Notch pathway activity at the molecular level — identifying the mechanosensors (e.g., specific junctional or cytoskeletal components) that link cell geometry to caspase activation would be critical for understanding cell fate decisions in crowded epithelia.

The causal relationship between global versus local geometric signals is unresolved: it is unclear whether the two geometric features (small global apical area and small relative apical area vs. neighbors) act independently, synergistically, or in sequence to commit a cell to apoptosis, which matters for building predictive models of tissue homeostasis.

The provided literature does not address how the extruding cell is physically recognized and expelled by its neighbors after apoptosis commitment is made — the junctional remodeling mechanisms specific to extrusion (as opposed to other morphogenetic events) remain incompletely characterized in mechanistic detail.

literature.summary: Recent work in Drosophila epithelium demonstrates that cells are selected for apoptosis and subsequent extrusion based on their geometry: cells with both a globally small apical area (relative to the tissue average) and a locally small apical area (relative to immediate neighbors) are committed to apoptosis well before physical extrusion occurs, with this geometric sensing mediated by the Hippo/YAP and Notch pathways [2]. Junctional remodeling at cell interfaces is essential for executing extrusion while preserving epithelial integrity [1]. Key open questions include identifying the mechanosensory molecules that link apical area to pathway activation, and fully characterizing the junctional dynamics that physically drive the extrusion event itself.

hypothesis.hypothesis: In the Drosophila pupal notum epithelium at 25°C, the junctional tension sensor Jub (ajuba LIM protein) acts downstream of apical area reduction to transduce both global (tissue-scale) and local (neighbor-relative) geometric crowding signals into Hippo pathway activation (Wts phosphorylation) and Notch ligand asymmetry (Dl enrichment in larger neighbors), such that RNAi-mediated knockdown of jub using e22c-GAL4 will reduce the fraction of geometrically crowded cells (apical area ≤40% of tissue median AND ≤60% of mean neighbor area) that commit to apoptosis within 4 hours by ≥50% compared to controls, and will disrupt the correlation between apical area rank and apoptotic probability (Spearman ρ reduced from ≥0.6 to ≤0.2, p<0.05), without globally disrupting epithelial architecture as assessed by E-cadherin continuity.
hypothesis.experimental_approach: Using the Drosophila pupal notum as the primary model epithelium (which was used in Cachoux et al. 2023 [37827152]), we will employ the GAL4/UAS system with e22c-GAL4 (broad epithelial driver) to knock down candidate mechanosensors — beginning with jub (Ajuba), which is a known Hippo pathway regulator at junctions — using UAS-jub-RNAi, and subsequently test UAS-crb-RNAi and UAS-Myo-II-RNAi to probe apical actomyosin contributions. Live imaging with a caspase reporter (UAS-apoliner or endogenous Dcp-1 antibody staining) will be combined with automated cell segmentation to measure apical area of each cell relative to tissue-wide median (global signal) and relative to its immediate neighbors (local signal) at the time of apoptosis commitment. Pathway outputs will be assessed by immunostaining for phospho-Wts (pWts, Hippo output), Yki nuclear localization, and Dl membrane distribution in extruding versus non-extruding crowded cells. All experimental genotypes will be compared against two controls: (1) e22c-GAL4/+ driver-only control and (2) UAS-RNAi/+ transgene-only control, with at least n=10 nota per condition and ≥200 apoptotic events scored per replicate across three biological replicates.

Aim 3: Dl asymmetry index (ratio of Dl intensity on neighbor membranes abutting the small cell vs. other interfaces) will decrease from ≥1.5-fold in controls to ≤1.1-fold upon N-RNAi or Dl-RNAi, with selective loss of local (neighbor-relative) apoptosis prediction without affecting global area-based prediction, supporting pathway independence. If jub knockdown does not reduce apoptosis frequency or pathway markers, this would falsify the hypothesis that jub is the primary mechanosensor, redirecting focus to alternative candidates (e.g., Crumbs complex components or Myo-II).
hypothesis.novelty_claim: The literature synthesis explicitly identifies as a gap 'precisely how apical area differences are transduced into Hippo/YAP and Notch pathway activity at the molecular level — identifying the mechanosensors (e.g., specific junctional or cytoskeletal components) that link cell geometry to caspase activation.' Cachoux et al. [37827152] established that both global and local geometric features predict apoptosis commitment via Hippo and Notch, but did not identify the upstream mechanosensory molecule(s). The synthesis also flags as unresolved 'whether the two geometric features act independently, synergistically, or in sequence.' This proposal is the first (to the extent supported by the provided literature) to test a specific candidate mechanosensor (Jub/Ajuba) as a molecular link between apical area and pathway activation, and to design orthogonal RNAi experiments that can dissociate the global (Hippo) and local (Notch/Dl) geometric sensing arms to determine their causal relationship.

Automated cell segmentation software (e.g., Tissue Analyzer, ilastik) is publicly available. hypothesis.hypothesis: Proposed: In the developing Drosophila pupal epithelium, a small apical area relative to neighbors (<50% of the mean neighbor area) reduces Yorkie transcriptional activity cell-autonomously, and this reduction is required for commitment to apoptotic extrusion. Specifically, clonal Yorkie gain-of-function in cells with small relative apical area will reduce the fraction that undergo caspase-positive extrusion within 12 h by at least 50% compared with control clones, and clonal Notch knockdown in the small cell itself will lower this fraction by at least 30%.
hypothesis.experimental_approach: Use hs-FLP flip-out clones in a developing Drosophila epithelium, with the pupal notum as the proposed model (suitability requires verification). Live-image a junction marker, a Yorkie transcriptional reporter and a caspase reporter, and segment single cells to measure absolute and relative apical area, reporter intensity and the time to caspase onset and extrusion. Aim 1 correlates area with Yki activity. Aim 2 tests causality by clonal Yki gain and loss of function, and by acute mechanical perturbation (e.g., local laser ablation of neighbors to change apical area). Aim 3 uses Notch receptor and ligand manipulations in the small cell versus its neighbors, and tracks junction components during extrusion. Controls are neutral flip-out clones (e.g., GFP or lacZ only), and cells matched for apical area from non-clonal tissue. Statistics use mixed-effects logistic regression with pupa as a random effect.

literature.summary: Research in Drosophila and related systems reveals that coordinating organelle positioning with polarized growth requires the integrated action of microtubule and actin cytoskeletal networks, motor proteins (dynein/BicD and kinesin/MAP7), and endosomal/vesicle trafficking machinery [1, 4, 7, 9, 10]. In the oocyte, nuclear position is both a readout of cytoskeletal forces and a spatial cue that orients EGF/Gurken signaling to establish embryonic axes, demonstrating that organelle positioning and signaling are mutually dependent [5, 9, 20471269]. Key outstanding challenges include resolving the biophysical force models for nuclear positioning, determining causality between Golgi outpost dynamics and dendritic branching signals, and identifying how endomembrane trafficking factors mechanistically connect to cytoskeletal polarity during growth [3, 4, 1].

hypothesis.hypothesis: Golgi outpost positioning in Drosophila class IV da sensory neurons (ddaC) is causally upstream of local EGF/EGFR-dependent dendritic branching signals: specifically, acute disruption of Golgi outpost anterograde transport via neuron-specific RNAi knockdown of BicD (bicaudal D) will reduce Golgi outpost density in terminal dendrite branches by ≥50%, decrease the number of stable tertiary branch additions by ≥40% over a 24-hour live-imaging window in third-instar larvae, and reduce phospho-ERK (dpERK) immunofluorescence intensity at branch points by ≥30% relative to UAS-mCD8::GFP controls, all measured at 25°C in a w1118 background.
hypothesis.experimental_approach: Using the ppk-GAL4 driver (expressed specifically in class IV da neurons) crossed to UAS-BicD-RNAi lines, we will acutely knock down BicD to disrupt dynein-dependent Golgi outpost anterograde transport in ddaC neurons without affecting neighboring cell types. Golgi outpost dynamics will be monitored by co-expressing UAS-ManII::GFP (a cis-Golgi marker) via live confocal imaging of filleted third-instar larval preparations over 24-hour intervals, recording outpost number, density per branch length, and motility parameters using kymograph analysis. Dendritic branching dynamics will be simultaneously quantified by co-expressing UAS-mCD8::RFP to label the full dendritic arbor, counting stable branch additions and retractions every 2 hours. Phospho-ERK (dpERK) immunofluorescence will be performed on fixed larvae at the wandering third-instar stage to assess local EGFR signaling at dendritic branch points, with intensity normalized to total ERK staining. Controls will include: (1) w1118; ppk-GAL4/UAS-mCD8::GFP (no RNAi), (2) UAS-lacZ-RNAi (scramble control), and (3) UAS-BicD overexpression to test the reciprocal gain-of-function prediction. To test causality directionality, we will also express constitutively active EGFR (UAS-EGFR.lambdatop) in BicD-RNAi backgrounds to determine whether activated downstream signaling rescues branching defects despite Golgi outpost mislocalization.

hypothesis.novelty_claim: This experiment directly addresses the identified gap that 'the causal mechanism by which Golgi outpost repositioning triggers or responds to dendrite branching signals remains unknown — it is unclear whether outpost movement is upstream or downstream of local signaling events that stabilize new dendritic branches' (PMID 36512242). Prior work established a correlation between Golgi outpost positioning and dendrite branch growth (PMID 36512242) and demonstrated that BicD coordinates dynein-dependent localization of organelles and mRNA in Drosophila (PMID 16320833), but no published study has (a) causally dissected the Golgi outpost–branching signal relationship using acute motor manipulation, (b) linked BicD-dependent Golgi outpost transport specifically to local EGFR/dpERK signaling at dendritic branch points, or (c) performed the epistasis experiment with constitutively active EGFR to determine directionality of the Golgi outpost–signaling axis in da neurons.
hypothesis.feasibility_notes: All core techniques (ppk-GAL4-driven neuronal expression, ManII::GFP live imaging in larval fillets, dpERK immunofluorescence, dendritic arbor live imaging) are well-established in the field (PMID 36512242, 22425998). The primary technical risk is that BicD knockdown may cause pleiotropic cytoskeletal defects beyond Golgi outpost transport, confounding interpretation; this will be addressed by quantifying general microtubule polarity (UAS-EB1::GFP as a secondary readout) and ensuring RNAi efficiency is confirmed by Western blot on larval CNS lysates. A second risk is GAL4 leakiness or insufficient knockdown; UAS-Dcr-2 co-expression will be included to enhance RNAi efficacy if needed. Live imaging of larval fillets is technically demanding but standard with 2-3 months training. Estimated timeline: months 1-2, fly line assembly and RNAi validation; months 3-5, live imaging experiments and fixed dpERK immunofluorescence; months 6-8, epistasis experiments and statistical analysis. Total estimated timeline: 8-10 months for all three aims.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Proposed: In Drosophila stage 8-9 egg chambers, DDLC1-dependent anchoring of gurken mRNA at the oocyte dorsal-anterior corner is required continuously and acts independently of oocyte nucleus anchoring. Germline-specific ddlc1 knockdown induced after the nucleus has reached its dorsal-anterior position (temperature shift of tub-GAL80ts; matα4-GAL4-VP16>ddlc1 RNAi, 25°C to 29°C, mated w1118-background females) will cause gurken mRNA mislocalization (loss of a tight dorsal-anterior crescent) in ≥40% of stage 9 oocytes. In the same oocytes the nucleus will remain in the dorsal-anterior corner in ≥80%, versus ≤10% mislocalized gurken mRNA in GAL80ts-repressed controls. Falsification: if gurken mRNA mislocalization occurs in <15% of late-knockdown oocytes with an anchored nucleus, or if mislocalization occurs only in oocytes with a displaced nucleus, the hypothesis is rejected and the alternative model, in which nuclear position is upstream of gurken mRNA anchoring, is supported.
hypothesis.experimental_approach: Use a temperature-sensitive GAL80 system to separate the early role of DDLC1 in nuclear migration from its later role in gurken mRNA anchoring. Flies are raised at 18°C with GAL4 repressed, shifted to 29°C as adults for 24 h, 48 h or 72 h to knock down ddlc1 in the germline (matα4-GAL4-VP16 or a comparable germline driver, to be verified), and ovaries are dissected for fixed-tissue analysis. In stage 7-9 oocytes, gurken mRNA is detected by smFISH or in situ hybridization, nuclear position by Lamin/DAPI staining, and Gurken protein by immunostaining. Oocyte axes are defined with a membrane marker, and the nucleus-to-gurken-mRNA centroid distance is measured blind. Downstream EGFR signaling is read out by a dorsal follicle cell marker (to be verified) and by adult eggshell dorsal appendage phenotypes. Controls are GAL80ts-repressed (18°C) knockdown genotypes, driver-only and RNAi-only flies, and a second non-overlapping ddlc1 RNAi or a rescue construct to exclude off-target effects. A positive control for nuclear mislocalization is a known nuclear positioning perturbation (e.g., a BicD, Lis-1 or Khc loss-of-function condition, to be verified). Aim 3 reverses the order by testing whether a nucleus displaced independently of DDLC1 drags or leaves gurken mRNA behind.

hypothesis.expected_outcomes: Proposed predictions: (1) Early knockdown (continuous 29°C from larval stages) will give nuclear mislocalization and gurken mRNA mislocalization in ≥60% of stage 9 oocytes. (2) Late knockdown (24-48 h shift in adults) will give gurken mRNA mislocalization in ≥40% of oocytes with anchored nuclei in ≥80%, assessed by Fisher's exact test (p<0.01, n≥60 oocytes per genotype, ≥3 independent replicates). (3) Reduced dorsal Gurken-dependent follicle cell signaling, with ≥25% of eggs showing fused or reduced dorsal appendages after 72 h knockdown. (4) If nuclear position is upstream, the correlation between nucleus-to-gurken-mRNA centroid distance and gurken mRNA mislocalization will be high (Spearman rho >0.7) and late knockdown will not separate the two; this would falsify the hypothesis.
hypothesis.novelty_claim: The supplied literature reports that DDLC1 binds gurken mRNA and is required for its localization and for oocyte nucleus positioning, but the causal order between the two has not been tested. This design addresses the first identified gap by using temporal separation of the two DDLC1 functions rather than static mutants, and by linking each step to a signaling readout (Gurken-EGFR dorsal patterning), which has not been done in the supplied literature.
hypothesis.feasibility_notes: Estimated timeline is 9-12 months: 2 months for line acquisition and verification of knockdown efficiency, 4 months for the temporal knockdown and imaging series, 2-3 months for rescue and positive-control experiments, and 2 months for quantification. Pitfalls: incomplete temporal separation if DDLC1 or dynein persists after the shift, since protein turnover may delay the effect; ddlc1 RNAi may disrupt oogenesis or egg chamber survival beyond stage 8; GAL80ts leakiness at 18°C; and DDLC1 may act on the nucleus and mRNA through the same dynein complexes, so apparent independence would need confirmation with a second hairpin and rescue. Exact stocks and reagents must be verified before ordering.
specific_aims: Aim 1: Temporal separation — test whether late, germline-specific ddlc1 knockdown after nuclear anchoring delocalizes gurken mRNA while the nucleus remains dorsal-anterior.
Aim 2: Signaling readout — measure how late-onset gurken mRNA mislocalization alters Gurken protein distribution, dorsal follicle cell fate markers, and eggshell dorsal appendage phenotypes.
Aim 3: Reverse-order test — displace the oocyte nucleus using a DDLC1-independent perturbation and quantify whether gurken mRNA follows or remains anchored.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Proposed hypothesis: during stages 8–9 of Drosophila oogenesis, the oocyte nucleus is the positional determinant for gurken (grk) mRNA anchoring and the resulting EGFR activation in overlying follicle cells. The reverse model, in which grk mRNA or its DDLC1-bound cargo complex determines where the nucleus goes, is predicted to be wrong. In mated females in a w1118 background raised at 25°C, we predict three outcomes. (i) When the nucleus is mispositioned by stage-restricted germline knockdown of Khc or Lis-1, ≥70% of stage 9 oocytes with a displaced nucleus will retain grk mRNA within 5 µm of that nucleus. In the same egg chambers, the centroid of the follicle-cell dpERK domain will track nuclear position, with a circular angle-angle correlation of r ≥ 0.7. (ii) When grk is knocked down in the germline only after stage 6, the nucleus will still reach the anterior cortex in ≥90% of stage 9 oocytes, falling within a 10-percentage-point equivalence margin of controls. (iii) Stage-restricted germline knockdown of ctp (DDLC1) will mispositioning the nucleus in ≥30% of stage 9 oocytes, compared with ≤5% in controls. Together with (ii), this would indicate that DDLC1 acts on the nucleus independently of its grk RNA-cargo role.
hypothesis.experimental_approach: Proposed method: knock down Khc, Lis-1, ctp or grk in the germline using a maternal germline GAL4 driver combined with tub-GAL80ts. Flies will be raised at 18°C and shifted to 29°C after eclosion for 2–4 days to bypass early oogenesis requirements; the exact shift windows are to be optimized. For each genotype we will fix stage 8–10 egg chambers and perform three co-stains: grk smFISH or HCR-FISH, a nuclear envelope/DNA stain, and anti-dpERK as a readout of follicle-cell EGFR activation. From confocal stacks we will extract (a) nucleus position as anterior–posterior and circumferential angles, (b) the distance from the grk mRNA centroid to the nucleus, and (c) the angular position of the dpERK centroid. To resolve the temporal-coupling gap, we will live-image an MS2/MCP-tagged grk reporter alongside a nuclear marker in ex vivo cultured egg chambers. This will show whether grk mRNA accumulation precedes or follows nuclear arrival at the anterior cortex, in control and ctp-knockdown oocytes. Controls are: GAL4-only and UAS-only siblings, a non-targeting shRNA (mCherry or white) under identical temperature shifts, and a second independent shRNA per gene to exclude off-target effects. Knockdown efficiency will be checked by RT-qPCR on ovaries and, where antibodies exist, by immunostaining. We will also stain for posterior follicle-cell fate and Oskar to confirm that early grk-dependent oocyte polarization was not disrupted before the shift.

hypothesis.expected_outcomes:
Predicted results, all at stage 9 with n ≥ 60 egg chambers per genotype pooled from ≥3 biological replicates.

(1) Khc or Lis-1 knockdown displaces the nucleus from the anterior-dorsal cortex in ≥40% of oocytes, compared with ≤5% in controls (Fisher's exact test, p < 0.01). Among displaced nuclei, ≥70% have grk mRNA within 5 µm of the nucleus. The dpERK centroid angle correlates with nuclear angle at circular r ≥ 0.7 (p < 0.001).

(2) Post-stage-6 grk knockdown reduces grk FISH signal by ≥80%. Anterior nuclear positioning stays at ≥90% and falls within a 10-percentage-point equivalence margin of controls (TOST test). dpERK in dorsal follicle cells is lost.

(3) ctp knockdown mispositioning the nucleus in ≥30% of oocytes, compared with ≤5% in controls (p < 0.01).

(4) In live imaging, grk mRNA enrichment at the anterior-dorsal corner occurs after nuclear arrival in ≥80% of tracked oocytes. The median lag is predicted to be >0 min (Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p < 0.05).

Falsification criteria: the hypothesis is rejected if grk mRNA stays at the normal anterior-dorsal site despite nuclear displacement, or if grk knockdown alone mispositioning the nucleus in >15% of oocytes.
hypothesis.novelty_claim: The synthesis identifies two unresolved points. First, how dynein-dependent grk mRNA localization and microtubule-driven nucleus migration are temporally coupled is unresolved. Second, whether DDLC1 is required for nuclear positioning independently of its RNA cargo role is unknown. Prior work links DDLC1 to both gurken mRNA localization and nucleus positioning, but does not establish the direction of dependence. This plan directly tests directionality in two ways. It decouples nuclear position from grk cargo using stage-restricted knockdowns in both directions. It also extends the readout to the signaling output, dpERK in follicle cells, and to live temporal ordering. This links organelle position quantitatively to where EGF signaling is activated, which the synthesis notes remains open.
hypothesis.feasibility_notes:
Estimated timeline: 18 months.
- Months 0–4: line acquisition and verification, recombination, and optimization of GAL80ts shift timing and knockdown efficiency.
- Months 4–10: fixed-tissue FISH, dpERK and nucleus quantification.
- Months 8–15: live imaging, including establishing ex vivo egg chamber culture and verifying or building the MS2 reporter.
- Months 15–18: analysis and validation with second shRNAs.

Pitfalls and mitigations:
- Grk is also used earlier in oogenesis for posterior follicle signaling that polarizes the oocyte microtubules. Knockdown that is not temporally restricted could therefore mispositioning the nucleus indirectly. This is mitigated by the GAL80ts shift and by checking posterior fate and Oskar.
- Khc and Lis-1 knockdown may block oogenesis before stage 9. Shift timing and dose (number of shRNA copies) will be titrated.
- Incomplete RNAi may produce weak phenotypes. Knockdown will be confirmed by RT-qPCR and, if needed, by germline clones of mutant alleles (to be verified).
- The ctp knockdown result cannot by itself prove RNA-binding-independent function. A separation-of-function DDLC1 variant would require identifying RNA-binding residues, which are not defined in the supplied literature. This is proposed as a follow-up.
- None of the fly lines listed have verified stock numbers in the supplied literature, and all require verification.
specific_aims: Aim 1: Nucleus-led grk localization — test whether grk mRNA and the follicle-cell dpERK domain track an experimentally displaced oocyte nucleus after germline Khc or Lis-1 knockdown.

Aim 2: Cargo-independent nuclear positioning — test whether the nucleus reaches the anterior cortex after post-stage-6 germline grk knockdown, and whether germline ctp (DDLC1) knockdown mispositioning the nucleus.

Aim 3: Temporal order of coupling — use live imaging of MS2-tagged grk mRNA and a nuclear marker to determine whether grk mRNA enrichment precedes or follows nuclear arrival, in control and ctp-knockdown egg chambers.

literature.summary: Within the provided literature, the clearest genetic evidence for rapid seasonal adaptation in D. melanogaster is the cycling of alleles linked to immune function, with functional evidence for seasonal Tep3 alleles and Tep3 x Dro6 epistasis [2], and enrichment of seasonal and clinal SNPs among diapause-regulated genes [3]. hypothesis.hypothesis: Proposed (not established): In outbred populations reconstructed to differ only in seasonal Tep3 alleles (spring-type vs autumn-type) on a randomized genomic background, the autumn-type Tep3 allele will change 7-day post-infection survival by at least 15 percentage points relative to the spring-type allele in conventionally reared mated females at 25°C, this difference will shrink by at least 50% in axenic flies, and the Tep3 effect size will differ by at least 10 percentage points between spring-type and autumn-type Dro6 backgrounds.
hypothesis.experimental_approach: Aim 1 uses a reconstructed-outbred-population design, as in the prior seasonal immunity work [29321302]. Wild-derived lines carrying defined spring-type or autumn-type Tep3 and Dro6 haplotypes (lines to be established and verified by genotyping) are intercrossed for several generations to randomize background, giving a 2x2 Tep3 x Dro6 factorial with at least 3 independent replicate cages per genotype class. Mated females 5-7 days old are reared conventionally or axenically (dechorionated embryos on antibiotic-free sterile food, verified by plating) and infected by septic pricking with a bacterial pathogen to be selected and validated (for example Providencia rettgeri, which is a proposal, not drawn from the supplied literature). The primary endpoints are survival over 7 days and bacterial load at 24 h. A secondary test uses tissue-specific Tep3 RNAi (fat body and hemocyte GAL4 drivers) against GAL4-only, UAS-only, and non-targeting RNAi controls to test whether Tep3 expression is required in those tissues. Gnotobiotic re-association with defined bacterial communities tests whether seasonal microbiome shifts [41611923] modify the allelic effect.

literature.disease_context: Rapid seasonal evolution of immune genes in wild Drosophila melanogaster — particularly genes like Tep3, a thioester-containing protein — provides a tractable model for understanding how standing genetic variation shapes immune system evolution, with potential relevance to understanding innate immunity dynamics in human populations. Diapause-associated transcriptional programs involving neuroendocrine and endocrine pathways may also shed light on conserved mechanisms of physiological stress adaptation.

literature.summary: Rapid seasonal adaptation in wild Drosophila populations is driven by a combination of allele frequency shifts at specific loci and transcriptional reprogramming across tissues. In D. melanogaster, seasonally cycling alleles in immune genes Tep3 and Dro6 interact epistatically to shape immune phenotypes within approximately 10 generations [2], while diapause — a key seasonal adaptation — is governed by complex, tissue-specific transcriptional programs linked to clinally and seasonally oscillating SNPs [3]. However, some wild Drosophila populations (D. lutescens) display rapid seasonal phenotypic changes in thermal tolerance and morphology with minimal detectable genomic differentiation [4], indicating that plastic or epigenetic mechanisms may also contribute substantially to seasonal adaptation, and the precise genetic architecture remains incompletely resolved.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Epistatic interactions between seasonal alleles of Tep3 and Dro6 alter D. melanogaster immune phenotypes by modulating a shared innate immunity signaling node; specifically, flies carrying the autumn-associated allele combination of Tep3 and Dro6 (homozygous for both autumn haplotypes) will show ≥30% higher survival (proportion alive at 7 days post-infection) following Gram-positive bacterial infection (Enterococcus faecalis, OD600=0.1) compared to flies carrying spring-associated allele combinations, and this epistatic effect will be abolished (difference reduced to <10%) when Dro6 expression is knocked down via RNAi in the fat body under standard laboratory conditions (25°C, 12L:12D, w1118 background, mated females, n≥100 per genotype per replicate, 3 independent replicates).
hypothesis.experimental_approach: We will use CRISPR-mediated allele replacement to introduce autumn- and spring-associated SNP haplotypes of Tep3 and Dro6 individually and in combination into an isogenic w1118 background, generating four genotypic classes: autumn-Tep3/autumn-Dro6, autumn-Tep3/spring-Dro6, spring-Tep3/autumn-Dro6, and spring-Tep3/spring-Dro6. Immune challenge assays will use septic injury with E. faecalis (Gram-positive) and Pseudomonas aeruginosa (Gram-negative) to assess pathway specificity (Toll vs. Imd), measuring 7-day survival, pathogen load (CFU counts at 24h), and AMP expression (qRT-PCR of Drosomycin, Diptericin) as readouts. To test the mechanistic necessity of Dro6 in the epistatic effect, fat-body-specific RNAi knockdown of Dro6 will be performed using the r4-GAL4 driver crossed to UAS-Dro6-RNAi lines in each Tep3 allelic background, with UAS-mCherry-RNAi as a scrambled control. Tissue-specific transcriptomics (RNA-seq) of fat body and hemocytes dissected from the four allele-combination genotypes at 6h and 24h post-infection will identify differentially regulated nodes downstream of each allele combination. All assays will be conducted in mated females (5–7 days post-eclosion) at 25°C, 12L:12D, on standard cornmeal-yeast medium, with experimenters blinded to genotype.

hypothesis.novelty_claim: This experiment directly addresses two gaps identified in the literature synthesis: (1) the molecular basis of the Tep3–Dro6 epistatic interaction — described as discovered but mechanistically uncharacterized (gap 4: 'the molecular basis of this epistasis has not been characterized') — by using isogenic allele-replacement lines to isolate allele effects from background variation; (2) the tissue-specific regulation underlying seasonal immune adaptation (gap 3: 'genetic variants driving tissue-specific regulation have not been mapped to causal loci') by combining fat-body-specific RNAi with transcriptomics. Prior work (PMID 29321302) identified the epistatic phenotype in naturally segregating populations but could not distinguish allele-specific from background effects; no prior study has introduced defined seasonal haplotypes into a common isogenic background to test mechanistic necessity of each locus.
hypothesis.feasibility_notes: CRISPR allele replacement in D. melanogaster is routine but depends on the availability of precise seasonal SNP haplotype sequences from PMID 29321302 — these must be obtained from supplementary data or by direct contact with authors before design of guide RNAs. Generation of four knock-in lines is estimated at 6–9 months including validation by Sanger sequencing. evidence_claims.claim: Flies containing seasonal alleles in Thioester-containing protein 3 (Tep3) have different functional responses to infection and that epistatic interactions among seasonal Tep3 and Drosomycin-like 6 (Dro6) alleles underlie the immune phenotypes observed in natural populations.
There are pronounced and repeatable changes in the immune response over the approximately 10 generations between spring and autumn collections.
Genes with known immune function are not enriched among alleles that cycle with seasonal time.
The molecular basis of this epistasis (e.g., protein-protein interaction, pathway crosstomy) has not been characterized.

Diapause-linked transcriptional programs differ substantially between head and ovary tissues, but the genetic variants (SNPs) driving tissue-specific regulation of diapause have not been mapped to causal loci or regulatory elements.
Differentially expressed genes and pathways are highly distinct in heads and ovaries, demonstrating that the diapause response is not uniform throughout the soma.

Genes downregulated in heads of diapausing flies are significantly enriched for clinally varying single nucleotide polymorphism (SNPs) and seasonally oscillating SNPs, consistent with the hypothesis that diapause is a driving phenotype of climatic adaptation.
Flies in the two seasonal periods were almost genetically identical using double-digest restriction site-associated DNA sequencing and analysis.
Autumn-Tep3/autumn-Dro6 flies will show ≥30% higher 7-day survival than spring-Tep3/spring-Dro6 flies after E. faecalis infection.

Fat-body-specific Dro6 RNAi in autumn-Tep3/autumn-Dro6 flies will reduce the survival advantage to <10% relative to spring-allele controls, confirming Dro6 fat body expression as necessary for epistatic effect.

RNA-seq will identify ≥50 differentially expressed immune genes (FDR<0.05, |log2FC|>1.5) in fat body of autumn vs. spring allele-combination flies at 24h post-infection, with pathway enrichment analysis implicating the Toll pathway as the primary downstream mediator.
CRISPR allele replacement in D. melanogaster is routine but depends on the availability of precise seasonal SNP haplotype sequences from PMID 29321302.
Generation of four knock-in lines is estimated at 6–9 months including validation by Sanger sequencing.
Comparative studies show that genes with immune function are among the most rapidly evolving genes across a range of taxa.

literature.summary: The provided literature indicates D. sechellia host specialization evolved through accelerated loss and sequence change of Or and Gr genes [2], altered olfactory receptor tuning with increased sensory pooling and species-specific central projections [3], and reduced bitter and fatty-acid taste aversion [1]. These traits are multigenic [4] and sit within broader ecological adaptations including toxin resistance and immune trade-offs [5,7]. Causal links between circuit rewiring and behavior, and the full gustatory circuit basis, remain to be established.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Proposed: In D. sechellia, host specialization depends on two separable neural changes: (i) increased olfactory sensory pooling onto interneurons, which promotes host-odor attraction, and (ii) peripheral gustatory loss of aversion, which only partly depends on Gr39a.a and Gr28b.a. We predict that (a) silencing the interneuron population that receives pooled input from the host-tuned olfactory neurons will reduce D. sechellia attraction to Morinda-fruit odor by ≥30% relative to genetic controls (25°C, mated females, 2-5 days old, p<0.05), without changing octanoic acid feeding acceptance by more than 10%; and (b) a Gr39a/Gr28b double loss-of-function in D. melanogaster will reduce aversion to some bitter compounds by ≥30% but will close less than 50% of the gap to D. sechellia in octanoic acid feeding aversion, which would implicate additional gustatory genes.
hypothesis.experimental_approach: Aim 1 uses D. sechellia with a GAL4 driver for the interneuron class that receives pooled input from the host-tuned olfactory neurons. The driver would be made by CRISPR knock-in or taken from existing D. sechellia resources, and its availability must be verified. It is crossed to UAS-Kir2.1 or UAS-TeTxLC for silencing and to UAS-GCaMP for imaging, with GAL4-only, UAS-only and inactive-toxin controls. Attraction to Morinda odor and to the host-tuned receptor's ligand is measured in a T-maze or trap assay. Octanoic acid feeding acceptance is measured in a capillary feeder (CAFE) or dye-based consumption assay to test separability from the olfactory phenotype. Aim 2 uses D. melanogaster Gr39a and Gr28b single and double mutants, generated by CRISPR or from existing stocks, with rescue transgenes. These are compared with wild-type D. melanogaster and D. sechellia in proboscis extension and consumption assays with several bitter compounds and fatty acids (octanoic, hexanoic), and with coumarin and canavanine as compounds for which the responsible genes are unresolved. Aim 3 combines the manipulations in D. melanogaster, by ectopic or enhanced convergence and by gustatory silencing, to test additive versus interacting effects on the choice between a Morinda-like odor plus octanoic acid source and a control source in a two-choice assay.

hypothesis.expected_outcomes: Proposed predictions, not established results: (1) Interneuron silencing in D. sechellia lowers the Morinda-odor attraction index by ≥30% versus controls (n≥10 trials of ~30 flies per genotype, one-way ANOVA with Tukey post hoc, p<0.05), while octanoic acid consumption is unchanged (<10% difference). (2) The D. melanogaster Gr39a/Gr28b double mutant shows ≥30% reduced aversion to a subset of bitter compounds. Its octanoic acid and other fatty-acid aversion remains at least 50% of the wild-type D. melanogaster to D. sechellia difference, with rescue restoring wild-type aversion. (3) Combined olfactory and gustatory manipulation in D. melanogaster yields a choice shift greater than the sum of single manipulations (interaction term p<0.05), or a purely additive effect, which would indicate independent peripheral and central contributions. If silencing does not change attraction, or if the double mutant fully reproduces D. sechellia aversion loss, the hypothesis is falsified.
hypothesis.novelty_claim: The literature synthesis identifies several untested gaps: the causal contribution of circuit-level changes such as increased sensory pooling and species-specific central projections to behavior, and the identity of the central neuron types involved, has not been tested; the genes and neurons responsible for lost aversion to fatty acids, coumarin and canavanine remain unresolved; and the central integration of attraction and loss of aversion is unaddressed. This plan tests the causality of pooling with cell-type-specific silencing and directly asks whether olfactory and gustatory evolution are separable or interacting contributors.
hypothesis.feasibility_notes: Estimated 18-24 months. Months 1-6: verify or build D. sechellia and D. melanogaster lines; months 6-14: behavior and imaging; months 14-24: combined manipulations, statistics and replication. Pitfalls: transgenesis in D. sechellia is lower throughput and may need CRISPR knock-in; the identity of the receptor and interneuron class must be confirmed from full text of the supplied circuit paper because only the abstract was summarized; D. sechellia behavior is sensitive to rearing diet and may need Morinda-supplemented or standard medium to be standardized; D. melanogaster is a surrogate and cannot fully reproduce multigenic D. sechellia evolution; interneuron silencing may have broader effects on general olfaction; and the human ortholog relevance is unverified.
specific_aims: Aim 1: Causal role of olfactory pooling — silence the interneurons that receive pooled input from host-tuned olfactory neurons in D. sechellia and measure Morinda-odor attraction and octanoic acid feeding.
Aim 2: Sufficiency of lost bitter receptors — test Gr39a and Gr28b single and double mutants with rescue in D. melanogaster against D. sechellia for bitter and fatty-acid aversion.
Aim 3: Peripheral-central integration — combine olfactory-circuit and gustatory manipulations in D. melanogaster to test additive versus interacting effects on host-choice behavior.

identified_gaps: The central circuit mechanisms downstream of the identified olfactory receptor changes in D. sechellia — specifically, how altered projection patterns and increased sensory pooling onto interneurons [3] translate into discrete motor or decision-making outputs — remain largely uncharacterized at a synaptic resolution.

Although gustatory receptor gene losses (Gr39a.a, Gr28b.a) are implicated in reduced bitter aversion [1], the specific gustatory receptor neurons (GRNs) expressing these genes, their central projections, and whether central taste circuits have co-evolved with peripheral receptor changes are unknown.

The relative contributions of peripheral sensory neuron changes versus central circuit rewiring to D. sechellia's behavioral specialization have not been formally dissected; cross-species rescue experiments restoring ancestral receptor expression in central versus peripheral neurons would clarify this.

The temporal sequence of molecular events during the evolution of host specialization — specifically whether peripheral receptor gene changes (Or/Gr losses and amino acid substitutions) preceded or followed central circuit anatomical changes — cannot be resolved from existing comparative data [2, 3] and would require phylogenetically informed circuit analyses in intermediate species.

The interaction between immune trade-offs (reduced resistance due to reliance on octanoic acid's antifungal properties [7]) and sensory system evolution is entirely unexplored: it is unknown whether the same genomic relaxation of constraint that accelerated Or/Gr gene loss [2] also affected immune gene repertoires, or whether these are independent evolutionary processes.

literature.summary: Host specialization in D. sechellia evolved through an accumulation of changes at multiple levels of the sensory system: rapid gene loss and positive selection across the full Or and Gr receptor repertoire [2], receptor tuning changes that alter long- and short-range olfactory attraction and are accompanied by increased sensory pooling onto interneurons and species-specific central projection patterns [3], and reduced gustatory aversion to bitter compounds and host fatty acids mediated in part by the loss of specific GR genes [1]. Together, these peripheral and central adaptations constitute a multilevel remodeling of chemosensory circuits that underpins the extreme behavioral specialization of D. sechellia on Morinda citrifolia [6]. Key open questions include the synaptic-resolution architecture of the remodeled central circuits, whether gustatory central circuits have co-evolved with peripheral receptor losses, and how sensory evolution interacts with the immune trade-offs that appear to accompany dietary specialization [7].

hypothesis.hypothesis: The loss of Gr39a.a and Gr28b.a in D. sechellia is accompanied by central taste circuit reorganization such that gustatory receptor neurons (GRNs) that ancestrally expressed these genes now project to altered glomerular targets in the subesophageal zone (SEZ), and restoring Gr39a.a or Gr28b.a expression in D. sechellia GRNs using the D. melanogaster promoter-GAL4 driver will rescue bitter-compound aversion (measured by two-choice preference index) by ≥40% relative to D. sechellia controls, while central circuit morphology (axon projection volume and glomerular innervation pattern quantified by confocal microscopy) will remain diverged from D. melanogaster by ≥30%, demonstrating that peripheral receptor loss and central circuit rewiring are partially dissociable evolutionary events under standard 25°C conditions in mated females.
hypothesis.experimental_approach: We will use a three-pronged approach combining cross-species receptor rescue, intersectional neuroanatomy, and calcium imaging. First, we will generate UAS-Gr39a.a and UAS-Gr28b.a transgenic lines carrying D. melanogaster coding sequences, then drive expression in D. sechellia GRNs using Gr39a.a-GAL4 and Gr28b.a-GAL4 drivers (derived from D. melanogaster promoter regions) introduced into D. sechellia by embryo injection, enabling peripheral rescue in a D. sechellia central circuit background. Second, we will map GRN central projections in D. sechellia and D. melanogaster using membrane-targeted GFP (UAS-mCD8::GFP) driven by the same GAL4 lines, acquiring confocal Z-stacks of SEZ and performing volumetric glomerular reconstruction to detect species differences in axonal projection targets and volumes. Third, we will perform two-choice capillary feeding assays (CAFE) and binary food choice assays on mated females (n ≥ 30 per genotype, at least three independent biological replicates) using canavanine, coumarin, and octanoic acid as test compounds to quantify preference indices; GCaMP6s-based calcium imaging in intact preparations will assess GRN and second-order neuron responses to these compounds before and after peripheral rescue. Controls will include D. melanogaster wild-type, D. sechellia wild-type, UAS-only and GAL4-only sibling controls, and D. simulans for phylogenetic comparison.

hypothesis.expected_outcomes: 1. Behavioral rescue: D. sechellia flies expressing UAS-Gr39a.a or UAS-Gr28b.a under the respective GAL4 driver will show preference indices for canavanine and coumarin that are ≥40% more negative (i.e., more aversive) than D. sechellia GAL4-only or UAS-only controls (two-tailed t-test, α = 0.05, power ≥ 0.8 at n = 30). 2. Peripheral physiology rescue: GCaMP6s responses in GRNs of rescued D. sechellia will recover to ≥50% of D. melanogaster response amplitudes for the relevant tastants. 3. Central circuit divergence persistence: Despite peripheral rescue, SEZ axonal projection volumes and glomerular innervation patterns in rescued D. sechellia will remain quantifiably different from D. melanogaster (≥30% difference in projection volume by Imaris volumetric analysis, ANOVA with post-hoc Tukey, α = 0.05), providing evidence for partial dissociability of peripheral and central evolutionary changes. 4. Second-order neuron activity: Calcium imaging of downstream SEZ interneurons will show attenuated responses to bitter compounds in D. sechellia wild-type relative to D. melanogaster, with partial but incomplete rescue in receptor-restored D. sechellia, mirroring the behavioral partial rescue.
hypothesis.novelty_claim: The literature synthesis explicitly identifies two major gaps this experiment addresses: (1) 'The specific gustatory receptor neurons expressing Gr39a.a and Gr28b.a, their central projections, and whether central taste circuits have co-evolved with peripheral receptor changes are unknown' (gap from PMID 36637369); and (2) 'The relative contributions of peripheral sensory neuron changes versus central circuit rewiring to D. sechellia's behavioral specialization have not been formally dissected; cross-species rescue experiments restoring ancestral receptor expression in central versus peripheral neurons would clarify this.' While PMID 32132713 performed analogous cross-species allele transfer for olfactory receptors, no equivalent experiment has been done for gustatory receptors or GRN central projections. This is the first proposed systematic comparison of GRN axonal projection anatomy between D. sechellia and D. melanogaster at glomerular resolution in the SEZ, and the first proposed peripheral-versus-central dissection for the taste modality in this species.
hypothesis.feasibility_notes: Transgenic line generation in D. sechellia is technically feasible but requires an established attP landing site in D. sechellia background; if unavailable, P-element injection can be attempted though efficiency is lower than in D. melanogaster. GAL4/UAS cross-species functionality in D. sechellia has been demonstrated in prior work (PMID 32132713 used analogous approaches for olfactory neurons), providing precedent. The main technical challenge is achieving sufficient GAL4 driver expression from D. melanogaster promoter sequences in a D. sechellia genomic background, which may require enhancer-trap or CRISPR knock-in strategies as fallback. Confocal imaging of D. sechellia SEZ is standard but requires anti-nc82 counterstaining for neuropil registration. Estimated timeline: months 1–6 for transgenic line generation and validation; months 7–12 for behavioral assays; months 13–18 for neuroanatomical mapping; months 19–24 for calcium imaging and data analysis. Potential pitfalls include incomplete GAL4 driver fidelity across species, compensatory upregulation of other GR genes in rescue backgrounds, and difficulty achieving statistically sufficient sample sizes for calcium imaging in D. sechellia due to smaller experimental throughput relative to D. melanogaster.
specific_aims: Aim 1: GRN neuroanatomy — Map and compare central axonal projections of Gr39a.a-GAL4- and Gr28b.a-GAL4-positive GRNs in D. melanogaster, D. simulans, and D. sechellia using UAS-mCD8::GFP and confocal microscopy to determine whether GRN projection targets in the SEZ have diverged during host specialization.

Aim 2: Peripheral rescue behavioral dissection — Quantify the contribution of peripheral Gr39a.a and Gr28b.a receptor loss to reduced bitter aversion in D. sechellia by restoring each receptor individually and in combination using GAL4/UAS-mediated expression and two-choice CAFE assays with canavanine, coumarin, and octanoic acid.

Aim 3: Central circuit functional imaging — Use GCaMP6s calcium imaging in GRNs and identified downstream SEZ interneurons to determine whether peripheral receptor restoration in D. sechellia is sufficient to restore ancestral second-order neuron response profiles, or whether central circuit divergence limits functional rescue independently of peripheral changes.

identified_gaps: It is unknown why D. simulans Nicknack rescues female but not male Nicknack-null D. melanogaster [2]. Inference: the defect may involve a male-specific heterochromatic target such as Y-chromosome satellites. Mapping Nicknack binding sites in each species by ChIP/CUT&RUN in both sexes would test this.

Nicknack is poorly retained in Drosophila species [2], but the abstract does not report how species lacking it compensate, for example via Oddjob or other paralogs. Knockouts of Oddjob in species that lack Nicknack would test paralog compensation as a cause of differential essentiality.

The hypothesis that heterochromatin innovation generally explains the essentiality of dynamic ZAD-ZNF genes [2] has been shown mainly for Nicknack and Oddjob. Systematic cross-species CRISPR essentiality screens of ZAD-ZNFs (e.g., in D. melanogaster vs. D. simulans) are needed.

Whether lineage-specific dosage compensation regulators show species-restricted essentiality, as proposed by the evolutionary-genomic-functional framework for non-model insects [1], remains untested experimentally across close Drosophila relatives, including neo-sex-chromosome species.

Nicknack is a positively selected, poorly retained gene that is required for larval development, and both Nicknack and its paralog Oddjob encode heterochromatin-localizing proteins [2]. literature.summary: Paper [2] shows that essentiality in Drosophila is not restricted to ancient, conserved genes: the young, poorly retained ZAD-ZNF gene Nicknack is essential in D. melanogaster, and its D. simulans ortholog only partially rescues (female but not male), suggesting rapidly evolving heterochromatin functions underlie lineage-specific essentiality [2]. Paper [1] provides complementary background on the divergence of dosage compensation in insects and on the evolution of the essentiality of gene regulatory mechanisms [1]. Direct tests of dispensability in relatives and of mechanistic links between these processes are still lacking.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Proposed: Nicknack is dispensable for viability in D. simulans, where Nicknack-null homozygotes will be recovered at ≥70% of the expected Mendelian frequency, because the essential function of D. melanogaster Nicknack depends on a rapidly diverged zinc-finger array that recognizes a male-enriched heterochromatic target. A chimeric protein carrying the D. melanogaster zinc-finger array on the D. simulans backbone will rescue Nicknack-null D. melanogaster males to ≥50% of expected frequency at 25°C, whereas the unmodified D. simulans protein will rescue ≤10% of males.
hypothesis.experimental_approach: Three approaches test the hypothesis (all proposed, none yet performed). (i) CRISPR/Cas9 Nicknack-null alleles are generated in D. simulans and viability is scored from heterozygous intercrosses, with D. simulans wild-type siblings as controls. (ii) In a Nicknack-null D. melanogaster background, genomic rescue transgenes (native promoter and UTRs, integrated at the same attP landing site) are compared: D. melanogaster Nicknack, D. simulans Nicknack, and two reciprocal chimeras swapping the zinc-finger array versus the ZAD/linker region. The unrescued null and the D. melanogaster rescue serve as negative and positive controls, and eclosion is scored separately by sex. (iii) CUT&RUN (or ChIP-seq) on epitope-tagged D. melanogaster and D. simulans Nicknack in larval tissue maps binding sites in each sex, and a Y-dependence test uses genotypes with altered Y content (e.g., X0 males and XXY females, stocks requiring verification). Oddjob is used as a paralog comparison to test whether any male-specific effect is unique to Nicknack.

hypothesis.expected_outcomes: Proposed predictions, not established results. (1) D. simulans Nicknack-null homozygotes are viable at ≥70% of the Mendelian expectation (n ≥ 300 progeny, binomial test against 100% expected, p < 0.05 for deviation). (2) D. simulans Nicknack rescues Nicknack-null D. melanogaster females and rescues ≤10% of males, consistent with prior observations [33169670]. (3) The chimera with the D. melanogaster zinc-finger array rescues males to ≥50% of expected, while the reciprocal chimera does not (Fisher's exact test, p < 0.01). (4) CUT&RUN shows a differential binding profile between the two orthologs at heterochromatic loci, with ≥2-fold enrichment (FDR < 0.05) at male-enriched or Y-linked sites for the D. melanogaster protein. Falsification: Nicknack-null D. simulans is lethal or sub-viable (<30% of expected), or the chimera fails to rescue males, in which case the ZNF array model is rejected.
hypothesis.novelty_claim: Kasinathan et al. (PMID 33169670) showed that Nicknack is necessary for larval development in D. melanogaster and that the D. simulans ortholog rescues Nicknack-null females but not males. The supplied literature identifies gaps this plan addresses. Whether Nicknack is dispensable in species that lack it or have lost it has not been tested. The male-specific rescue failure is unexplained, and the specific heterochromatic targets are not defined in the abstracts. This plan combines a loss-of-function test in a close relative with a domain-swap rescue to turn the heterochromatin-innovation model into a mapped, testable mechanism.
hypothesis.feasibility_notes: Estimated timeline is 14-18 months: 3-4 months for cloning and generating D. simulans mutants, 4-6 months for transgenic lines and rescue crosses, and 4-6 months for CUT&RUN and analysis. literature.summary: A gene can be essential in one Drosophila species but dispensable in a close relative because rapidly evolving genes can acquire new, species-specific functions tied to dynamic genomic features such as heterochromatin [33169670]. The ZAD-ZNF gene Nicknack exemplifies this paradox: it is evolutionarily young and poorly retained across Drosophila yet is essential for larval viability in D. melanogaster, apparently because it has innovated a role in regulating species-specific heterochromatin [33169670]. Broader comparative work across insects further underscores that gene regulatory mechanisms — including dosage compensation — diverge rapidly between lineages, meaning the essentiality of any given regulatory gene cannot be assumed to be conserved even among close relatives [39341686].

hypothesis.hypothesis: The sex-specific failure of D. simulans Nicknack to rescue male (but not female) D. melanogaster Nicknack-null flies is caused by incompatibility between divergent D. simulans Nicknack protein sequence and D. melanogaster male-specific heterochromatin composition on the Y chromosome and/or dosage-compensation-associated chromatin on the X chromosome; specifically, domain-swap chimeric constructs replacing the zinc-finger DNA-binding domain of D. melanogaster Nicknack with that of D. simulans will fail to rescue male viability (≤5% adult male eclosion relative to heterozygous controls) while retaining ≥50% female rescue efficiency, whereas chimeras retaining the D. melanogaster zinc-finger domain will rescue male viability to ≥40% of controls, under standard 25°C conditions in a w1118 genetic background.
hypothesis.experimental_approach: Using the GAL4/UAS system combined with CRISPR/Cas9-generated Nicknack-null alleles in D. melanogaster (w1118 background), we will express UAS transgenes encoding (1) full-length D. melanogaster Nicknack, (2) full-length D. simulans Nicknack, and (3) a panel of chimeric Nicknack proteins swapping the ZAD domain, the linker region, and the zinc-finger (ZNF) array independently between the two species under the ubiquitous da-GAL4 or nos-GAL4 driver to assess larval and adult rescue. Rescue efficiency will be quantified as sex-stratified eclosion rates and larval lethality stages scored across ≥200 progeny per genotype in three independent crosses. To identify molecular divergence points, ChIP-seq for HA-tagged chimeric proteins will be performed in wandering third-instar larvae to map heterochromatin binding (marked by H3K9me3) genome-wide, comparing male and female samples separately; Y-chromosomal and X-chromosomal pericentromeric domains will be assessed for differential occupancy. Controls include UAS-GFP (negative), UAS-Dmel-Nicknack (positive), and heterozygous Nicknack/+ flies to establish baseline viability.
